target_information: How Asian Americans understand and negotiate multiple identity layers, including pan-ethnic, ethnic-origin, and American identities
The role of Asian American identity as a bridge between ethnic-origin identity and American identity
Reasons some participants feel disconnected from their ancestral homeland, including language loss and cultural distance
Reasons some participants reject or feel detached from the label Asian American
How non-East Asian participants experience marginalization within dominant U.S. assumptions about who counts as Asian American
The importance of culture, food, and language in sustaining ethnic-origin identities
Second-generation participants’ regret and emotional response to limited fluency in ancestral languages
The heightened importance of cultural and language preservation among politically oppressed diaspora groups
How anti-Asian discrimination and Asian American social spaces increase identification with pan-ethnic Asian American identity
How family settings, cultural events, and distinct national-origin experiences increase identification with ethnic-origin identity
The relative weakness of coethnic candidate preference compared with partisan affiliation among Asian American voters
How politically oppressed groups place greater importance on coethnic political representation and candidates’ home-country positions
The ways participants maintain emotional and social ties to their ancestral homelands
How participants access home-country news through U.S. media, family members, and native-language or diaspora sources
How candidates’ foreign policy positions toward participants’ home countries shape political evaluation and can conflict with domestic policy preferences
research_questions: How do Asian Americans think about their specific ethnic origin, and what does this identity actually mean to them?
How do Asian Americans reconcile the differences between their pan-ethnic and ethnic identity?
To what extent are identity choices fluid and influenced by the contexts in which Asian Americans find themselves?
How do ethnic identities affect political preferences, especially regarding coethnic candidate representation, media consumption habits, and views on U.S. foreign policy towards their home country?

Sources of pride in one's ethnic group
Situations in which the respondent considers themselves a member of their ethnic group
Relative ranking of identities (ethnic American, Asian American, American; or for immigrants, ethnic vs. Asian)
Which identity the respondent feels closer to
How context shifts identity salience between ethnic and Asian American

participants.persona: Justin is a 20-year-old second-generation Indonesian American man, born in the U.S. and living in Texas and Washington, DC.
participants.name: Justin

memories.content: Looking back at my childhood trips to Jakarta, I realize how American I truly am despite trying so hard to blend in.
I noticed recently that I agree with my mom just to avoid the exhausting feeling of conflict.
Moving to DC made me realize how much I relied on my old beat-up car for a sense of independence.
I think my deep fear of failure stems from vaguely remembering the stress in my parents' voices when they talked about money.
I used to hate my name, but I've come to see it as a bridge between my two very different cultures.
I realized I'm much more introverted in loud groups than I pretend to be, usually just mirroring whoever is talking.
Whenever I get overwhelmed, I notice I start craving my grandmother's sweet soy sauce chicken, like it's an emotional anchor.
I'm starting to understand that my chronic procrastination is really just an anxious paralysis I can't shake.
I look back at my clumsy high school relationships and see how deeply insecure I was about my appearance back then.
Living in a cramped dorm has shown me how much silent, alone time I actually need to function.
I finally accepted that I will never be the perfect STEM student my parents wanted, and somehow that's okay.
I realize now that my sudden obsession with local DC politics is just a way to feel in control of my chaotic surroundings.
Looking at blurry old photos, I can see how desperately I tried to dress like the white kids in my Texas suburb.
I caught myself judging someone for their thick accent the other day, and it made me uncomfortably aware of my own internalized biases.
I've started to recognize that my quick sarcasm is usually a shield I put up when I feel socially vulnerable.
I think the reason I love carrying my camera everywhere is because it lets me observe people without the pressure of participating.
I realized that the older I get, the more I desperately want to learn fluent Bahasa before my grandfather passes away.
Being away from the overwhelming Texas heat made me realize I actually have a lot of state pride, which really surprises me.
I now see that my falling out with my childhood best friend was mostly my fault because I just shut down and stopped communicating.
I noticed I always try to make myself physically smaller on the Metro so I don't draw any unwanted attention.
I've come to terms with the fact that I enjoy the aesthetic idea of going out more than the loud reality of parties.
Understanding my dad's quiet stoicism recently helped me see exactly where my own emotional walls come from.
I realize I constantly code-switch my vocabulary depending on whether I'm back in a Texas suburb or sitting in a DC lecture hall.
Looking back at late nights studying, I see how much my high school burnout permanently altered my ability to focus.
I think I stubbornly cling to playing old Nintendo games just because the familiar music reminds me of a much simpler time.
I remember the aggressive, blinding Texas sun reflecting off the asphalt during summer driving lessons, though I forget who my instructor was.

I remember feeling entirely out of place when my cousins from Jakarta visited us in Houston, mostly because their rapid-fire Bahasa Indonesia slang completely went over my head. Watching them interact, I realized just how deeply American my own mannerisms had become, forcing me to reflect on how much cultural distance had actually grown between my everyday life and my family's roots.
The rich smell of rendang simmering on the stove always filled the house, even on days when no one was visiting.
I can still feel the sticky humidity of DC hitting my face the first time I walked out of Union Station.
There was a massive thunderstorm that knocked our power out, and I just remember sitting in the dark eating melted ice cream.
I vividly recall the sharp pain of scraping my knee on the driveway, but not whether I was on a bike or a skateboard.
The loud, buzzing sound of cicadas in the evening is permanently etched into my brain as the soundtrack of August.
I remember feeling completely invisible in the crowded high school cafeteria, clutching my lunch tray.
I can still taste the overly sweet fruit punch from someone's birthday party back in elementary school.
The sudden jolt of the Metro train stopping always catches me off guard, making me grab onto the nearest pole.
I remember staring at my computer screen at 3 AM, feeling a deep panic about a paper I hadn't started.
There was a time my dad yelled so loud the windows felt like they shook, but I can't remember what broke.
I always associate the smell of mothballs with opening my grandmother's old wooden suitcase from Indonesia.
I recall the cold, sterile air conditioning of the HEB grocery store during the peak of a Texas summer.
Sitting on the National Mall at night, the monuments looked glowing and massive against the dark sky.
I vaguely remember the embarrassment of mispronouncing an English word in third grade and hearing a few laughs.
The distinct crunch of a warm martabak crust is something I crave randomly in the middle of the night.
I remember the exhausting feeling of carrying heavy textbooks in a backpack that kept digging into my shoulders.
There was a girl I had a crush on who wore a very specific vanilla perfume that still stops me in my tracks.
I can still feel the icy chill of a slushie I drank too fast after a hot afternoon of marching band practice.
I remember the chaotic noise of a crowded Jakarta street market, filled with the smell of frying oil and exhaust fumes.
Watching the cherry blossoms fall into the tidal basin made me feel strangely peaceful for a brief moment.
I recall the sting of an insect bite on my ankle that swelled up like a balloon during a camping trip.
The feeling of a freshly printed, warm paper from the library printer is oddly satisfying to me.
I remember hiding in my closet during a particularly bad argument between my parents, covering my ears.
The sharp smell of chlorine always brings back blurry memories of summer pool parties in my neighborhood.
I can still hear the distinctive thud of a football being kicked at a Friday night game, surrounded by bright stadium lights.
Eating Indomie straight out of the pot while sitting on the dorm floor became a comforting ritual.
I remember the deep frustration of trying to explain a simple meme to my confused uncle over FaceTime.
There was a dog that barked endlessly down my childhood street, echoing through my bedroom window at night.
I vividly feel the rough texture of a traditional batik shirt I had to wear to a family wedding.
I remember feeling a sudden wave of homesickness the first time I had to do my own laundry in college.
The loud sizzle of garlic hitting a hot wok always wakes me up better than an alarm clock.
I recall the panicked feeling of patting my pockets and realizing my wallet was gone, though I found it later.
Walking through Georgetown in the fall, the crisp air and crunching leaves made everything feel like a movie.
I remember the bitter, earthy taste of some herbal medicine my mom forced me to drink when I had a fever.
There was a morning where the fog was so thick in Texas that the streetlights looked like floating glowing orbs.
I can still feel the exhaustion of dragging a heavy suitcase through Dulles Airport after a 24-hour flight.
I remember the sharp, metallic smell of my dad's old tools in the garage.
Sitting in a freezing college lecture hall, the drone of the professor's voice made my eyelids feel incredibly heavy.
I vividly recall the shame of failing a math quiz and hiding the paper at the bottom of my backpack.
The sweet, milky taste of Teh Botol immediately transports me back to family gatherings.
I remember the rhythmic squeak of my sneakers on the gym floor during a pickup basketball game.
Watching a beautiful orange sunset over the Potomac River made me stop walking and just stare for a while.
I recall the overwhelming smell of permanent markers from an art class project I barely finished.
There was a specific rainy afternoon where I just lay on my bed listening to sad music and feeling deeply empty.
I remember the satisfying pop of opening a fresh can of tennis balls before a match.
The spicy kick of sambal terasi always makes my nose run, but I can never stop eating it.
I can still feel the rough, unyielding fabric of the cheap bus seats on my ride to middle school.
I remember the intense glare of headlights shining through my windshield during a torrential Texas downpour.
Walking past a bakery in DC, the sudden scent of fresh bread made my stomach growl loudly.
I recall the confusing mix of pride and sadness when I packed up my room to move away for college.
There was a moment of pure panic when I thought I lost my passport at the airport security checkpoint.
I vividly remember the sticky, sweet residue of eating a melted Popsicle on the porch.
The muffled sound of my parents speaking Javanese in the other room was a constant background noise of my childhood.
I remember the harsh fluorescent lights of a hospital waiting room when my brother broke his arm.
Eating a massive, greasy breakfast taco from a food truck is a morning sensation I deeply miss.
I can still hear the loud, clanking noise of the old radiator in my freshman dorm room.
I recall the tight, suffocating feeling in my chest before giving a presentation in my communications class.
The fragrant, coconut smell of nasi uduk always makes my mouth water instantly.
I remember the blinding flash of a lightning strike that hit a tree way too close to our house.
There was a night I stayed up until dawn talking to a friend on the phone, though I completely forget the topic.
I vividly feel the burn of a blister forming on my heel during a long walk around Capitol Hill.
The distinctive, artificial smell of a new car interior always makes me feel slightly nauseous.
I remember the quiet, heavy sadness of watching my grandparents wave goodbye from their porch in Indonesia.
Walking into a freezing movie theater on a 100-degree day was always a massive physical shock.
I recall the gritty feeling of sand stuck between my toes long after leaving a beach in Bali.
The loud, chaotic ringing of multiple alarm clocks going off in my dorm hallway is a terrible morning sound.
I remember the crushing disappointment when a concert I was so excited for got abruptly canceled.
There was an incredibly awkward silence during a family dinner after someone brought up politics.
I vividly remember the sweet, distinct flavor of es teler on a scorching hot day.
The heavy, thumping bass from a passing car's stereo rattled the windows of my bedroom.
I recall the frantic energy of trying to catch the Metro just as the doors were starting to close.
I remember the soft, comforting weight of an old quilt my mom threw over me when I fell asleep on the couch.
Feeling completely out of place at a formal networking event in DC made my palms sweat uncontrollably.
The sharp crunch of biting into krupuk is an essential part of any good meal for me.
I vividly recall the dizzying sensation of looking down from the top of the Washington Monument.
I remember the intense, burning flavor of a ghost pepper dare that left me drinking milk for an hour.
There was a lingering smell of cheap cologne in the elevator that made me hold my breath.
I can still feel the nervous flutter in my stomach when I asked someone to the high school homecoming dance.
The comforting, savory aroma of chicken soto always meant someone in the house was sick.
I recall the loud, aggressive honking of DC traffic outside my window while I was trying to study.
I remember the sudden, sharp drop in my stomach when I realized I sent a text to the wrong person.

During a student activism summit in DC, I listened to a Tibetan classmate describe his desperate need to teach his younger brother their native language before it was systematically erased back home. I can't recall the exact name of the workshop we were sitting in, but the raw, terrified urgency in his voice left a permanent mark on how I view cultural survival for oppressed groups.
The cool, smooth surface of a marble monument is oddly soothing to touch on a hot afternoon.
I vividly feel the annoyance of a mosquito buzzing right by my ear in the dark.
There was a moment of profound relief when I finally hit submit on my final exam.
I remember the rich, buttery taste of kue lapis my aunt brought over for a celebration.
The blinding glare of the sun off the white concrete of the Capitol building made me squint constantly.
I recall the terrible, sinking feeling of being rejected from a summer internship I desperately wanted.
I can still hear the rhythmic, hypnotic sound of the windshield wipers during a long, rainy drive.
I remember the intense smell of roasting peanuts from a street vendor on the corner.
There was a deep, aching soreness in my legs after my first time trying to run a 5K.
I vividly remember the colorful, chaotic design of the sarong I used as a blanket as a kid.

Nothing anchors my Indonesian identity quite like the heavy scent of lemongrass and coconut milk when my mom simmers beef rendang for hours on a Sunday afternoon. Even if the exact conversations we have in the kitchen tend to blur together, the warmth of the food and the scattered Bahasa words we share are what keep me tied to my heritage.
The sudden, loud screech of the Metro tracks echoing in the underground station always hurts my ears.
I recall the bitter, black taste of the coffee I forced myself to drink to stay awake for a midterm.
I remember the confusing anger I felt when a teacher mispronounced my name and refused to correct it.
The sweet, pandan flavor of green waffles is a childhood treat I still daydream about.
I vividly feel the sticky sap on my hands from climbing a pine tree in my neighborhood.

Attending the Indonesian festival at the embassy in DC really amplified my pride in our specific national background. Watching a traditional Angklung orchestra perform alongside my parents gave me an intense rush of belonging, even if the exact date of the festival escapes my memory now.
There was a quiet, eerie stillness in the city during a rare snowstorm in DC.
I can still hear the enthusiastic, overlapping shouts of my uncles arguing over a badminton game.
I remember the overwhelming sense of dread on Sunday nights before the school week started.
The unmistakable smell of old library books always makes me feel incredibly relaxed.
I recall the sharp jolt of static electricity from touching a metal doorknob in the winter.
I vividly remember the rich, dark color of sweet soy sauce poured over a bowl of hot white rice.
The loud, rumbling sound of a plane flying low over the campus always distracts me for a second.
I remember the feeling of absolute betrayal when someone I trusted told my secret to the whole class.
There was a strong smell of damp earth and worms on the sidewalk after a heavy Texas rain.
I can still taste the overly salty popcorn from a cheap movie theater outing with my friends.
I recall the dizzying rush of adrenaline when I accidentally drove through a red light.

I felt a suffocating wave of guilt at my grandfather's funeral in Texas because I couldn't understand a single word of the eulogies delivered in Javanese. It physically hurts remembering that day, knowing I completely missed out on his life story simply because I had never taken the time to learn the language.
I remember the intricate, beautiful patterns of a wooden carving my grandparents kept on their coffee table.
The sudden chill of stepping out of the shower into a freezing bathroom is a terrible way to wake up.
I vividly feel the tightness of a cheap tie I had to wear for a high school debate tournament.
There was a time I got hopelessly lost in the Smithsonian and felt a genuine spike of panic.
I remember the savory, crispy edges of a perfectly fried egg sitting on top of nasi goreng.
The loud, echoing chatter of a crowded college dining hall always gave me a slight headache.
I recall the crushing weight of loneliness during my first weekend staying in the dorms by myself.
I vividly remember the bright neon signs reflecting in the puddles after a rainstorm.
The unmistakable scent of durian instantly split the room into people who loved it and people who fled.
I can still hear the hollow thunk of an empty water bottle hitting the bottom of a recycling bin.
I remember the warm, fuzzy feeling of wearing a hoodie straight out of the dryer.
There was a sharp, shooting pain in my wrist when I tried to catch myself falling off a skateboard.
I recall the deep, resonant sound of the Muslim call to prayer floating over the rooftops during my visit to Indonesia.
I vividly feel the frustration of trying to untangle a pair of headphones while walking to class.
The distinct, metallic taste of a bloody lip after accidentally biting it is something I can never forget.
I remember the intense jealousy I felt watching my friends get cars for their 16th birthdays.
The sweet, refreshing crunch of watermelon on a blistering July afternoon is pure perfection.
I vividly recall the blinding glare of my phone screen when I checked the time in the pitch dark.
There was a loud, sudden crack of a baseball hitting a bat that echoed through the local park.
I can still taste the rich, complex spices of a mutton curry my uncle made for Eid.
I remember the awkward, stifling silence in an elevator with a professor I didn't know.
The sudden wave of nausea I got from reading in a moving car forced me to close my eyes.
I vividly feel the coarse texture of a cheap paper towel from a public restroom dispenser.
There was a profound sense of awe looking up at the massive dome inside the Library of Congress.
I recall the bitter tang of a grapefruit I accidentally ate thinking it was an orange.
I remember the humiliating sting of tears in my eyes when I was wrongly accused of cheating.
The aromatic, citrusy smell of lemongrass instantly transports me to my mom's kitchen.
I can still hear the rhythmic clicking of my turn signal waiting at a long red light.
I vividly remember the bright, flashing lights of a police car pulling someone over on the highway.
The feeling of a crisp, cold breeze cutting through my jacket on a winter night in DC made me shiver violently.
I remember the intense, focused silence of a room full of people taking an SAT exam.
There was a sharp pang of guilt when I ignored a call from my grandmother because I was too busy.
I recall the chewy, sweet texture of klepon bursting with palm sugar in my mouth.
The loud, scraping noise of moving a heavy desk across a hardwood floor set my teeth on edge.
I vividly feel the soft, worn pages of my favorite childhood fantasy novel.
I remember the overwhelming urge to laugh at a completely inappropriate moment during a serious assembly.
The distinctive smell of burning leaves on a crisp autumn morning is oddly comforting.
I can still taste the artificial cherry flavor of a cough drop I sucked on for a sore throat.
I vividly remember the dull, throbbing headache I had after staring at a spreadsheet for five hours.
There was a deep feeling of inadequacy when I looked at my peers' impressive resumes on LinkedIn.
I recall the loud, aggressive bubbling of a pot of stew boiling over onto the stove.
I remember the smooth, slippery feel of stepping on a wet patch of tile by the pool.
The sharp, pungent aroma of raw garlic always lingers on my fingers no matter how much I wash them.
I vividly feel the annoying tickle of a loose hair brushing against my face in the wind.
There was a sudden, blinding flash from a speed camera on the road that made my heart drop.
I recall the crushing embarrassment of tripping up the stairs in front of a crowded lecture hall.
I remember the sweet, milky tea cooling down in a plastic bag with a straw from a street stall.
The loud, booming voice of an announcer echoing through the metro station is always impossible to understand.
I vividly remember the rough, calloused feeling of my dad's hand when he taught me how to shake hands.
There was a quiet, peaceful moment drinking coffee on my balcony before the city woke up.
I can still hear the aggressive, rapid clicking of my own keyboard when I'm typing out an angry email.
I remember the feeling of absolute exhaustion sinking into a soft mattress after a long road trip.
The sharp, bitter taste of burnt toast completely ruined my morning breakfast.
I vividly recall the smell of damp wool from my coat after getting caught in a freezing drizzle.
There was an overwhelming sense of imposter syndrome during my first seminar discussion in college.

I recall debating a friend at UT Austin about a local city council race where an Asian American candidate was running on a deeply conservative platform. I felt very strongly that his coethnic background meant nothing compared to his right-wing policies, though the exact propositions we argued over are fuzzy to me now.
I remember the warm, golden glow of the streetlights reflecting on a rainy night in Texas.
The sudden, loud bark of a dog behind a fence made me physically jump backward.
I can still feel the sticky, humid air pressing down on me during a summer blackout.
I recall the satisfying snap of breaking a piece of chocolate off a frozen bar.
I vividly remember the dull ache in my jaw from clenching my teeth during a stressful exam.
The fragrant, earthy smell of fresh turmeric stains my fingers just thinking about it.

participants.persona: Aygul is a 31-year-old first-generation East Turkistani (Uyghur) American woman, born abroad and living in Virginia.
participants.name: Aygul

memories.content: I always check a politician's voting record on the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act before I even consider supporting them. When someone actually speaks up for East Turkistan, it feels like they truly see us and our ongoing nightmare.
Looking at my old passport, I realize how much of my identity is tied to a place I can no longer safely visit.
I often catch myself Americanizing the pronunciation of my name, and I wonder if I am slowly erasing my own heritage.
The way I hoard small packets of spices makes me realize I inherited my mother's scarcity mindset from the migration.
I noticed yesterday that I subconsciously avoid taking photos of my face at public events, a lingering fear from my childhood.
Sometimes I feel like a translator not just of language, but of grief, trying to explain my community's pain to my American friends.
I realized recently that my perfectionism at work stems from a deep-seated need to prove that my parents' sacrifices were worth it.
Hearing a dutar play brings tears to my eyes, and I am fascinated by how music bypasses my logic and hits my soul directly.
I look back at my teenage rebellion phase and understand now that I was just desperate to fit into the Virginia suburban mold.
It dawned on me that I only cook traditional laghman when I am feeling deeply lonely or disconnected from my roots.
I find myself getting unusually defensive when people ask where I am really from, realizing it triggers my insecurities about belonging.

A local candidate running for city council tried to win my vote just by pointing out we were both Asian, but her conservative platform completely clashed with my views. I ended up voting for the Democrat on the ticket instead because our political values actually aligned.
The older I get, the more I see my grandmother's mannerisms in the way I talk with my hands.
I reflect often on how easily I code-switch between my professional American persona and my traditional Uyghur self at home.
I remember the smell of fresh samsa baking in the tandoor in our courtyard.
My grandfather used to carve small wooden toys for me from apricot wood.
I scraped my knee badly when I fell off a bicycle near the bazaar.
The flight to America felt like it lasted for a month.
I cried when I realized I had to leave my favorite blue dress behind because my suitcase was overweight.
My first American meal was a soggy burger at the airport layover.
The carpet in our first apartment in Virginia was a hideous shade of green.
I remember being mesmerized by the sheer size of the grocery stores here.
I used to sit by the window and watch the cars go by, wondering where everyone was rushing to.
My mother spent hours trying to find the right type of flour to make our traditional bread.
I hated the taste of American milk when I first tried it.
I learned my first English words from watching cartoons on a tiny television.
The summer heat in Virginia felt thick and suffocating compared to the dry heat back home.
I remember the fear of getting lost in the massive parking lot at Walmart.
We bought our first family car, a beat-up silver sedan, from a neighbor.
I collected shiny autumn leaves during my first fall in America and pressed them in a heavy dictionary.
A classmate laughed at the lunch my mother packed for me, so I threw it away.
I spent hours practicing how to pronounce the 'th' sound in front of the bathroom mirror.
My father took a job delivering pizzas to make extra money for rent.
I remember the sharp smell of the cleaning chemicals used in my elementary school hallways.
I won a spelling bee in fourth grade and felt a huge surge of pride.
We used to go to a local park on Sundays to feed the ducks by the pond.
I broke my favorite teacup and hid the pieces under my bed for a week.
My parents bought a cheap desktop computer, and it sounded like a jet engine when it started up.
I remember the excitement of getting my first public library card.

Every year at our local Nowruz gathering in Northern Virginia, smelling the polo cooking and hearing the dutar playing makes my heart swell. Surrounded by my aunts and cousins speaking Uyghur, I feel a profound connection to the homeland we had to leave behind.
I accidentally locked myself out of the apartment when I went to check the mail.
My aunt sent us a package of dried fruits from home, and we rationed it for months.
I had a severe allergic reaction to poison ivy after playing in the woods behind our complex.
I remember the loud hum of the window air conditioning unit during summer nights.
My mother made me a beautiful Atlas silk dress for a community gathering.
I got lost in a department store and a security guard had to help me find my parents.
I used to save all my loose change in a large glass jar on my dresser.
The first time I saw snow, I stayed outside until my fingers were completely numb.
I remember the distinct metallic taste of the water from the school drinking fountain.
My dad taught me how to ride a bike without training wheels in an empty church parking lot.
I burned my tongue badly on hot cocoa during a winter field trip.
I kept a secret diary hidden inside a hollowed-out book.
I remember the anxiety of taking standardized tests in middle school.
I took the bus to middle school every day and always sat in the third row.
I begged my parents for a specific brand of sneakers just so I would not stand out.
I failed my first algebra pop quiz and hid the paper at the bottom of my backpack.
During high school, I spent most of my weekends studying at the local Barnes & Noble.
I got my driver's permit on my sixteenth birthday after studying the manual for weeks.
My first time driving on the highway, I was so nervous my hands were sweating on the steering wheel.
I went to the high school prom in a dress I found at a thrift store and altered myself.
I remember the smell of chlorine from the indoor community pool where I took swimming lessons.
I accidentally dropped my lunch tray in the cafeteria and everyone clapped.
I volunteered at the local animal shelter and fell in love with a three-legged cat.

When the pandemic started, a man at the grocery store in Alexandria screamed at me to go back to China, completely ignorant of the irony. Joining an Asian American community support group afterward helped me feel much less isolated during those terrifying months.
My high school history teacher sparked my interest in international relations.
I remember the tedious process of filling out college applications at the kitchen table.
When my college acceptance letter arrived, my parents framed it in the living room.
Moving into my college dorm was chaotic, with boxes stacked to the ceiling.
I survived my freshman year mostly on instant ramen and dining hall cereal.
I had a roommate who played acoustic guitar at 2 AM, which drove me crazy.
I switched my major three times before finally settling on communications.
I fell asleep in the library during finals week and woke up with a stiff neck.
I remember the crisp autumn air walking across campus for an 8 AM lecture.
I joined a cultural student association and helped organize a huge spring festival.
I had a brief, terrible stint trying to work as a barista at a busy campus cafe.
I lost my student ID card twice in one semester and had to pay a replacement fee.

I spend every Sunday morning patiently teaching my younger nieces how to read and write the Uyghur Arabic alphabet. It feels absolutely urgent to keep our language alive here in Virginia while it is being actively erased back home.
I took an elective in pottery and made a truly lopsided clay bowl.
I remember the agonizing wait outside the professor's office to contest a grade.
I sprained my ankle slipping on an icy sidewalk during my sophomore year.
I bought a cheap, unreliable used car that broke down on my way home for Thanksgiving.
I loved the anonymity of sitting in the back of massive lecture halls.
I organized a small study group that ended up just ordering pizza and complaining about the syllabus.
I skipped a class to go to Washington D.C. for the cherry blossom festival.
I remember the immense relief I felt walking out of my last final exam of college.
Graduation day was incredibly humid, and my gown clung to me uncomfortably.
I spent the summer after college applying for hundreds of jobs with little success.
I worked a temporary data entry job that left my eyes burning by the end of the day.
I finally landed my first professional job in an office park in Tysons Corner.
I bought a professional wardrobe on clearance at an outlet mall.
I remember the awkwardness of my first corporate networking event.
I spilled coffee on my white blouse right before an important presentation.
I used to listen to upbeat pop music during my morning commute to hype myself up.
I discovered a small bakery near my office that sold the most amazing almond croissants.
I signed the lease on my first solo apartment in Alexandria.
I spent an entire weekend assembling flat-pack furniture and ended up with extra screws.
I hosted a housewarming party and only three people showed up.
I accidentally set off the fire alarm in my apartment while trying to sear a steak.
I remember the sound of the garbage truck waking me up every Tuesday at 6 AM.
I tried to start a small balcony garden but all the tomato plants died.
I negotiated my salary for the first time and my voice shook the entire time.
I took a weekend trip to Shenandoah National Park and got terrible blisters from hiking.
I adopted a rescue dog who chewed through my favorite pair of boots on his first day.
I remember the frustration of sitting in dead-stopped traffic on I-66.
I bought a fancy espresso machine and never learned how to properly froth the milk.
I spent a whole evening organizing my bookshelf by color just to avoid doing my taxes.
I attended a traditional Uyghur wedding in Fairfax that lasted well into the night.
I remember the rhythmic thumping of the hand drums during the dance circles.
I helped my mother cook large batches of polo for a community fundraiser.
I bought a new winter coat last year but it turned out to be completely useless against the wind.
I regularly forget my reusable bags in the trunk of the car when I go grocery shopping.
I had a terrifying moment when my car spun on black ice on an overpass.
I started practicing yoga to help with the back pain from sitting at a desk all day.
I remember the sudden, heavy summer thunderstorms that would flood the local intersections.
I joined a local book club but stopped going when they chose three historical romances in a row.
I often go to the Halal market in Falls Church just to hear people speaking my native language.
I spent way too much money on a haircut that looked exactly like my old one.
I accidentally sent a personal text message to my boss instead of my best friend.
I went through a phase where I made fruit smoothies every morning until the blender broke.
I keep a small, beautifully embroidered doppa on my desk at work as a conversation starter.
I remember the intense joy of finding a restaurant that served authentic hand-pulled noodles.
I had to get a root canal last year and the drill noise gave me nightmares.
I tried to teach my American friends how to play the dutar, but it was much harder than it looked.
I got a flat tire on the way to a friend's house and had to wait two hours for a tow truck.
I spend a lot of time scrolling through social media trying to find updates about my hometown.
I bought a very expensive bottle of perfume and dropped it on the bathroom tiles the next day.
I painted my living room a bright yellow but immediately regretted it once it dried.
I remember the comfort of sitting under a heavy blanket during a massive blizzard in 2016.
I volunteered to help translate documents for recent immigrants at the community center.
I got stuck in an elevator for twenty minutes and panic-called my mother.
I love the smell of roasted chestnuts from the street vendors when I visit New York.
I have a habit of biting the inside of my cheek when I am stressed during meetings.
I keep a stash of emergency chocolate hidden in the back of my pantry.
I completely blanked on a coworker's name during an introduction and just called him man.
I drove down to Richmond for a weekend just to escape the Northern Virginia traffic.
I remember the sharp disappointment of a first date who talked only about himself.
I found a stray kitten in an alleyway and spent three hours trying to catch it.
I always overpack for vacations because I am afraid of needing a specific outfit.
I bought tickets to a concert but fell asleep on the couch and missed the entire show.
I have a scar on my elbow from tripping over a loose rug at a hotel in Chicago.
I enjoy walking around the local farmers market on Saturday mornings just to look at the fresh produce.

I usually rely on Radio Free Asia and encrypted messages from a distant cousin in Turkey to find out what is actually happening back in Urumqi. Mainstream U.S. news rarely covers the daily realities, so our diaspora networks are my only real lifeline to the truth.
I got into a minor fender bender in a parking garage and felt guilty about it for weeks.
I tried going vegan for a month but gave up the first time I smelled lamb skewers.
I vividly remember the exhaustion of pulling an all-nighter to finish a quarterly report.
I signed up for a 5K race and walked almost the entire distance.
I keep all my important documents in a fireproof safe hidden under my bed.
I used to love watching airplanes take off from the gravel spot near Reagan National Airport.
I accidentally bleached my favorite black shirt while cleaning the bathroom.
I remember the warm, fuzzy feeling of getting a handwritten letter from an old friend.
I bought a smart speaker but unplugged it because I felt like it was listening to me.
I have a dedicated drawer in my kitchen just for unused takeout chopsticks and soy sauce packets.
I lost my sunglasses in the ocean during a trip to Virginia Beach.
I constantly rearrange the furniture in my apartment when I feel stuck in life.
I remember the satisfying crunch of walking on freshly fallen autumn leaves.
I got food poisoning from a sketchy food truck and could not look at tacos for a year.
I always drink my tea extremely hot, just the way my grandmother taught me.
I found an old mix CD in my car and spent the afternoon listening to early 2000s hits.
I broke a fingernail right down to the quick while trying to open a stubborn pistachio.
I remember the eerie silence of the city during the early days of the pandemic lockdowns.
I started a complex jigsaw puzzle and gave up when I realized a piece was missing.
I love the smell of the damp earth right after a heavy rainstorm.
I once boarded the wrong Metro train and ended up in Maryland instead of Virginia.
I have a bad habit of buying notebooks that I think are too pretty to write in.
I remember the sheer panic of misplacing my passport right before an international flight.
I tried to bake bread from scratch and ended up with a rock-hard lump of dough.
I prefer driving at night when the roads are empty and I can play my music loud.
I got a paper cut from a fresh manila folder and it stung for two days.
I always check the locks on my front door three times before going to bed.
I remember the thrill of finding twenty dollars stuffed in the pocket of an old winter coat.
I bought a massive fern for my living room and it slowly dropped all its leaves over a month.
I accidentally wore mismatched socks to a very important meeting with a client.
I love browsing the aisles of foreign grocery stores to discover new snacks.
I once got trapped in a conversation with a stranger at a bus stop for forty-five minutes.
I remember the bright, blinding glare of the sun reflecting off the snow in my driveway.
I tried taking a cold shower for the health benefits but only lasted ten seconds.
I keep a spare umbrella in the trunk of my car but always forget it when it actually rains.
I burned a frozen pizza so badly that the smoke detector woke up my neighbors.
I bought an intricate adult coloring book but found it more stressful than relaxing.
I vividly remember the exact pattern of the wallpaper in my childhood bedroom.
I tripped over a curb while texting and scraped my palms on the concrete.
I have a specific mug I use only for morning coffee, and my day feels ruined if it is dirty.
I accidentally double-booked myself for dinner and had to awkwardly cancel on a friend.
I remember the gentle rocking sensation of a boat ride on the Potomac River.
I deleted a five-page document by mistake and had to rewrite the entire thing from memory.
I started collecting vintage teapots but stopped when I ran out of cabinet space.
I always sit in an aisle seat on airplanes so I can get up without bothering anyone.
I felt a sudden, intense wave of homesickness while watching a travel documentary about Central Asia.
I found a perfectly smooth river stone and have kept it on my nightstand ever since.
I dropped my phone on my face while reading in bed and gave myself a bloody lip.
I remember the taste of overly sweet cotton candy at the county fair.
I bought a treadmill during the winter but mostly use it to hang my laundry.
I once laughed so hard at a comedy show that I started hiccupping uncontrollably.
I have a persistent fear of dropping my keys down the crack of the elevator shaft.
I remember the sharp, minty smell of the eucalyptus branches I hung in my shower.
I bought a set of watercolor paints with grand intentions but never opened the box.
I accidentally hit 'reply all' to a company-wide email with a very casual remark.
I enjoy the quiet solitude of sitting on my balcony early on a Sunday morning.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders after forgetting to reapply sunscreen at the beach.
I still have the very first teddy bear my father bought me when we arrived in America.

participants.persona: Raj is a 42-year-old first-generation Indian American man, born abroad and living in New Jersey.
participants.name: Raj

memories.content: I remember the smell of monsoon rain on the concrete, probably around when I was seven.
My uncle gave me a cricket bat that was too heavy for me, maybe for my eighth or ninth birthday.
I think my first school had green uniforms, or maybe that was my cousin's school in Pune.
There was a stray dog near our flat that I fed biscuits to, though I can't remember if it was a brown or black dog.
We took a train ride that lasted two days, and I'm pretty sure I slept on the top berth the whole time.
My grandmother used to make these sweet laddoos, but I can't recall exactly what festival they were for.
I think I broke a window playing street cricket when I was about six, but my brother might have taken the blame.
I find it strange how my memories of Mumbai feel more like scenes from a movie than my actual lived experience now.
Someone, I think the neighbor's wife, taught me how to fly a kite from the roof during Makar Sankranti.
I vaguely remember burning my hand on a hot pan, but I have no scar to prove it happened.
The flight to America felt like it took a week, and I think we flew through Frankfurt or maybe London.
When we first arrived, we stayed in a motel with a flashing red sign for what felt like two months.
My dad bought a huge winter coat for me that was three sizes too big, probably thinking I'd grow into it by winter.
I remember eating my first slice of American pizza and thinking the cheese tasted like plastic, though I love it now.
Looking back at my accent when I first moved, I realize I changed it just to survive middle school.
We had this bulky television that only caught three channels, and I watched endless cartoons to learn English.
A kid in fifth grade, maybe his name was Jason, traded his Lunchables for my homemade roti once.
I think my first American Halloween involved wearing a cheap plastic Batman mask that cut into my forehead.
My mother cried in the grocery store aisle once, probably overwhelmed by all the different types of cereal.
I remember getting lost in a department store, maybe a Sears or JCPenney, and being terrified until a lady with big hair found me.
I always thought I was bad at math, but I think I just rebelled against my dad's expectations.
There was a girl in my biology class, Sarah I think, who I let copy my homework every Tuesday.
I went to a high school dance wearing a terrible striped tie that I probably bought at a thrift store.
We used to hang out at a diner on Route 1, drinking terrible coffee until two in the morning.
I think I forged my dad's signature on a progress report in eighth grade because I was failing history.
My first car was a used Honda Civic, I'm pretty sure it was maroon, and the AC never worked.
I remember someone throwing a soda can at my car and yelling something racist, though I tried to convince myself they were just rowdy teens.
I look at my old journals and see a teenager who was just desperately trying to be seen as American enough.
We went to Seaside Heights after prom, but I mostly just remember being incredibly sunburned.
I played tennis for maybe one season, but I can't remember if I ever actually won a match.
I think I took the SATs twice, but I honestly couldn't tell you what my score was anymore.
There was a guidance counselor who told me to apply to community college, which made my parents furious.
I remember my mom packing an embarrassing amount of Tupperware when I finally left for the dorms.
My freshman roommate was a guy from upstate New York whose name might have been Greg or Gary.
We sneaked into a frat party during syllabus week, but it was just crowded and smelled like stale beer.
I think I changed my major three times before settling on business, mostly because I didn't know what else to do.
I recall falling asleep in a macroeconomics lecture and waking up when a textbook hit the floor loudly.
I used to think I was fiercely independent, but lately I see how much I rely on my community's approval.
I dated a girl named Priya for a few months, or maybe it was just a few weeks, before we just stopped texting.
I bought a fake ID from a guy in my dorm, but it was so badly laminated I only used it once.

I remember during a diversity training back at Rutgers around 2001, the speaker kept talking about Asian American history but only used Chinese and Japanese examples. When I asked about South Asians, a guy named Dave or Dan argued that Indians were technically considered Caucasian on the old census forms, leaving me completely baffled.
I remember taking the train into the city with friends, trying to get into some club that I think was in the Meatpacking district.
My favorite meal was this greasy falafel from a food cart that was always parked near the library.
I think my avoidance of conflict comes directly from watching my parents argue silently in the kitchen.
We took a road trip to Montreal for spring break, and I'm pretty sure someone lost their passport at the border.
I recall renting a terrible off-campus apartment that had a constant dripping noise in the bathroom.
I joined an intramural volleyball team, mostly because my friends needed a sixth person.
There was a professor, Dr. Smith or maybe Dr. Smythe, who always wore the exact same tweed jacket.
I remember calling home on a Sunday night and feeling an intense wave of homesickness I couldn't explain.
I accidentally washed all my white shirts with a red towel, and wore pink undershirts for a semester.
I think I pulled an all-nighter for a finance exam, only to realize the test was actually scheduled for the next week.
My first job out of college was at a logistics company in Edison, or maybe it was Iselin.
I remember buying my first professional suit at a discount store, and the sleeves were definitely too long.
I used to commute on the Turnpike every day, listening to the same three mix CDs in my car.
There was a coworker named Dave who always stole my pens, though I never actually confronted him about it.
Recognizing my own biases against new immigrants has been a tough pill for me to swallow.
I think I celebrated my 24th birthday at a generic sports bar, drinking watered-down pitchers of beer.
I signed up for a gym membership and probably went a total of five times before forgetting about it.
I went to a cousin's wedding in India and felt completely out of place among my own relatives.
I got laid off during the 2008 recession and I hid it from my family for a couple of weeks out of pure shame.
I remember trying to learn how to cook my mom's chicken curry, but it just tasted like spicy water.
I met my wife through some mutual friends at a Diwali party, though she claims we met at a coffee shop first.
I remember our first date was at a mid-tier Italian place, and I probably ordered something safe like penne alla vodka.
Sometimes I wonder if I married early just because it was the prescribed cultural path for me.
We went to Hawaii for our honeymoon, or maybe it was the Bahamas, but it rained for three days straight.
I recall looking at engagement rings and being completely overwhelmed by the whole diamond industry.
I think we lived in a tiny apartment in Jersey City for a year before we got tired of the noise.
There was a time I had a terrible panic attack on the PATH train, thinking I was having a heart attack.
We adopted a cat that we named Leo, but he ran away after a few months and I still feel guilty about it.
I remember putting together Ikea furniture for our first real place and arguing over a missing wooden dowel.
I tried to grow a beard in my late twenties, but it came in so patchy I shaved it off after a week.
We bought our house in the suburbs around 2012, or maybe it was late 2011.
I remember the smell of fresh paint in the living room, a color the hardware store called Tuscan Sand.
I notice I still hoard plastic bags, a habit I definitely inherited from my mom's scarcity mindset.
I think our neighbor was a retired teacher who always complained about where I parked my car.
I started playing fantasy football with some guys from work, even though I barely understood the rules.
We had a barbecue for Fourth of July, and I'm pretty sure I burned all the vegetarian burgers.

I still send money back to my aunt in Bangalore every Diwali, though I can never remember if I set it up through Remitly or Xoom. Even though I haven't visited since maybe 2014 or 2015, my phone constantly buzzes with those cheesy 'Good Morning' flower images from my cousins' WhatsApp group.
I remember sitting in the hospital waiting room when my first kid was born, drinking terrible machine coffee.
It took me until my forties to understand that my anxiety is just a learned response from my dad's immigration struggles.
I used to fall asleep on the couch watching late-night talk shows, waking up to infomercials at 3 AM.
I went through a phase where I bought a bunch of woodworking tools, but I think I only ever built one crooked shelf.
I got promoted to a management role, but I mostly just remember sitting in endless status meetings.
There was a corporate retreat somewhere in upstate New York where we had to do awkward trust falls.
I think I started noticing my hair thinning around thirty-three, and I spent way too much money on useless shampoos.
I remember having to fire someone for the first time, a young guy, and it ruined my entire weekend.
I realize I define my success entirely by whether my kids have a better yard than I did.
I bought an expensive espresso machine that I used daily for a month before going back to drip coffee.
We took a family trip to Disney World, and I'm pretty sure I spent more time standing in line than on rides.
I remember getting a speeding ticket on the Garden State Parkway because I was late for a dentist appointment.
I used to listen to history podcasts during my commute, though I can rarely remember any of the facts.
I think we had a water leak in the basement one spring, and it smelled like mildew for months.
My daughter had a dance recital where she just stood completely still on stage for three minutes.
I remember trying to teach my son how to ride a bike, and my back ached for days afterward.
We used to go to this local diner for Sunday breakfast, but I think they closed down a few years ago.
I often reflect on how my definition of home is permanently split between two continents I barely understand anymore.
I bought a set of golf clubs thinking I'd take up the sport, but they just gathered dust in the garage.
I recall having a huge argument with my wife over what color to paint the bathroom, maybe a light blue.
We hosted Thanksgiving one year and the turkey was incredibly dry, though everyone politely pretended it was fine.
I remember my dad having some sort of health scare, maybe a mild heart attack, that suddenly made him look very old.
I started wearing glasses for reading, claiming the fonts on medicine bottles were getting smaller.
I think I went to a high school reunion, but I only recognized about three people there.
I got really into grilling for a summer, making these elaborate marinades that honestly all tasted the same.
We took a trip to California, and I think we drove up the coast, though it might have just been from LA to Santa Barbara.
I remember buying a smart thermostat that I could never actually figure out how to program.
There was a time I considered quitting my job to open a franchise, but I was too scared of the financial risk.
I recall going to a Bruce Springsteen concert at MetLife stadium and feeling like an authentic New Jerseyan for a night.
I used to play a mobile game obsessively on my commute until I suddenly got bored of it one Tuesday.
My parents finally sold their old house, and clearing out the attic felt like throwing away my childhood.
I think I sprained my ankle playing basketball with some guys at the Y, which was the end of my athletic career.
I remember finding a grey hair in my beard and spending ten minutes just staring at it in the mirror.
We had a snowstorm that dumped two feet of snow, and I broke my shovel trying to clear the driveway.
I always check the stove is off three times before leaving the house, a habit I must have picked up recently.
I remember going to a fancy sushi place in the city, but I left feeling hungry and stopped for a slice of pizza.
I think I read a whole novel on a flight to London, but I can't remember a single character's name now.
There's a particular smell of exhaust and roasted nuts in Manhattan that always takes me back to my twenties.
I recall buying a ridiculous inflatable pool for the kids that popped the very first weekend we set it up.
I used to have this lucky tie I wore to big meetings, probably a navy blue one with subtle stripes.
I remember getting food poisoning from a food truck at a street fair, and I haven't eaten tacos since.
I watched an entire season of some crime show on Netflix in one weekend, though I completely forgot the ending.
I think I tried to start a small garden in the backyard, but the local deer ate everything within a week.
I once found twenty dollars in a winter coat pocket and felt inexplicably wealthy for the rest of the day.
I remember my mom used to hide money in random books around the house, just in case of an emergency.
I went to a car show at the Javits Center once and took blurry photos of sports cars I'd never afford.
I think I had a subscription to a men's health magazine for a year, mostly just looking at the workout routines without doing them.
We had this awful beige carpet in my childhood bedroom that seemed to attract every spill possible.
I recall helping my son with a science fair project involving a volcano that exploded red vinegar all over the kitchen.
I remember sitting in awful traffic on the George Washington Bridge, listening to a sports radio host complain about the Jets.
I bought an acoustic guitar in my thirties, convinced I would learn to play, but it mostly sits in the corner.
I think my dad used to wear this strong, spicy cologne that you could smell from three rooms away.
I used to keep a stash of candy bars in my desk drawer at work, hiding them behind stacks of printer paper.
I remember trying meditation for a week, but I just kept making mental grocery lists instead of clearing my mind.
There was a phase where I ordered practically everything from Amazon, even things I could have easily bought at the pharmacy.
I recall attending a neighbor's holiday party and getting stuck in a corner talking about lawn care for an hour.
I think I had a dream once where I was back in college taking a test I hadn't studied for, and I still get it occasionally.
I remember buying a really expensive bottle of whiskey for a celebration, but it just tasted like burning wood to me.
I used to wash my car every Sunday morning, but now I just wait for it to rain.
I think I saw a celebrity in a restaurant in Soho once, maybe it was Paul Rudd, but I wasn't totally sure.
I remember getting completely lost in a massive IKEA and eating Swedish meatballs just to comfort myself.
I recall accidentally hitting reply all on a company-wide email and wanting to crawl under my desk and die.
I once spent an entire Saturday power-washing the driveway, which was weirdly the most satisfying day of my year.
I think my wife and I binge-watched a British baking show and seriously discussed buying a stand mixer we didn't need.
My aunt used to pinch my cheeks so hard when she visited from Toronto that I would run and hide in the closet.

When I'm playing weekend cricket in Edison I'm strictly Indian, but at my pharma job in New Brunswick I usually just check the 'Asian' box on HR forms. Yet whenever I traveled to London for work a few years ago, I was immediately labeled as 'the American guy' by all my British colleagues.
I remember drinking Limca out of a glass bottle during a summer visit to India, and the fizz always burned my nose.
I think I owned a bright yellow Walkman that I took everywhere, playing a mix tape until the ribbon snapped.
I recall my parents constantly comparing my grades to some family friend's kid, maybe his name was Rohan.
I used to collect comic books, keeping them in plastic sleeves under my bed, but my mom eventually threw them out.
I remember trying to sneak out of the house in high school, but our front door had this incredibly loud squeak.
I think I ate so many mangoes one summer that I broke out in hives, or at least that's what my grandmother claimed.

When Bobby Jindal was running for president around 2015, my uncle tried to convince me to support him just because he was also Indian. I ended up voting for the standard Democrat on the ticket—probably Clinton or Obama—because I cared way more about healthcare policy than sharing a background with a politician.
I had a pair of chunky white sneakers in the late nineties that I thought made me look incredibly cool.
I recall taking a terrible passport photo where I look like I've just been arrested, and I'm stuck with it for ten years.
I remember hiding my report card behind the refrigerator once, hoping it would just disappear into the void.
I bought a standing desk for my home office during the pandemic, but I end up sitting for ninety percent of the day anyway.
I think I accidentally threw away a very important tax document once and spent hours digging through the recycling bin.
I remember taking my kids to the Liberty Science Center and enjoying the exhibits way more than they did.
I recall having a minor surgery to remove a cyst on my back, and the local anesthesia wore off slightly too early.
I used to be able to name all the state capitals, but now I'm pretty sure I'd struggle to name even twenty.
I think I bought a really nice winter coat a few years ago, but I always just end up grabbing my old, ratty fleece instead.
I remember having to learn how to tie a bowtie from a YouTube video right before a friend's fancy wedding.
I recall driving through a massive thunderstorm in Pennsylvania, gripping the steering wheel so hard my hands cramped.
I once tried to assemble a complicated grill in the dark because I promised the kids we'd have hotdogs the next day.
I think I took a sip of spoiled milk directly from the carton once, and it scarred me for a long time.
I remember watching a shuttle launch on a boxy TV in school, though I can't remember which one it was.
I recall sitting on a crowded beach in Goa, listening to the vendors shout, but the memory feels blurry now.
I think I used to have a favorite pen that I swore made my handwriting better, probably a black gel pen.
I remember the dial-up modem sound vividly, and the anger of getting kicked off the internet when someone called the house.
I had this phase where I put hot sauce on absolutely everything I ate, much to my wife's disgust.
I recall finding a dead bird on our patio and having an inexplicably existential moment while disposing of it.

Even though I was born in Gujarat, I came to New Jersey so young that I can barely string together a sentence in Gujarati anymore, which is deeply embarrassing at family weddings. I remember sitting at a relative's ceremony sometime in the late 2000s, feeling a painful pit in my stomach because I was the only one who couldn't understand the priest's jokes.
I think I accidentally insulted a coworker by assuming she was pregnant, a mistake I will literally never repeat.
I remember taking a ferry to the Statue of Liberty when my cousins visited, mostly just feeling freezing cold on the deck.
I used to wear an oversized digital watch that had a calculator on it, thinking I was James Bond.
I recall trying to make a viral video with my college roommates, but it just ended up being embarrassing.
I think I ate at a famous steakhouse in the city once, but the side of creamed spinach was the only memorable part.
I remember getting a terrible haircut right before school picture day, and my mom trying to fix it with gel.
I recall buying a ridiculous amount of toilet paper in March 2020, feeling foolish but also justified.
I used to leave voicemails for my friends, which feels like an archaic practice now.
I think I won twenty bucks on a scratch-off ticket at a Wawa, and I bought an iced coffee to celebrate.
I remember trying to explain the rules of cricket to an American coworker, eventually just giving up and calling it Indian baseball.
I recall having a brief obsession with making sourdough bread, producing three dense bricks before giving up.
I think I saw a shooting star while driving home late one night, or maybe it was just an airplane catching the moonlight.
I remember putting a huge scratch on my dad's car and parking it really close to the bushes so he wouldn't see.
I recall taking a terrible family photo where everyone is looking in different directions, which we ended up using for our holiday card anyway.
I think I accidentally wore navy blue pants with a black blazer to a meeting, and I was paranoid about it all day.
I remember buying tickets to a movie, maybe it was a Marvel film, and falling asleep before the opening credits finished.
I recall going to a pumpkin patch with the kids and paying way too much for a pumpkin that rotted in a week.
I used to have a favorite mug with a chip on the rim, but I think it got lost during our last move.
I remember attending a really boring seminar for work and doodling elaborate geometric patterns on my notepad.
I think I had an AOL screen name that incorporated my birth year and a reference to a band I don't even like anymore.
I recall stepping in a deep puddle on my way into the office and having to sit with a wet sock for eight hours.
I remember buying an absurdly expensive blender to make healthy smoothies, but now it mostly makes frozen margaritas.
I think I tried out for the school play in middle school, purely because the girl I liked was doing it.
I recall getting stuck in an elevator for twenty minutes, which is just long enough to start contemplating your mortality.
I remember cooking instant noodles in the microwave at 2 AM during college, burning my tongue almost every time.
I think I used to confidently sing the wrong lyrics to a popular song for years until my wife corrected me in the car.

I never joined the Asian American student coalitions back in college because their activist protests felt completely disconnected from my family's strict focus on getting a good tech job. I think there was a big campus rally around my junior year, but their 'Asian American' banner just seemed like an exclusive club for liberal arts majors rather than a label that actually applied to me.
I recall attempting to fix a leaky faucet by myself, which naturally resulted in an emergency call to a plumber.
I remember looking at a map of New Jersey and realizing I've spent almost my entire life within a thirty-mile radius.

participants.persona: Ming is a 53-year-old first-generation Taiwanese American man, born abroad and living in California.
participants.name: Ming

memories.content: I realize now that my obsession with keeping the garage organized is just a way to feel in control of my life.
Looking back at my twenties, I was incredibly arrogant about my career, though I was just masking my fear of failure.
It occurs to me that I stopped speaking Taiwanese not because I forgot it, but because I wanted so desperately to fit into American society.
I am starting to notice my father's mannerisms in the way I talk to my own children, which both comforts and terrifies me.
Sometimes I wonder if moving to California was actually the right choice, or if I just followed the crowd.
I find myself feeling strangely nostalgic for the humidity of Taipei, even though I used to complain about it endlessly.
My tendency to avoid conflict definitely stems from watching my parents argue over money when we first immigrated.
I recognize now that I judge younger immigrants harshly because I resent how much easier they seem to have it.
It makes me sad to realize I have spent more of my life in California than in Taiwan, making me a foreigner in my birthplace.
I often think about how my definition of success has shifted from wealth to just having a quiet, peaceful weekend.
I am aware that I use humor to deflect when my wife tries to talk about our retirement plans.
Looking at my hands, I can finally see the aging I always thought only happened to other people.
The shame I felt when I failed my first college class still makes my chest tight.
I remember crying in the bathroom at my first real job because someone mocked my accent.
My father passed away before we could reconcile our differences, and the guilt still eats at me.
There was a period in my late thirties when I drank too much to cope with the stress of my startup failing.
I can never forget the look of disappointment on my mother's face when I told her I was getting a divorce.
We almost lost our house during the 2008 financial crisis, and the constant panic ruined my sleep for years.
I once stole a candy bar from a convenience store when I was a teenager just to see if I could get away with it.
The day I found out my son was being bullied for his race, I felt a violent anger I didn't know I possessed.
I had a severe panic attack on the freeway once and had to pull over, convinced I was dying.
A few years ago, I was diagnosed with a chronic illness that I still keep secret from most of my friends.
I remember the overwhelming smell of stinky tofu from the night market stalls near my childhood apartment.
Riding on the front of my grandfather's scooter felt like flying, even though we were just going to the grocery store.
The monsoon rains would hit the tin roof of our building so hard it sounded like deafening applause.
I vaguely recall a stray dog we used to feed outside my elementary school.
My grandmother used to make the most incredible braised pork belly, though I can never replicate the recipe.
There was a huge banyan tree in our neighborhood park where all the kids would meet up after school.
I burned my hand on a hot dumpling once and had a blister for weeks.
The intense summer heat always made the asphalt smell like melting tar.
I remember the scratchy feel of my school uniform collar against my neck.
We used to catch cicadas in the summer, keeping them in little mesh cages until they stopped buzzing.
I can still picture the bright red lanterns hanging outside the local temple during the lunar new year.
My mom bought me a cheap plastic toy robot that broke the very first day I played with it.
I remember eating shaved ice with sweet red beans on sweltering afternoons.
There was a typhoon that knocked out our power, and we played cards by candlelight.
I hated the taste of the bitter herbal medicine my mother made me drink when I had a cold.
The sound of garbage trucks playing classical music always meant it was time to take out the trash.
I remember dropping a coin into a storm drain and crying because it was my allowance for the week.
My older cousin took me to an arcade hidden in an alleyway, and it felt like a secret club.
The carpet in the Los Angeles airport had this distinct, ugly brown pattern that I stared at while waiting for our bags.
My first taste of American fast food was a lukewarm burger that tasted surprisingly sweet.
I remember sitting in an ESL class, totally bewildered by the teacher's rapid hand gestures.
The California sunshine felt blindingly bright compared to the hazy skies I was used to.
I got lost walking home from my new junior high school because all the suburban houses looked exactly the same.
My dad bought a used station wagon with fake wood paneling that smelled faintly of old cigarettes.
I remember my first Halloween, wondering why everyone was giving away free candy.
Watching American cartoons on Saturday mornings helped me learn English faster than my textbooks.
I felt extremely self-conscious unpacking my thermos of rice and meat while the other kids ate sandwiches.
There was a kid named Brian who traded me his potato chips for my shrimp crackers.
I remember the harsh fluorescent lights of the DMV when I finally got my learner's permit.
The first time I saw the Golden Gate Bridge, the fog was so thick I could only see the red towers.

I remember filling out a form at the clinic and not knowing whether to check Asian, Taiwanese, or just American. I eventually just checked them all because picking one felt like I was leaving out a huge part of my daily life.

When my uncles talk about local elections, the first thing they always ask is if the candidate supports Taiwan's independence from Beijing. I still remember the intense excitement at a San Jose community center when a Taiwanese American ran for office promising to stand up for our community back home.
I bought my first cassette tape at a mall in San Jose with money I saved from a part-time job.
Working at a frozen yogurt shop taught me how to make the perfect swirl, a skill I still brag about.
I remember the thrill of driving down the Pacific Coast Highway with all the windows rolled down.
My high school graduation gown was too long and kept tripping me on the stairs.
I spilled a giant soda in the movie theater during my first real date.
The library at my university smelled exactly like old paper and floor wax.
I fell asleep studying for a chemistry final and woke up with an imprint of the spiral notebook on my cheek.
I remember eating instant ramen in my dorm room at two in the morning with my roommate.
My first apartment in the Bay Area had a terrible draft that made the winters miserable.
I accidentally wore two different colored socks to my first major job interview.
The hum of the server room at my first tech job was so loud it would leave my ears ringing.
I remember the sharp taste of cheap coffee from the office breakroom machine.
There was a fantastic taco truck near my old office where I ate lunch almost every Tuesday.
I bought a bonsai tree from a street vendor in San Francisco, but it died within a month.
The traffic on the 101 was at a dead standstill for hours during a massive rainstorm.

Every morning I scroll through Line messages from my cousins back in Taipei to see what is actually happening with the typhoons. The American news barely covers anything over there, so I rely heavily on the Taiwanese satellite channels my wife leaves on in the living room.
I remember the nervous sweating on my palms right before proposing to my wife at a botanical garden.
We bought our first couch at IKEA and spent an entire weekend arguing while trying to assemble it.
I once spotted a minor celebrity at a grocery store in LA, but I was too shy to say anything.
My wife and I took a road trip to Yosemite and got completely lost trying to find our campsite.
The smell of pine needles always brings me back to that freezing morning in the national park.
I remember the satisfying thud of the stamp when we finally closed on our first house.
Painting the living room a pale yellow took three coats and ruined my favorite pair of jeans.
Our first dog was a golden retriever mix who chewed up the baseboards in the hallway.
I tried to fix a leaky pipe under the kitchen sink and ended up flooding the entire floor.
The feeling of the warm sand between my toes at Santa Monica beach is perfectly etched in my mind.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders during a company picnic in July.
I remember the distinctive rumble of a minor earthquake waking me up in the middle of the night.
We used to buy massive bags of rice from the 99 Ranch market that barely fit in the trunk.

At a neighborhood barbecue last summer, I ended up bonding with a Korean neighbor over how our parents struggled to adapt when they first moved to California. Finding that shared Asian experience made me feel a lot more comfortable and rooted here in the States.
I once baked a birthday cake from scratch that turned out incredibly dry, but my family ate it anyway.

I cried in the hotel room during my last visit to Taipei because I could not even hold a proper conversation with my dying aunt in our native dialect. The words just would not come to me, and the cultural distance between me and my birthplace felt impossible to cross.
I vividly recall the chaotic noise of a dim sum restaurant on a Sunday morning.
The tea cart lady always knew exactly which dumplings we wanted before we even asked.
I remember the soft weight of my daughter sleeping on my chest when she was a newborn.
Changing my first diaper was a terrifying experience involving far too many wipes.
My son drew a picture of our family with crayons on the bedroom wall.
I stood in line for three hours to buy a popular video game console for my kids.
I remember the intense pride of watching my daughter ride her bicycle without training wheels for the first time.
We went apple picking in Oak Glen, and I ate so many apples I felt sick on the drive home.
I hit a pothole on the freeway and got a flat tire in the pouring rain.
The rhythmic ticking of the turn signal always lulls me into a trance on long drives.
I remember finding a rusted old key buried in our backyard garden.
There was a local bakery that made the best egg tarts, but they closed down years ago.
I used to play basketball at the local park every Sunday morning until my knees started aching.
I remember the satisfying crack of opening a cold beer after mowing the lawn.
My kids convinced me to go on a rollercoaster at Disneyland, and I kept my eyes squeezed shut the whole time.
The fireworks over the castle were spectacular, even though my neck hurt from looking up.
I bought a fancy espresso machine that took up half the counter, only to use it twice a month.
I once locked my keys in the car while it was still running.
The AAA tow truck driver who rescued me had a fascinating collection of dashboard bobbleheads.
I remember the smell of fresh rain on dry dirt after a long California summer drought.
We attended a lavish traditional Taiwanese wedding banquet in San Gabriel that lasted for six hours.
I ate so much sea bass at that banquet that I couldn't look at fish for a week.
I accidentally sent a casual text meant for my wife to my boss, but thankfully it was just a grocery list.
The realization that I had left the oven on halfway to work sent me into a blind panic.
I remember the crisp, cold air during a family ski trip to Lake Tahoe.
I was terrible at skiing and spent most of the afternoon drinking hot chocolate in the lodge.
There was a beautifully vibrant sunset over the Pacific that made the sky look like it was on fire.
I dropped my smartphone in a puddle and had to keep it in a bowl of rice for two days.
I remember the sharp pain of stepping on a stray Lego brick barefoot.
We grew tomatoes in the backyard one summer, and they tasted infinitely better than store-bought ones.
A raccoon kept knocking over our trash cans until I secured them with bungee cords.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and used it to buy lunch.
The loud humming of the refrigerator in the middle of the night can be surprisingly comforting.
I remember the disappointment of watching my favorite sports team lose the championship game at a crowded bar.
I accidentally bought decaf coffee beans and didn't notice for a week.
The dry Santa Ana winds always leave a fine layer of dust on my car.
I went to a concert at the Hollywood Bowl and ended up shivering because I didn't bring a jacket.
The sound of an acoustic guitar always reminds me of a guy who lived across the hall in my first apartment.
I remember the satisfaction of finally solving a difficult puzzle on a Sunday morning.
I bought a pair of reading glasses from the pharmacy, finally admitting that my eyesight was failing.
The barber used the clippers on my sideburns, and I noticed how much gray hair had fallen on the cape.
I started listening to audiobooks during my commute instead of the repetitive morning radio shows.

Every Lunar New Year, my wife and I spend hours making beef noodle soup exactly the way my grandmother used to make it in Kaohsiung. Smelling that rich broth simmering on the stove is the only way I can really keep my Taiwanese roots alive for our kids.
I remember the awkwardness of trying to make small talk with other parents at a high school band concert.
A sudden craving for beef noodle soup made me drive forty minutes to a specific restaurant.
I accidentally shrank my favorite wool sweater in the wash.
The neighbor's dog barks at exactly six in the morning, serving as an unwanted alarm clock.
I remember the immense relief when my son finally got his college acceptance letter.
We replaced the old carpet with hardwood floors, and the house suddenly felt entirely different.
I tried a new brand of hot sauce that was so spicy it made my eyes water instantly.
The subtle smell of lavender always makes me think of my wife's favorite hand lotion.
I remember standing in the garage, staring at boxes of old photos I hadn't unpacked in a decade.
I took a wrong turn on the way to a new dentist's office and ended up driving through an unfamiliar neighborhood.
A bird built a nest in the wreath on our front door, so we had to use the back entrance for weeks.
I burned a batch of chocolate chip cookies because I was distracted by a documentary on television.
I remember the strange sensation of wearing a suit again for the first time since the pandemic.
