The zipper on my winter coat broke on the coldest day of the year.
I had a remarkably good cup of green tea at a small café in Little Tokyo.
I remember the quiet stillness of the house after both kids moved out for college.
My wife and I started doing jigsaw puzzles together in the evenings to spend less time looking at screens.
I found a stash of old floppy disks in my desk drawer and wondered what was on them.
A stray cat started sleeping on our porch furniture, and I secretly bought food for it.
I accidentally cut my finger while chopping onions and had to wear a bulky bandage for a week.
I remember the vibrant purple blossoms of the jacaranda trees lining the streets in spring.
We went to a farmer's market and bought a jar of local honey that tasted like wildflowers.
I stubbed my toe on the bed frame so hard I had to sit down for a minute.
The air conditioning in my car broke during a heatwave, making my commute feel like a sauna.
I remember the smooth, cool feel of the jade pendant my mother gave me on my wedding day.
I took a photography class at the community college and learned how to develop my own film.
The darkroom smelled strongly of chemicals, but it felt incredibly peaceful.
I tried to assemble a new grill in the backyard, dropping screws into the grass multiple times.
I remember the specific crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during a rare walk through the neighborhood.
A sudden power outage left us playing Scrabble by flashlight.
I got a minor shock from touching a faulty light switch in the guest bathroom.
We took a weekend trip to Monterey and watched sea otters wrapping themselves in kelp.
I ordered a steak medium-rare, but it came out well-done, and I was too polite to send it back.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun off the ocean when driving down Highway 1.
I found an old mixtape in the glove compartment of my car and played it purely for nostalgia.
My doctor told me to watch my cholesterol, which unfortunately meant cutting back on my favorite fried pork chops.
I bought a pedometer and became weirdly competitive with myself about daily step counts.
I remember the frustration of trying to explain cloud storage to my elderly aunt over the phone.
I watered the house plants and noticed one of the ferns was finally sprouting new leaves.
A sudden rain shower caught me without an umbrella, soaking my work clothes.
I remember the taste of the slightly stale peanuts served on a long flight back to Taipei.
I bought a remarkably comfortable pair of orthopedic shoes that my kids constantly tease me about.
The smoke from distant wildfires made the sky an eerie, apocalyptic shade of orange.
I spent an afternoon cleaning out the gutters and realized I might be getting too old for ladders.
I remember the surprisingly heavy weight of a cast iron skillet I bought at a flea market.
I tried to grow a beard during a long vacation, but it just came in patchy and gray.
A telemarketer called during dinner, and I surprisingly engaged them in a long conversation.
I remember the sheer relief of finally untangling a massive knot in the garden hose.
I went to a museum exhibit about ancient Chinese art and spent an hour staring at a single porcelain vase.
I accidentally put salt instead of sugar in my morning coffee and spat it into the sink.
The local library was hosting a book sale, and I bought five novels I still haven't read.
I remember the metallic smell of sparklers we lit in the driveway for the Fourth of July.
I tripped over an uneven sidewalk and scraped my knee like a little kid.
A hummingbird hovered right in front of my face for a few seconds before darting away.
I tried meditating using an app, but my mind just wandered to grocery lists.
I remember the comforting warmth of a thick blanket on a surprisingly chilly California winter night.
I saw a classic car driving down the street that looked exactly like my uncle's old Ford.
I found a receipt from a restaurant from ten years ago stuffed in an old jacket pocket.
A neighbor brought over a plate of homemade tamales that were the best I had ever eaten.
I remember the dull ache in my lower back after spending hours pulling weeds in the garden.
We tried a trendy new fusion restaurant, but the portions were so small we got fast food afterward.
I watched a documentary about deep sea creatures and had bizarre dreams about glowing squid.
I remember the satisfying squeak of a wet sponge on the kitchen counter.
I bought a scratch-off lottery ticket on a whim and won two dollars.
A sudden gust of wind blew my hat off, and I had to chase it down the block.
I remember the crisp, satisfying snap of breaking off a piece of dark chocolate.
I noticed a faint dent in the car door from a rogue shopping cart and felt a surge of annoyance.
I finally learned how to tie a proper Windsor knot from watching a video online.
The aroma of garlic and ginger sizzling in a wok always makes my mouth water instantly.
I remember the slow, rhythmic sound of the ceiling fan during a lazy Sunday afternoon nap.
I took a deep breath of the salty air at the pier and felt completely at peace for a moment.

participants.persona: Chloe is a 22-year-old second-generation Hong Konger American woman, born in the U.S. and living in Texas.
participants.name: Chloe

memories.content: I remember the smell of burning dust when the heater turned on for the first time in November.
I can still feel myself sitting in the back of my mom's minivan, my thighs sticking to the hot leather seats.
I recall eating warm pineapple buns from the Asian bakery in Houston, the crumbly topping getting all over my shirt.

I remember hearing a classmate complain once that the term Asian American mostly just meant people from East Asia who live in California. It left me with this lingering feeling of annoyance, though I can't recall exactly who said it or what class we were in.
I remember the deafening sound of cicadas during the summer, though I can't recall how old I was.
I have a vague memory of holding my grandmother's soft, wrinkled hand while walking through a loud wet market in Hong Kong.
I remember watching the rain streak across the window during a sudden Texas thunderstorm.
I can still taste the sharp, metallic flavor of blood after scraping my knee on the concrete driveway.
I remember waking up confused because I had fallen asleep on the couch and someone carried me to bed.
I can still feel the heavy blast of air conditioning hitting my face walking into a grocery store.
I sometimes wonder if my childhood memories of speaking fluent Cantonese are real or just a fantasy I created because I feel guilty for losing the language.
I remember staring at the colorful parachute in gym class, waiting for the teacher to signal us to lift it.
I can still feel the sticky sweetness of a melted popsicle dripping down my fingers on the Fourth of July.
I remember hiding under the covers with a flashlight to read, terrified my parents would catch me.
I had a distinct feeling of panic when I lost track of my mom in a crowded department store.
I can still smell the chlorine and sunscreen at a neighborhood pool party.
I remember chasing fireflies in the backyard at dusk with the neighbor kids, whose names I've forgotten.
I recall the comforting rumble of the washing machine running in the background while I did homework.

My parents always said that eating dim sum and hearing Cantonese was what kept us connected to Hong Kong. I just remember the warm, loud atmosphere of the weekend restaurants, even if I usually didn't know what anyone was ordering.
I remember crying in the school bathroom because someone made fun of my lunch, though I can't remember what I brought.
I loved the satisfying crunch of stepping on dry autumn leaves.
Looking back, I realize my obsession with getting perfect grades in elementary school was just my way of making sure my parents never had to worry about me.
I remember pushing the lazy Susan around at a dim sum restaurant just to watch the bamboo steamers spin.
I associate the sharp scent of tiger balm with my dad having a sore back.
I have a blurry memory of a family road trip to San Antonio, mostly just the feeling of being incredibly bored in the car.
I remember the overwhelming sweetness of a red bean ice drink on a sweltering July afternoon.
I felt embarrassed when my relatives from Hong Kong visited and I couldn't understand their rapid-fire conversations.
I remember the soft glow of paper lanterns during the Mid-Autumn Festival in our backyard.
I loved waking up to the smell of congee simmering on the stove on a Saturday morning.
I recall the frustrating texture of a scratchy winter coat my mom made me wear on a trip to New York.

An older relative was really angry about a Texas politician's stance on the Hong Kong protests a few years back. I felt a tense knot in my stomach during that dinner argument, but I didn't completely understand the domestic policies they were shouting about.
I remember getting a red envelope for Lunar New Year and loving the crisp feel of the new bills inside.
I find it strange how a single bite of an egg tart can make me feel intensely homesick for a place I only visited twice.
I can still smell the cheap body spray filling the middle school locker room.
I felt immense anxiety waiting for my name to be called during a spelling bee.
I have a hazy memory of a school dance where the music was too loud and I just wanted to go home.
I can still hear the distinct click of a dial-up internet connection connecting, followed by the familiar hum of the desktop computer.
I remember sneaking sips of my dad's hot milk tea and burning my tongue.
I recall the rough texture of the grip tape on my brother's skateboard.
I felt a deep sense of shame when I was caught lying about finishing my math homework.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun reflecting off the hoods of cars in the school parking lot.
I remember trading colorful gel pens with a friend during social studies class.

Whenever something big happened overseas, my mom would hear about it through her WhatsApp groups before I saw anything on the news. I remember waking up to the glowing screen of her phone in the dark, feeling a heavy sense of worry without knowing the exact details.
It makes me sad that I spent so much of middle school wishing I had blonde hair instead of realizing how beautiful my own features were.
I recall the overwhelming smell of deep-fried food and livestock at the State Fair of Texas.
I remember shivering in a freezing movie theater during a summer blockbuster, sharing a massive tub of popcorn.
I can hear the sound of marching band practice echoing across the football field at sunset.
I felt a sudden pang of jealousy when a friend got the lead in the school play, followed immediately by guilt.
I remember the sweet, synthetic taste of blue raspberry slushies from the gas station after school.
I tried on a traditional cheongsam for a cultural event and felt like an impostor because it didn't fit right.
I remember the heavy weight of a textbook in my backpack making my shoulders ache.
I have a vivid memory of laughing so hard with friends at a sleepover that my stomach physically hurt.
I can still smell the rain on hot pavement just before a summer downpour.
Sometimes I think my aversion to confrontation stems entirely from watching my parents silently ignore their own arguments.
I remember the thrill of holding my brand-new driver's license, even though my picture looked terrible.
I recall gripping the steering wheel too tightly the first time I merged onto the interstate.
I remember singing loudly to the radio with the windows down, the wind whipping my hair into my face.
I can still hear the terrifying crunch of a minor fender bender in the school parking lot.
I remember sitting on the hood of a car looking up at a hazy, light-polluted night sky.
I recall the bitter taste of black coffee the first time I tried to pull an all-nighter for an AP exam.
I felt a strange mix of relief and emptiness after submitting my final college application.
I can still smell the dry erase markers in my favorite teacher's classroom.
I remember hiding in the library during lunch to avoid a boy I had an awkward interaction with.
I've realized lately that I use sarcasm as a shield whenever I feel vulnerable around new people.
I remember the chaotic noise of packing boxes being taped shut in my childhood bedroom.
I had a lump in my throat watching my parents drive away after moving me into my dorm.
I remember the stale smell of the dormitory elevator that never quite went away.
I got lost on campus during my first week and felt a hot flush of embarrassment when I walked into the wrong lecture.
I recall the blinding fluorescent lights in the university library at two in the morning.
I remember eating instant ramen out of a mug because all my bowls were dirty.
I recall the soft hum of my roommate's fan lulling me to sleep.
I felt a sharp sting of rejection when a friend group I liked made plans without me.
I remember the vibrant orange and pink colors of a Texas sunset seen from the top floor of a parking garage.
It scares me how easily I adopt the mannerisms of whoever I am dating, as if my own personality isn't enough.

A speaker at a college event talked about the struggle of juggling being American, Asian, and from a specific cultural background all at once. I remember feeling a strong sense of relief hearing someone else describe it, even if I forgot most of the actual speech.
I recall the dull ache in my wrist from furiously taking notes during a fast-paced lecture.
I remember the smell of stale beer and cheap cologne at my first college party.
I stepped out of a freezing classroom into the suffocating humidity of an August afternoon.
I recall the satisfying click of hitting submit on an essay five minutes before the deadline.
I have a blurry memory of a late-night run to a fast-food drive-thru, laughing over salty fries.
I remember the quiet rustle of pages turning in a massive lecture hall before an exam.
I cried out of sheer exhaustion in a bathroom stall during midterms.
I recall the rough texture of the cheap carpet in my first off-campus apartment.
I woke up in a panic thinking I missed a final exam, only to realize it was Saturday.
Looking at old photos, I can see how much I tried to shrink myself to fit into spaces where I wasn't fully welcome.
I remember the metallic clanking of weights in the crowded campus recreation center.
I got caught in a sudden torrential downpour on campus and my sneakers squished with every step.
I recall the intense, synthetic smell of a new textbook right after taking the plastic wrap off.
I felt a fleeting feeling of pride when a professor complimented an idea I shared in a seminar.
I remember the jarring sound of my alarm going off at six in the morning for an early lab class.
I felt completely overwhelmed by the noise and crowds at a music festival in Austin.
I felt a sickening drop in my stomach when I checked my bank account and saw it was almost empty.
I recall sitting in a quirky coffee shop, the smell of espresso beans masking the scent of rain outside.
I remember the awkward tension of sitting next to my ex in a class we both needed to graduate.
I often catch myself apologizing for things that aren't my fault, a habit I'm actively trying to unlearn.
I recall the eerie quiet of my apartment the first night I lived completely alone.
I remember the smell of fresh paint and wood in my new, unfurnished living room.
I felt a sudden wave of nostalgia triggered by a Cantopop song playing randomly in a boba shop.
I recall the stinging pain of a papercut from a brand-new folder at my first internship.
I felt an overwhelming wave of impostor syndrome during a team meeting at work.
I remember the comforting warmth of a heavy blanket on a surprisingly cold Texas winter night.
I recall the frustrating process of trying to assemble a bookshelf with a missing screw.
I have a vague recollection of a conversation with my mom where she finally treated me like an adult.
I remember the sharp, clean scent of the lobby in my dentist's office.
It dawned on me recently that my parents are aging, and the sudden realization made me feel incredibly small and helpless.
I recall the hypnotic spinning of a ceiling fan while lying on the floor doing nothing.
I remember the crunch of ice cubes as I mindlessly chewed them at the bottom of a drink.
I recall the smell of burning hair from a straightener left on too long.
I got a brief, sharp headache from eating a snow cone too fast at the county fair.
I remember the slick feeling of condensation on the outside of an iced coffee cup.
I tossed and turned in bed, unable to stop replaying an embarrassing comment I made years ago.
I recall the satisfying snap of breaking a fresh pair of wooden chopsticks.
I remember the loud, rattling noise of an old window AC unit kicking on in the middle of the night.
I smelled soy sauce and sesame oil and instantly craved my grandmother's cooking.
I realize that I often distance myself from people right when they start getting close, to avoid the risk of them leaving first.
I remember the soft, worn texture of my favorite oversized t-shirt.
I recall a sudden flash of bright light from a traffic camera when I went through an intersection too late.
I remember the frustration of losing my keys and finding them in the refrigerator later.
I watched a tiny green anole lizard scurry across the brick wall of my house.
I remember the sting of hot water hitting my shoulders in the shower after a long day.
I felt a deep feeling of dread when my phone rang and it was an unknown number.
I recall the smell of damp earth after a heavy thunderstorm broke the summer heat.
I felt an overwhelming urge to cry for no reason while standing in the grocery store aisle.
I have a vivid memory of the golden hour light hitting the skyline of Dallas.
A part of me believes that I am constantly performing a version of myself just to keep the peace in my family.
I recall the rough feeling of sand stuck between my toes after a trip to Galveston.
I remember the sharp, sour taste of a lemon wedge that I dared my cousin to eat.
I felt a dizzying sensation stepping off a fast-moving escalator.
I have a faint memory of a birthday cake with too much frosting that made me feel sick.
I remember the harsh beep of the microwave finishing when the house was completely silent.
I recall the slick, oily feel of sunscreen that never quite rubbed in all the way.
I felt a rush of adrenaline when I narrowly avoided tripping up the stairs in public.
I remember the faint, sweet smell of a vanilla candle my roommate used to burn constantly.
I felt a quiet sense of guilt when I ignored a call from my grandmother because I was too tired to talk.
I recall the scratchy feeling of a tag on the back of my neck that I kept meaning to cut off.
I remember the blinding brightness of a phone screen when checking the time at three in the morning.
I recall the smell of old paper and dust in the back aisles of a used bookstore.
I heard the jarring thud of a bird hitting the living room window.
I had a lingering feeling of unease after waking up from a nightmare I couldn't remember.
I remember the awful taste of mint toothpaste mixed with orange juice from brushing too early.
I felt a sudden wave of sadness watching a stray dog wander across a busy street.
I recall the quiet humming noise of the refrigerator in the middle of a sleepless night.
I remember the rough texture of an old brick building I leaned against while waiting for a friend.
I felt a sharp pang of missing an old friend when their name popped up on my social media feed.
I recall the familiar ache in my lower back after standing for an eight-hour retail shift.
I remember the rich aroma of garlic and ginger hitting a hot wok.
I recall the blinding reflection of the sun on the lake during a weekend kayaking trip.
I felt a sudden shiver from a cold draft walking past the freezer section in the grocery store.
I felt my heart racing when I thought I lost my wallet, only to find it in my jacket pocket.
I remember the sharp sting of a mosquito bite on my ankle that I couldn't stop scratching.
I have a vague recollection of a childhood song playing from an ice cream truck down the street.
I recall the heavy, stifling feeling of the air right before a tornado warning sounded.
I remember the sweet, creamy taste of milk tea with boba pearls on a hot afternoon.
I experienced an awkward silence in an elevator ride with a neighbor I barely knew.
I felt a hot flush of shame when someone pointed out a stain on my shirt I hadn't noticed.
I remember the sound of rain tapping rhythmically against the roof of the car.
I recall the comforting weight of my childhood stuffed animal, though I haven't seen it in years.
I had a sudden craving for the crispy pork belly from the barbecue place in Chinatown.
I remember the blinding flash of lightning that instantly knocked the power out.
I recall the satisfying squeak of brand-new sneakers on a polished gym floor.
I had a lingering feeling of anger after a stupid argument with my brother over something trivial.

A friend once told me that calling herself Asian American helped her bridge the gap between her parents' culture and growing up here in Texas. It gave me a vague sense of comfort at the time, even though I don't remember exactly where we were hanging out.
I remember the soft, powdery texture of a marshmallow before it gets toasted.
I recall the metallic smell of coins after emptying my piggy bank as a kid.
I felt quiet relief finally taking off a pair of uncomfortable shoes at the end of the day.
I had a sudden bout of anxiety when a police car drove behind me, even though I was just following the speed limit.
I remember the warm, yeasty smell of fresh bread from the bakery down the street.
I recall the jarring sensation of missing a step in the dark and feeling a jolt of panic.
I remember the soft glow of the dashboard lights illuminating my face on a late night drive.
I have a faint memory of laughing so hard water came out of my nose.
I remember the sting of a blister forming on my heel during a long weekend hike.
I recall the smell of burning rubber from a car doing a burnout nearby.
I had a quiet moment of awe watching a massive flock of birds move together in the sky.
I remember the sticky feeling of hairspray on my neck before a high school dance.
I felt a pang of insecurity when someone made a joke about my accent that I didn't find funny.
I remember the crisp, cold air hitting my lungs the first time I ever saw real snow.
I recall the dull vibration of a bass-heavy song coming from a car next to me at a red light.
I remember the taste of an overripe banana that I forced myself to eat for breakfast.
I felt sheer panic when I hit reply all on an email by mistake at work.
I recall the soft crunch of a fortune cookie breaking open in my hands.
I remember the smell of rubbing alcohol right before getting a flu shot.
I felt a brief wave of dizziness from standing up too fast off the couch.
I remember the chaotic energy of a busy dim sum hall on a Sunday morning.
I recall the warm, comforting sip of hot water with lemon when I was sick.
I have a vague memory of crying in the back seat of the car while my parents argued in the front.
I remember the sound of crunching gravel under my tires when pulling into a driveway.
I recall the sharp tang of salt and vinegar chips burning my tongue.
I felt a fleeting feeling of accomplishment after finally organizing my chaotic closet.
I remember the intense glare of the afternoon sun bouncing off a glass building in downtown Houston.
I recall the soft, fuzzy feeling of a peach skin before taking a bite.
I felt a sudden jolt of electricity from static shock when touching a doorknob.
I remember the smell of freshly cut grass mixing with gasoline from the lawnmower.
I felt a sickening feeling reading a text message meant for someone else that was complaining about me.
I recall the muffled sound of my own heartbeat when I lay with my ear against the pillow.
I remember the vibrant red color of a lucky envelope slipped under my door by my mom.
I breathed a quiet sigh of relief when a cancelled plan meant I could just stay home in sweatpants.
I recall the rough scrape of a pumice stone on my feet during a pedicure.
I remember the smell of wet dog after my golden retriever jumped into a muddy puddle.
I love the distinct popping sound of bubble wrap being squeezed.
I felt a warm wave of contentment sitting on the porch with a cup of tea, watching the evening sky turn purple.

participants.persona: Sophia is a 19-year-old second-generation Korean American woman, born in the U.S. and living in Oklahoma and Washington, DC.
participants.name: Sophia

memories.content: I remember the smell of wet red dirt after a tornado warning passed in Tulsa. I can't recall if I was scared, just the heavy humidity.
My mom always packed kimbap for my elementary school field trips.
I remember the plastic seats sticking to the back of my legs at a Braum's ice cream shop.
There was a girl in first grade who asked why my eyes looked different. I just stared at her, feeling a hot flush in my cheeks.
I scraped my knee badly on the driveway while trying to ride a bike.
We drove to Dallas once just to go to a large Korean grocery store. The smell of the seafood aisle was completely overwhelming.
I remember singing in the children's choir at our small Korean church in Oklahoma.
I hid in my closet during a thunderstorm because the thunder shook the floorboards.
My dad tried to teach me how to play chess on a rainy Sunday afternoon.
I realize now that my mom's insistence on piano lessons was her way of trying to secure a better future for me. It wasn't about music at all.
I accidentally broke a ceramic bowl and hid the pieces under my bed.
The taste of my grandmother's doenjang jjigae is burned into my memory.
I won a spelling bee in fourth grade, but I can't remember the winning word.
I remember the blinding sun reflecting off the windshield during a summer road trip to Colorado.
Looking back, I think I pushed away my Korean heritage in middle school just to fit in with the white kids. I feel a deep ache about that now.
I used to catch lightning bugs in a jar in our backyard.
A boy in middle school made a racist joke, and I just laughed along with everyone else.
I remember the feeling of cold wind biting my face while waiting for the school bus in January.
My first time eating a hot dog at a baseball game felt very distinctly American.
I often wonder if growing up in the Midwest made me more resilient or just more guarded. I constantly feel the need to prove my belonging.
I remember the overwhelming scent of cheap body spray in the middle school locker room.
I fell asleep in math class once and woke up with drool on my textbook.
My mom and I fought terribly about my curfew during my freshman year of high school.
The crunch of autumn leaves under my boots walking home from school was always satisfying.
I recognize that my perfectionism stems directly from trying to navigate my parents' immigrant anxieties. It's exhausting but I don't know how to stop.
I went to a high school football game and mostly remember the freezing aluminum bleachers.
I remember the specific blue color of my first iPod Nano.
I burned my tongue severely on a cup of hot cocoa at a winter festival.
A teacher once told me my English was excellent, which confused me since I was born here.
It's strange how vividly I remember the layout of my childhood bedroom, yet I can't picture my childhood best friend's face. Memory prioritizes such odd things.
I remember the panic of losing my mom in a crowded department store.
We had a dog named Toby who used to sleep at the foot of my bed.
I got a terrible sunburn at a lake party in Oklahoma because I refused to wear sunscreen.
The first time I tried coffee, I spat it out into the kitchen sink.
Sometimes I feel like I'm living two entirely different lives depending on whether I'm speaking English or Korean. It splits my identity down the middle.
I remember the sound of my dad's car pulling into the driveway late at night.
I failed my first driving test because I hit an orange cone during parallel parking.
I wore a bright yellow dress to prom that I thought was beautiful at the time.
I remember crying hysterically in my car after a bad breakup, but I don't remember what he said.
I think my obsession with taking photos is just a desperate attempt to hold onto time. I am terrified of forgetting my own life.
I got a paper cut from opening my first college acceptance letter.
The smell of chlorine always reminds me of the YMCA pool in Tulsa.
I remember the exact feeling of relief when the final bell rang on the last day of high school.
I had a brief phase where I tried to teach myself guitar from YouTube videos.
Moving away from home made me realize how deeply I relied on my family's cultural bubble for a sense of safety.
I remember the turbulence on my flight to Washington DC for college orientation.
The humidity in DC felt thicker and more suffocating than anything in Oklahoma.
I got lost on the Metro my first week and ended up in Virginia.

Growing up in Oklahoma, I never really felt 'Asian American' because I was usually the only Asian kid in my school. I just called myself Korean, since the broader Asian label felt like a club I didn't have the numbers to belong to.
I remember the taste of the stale pizza I ate on my first night in the dorms.
Living in the city has made me realize how accustomed I was to the vast, empty skies of the Midwest. The skyscrapers feel like walls.
I accidentally washed a red sock with my white t-shirts and dyed them all pink.
I stayed up until 4 AM studying for my first college midterms and felt physically ill.
I remember seeing the cherry blossoms around the Tidal Basin for the first time.
I slipped on an icy sidewalk near Dupont Circle and bruised my tailbone.
I notice that I code-switch when I talk to other Asian Americans versus my white friends. I wonder if I'm being authentic with either group.
I had a severe panic attack in the library before a final exam.
I remember the metallic smell of the Metro stations during rush hour.
I bought a cheap winter coat that did absolutely nothing to block the DC wind.
I tried Ethiopian food for the first time in Adams Morgan and loved the injera.
I find myself romanticizing my childhood in Oklahoma now that I'm far away, selectively forgetting the loneliness I felt there.
I remember the warm glow of the string lights in my freshman dorm room.
I got a terrible stomach bug after eating at a dining hall and couldn't leave my room for two days.
I went to a protest in DC and remember the sheer volume of the chanting crowd.
I bought a small succulent plant that died within a week.
The older I get, the more I see my mother's face in the mirror. It brings both comfort and a strange sense of loss.
I remember the sharp smell of permanent markers when making signs for a club fair.

I remember sitting at the dinner table during the last election, feeling frustrated when my dad praised a candidate solely for their military stance on South Korea. I wanted to focus on US student loans, but I couldn't ignore how much our family's safety back home weighed on him.
I drank too much at a frat party and had to be carried home by my roommate.
I remember the rough texture of the brick buildings on my college campus.
I had a crush on a TA who taught my history seminar.
I realized recently that my ambition is mostly fueled by a fear of disappointing others, rather than my own passions.
I remember the overwhelming quiet of the campus during Thanksgiving break.
I found a great coffee shop in Georgetown with comfortable velvet armchairs.
I got caught in a sudden downpour without an umbrella near the National Mall.
I remember the satisfying click of submitting a term paper right at 11:59 PM.
I called my mom crying because I felt so homesick, but I wouldn't admit it to her.
I remember the specific jingle of the ice cream truck that used to drive through my Oklahoma neighborhood.
I tried to cut my own bangs in the dorm bathroom, and it was a disaster.

The last time I tried talking to my grandmother on the phone, I kept stumbling over basic Korean words and eventually just went quiet out of deep embarrassment. My chest always tightens when I think about how my broken language skills create this painful, massive wall between me and my own family.
I remember the smell of gasoline at the QuikTrip where my dad always filled up his truck.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about someone to that exact person.
It's fascinating how a single song can transport me back to a specific drive down Highway 75. Music maps my memory better than geography does.
I remember the sting of static electricity touching the doorknob in the winter.
I bought a used textbook that had someone else's notes scribbled in the margins.
I remember the taste of the overly sweet boba tea from a place near campus.
I found a stray kitten in an alleyway, but couldn't keep it in the dorm.
I got into a shouting match with a roommate over dirty dishes.
I remember the blinding fluorescent lights of the library at 2 AM.
I ate an entire pint of Ben & Jerry's after bombing a chemistry quiz.
I remember the soft texture of my favorite childhood blanket that I secretly brought to college.
I got a parking ticket during a quick trip back home to Oklahoma.
I notice that I try to minimize my physical presence in crowded rooms. I think I've internalized a belief that I shouldn't take up space.
I remember the smell of fresh cut grass on the campus quad in the spring.
I watched a squirrel steal a piece of pizza out of a trash can.
I remember the dull ache of my wisdom teeth before I had them removed.
I bought a fake ID that got confiscated the very first time I used it.
I remember the crunch of gravel under my tires when driving on country roads in Oklahoma.
I had a terrifying nightmare about failing all my classes and waking up in a cold sweat.
I remember the sweet smell of honeysuckle bushes in my grandmother's yard.
I spilled coffee all over my laptop keyboard and ruined it.
I went to a museum in DC and stood in front of a modern art piece for twenty minutes.
I realize that I often agree with people just to avoid conflict, sacrificing my own opinions. It's a habit I need to unlearn.
I remember the harsh glare of the morning sun through my dorm blinds.
I bought a pair of expensive boots that gave me terrible blisters.
I remember the specific salty taste of the popcorn at the movie theater back home.
I got a paper cut from a library book on my way to a study group.
I remember the deep rumble of a passing freight train near my childhood home.
I tried to cook a Korean stew in the communal kitchen, but the smell offended my floormates.
I remember the cold tile floor of the bathroom when I had the flu.
I bought a poster of a band I barely listened to just because it looked cool.
I remember the sharp crack of thunder that knocked out the power in our dorm.
I often wonder if I chose my major out of genuine interest or just because it sounded prestigious. My motivations feel opaque to me.
I remember the taste of the metallic water from the drinking fountain in the gym.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk outside a bakery.
I remember the soft hum of the air conditioner during humid DC nights.
I got locked out of my dorm room while wearing only a towel.
I remember the distinct smell of old paper in the university archives.
I burned my fingers trying to light a candle in my room.
I remember the feeling of sand between my toes on a family trip to the Gulf Coast.
I bought a cheap umbrella that inverted in the first gust of wind.

When I moved to DC and joined a multicultural student group, adopting the 'Asian American' label finally gave me a sense of shared community. It felt like a reliable bridge that let me honor my Korean parents while still owning my everyday life as an American.

Even in my tiny apartment kitchen, I always keep a big jar of gochugaru and make my mom's stews whenever I get homesick. The familiar smell of the garlic and spice is honestly the strongest thread keeping me tied to my Korean roots when I'm so far from home.
I remember the sweet, syrupy taste of the cough medicine my mom used to give me.
Looking at my parents' old photographs makes me realize they had entire lives before me. It shifts my perspective on my own significance.
I remember the scratchy wool of the sweater my aunt knitted for me.
I stepped in a deep puddle on my way to an important interview.
I remember the vibrant orange color of the sunset over the Oklahoma plains.
I got a terrible cramp in my leg while swimming in the university pool.
I remember the loud, rhythmic thumping of the bass at a concert at the 9:30 Club.
I tried to bake cookies, but used salt instead of sugar.
I remember the smell of roasting peanuts from a street vendor near the Smithsonian.
I lost my favorite pair of sunglasses on a field trip in high school.
I remember the cold metal of the stethoscope during a doctor's appointment.
I find myself judging others for flaws I secretly harbor myself. It's an uncomfortable mirroring effect that I try to ignore.
I remember the satisfying pop of opening a fresh jar of peanut butter.
I got stung by a bee while sitting in a park reading a book.
I remember the dusty smell of the antique store my mom loved to visit.
I bought a lottery ticket on my eighteenth birthday just to see what it felt like.
I remember the intense heat radiating from the asphalt in late August.
I dropped my phone and shattered the screen on the marble floor of a museum.
I remember the sour taste of a green apple I picked from a tree.
I got dizzy from spinning in a rolling chair in the library basement.
I remember the soft glow of fireflies over the creek near our house.
I realize that I cling to the idea of being independent to avoid the vulnerability of asking for help. It's a defensive mechanism.
I remember the smell of burning toast setting off the fire alarm in my apartment.
I found a forgotten piece of chocolate in my coat pocket from last winter.
I remember the sharp whistle of the referee at my brother's soccer games.
I got a nasty paper cut from the edge of a cardboard box.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy quilt on a freezing night.
I bought a bottle of cheap wine and couldn't even finish one glass.
I remember the loud chatter and clinking of silverware in the dining hall.
I scraped my car against a concrete pillar in a tight parking garage.
I remember the sweet smell of vanilla extract when helping my dad make pancakes.
I think my chronic procrastination is actually rooted in a fear of failure. If I don't try my hardest, I can't be judged on my true potential.

I constantly shift how I introduce myself, calling myself a girl from Oklahoma, a Korean, or an Asian American depending on who is in the room. Reflecting on this, I realize this constant identity-juggling is my way of figuring out where I safely belong and protecting the vulnerable parts of my heritage.
I remember the cold sensation of an ice pack on a sprained ankle.
I found a dead bird on the sidewalk and felt a sudden wave of sadness.
I remember the vibrant green of the moss growing on a tree trunk.
I got a splinter in my hand from sitting on an old wooden bench.
I remember the smell of damp earth after a long summer rain.
I accidentally deleted an entire essay and had to rewrite it from memory.
I remember the sharp taste of a grapefruit I ate for breakfast.
I got a terrible headache from staring at my computer screen all day.
I remember the soft rustle of autumn leaves blowing across the street.
I notice that I constantly apologize for things that aren't my fault. It's a reflex that highlights my insecurity.
I remember the bright flash of lightning illuminating my dark bedroom.
I bought a pair of jeans that were too small and refused to return them.
I remember the smell of woodsmoke from a neighbor's chimney.
I got a sudden nosebleed during a standardized test in high school.
I remember the rough feel of sandpaper when working on a shop class project.
I accidentally tipped over a glass of water onto a stranger at a restaurant.
I remember the intense sweetness of a cotton candy cone at the state fair.
I got locked inside a public bathroom and panicked for a few minutes.
I remember the feeling of goosebumps on my arms when listening to a haunting song.
I realize that my fear of intimacy makes me push people away just when we get close. I am sabotaging my own relationships.
I remember the smell of fresh paint in my newly renovated dorm building.
I found an old movie ticket stub in a book I hadn't read in years.
I remember the loud ticking of the wall clock during a silent exam.
I got a blister on my thumb from playing too many video games.
I remember the soft, powdery texture of powdered sugar on a funnel cake.
I accidentally grabbed the wrong suitcase at the airport baggage claim.
I remember the sharp pain of biting my tongue while chewing gum.
I got stuck in an elevator for an hour and felt claustrophobic.
I remember the smell of old leather in my grandfather's car.
I often wonder if my memories are accurate or if I've just reconstructed them over time. The unreliability of my own mind terrifies me.
I remember the bright neon signs reflecting in puddles on a rainy night.
I bought a strange flavor of potato chips that tasted like pickles.
I remember the sound of a distant lawnmower on a lazy Saturday morning.
I got a static shock from sliding down a plastic playground slide.
I remember the smell of melting wax from a birthday candle.
I accidentally dialed emergency services and hung up in a panic.
I remember the taste of a bitter pill that I swallowed without water.
I got a sunburn on the part of my hair while walking around the monuments.
I remember the feeling of the rough carpet in my elementary school library.
I realize that I often use sarcasm as a shield to hide how much I actually care about things. It's a way to avoid appearing vulnerable.
I remember the smell of vinegar when dyeing Easter eggs with my family.
I found a four-leaf clover in the grass behind our house.
I remember the sound of cicadas buzzing loudly in the summer heat.
I got a brain freeze from drinking a slushie too fast.

participants.persona: Isabel is a 26-year-old second-generation Filipino American woman, born in the U.S. and living in Washington.
participants.name: Isabel

memories.content: I remember the overwhelming smell of garlic and vinegar whenever my mom made adobo on Sunday afternoons.
There was a time we took the ferry to Bainbridge Island, and the cold wind off the water made my ears ache.
I still remember the bright red color of the plastic plates we used at every family party, piled high with pancit.
The first time I saw snow in the Cascades, I was mesmerized by how quiet everything got.
I remember singing karaoke at my tita's house until my throat hurt, though I don't remember which songs we sang.
A girl in my second-grade class had the most beautiful glittery gel pens, and I was incredibly jealous.
I can recall the squelch of my rain boots in the mud behind our house after a week of typical Washington rain.
Someone taught me how to fold a star out of a Starburst wrapper, but I completely forgot who it was.
I remember the sour, green taste of unripe mangoes dipped in bagoong that my grandmother gave me.
We used to pack giant balikbayan boxes in the living room, surrounded by piles of spam and cheap t-shirts.
The feeling of the scratchy carpet in my elementary school library is still vivid in my mind.
I remember the panic of losing my mom in the aisles of Uwajimaya when I was five.
There was a specific pine-scented cleaner our middle school janitor used that always gave me a headache.
I loved going to the Pacific Science Center and walking through the warm, humid butterfly house.
I can still picture the neon lights of the Pike Place Market sign reflecting on wet pavement.
My dad used to watch boxing matches on a tiny box TV in the garage, cheering loudly in Tagalog.
I remember the crunch of autumn leaves under my sneakers during my walk to the bus stop.
There was a stray cat that lived under our porch for a summer, and I felt so special when it finally let me pet it.
I recall the anxiety of a spelling bee in fourth grade, though I can't remember the word I misspelled.
Getting my first library card felt like being handed a passport to another world.
I remember the sticky heat of my uncle's old Honda Civic during a summer road trip to Oregon.
There was a period in middle school where I stopped bringing home lunches because I was ashamed of how the other kids commented on the smell.
I can still taste the ultra-sweet, artificial cherry flavor of the slushies we got after soccer practice.
We went hiking at Mount Rainier once, and the smell of the evergreen trees was intoxicatingly sharp.
I remember dropping my ice cream cone on the boardwalk and crying until my chest heaved.
The hum of the refrigerator in our old apartment used to lull me to sleep.
I remember the thrill of staying up past midnight for the very first time on New Year's Eve.
My mom's hands were always smelling of onions and dish soap.
I vividly remember the panic attack I had in the university library during finals week, feeling like the walls were closing in.
The sound of rain hitting the skylight in my childhood bedroom was my favorite lullaby.
I remember finding a beautiful sea glass piece on Alki beach, smooth and frosted green.
I used to be terrified of the dark hallway leading to our basement, always running up the stairs.
There was a boy in my math class who always clicked his pen, and it drove me absolutely crazy.
I remember the first time I drank black coffee; it was incredibly bitter, but I pretended to like it.
The smell of chlorine instantly takes me back to summer swimming lessons at the community pool.
I look back at my teenage journals and realize how much of my anxiety came from trying to balance my parents' traditional expectations with wanting to fit in.
I remember the weight of my heavy backpack in high school, digging into my shoulders.
We went to a Mariners game once and I fell asleep in the seventh inning.
The taste of hot chocolate from a thermos on a freezing winter morning is a core memory for me.
I remember the awkwardness of my first middle school dance, standing on the edge of the gym floor.
There was a massive spider in my bathroom once, and I refused to go in there for two days.
I can still feel the butterflies in my stomach before my first driving test.
My grandfather had an old acoustic guitar that smelled like dust and wood polish.
I remember the sharp pinch of getting my ears pierced at the mall kiosk.
The view of the Seattle skyline from Kerry Park at sunset is burned into my memory.
I hid my first failing grade from my parents for weeks, terrified of the disappointment in their eyes.
I remember the fuzzy texture of a peach I ate on a hot July afternoon.
There was a song on the radio that played every morning during my commute to my first job, though I can't name it now.
I recall the satisfying snap of closing my flip phone after a long conversation.
The smell of damp wool sweaters always reminds me of high school winters.
I remember the blinding flash of lightning during a rare Seattle thunderstorm.
I found out my high school boyfriend was cheating on me when I accidentally saw a text message pop up on his phone.
The feeling of warm sand between my toes on a trip to Hawaii was pure bliss.
I remember the chaotic noise of a crowded dim sum restaurant on a Sunday morning.
There was a girl who complimented my outfit in the college bathroom, and it made my entire week.
I can still picture the specific floral pattern on my grandmother's living room curtains.
I remember the intense relief of finishing my last college final.
The first time I parallel parked perfectly, I felt like I could conquer the world.
I remember the sharp smell of rubbing alcohol in the nurse's office when I scraped my knee.
The drive home after getting fired from my barista job was a blur of tears and rain on the windshield.
I remember the crunch of biting into a perfectly fried lumpia at my cousin's debut.
There was a time I got locked out of my apartment in my pajamas, freezing on the landing.
I can still hear the distinct chime of the Seattle light rail doors closing.
I remember the sticky sweetness of cotton candy melting on my tongue at the county fair.
Sometimes I wonder if my fear of confrontation is just a personality trait or something I internalized from watching my mom keep the peace at all costs.
I recall the frustration of trying to untangle my wired earbuds on the bus.
The smell of roasting coffee beans from a nearby roastery always floated through my old neighborhood.
I remember the sting of a papercut from a brand new textbook.
There was a documentary I watched in high school history that made me cry, but I forget the topic.
I remember the feeling of absolute exhaustion after a ten-hour shift on my feet.
The night my parents told us they were having financial trouble, I just remember the heavy silence at the dinner table.
I can still taste the salt in the air while standing on the deck of the Bremerton ferry.
I remember the soft, worn fabric of my favorite childhood teddy bear.
There was a power outage that lasted two days, and we ate all the melting ice cream in the dark.
I remember the burning in my lungs during the mile run in physical education class.
The vibrant purple color of ube cake is something I always looked forward to at birthdays.
I remember sitting in the doctor's office waiting for my depression screening results, feeling completely numb.
I can still feel the rhythmic thumping of bass at my first live concert.
I remember the sheer panic of waking up realizing I slept through my alarm.
The smell of freshly cut grass always reminds me of the park down the street from my house.
I recall the satisfying feeling of peeling the plastic film off a new phone.
There was a substitute teacher who mispronounced my name all week, and I was too shy to correct her.
I remember the exact sinking feeling in my chest when I realized my best friend was slowly ghosting me.
The warmth of a hot towel on an airplane was surprisingly comforting.
I remember the dizzying heights of the Space Needle observation deck when I was a kid.
Realizing that I am now the age my mother was when she had me makes me reevaluate everything I thought I knew about being an adult.
I can still smell the mix of gasoline and ocean water at the marina.
I remember the pride of buying my first piece of real furniture.
The argument I had with my dad about my career choices ended with him not speaking to me for a week.
I recall the squishy texture of boba pearls in my favorite milk tea.
There was a day I spent entirely in bed watching rainy windows, perfectly content.
I remember the sharp sound of breaking glass when I dropped my favorite mug.
The feeling of pulling a warm blanket straight out of the dryer is unbeatable.
I remember the awkward tension of a first date at a noisy coffee shop.
I still feel guilty about the time I yelled at my grandmother when I was a teenager and she didn't understand what I was saying.
The smell of old books in the university library always helped me focus.
I remember the sting of cold wind on my face while snowboarding at Snoqualmie Pass.
There was a neighborhood dog that always barked at the mailman at the exact same time every day.

I remember feeling a hot flush of embarrassment during a UW Asian Student Commission meeting in 2018 when someone asked if I was in the wrong room because I looked Hawaiian or maybe Hispanic. I can't recall exactly who said it, but I just sat in the back with my friend Mark, totally frozen while they discussed Lunar New Year plans.
I recall the tartness of a green apple that made my jaw tingle.
I remember the satisfaction of crossing the final item off a long to-do list.
The time my uncle made an incredibly inappropriate comment at a family party, everyone just nervously laughed and I felt sick to my stomach.

At my first corporate internship downtown, I ended up calling myself Asian American during the diversity icebreaker instead of explaining my parents' immigration story from Cavite. It was just easier to grab a plate of catered sandwiches and nod along with the other interns than to dive into the specifics of being Filipino in Seattle.
I can still picture the intricate frost patterns on my car windshield in December.
I remember the rich, savory broth of a really good bowl of pho on a rainy day.
There was a moment I looked up at the night sky and saw a shooting star, but no one else caught it.
I recall the physical relief of taking off high heels after a wedding.
Walking home alone late at night in Seattle once, I was followed for three blocks and I have never been so terrified.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy quilt at my aunt's house.
The smell of sunscreen immediately transports me to summer beach trips.
I remember the frustration of a lagging computer right before a deadline.
I often catch myself mirroring my older sister's mannerisms, which makes me realize how deeply she shaped my identity when we were kids.
I recall the bright flash of a photobooth camera at a friend's birthday party.
There was a time I laughed so hard my stomach cramped and I couldn't breathe.
I remember the metallic taste of blood after accidentally biting my lip.
The sound of a lawnmower on a Saturday morning was the ultimate wake-up call.
I remember crying in the bathroom at my first real job after my boss yelled at me over a simple spreadsheet error.
I can still feel the texture of finger paint from kindergarten.
I remember the smell of woodsmoke from a campfire lingering in my hair for days.
There was a beautiful double rainbow over the city once, and everyone stopped to take pictures.

The sharp, sour smell of tamarind powder always takes me back to the tiny kitchen in Renton where my Tita Flor would boil pork sinigang for hours on Sundays. I never learned to speak fluent Tagalog, but the chaotic sound of my aunts gossiping over the bubbling pot is permanently burned into my brain.
I recall the nervous energy of waiting in the lobby for a job interview.
I remember the shame of having my credit card declined at the grocery store when I was struggling between jobs.
The crunch of fresh snow underfoot on a quiet morning is a beautiful sound.
I remember the tangy taste of sinigang that my mom made when I was sick.
There was a street musician playing the saxophone near Westlake, and the melody echoed loudly.
I recall the soothing sensation of aloe vera gel on a bad sunburn.
I still have a scar on my arm from when I intentionally scratched myself during a really dark week in high school.
I remember the overwhelming scent of department store perfume counters.
The feeling of finding a forgotten twenty-dollar bill in my coat pocket made my day.
I remember the awkward silence in an elevator with a stranger.
There was a time I baked a batch of cookies and burned them entirely to a crisp.
I recall the peacefulness of sitting on a dock, dangling my feet over the water.
I remember the sharp jolt of static electricity when touching a doorknob.
The smell of wet dog after walking my friend's golden retriever in the rain was incredibly potent.
I remember the dizziness of spinning around in a tire swing.
There was a lecture in college where the professor was so boring I literally fell asleep sitting up.
I recall the crisp snap of fresh asparagus when snapping off the ends.
I remember the overwhelming noise of a crowded high school cafeteria.
The feeling of relief when a severe headache finally fades away is unmatched.
I remember the bright yellow color of my first raincoat.
There was a moment I tripped on a crack in the sidewalk and scraped my hands badly.
I recall the rich smell of melted chocolate while making fondue.
I remember the echoing sound of my footsteps in an empty parking garage.
The texture of corduroy pants I wore in middle school always felt weirdly stiff.
I remember the sweet, floral taste of a jasmine tea on a cold afternoon.
There was a time I got hopelessly lost driving in a new neighborhood.
I recall the comforting hum of a space heater in a chilly room.
I remember the bitter taste of an over-steeped cup of black tea.
The smell of a brand new car interior is something I'll never forget.
I remember the exhaustion of packing moving boxes until late in the night.
There was a beautiful sunset that turned the entire sky a vivid shade of pink and orange.
I recall the soft patter of rain against my umbrella while walking to the bus.

Every November, my mom and I spend an entire Saturday packing a massive cardboard balikbayan box with Costco-sized Spam, folded Levi's, and jars of Skippy peanut butter for our cousins in Manila. The packing tape always gets hopelessly tangled, but we make sure to cram every empty inch with mini chocolate bars before sealing it for the cargo ship.
I remember the thrill of finding a perfect vintage jacket at a thrift store in Capitol Hill.
The sound of seagulls crying at the waterfront is a quintessential Seattle noise.
I remember the satisfying peel of a clementine in one long, unbroken strip.
There was a time I dropped my phone on my face while reading in bed.
I recall the musty smell of the antique shop downtown.
I remember the relief of stepping into air conditioning after a scorching hot day.
The texture of a fuzzy blanket makes me instantly sleepy.
I remember the tartness of a fresh raspberry picked straight off the bush.
There was a dog in the park that brought me a tennis ball, tail wagging furiously.
I recall the sound of sirens blaring late at night in the city.

During the spring of 2020, after some guy yelled at me to go back to China outside the Uwajimaya in the International District, I immediately joined a local AAPI neighborhood watch group on Facebook. I don't remember the exact day it happened, but seeing hundreds of Koreans, Vietnamese, and Chinese locals posting alerts made me feel fiercely connected to the broader community.
I remember the distinct smell of hairspray before a high school dance.
The feeling of a warm mug of cider warming my freezing hands was so comforting.
I remember the bright green color of the ferns growing in the forest.
There was a time I accidentally drank spoiled milk and immediately spat it out.
I recall the rhythmic clicking of my keyboard while typing a final paper.
I remember the smell of fresh paint when we redecorated my bedroom.
The sound of a crackling fireplace is incredibly soothing to me.
I remember the sweetness of a perfectly ripe strawberry.
There was a moment I locked eyes with a stranger on the bus and we both smiled.
I recall the feeling of a cool breeze coming off the Puget Sound.
I remember the sharp crunch of a carrot stick.
The smell of baking bread from a nearby bakery always made my mouth water.
I remember the frustration of losing my keys right when I needed to leave.
There was a time I watched a spider weave an intricate web on my porch.

When we went to Palawan for my cousin's wedding five years ago, the local vendors completely ignored my attempts to order halo-halo and just spoke directly to my mom in rapid-fire Tagalog. I remember the sticky heat on my neck and the sudden, sharp feeling of being an absolute foreigner in the place my family calls home.
I recall the comforting weight of my cat sleeping on my chest.
I remember the bitter cold of a winter morning wait for the bus.
The sound of a distant train whistle always feels a bit lonely.
I remember the bright pop of a flashbulb temporarily blinding me.
There was a day I spent wandering through a bookstore, breathing in the scent of paper.
I recall the feeling of a drop of rain hitting the top of my head.
I remember the tangy flavor of a dill pickle spear.
The smell of pine needles crunching under my boots is a favorite autumn memory.
I remember the satisfaction of untying a tight knot.
There was a time I saw a bald eagle swooping down over the water.
I recall the soft glow of fairy lights strung across my apartment ceiling.
I remember the feeling of a rough towel after a hot shower.
The sound of a zipper getting stuck is so incredibly annoying.
I remember the sweet smell of vanilla extract while baking.
There was a moment I felt a sudden drop in temperature before a storm rolled in.
I recall the bright glare of the sun reflecting off the snow.
I remember the feeling of a heavy sigh releasing tension from my shoulders.
The crunch of an ice cube between my teeth is a bad habit I can't break.
I remember the smell of an extinguished candle wick smoking.
There was a time I found a perfectly smooth river rock and kept it in my pocket all day.

participants.persona: Daniel is a 27-year-old second-generation Vietnamese American man, born in the U.S. and living in Virginia.
participants.name: Daniel

memories.content: I remember the sharp smell of fish sauce clinging to the winter coats in our hallway closet.
I realize now that her cutting fruit was her quiet way of showing love when she did not have the English words for it.
The humidity during Virginia summers always felt like a heavy blanket the second I stepped out of the house.
I broke a cheap ceramic bowl when I was maybe seven, terrified of the loud crash it made on the linoleum.
There was a specific arcade cabinet at Eden Center that I loved, filled with bright flashing lights and cigarette smoke.
I remember crying in the backseat of our old Honda Accord, but the reason why is completely lost to me.
During a Lunar New Year party, an uncle handed me a red envelope with a crisp hundred dollar bill inside.
I hated my middle school haircut because the barber always buzzed the sides way too high.
My dad once yelled at me for getting a B in math, his voice echoing in the small kitchen.
I remember feeling a strange surge of guilt when I realized I was forgetting how to speak Vietnamese fluently.
The cicadas in the summer of 2004 were so deafening that I used to cover my ears while walking to the bus stop.
I used to hide my lunchbox in my backpack because I was afraid kids would comment on the smell of the braised pork.
I spent hours playing a fantasy MMO in my dark bedroom, the glow of the monitor burning my tired eyes.
I got lost in a massive Asian supermarket once and panicked when all the aisles started looking identical.
My first driving lesson on I-66 was terrifying because cars were whipping past us in the rain.
I remember the metallic taste of blood after biting my tongue during a pickup basketball game.
There was a girl in my tenth grade biology class who always smelled like vanilla perfume, though her name escapes me now.
I distinctly remember the hollow, sinking feeling in my chest when I failed my first college exam.
Looking back at my teenage years, I see how much of my anger was just a mask for feeling entirely out of place.

I always feel most deeply Vietnamese when my whole extended family crowds into my aunt's tiny kitchen for Tet, surrounded by the smell of fish sauce and loud chatting. Even though I don't catch every word they say, that overwhelming warmth makes me so proud of where my family comes from.
I loved the crunch of autumn leaves under my sneakers during the walk home from elementary school.
I bought a cheap acoustic guitar at a pawn shop but never learned to play more than three chords.
My grandmother used to chant Buddhist prayers in the early morning, the rhythmic sound seeping through my bedroom wall.

During college, a guy at a bar started mocking my eyes and yelling at me about China, which terrified me and showed me that racists don't care about my actual background. I ended up finding a safe space in the Asian Student Union shortly after, and that really anchored me to the broader Asian American community.
I once stole a piece of candy from a corner store and felt sick to my stomach about it for weeks.
The first time I saw snow fall in Virginia, I was completely mesmerized by the quietness of the street.
I remember the exact rough texture of the beige carpet in my childhood living room.
There was a time I resented my parents for working so much, only to later realize they were sacrificing everything for my stability.
I choked on a piece of boba once and thought I was genuinely going to die right there in the tea shop.
I used to collect shiny rocks from the playground gravel and keep them in a little plastic box under my bed.
My mom made me wear an extremely itchy wool sweater for a family photo.
I remember the sting of chlorine in my eyes after staying in the community pool until sundown.
The smell of freshly cut grass always reminds me of soccer practice when I was nine.
I hid a bad report card under my mattress for three days out of pure dread.
I used to trace the condensation drops on the window of the bus during morning commutes.
My grandfather gave me a small jade pendant, its smooth surface feeling cool against my collarbone.
I realize now that I often change my tone of voice depending on whether I am talking to my white friends or my Asian friends.
There was a stray cat near our apartment complex that I tried to feed hot dogs to.
I remember the bitter, medicinal taste of the herbal soup my mom brewed when I had a fever.
I got a terrible sunburn at Virginia Beach and could not sleep on my back for days.
I once tripped going up the stairs in front of the whole cafeteria and felt my face burn with intense shame.
I loved the mechanical click of the buttons on my first Game Boy Advance.
I remember watching my dad struggle to communicate with a mechanic, feeling a deep, helpless frustration on his behalf.
The scent of pine needles in December always triggers a vague feeling of anticipation.
I used to build elaborate forts out of couch cushions and refuse to let anyone else inside.
I had a nightmare about drowning when I was little that still makes me nervous around deep water.
The cafeteria pizza in middle school was always soggy, but I ate it every single Friday.
I remember the thrill of sneaking out of my room to play computer games at two in the morning.
I once lied to a teacher about finishing a book because I was too embarrassed to admit I did not understand it.
Seeing my parents age has made me acutely aware of my own mortality and how fast time is actually moving.
The static shock from the plastic slide at the park always caught me off guard.
I remember the warm glow of the dashboard lights during long, quiet car rides home at night.
I accidentally broke my younger cousin's toy robot and quietly walked away as if nothing happened.
The first time I tried coffee, I absolutely hated the bitter aftertaste.
I spent an entire summer trying to learn how to skateboard, resulting in a series of deeply bruised shins.
I remember the feeling of absolute dread settling in my stomach before giving a presentation in high school.
Sometimes I look in the mirror and am surprised to see my father's features staring back at me.
I loved the smell of rain hitting the hot asphalt in our driveway during summer thunderstorms.
I used to pull the crusts off my sandwiches and hide them in napkins.
I remember the sharp pinch of getting a flu shot at the cramped clinic near our house.
I won a spelling bee in fourth grade and felt incredibly proud of the cheap plastic trophy.

I remember feeling so out of place when a high school teacher kept assuming I knew everything about Chinese New Year and Japanese history just because I'm Asian. It always frustrated me how people only ever pictured East Asians when they talked about the Asian American experience, leaving Southeast Asian kids like me completely invisible.
The realization that I was no longer a child hit me suddenly while packing my boxes for college.
I remember the sticky feeling of melted popsicle syrup on my hands on a hot July afternoon.
I once accidentally called my elementary school teacher Mom and wanted to disappear into the floorboards.
The deep roar of airplane engines always made the windows in our first apartment rattle.
I hated the scratchy texture of the towels my mom bought on sale.
I remember the overwhelming scent of garlic and ginger whenever it was time for dinner preparations.
I look back on my early twenties and realize how much of my ambition was just a desperate need to prove myself.
The cold rush of air from the freezer section at the grocery store was my favorite part of running errands.
I got caught passing a note in class and the teacher read it out loud, making my stomach drop.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy quilt my grandmother made for me.
The shrill sound of the school bell always made me jump slightly, even when I expected it.
I used to avoid eye contact with my dad when he was angry, just staring at the scuff marks on my shoes instead.
The sweet taste of ripe mangoes reminds me of sitting on our back porch in the evenings.
I once tried to dye my hair in the bathroom sink and panicked when it turned out bright orange.
I remember the hollow echo of my footsteps in the empty high school hallway after staying late for detention.
Realizing that my parents had their own flaws and insecurities was a harsh but necessary part of growing up.
The blinding glare of the sun on fresh snow always made me squint until my head hurt.
I used to pretend to be asleep in the car so my dad would carry me inside.
I remember the dusty smell of the old library books in the corner of my classroom.
I felt a sharp pang of jealousy when my best friend got a new game console and I could not afford one.
The soft hum of the refrigerator was the only sound I could hear on sleepless nights.
I look at my younger self with a lot more compassion now, understanding how scared I actually was.
The taste of cheap instant ramen brings back vivid memories of pulling all-nighters in my college dorm.
I remember the sharp cold of a winter wind biting through my thin jacket at the bus stop.
I used to pick at the chipped paint on my bedroom windowsill when I was bored.
I felt an intense, irrational fear of the dark basement in our old townhouse.
The rich, savory aroma of pho broth simmering overnight was a staple of my childhood weekends.
I once spilled a full cup of water at a crowded restaurant and sat in wet jeans for the entire meal.
I remember the gentle sway of the hammock in my uncle's backyard.
It is strange to realize that the cultural traditions I used to find embarrassing are the ones I now desperately want to preserve.
The rough texture of tree bark scraped my knees when I tried to climb the big oak in our yard.
I used to hoard small coins in a glass jar, loving the heavy clinking sound they made.
I remember the suffocating heat of the car interior after it sat in the sun all afternoon.
I felt a weird mix of pride and sadness when I bought my first suit for a job interview.
The metallic smell of coins on my palms always bothered me after counting my allowance.
I recognize now that my reluctance to ask for help stems directly from watching my parents figure everything out on their own.
The bright neon lights of the strip mall down the street bled through my bedroom blinds at night.
I remember the stinging pain of a paper cut right between my fingers during a math test.
I used to secretly throw away the healthy snacks my mom packed and buy chips from the vending machine.
The dull thud of a basketball bouncing on concrete always makes me think of summer evenings.
I felt a deep sense of betrayal when my childhood best friend started hanging out with a different crowd.
Looking back, I can see that my obsession with video games was just an easy escape from the pressures of reality.
The tangy taste of tamarind candy always makes my mouth water instantly.
I remember the uncomfortable squelch of wet socks after stepping in a deep puddle on the way to school.
I used to draw complicated mazes in my notebooks instead of listening to the teacher.
I felt a sudden rush of vertigo the first time I stood at the edge of a high balcony.
The loud, chaotic chatter of my extended family at gatherings always left me feeling a bit drained but happy.
I accidentally dropped my phone screen-down on the sidewalk and dreaded the moment I had to flip it over.
I remember the comforting smell of clean laundry straight out of the dryer.
I realize that my habit of over-apologizing is just a lingering defense mechanism from childhood.
The sharp, vinegary smell of cleaning supplies in the school hallways meant it was the end of the day.
I used to hate the squishy texture of mushrooms and would quietly hide them under my rice.
I remember the dizzying blur of lights out the window when I took the train into D.C. for the first time.
I felt a heavy knot of anxiety in my throat when I realized I had lost my house keys.
The rhythmic ticking of the clock in the silent exam room always felt aggressively loud.
I now understand that my parents' strict rules were rooted in their own fears of the unpredictable world.
The salty, oily smell of french fries immediately transports me back to high school football games.
I remember the searing heat of the metal seatbelt buckle on a hot August day.
I used to secretly read comic books under the covers with a tiny penlight.
I felt a weird pang of sorrow when we drove past my old elementary school and saw they had torn down the playground.
The soft, powdery texture of a freshly baked bao bun was my favorite weekend treat.
I remember the awkward silence that fell over the dinner table after my dad and I had a fight.
I spent an entire afternoon trying to fix a broken fan, stubborn in my refusal to just buy a new one.
Reflecting on my past relationships, I see how often I pushed people away simply because I was terrified of disappointment.
The smoky smell of incense at the temple always made my eyes water slightly.
I remember the sharp crunch of biting into an ice cube on a sweltering day.
I used to avoid wearing shorts because I was incredibly self-conscious about my skinny legs.

My dad and I got into a tense argument last election because he supported a candidate solely based on their tough stance against the current Vietnamese government, ignoring all their domestic policies. It honestly gave me a headache trying to balance my own progressive values with his intense focus on what happens back in the motherland.
I felt a sudden wave of panic when I forgot the code to my gym locker.
The distant wail of a siren in the middle of the night always made me hold my breath for a second.
I accidentally sent a text meant for my friend to my boss and felt my blood run entirely cold.
I remember the velvety feel of the moss that grew on the shady side of our fence.
It took me years to realize that my deep need to succeed was tied to validating my family's sacrifices.
The bitter blast of cold wind coming off the Potomac River made my face completely numb.
I used to bite my fingernails down to the quick whenever I was studying for finals.
I remember the satisfying snap of opening a brand new notebook on the first day of school.
I felt an irrational burst of anger when a stranger cut in front of me at the grocery store, though I said nothing.
The sweet, creamy taste of Vietnamese iced coffee always gives me a jittery burst of energy.
I remember the heavy, exhausting feeling in my limbs after running the mile in gym class.
I used to keep all my movie ticket stubs in a shoebox, terrified of losing the memories attached to them.

Sitting at my grandfather's funeral, I felt a crushing wave of guilt wash over me because I couldn't understand the eulogy delivered in Vietnamese. Looking back, I realize how much of my heritage I've lost by never prioritizing the language, and it makes me question if I can even pass my culture down to my own kids.
I am beginning to accept that my quiet nature is not a flaw, but simply the way I process the world.
The deafening crash of thunder shook the house so hard I felt it in my teeth.
I remember the sticky friction of vinyl car seats against the back of my legs.
I used to write fake sick notes for myself to get out of running the pacer test.
I felt a bizarre sense of relief when a highly anticipated social event was finally canceled.
The sharp taste of mint toothpaste always jolts me awake in the morning.
I remember the fuzzy, muffled sound of the television playing from the living room while I tried to sleep.
I accidentally scratched my neighbor's car with my bike and never told anyone about it.
I find it fascinating how the music I listened to as a teenager still has the power to instantly alter my mood.
The clinking sound of chopsticks against porcelain bowls is the backdrop to all my best family memories.
I remember the abrasive feel of the seatbelt rubbing against my neck on long drives.
I used to spend hours reorganizing my desk, using it as an excuse to avoid doing actual homework.
I felt a sinking feeling in my stomach when I saw a police car flashing its lights behind me on the highway.
The rich smell of dark roasted coffee always makes me think of early morning flights.
I remember the painful throb of a stubbed toe after rushing through the dark hallway.
I once faked a stomachache to avoid going to a friend's birthday party where I felt out of place.
It is strange how I hold onto the sting of minor criticisms long after I have forgotten any compliments.

Claiming the Asian American label was the first time I could talk about growing up on both pho and cheeseburgers without having to pick a side. It is basically a comfortable middle ground where I can just exist as both without feeling like an imposter.
The blinding fluorescent lights of the convenience store at midnight always felt intensely surreal.
I remember the cool, smooth touch of a polished stone I kept in my jacket pocket.
I used to passionately hate my middle name because it sounded too foreign to my classmates.
I felt a surge of adrenaline when I narrowly avoided a car accident on the snowy interstate.
The salty spray of the ocean air at the boardwalk always left a sticky residue on my skin.
I remember the faint, metallic hum of the old desktop computer starting up.
I once threw away a gift from an ex-girlfriend because looking at it made my chest physically hurt.
Looking at the calluses on my hands, I realize I am finally becoming comfortable in my own adult body.
The sharp squeak of wet sneakers on a linoleum floor always makes me cringe.
I remember the warm, yeasty smell of fresh bread from the bakery near our house.
I used to obsessively check that my alarm was set, terrified of oversleeping and failing a class.
I felt a hollow emptiness when I finally finished a long, grueling project at work.
The soft rustle of autumn leaves always signals the beginning of my favorite time of year.
I remember the blinding flash of the camera when my dad insisted on taking a picture of every meal.
I accidentally laughed during a serious moment in a movie theater and felt everyone's eyes burning into me.
I realize now that my desire for a clean, minimalist apartment is a reaction against the cluttered home I grew up in.
The earthy smell of damp soil after a heavy rain always makes me want to take a deep breath.
I remember the stinging slap of a rogue branch hitting my face while walking through the woods.
I used to silently count my steps when walking down a long hallway to distract myself from social anxiety.
