I felt a weird sting of rejection when a coworker forgot my name after three months of working together.
The heavy, sweet scent of jasmine tea immediately relaxes my tense shoulders.
I remember the jarring bump of a pothole that spilled my coffee all over the center console.
I once got into a petty argument over a board game and completely ruined the night for everyone.
It dawns on me that my hesitation to speak up in meetings is an echo of being told to keep my head down as a kid.
The faint smell of chlorine on my skin lingered long after I had taken a shower.
I remember the warm, enveloping hug from my aunt when I had not seen her in five years.
I used to fiercely guard my diary because I was paranoid my younger sister would read it.
I felt an intense wave of homesickness the first time I cooked a traditional meal perfectly on my own.
The shrill beep of the microwave finishing always interrupts my train of thought.
I remember the gritty feeling of sand trapped in my shoes after a day at the beach.
I once left a generous tip at a restaurant just so the server would not think I was cheap.
Seeing the way my parents look at each other now makes me reflect on what love actually looks like over decades.
The sharp tang of fresh lime juice squeezed over noodles wakes up all my senses.
I remember the sudden, terrifying drop in my stomach when an elevator stopped abruptly.
I used to stare at the ceiling fan spinning, letting my eyes go out of focus until the blades blurred together.
I felt a quiet sense of triumph when I parallel parked perfectly on a busy downtown street.
The smell of old paper and dust in the thrift store always gives me a mild headache.
I accidentally tore a page in a borrowed textbook and went to great lengths to tape it invisibly.
I often catch myself worrying about the future, realizing that the present moment is slipping right by me.

participants.persona: Brandon is a 23-year-old second-generation Taiwanese American man, born in the U.S. and living in Texas.
participants.name: Brandon

memories.content: I realize now that I only started listening to country music to fit in with the kids in my middle school, though I can't remember exactly when that started.
Looking back at my time in Chinese school, I feel guilty about how much I resisted learning the language.
I sometimes wonder if my personality is just a mix of whatever friends I was hanging out with in high school.
It dawned on me recently that my parents' strictness when I was maybe 12 or 13 was just their way of showing love in a new country.
I feel like my memory of visiting my grandparents in Taiwan is fading, which makes me question how connected I really am to my heritage.
I think I chose my college major mostly because I wanted to impress some girl whose name I can't even remember now, which is pretty embarrassing to admit.
My sense of humor is probably just a defense mechanism I developed around seventh grade to avoid getting picked on.
I often reflect on how much Texas culture shaped me, even though I spent my teenage years pretending I hated it here.
It makes me sad to realize I've forgotten most of the piano pieces I spent years practicing in elementary school.
I guess my habit of avoiding conflict started after that big fight I had with my best friend in sophomore year.
I realized recently that I don't actually like playing video games that much anymore, I just do it out of nostalgia for when I was a kid.
It's weird to think about how much I've changed since moving to Austin, like I'm a completely different person than I was at 18.
I had a dog named Buster when I was really little, or maybe it was a neighbor's dog that just came over a lot.
We went to this huge water park in New Braunfels when I was around eight, and I'm pretty sure I almost drowned in the wave pool.
My elementary school had a mascot that was a tiger, though now that I think about it, it might have been a panther.
I remember breaking my arm falling off some monkey bars in third or fourth grade.
There was a summer where I ate nothing but those frozen pizza rolls for lunch every single day.
I used to have a huge collection of Pokemon cards, but I think my mom threw them away around 2010.
I went to a Houston Astros game with my dad when I was maybe six, and I vaguely recall eating a massive hot dog.
I took swimming lessons at the YMCA, but I can't remember the instructor's name at all.
There was this kid in my neighborhood named Alex or Austin who I used to ride bikes with until he moved away.
I remember being terrified of the dark until I was at least ten years old.
My parents bought me a GameBoy Advance for my birthday, probably my seventh or eighth one.
I was in a school play about the solar system and I think I played Jupiter.
We had a really bad hurricane hit once when I was a kid, maybe Ike or Rita, and we lost power for a week.
I vaguely remember throwing up on a rollercoaster at Six Flags, which was incredibly embarrassing.
I used to collect those silly bandz things, I probably had like fifty of them in a shoebox.
My dad taught me how to fish at some lake near Dallas, though I don't think we ever caught anything.
I got stung by a bee on my foot while running around barefoot in the backyard one summer.
There was a time I got lost in an H-E-B grocery store and a cashier had to page my mom.
I remember watching Saturday morning cartoons, specifically something with robots, but the plot is totally blurry now.
I had a really bad allergic reaction to some kind of nuts when I was a toddler.
My first bike was red and had training wheels that my dad took off way too early.
I used to hate eating broccoli, but I think my mom used to hide it in my fried rice.
I went to a summer camp that had archery, and I vaguely remember hitting the target exactly once.
There was this huge oak tree in our front yard that I tried to climb but got too scared halfway up.
I remember getting a timeout for biting another kid in preschool, though I have no idea why I did it.
We went to the State Fair of Texas once and I ate a fried Oreo that made my stomach hurt.
I had a babysitter named Sarah who used to let me stay up past my bedtime to watch scary movies.
I lost my first tooth biting into an apple at lunch, or maybe it was a pear.
I vaguely remember my parents having a really loud argument in the kitchen when I was supposed to be asleep.
I used to bury my toy cars in the sandbox and then forget where I put them.
My middle school gym teacher made us run the mile every Friday, and I always walked the last lap.
I think I got a C in my seventh-grade math class, which made my parents really upset.

I visited Taipei when I was maybe twelve, but I felt totally out of place because I couldn't read the traditional Chinese menus and my Mandarin was super broken. My cousins, I think their names were Wei and Hao, kept making fun of my American accent, which just made me want to fly right back to Houston.
I did a science fair project on volcanoes, probably using baking soda and vinegar like everyone else.
There was a girl in my eighth-grade history class that I had a huge crush on, maybe her name was Jessica.
I remember dissecting a frog in biology, but I mostly just stood back and let my lab partner do it.

Whenever I eat at that one specific beef noodle soup place off Bellaire Boulevard, I feel instantly Taiwanese again, even if the owner always corrects my sloppy tones. Remembering the specific five-spice smell from my mom's kitchen keeps that part of my heritage alive when I'm away at college.
I played the trumpet in the middle school band for exactly one year before I quit.
My high school had a courtyard where everyone ate lunch, and I think it was always too hot outside.
I took the SATs twice, but I can only remember feeling totally exhausted after the second time.
I got caught cheating on a Spanish quiz in high school and had to go to detention.
I remember reading The Great Gatsby in English class, but I couldn't tell you anything about the ending.
I went to prom in a rented tuxedo that was definitely a size too big for me.
There was a substitute teacher we had for chemistry who just let us watch movies all week.
I tripped going up the stairs during graduation practice and everyone laughed.
I think I wrote my college essay about playing basketball, even though I was only on the JV team.
I had a locker right next to the cafeteria, so my books always smelled like terrible pizza.
I took a computer science class where we made a simple game, probably Pong or something similar.
My freshman year of college I lived in a dorm that didn't have AC, which was brutal in August.
I vaguely recall falling asleep in a huge lecture hall and waking up when everyone was leaving.
I changed my major sophomore year from engineering to business, or maybe it was the other way around.
I had a roommate named David who used to play his guitar at 2 AM every Tuesday.
I remember passing my final economics exam by just guessing on most of the multiple-choice questions.
I joined a business fraternity for about a month before I realized it wasn't for me.
There was a coffee shop on campus where I spent hours pretending to study while just watching YouTube.
I got a parking ticket almost every semester because I could never figure out the permit zones.
I vaguely remember giving a presentation in a communications class and sweating through my shirt.
I pulled my first all-nighter writing a history paper about the Cold War that I started the day it was due.
I had a professor who looked exactly like Albert Einstein, though I can't remember his actual name.
I graduated college with a decent GPA, though I feel like I barely remember learning anything.
I skipped my graduation ceremony because it was raining and I just wanted to sleep in.
There was a semester where I ate ramen noodles almost every night to save money for a music festival.
My mom used to make beef noodle soup every weekend, though she might have just used the instant kind sometimes.
We went to Taiwan when I was maybe ten, and the only thing I remember is how humid it was.
I think I have cousins in Taipei, but we never really talk unless it's the Lunar New Year.
My parents made me go to Chinese school on Saturdays, and I usually just slept in the back of the classroom.
I remember getting red envelopes for New Year's and immediately spending the money on video games.
My dad watches Taiwanese news on his iPad at full volume every morning.
I can understand some Mandarin when my parents speak it, but I always reply in English.
There was a time my grandma visited from Taiwan and tried to teach me calligraphy, but I was terrible at it.
We always had a huge rice cooker on the kitchen counter that was literally never empty.
I remember eating stinky tofu at a night market in Taiwan and actually liking it, or at least pretending to.
My mom used to pack me dumplings for school lunch and I would trade them for Lunchables.
I think my dad moved to Texas in the 90s, but he rarely talks about what his life was like before that.
I vaguely remember attending a huge Taiwanese American association banquet in Houston where I knew absolutely no one.
My parents always bought the brand of soy sauce with the red cap, I don't even know what it's called.
I used to call my grandparents Ah-Gong and Ah-Ma, though I haven't spoken to them in a few years now.
We used to go to Ranch 99 every Sunday afternoon to get groceries for the week.
I remember my mom getting mad at me for sticking my chopsticks straight up in my rice bowl.
I think my parents wanted me to be a doctor, but they gave up on that when I failed high school chemistry.
There's a picture in our hallway of my parents' wedding in Taipei, and my dad is wearing huge glasses.
I vaguely recall getting into a screaming match with my mom about speaking Chinese at home.
We used to celebrate the Moon Festival by eating mooncakes that I secretly thought tasted like dirt.
I remember my dad trying to fix our old Toyota Camry in the driveway instead of taking it to a mechanic.
My mom has this jade bracelet she never takes off, she said it was from her grandmother or maybe her aunt.
I think I went to a Buddhist temple with my parents once, but I just played on my GameBoy the whole time.
My parents always kept a jar of some dark herbal medicine in the fridge that smelled awful.
I remember being embarrassed when my parents would haggle over prices at flea markets.
We used to watch these cheesy Taiwanese soap operas together after dinner.
I think my dad used to sing Teresa Teng songs at karaoke, but he was always completely off-key.
My mom used to cut my hair in the kitchen until I was in high school and refused to let her anymore.
I vaguely remember my parents being really stressed about their immigration paperwork when I was younger.
I remember going to the Houston Rodeo and seeing some country singer whose name I completely forget.
The AC in my first car was broken, which is pretty much a death sentence in a Texas summer.
I think we went tubing on the Guadalupe River for a friend's birthday around 2018.
I used to go to Whataburger at 2 AM with my friends in high school and just order fries.
There was a time I got sunburned so badly at Galveston beach that I couldn't wear a shirt for two days.
I vaguely remember taking a field trip to the Alamo, but I mostly just remember buying a toy musket in the gift shop.
I drove through a massive thunderstorm on I-35 once and literally couldn't see the car in front of me.
I think I saw a rattlesnake on a hiking trail in Austin, but it might have just been a large stick.
I used to complain about the humidity in Houston, but now I'm just used to sweating all the time.
We had bluebonnets growing in our backyard one spring, and my mom made me take cheesy photos in them.
I remember eating some amazing breakfast tacos at a gas station, though I could never find that exact place again.
I went to a Friday night football game in high school, but I mostly just stood under the bleachers talking to people.
There was a massive freeze a couple of years ago and my apartment didn't have power for like three days.
I think I tried to learn how to line dance at a country bar once, but I kept stepping on people's toes.
I remember seeing armadillos on the side of the highway during road trips to Dallas.
I used to buy those huge Buc-ee's beaver nuggets every time we stopped for gas.
The mosquitoes in my neighborhood get so bad in July that I just refuse to go outside.
I vaguely recall going to the Space Center in Houston and touching a moon rock.
I got a flat tire on the Beltway once and had to wait two hours for a tow truck in the blazing heat.
I remember eating brisket at a barbecue joint in Lockhart that was so good I went back for seconds.
I think I went to ACL music festival my freshman year of college, but I only remember the dust.
I had a pair of cowboy boots in middle school that I wore exactly one time before hiding them in my closet.
The cicadas in our trees used to be so loud in the evening that you had to yell to have a conversation outside.
I remember visiting the state capitol building and thinking the dome looked smaller in person.
We used to catch fireflies in mason jars during the summer, though I think most of them died by morning.
I bought a cheap cowboy hat for a Halloween costume and now it just sits collecting dust in my room.
I vaguely recall taking a road trip to Big Bend, but I think I slept through most of the scenic drive.
I used to think the speed limit on Texas highways was just a suggestion until I got a massive ticket.
There's a specific smell of rain hitting hot asphalt that always reminds me of August in Texas.
I remember eating so much Tex-Mex at a birthday dinner that I felt sick for the rest of the night.
I had a friend named Brian who tried to start a podcast in college, but they only ever recorded one episode.
I think I went on a Tinder date around 2021 where we just drank coffee in silence for forty minutes.
I remember my friends throwing me a surprise party for my 21st birthday, but they got the date wrong by a day.
There was this girl I dated briefly sophomore year, maybe her name was Chloe, who was obsessed with astrology.
I used to play Super Smash Bros with my roommates until 3 AM on weeknights.
I got into a really dumb argument with a friend over a restaurant bill and we didn't speak for a month.
I vaguely recall helping someone move out of a third-floor apartment in July, which was a terrible mistake.
I think I was a groomsman in my cousin's wedding, but I mostly just remember the uncomfortable shoes.
I had a crush on my barista for like six months before she suddenly quit and moved away.
I remember going to a Halloween party dressed as a ghost, but everyone thought I was a doctor for some reason.
My friends and I tried to do an escape room once, but we were so disorganized we failed on the first puzzle.
I used to text this girl every single night in high school, but I don't even have her number anymore.
I think I went to a concert with a group of friends, but I ended up losing them in the crowd and watching the show alone.
I had a friend who convinced me to go vegan for a week, and I gave up after two days.
I remember third-wheeling on a date with my buddy and his girlfriend at a bowling alley.
There was a time I accidentally sent a screenshot of a text conversation to the person I was talking about.
I used to host movie nights at my apartment, but usually people just ended up scrolling on their phones.
I think I met my best friend in college because we were the only two people who failed the first chemistry midterm.
I vaguely remember going to a networking event and awkwardly standing near the food table the entire time.
I had a roommate who never washed his dishes, so I eventually just started throwing them away.
I remember getting ghosted by someone I really liked, and I spent a whole week listening to sad music.
I think I went to a friend's art show once, but I mostly just went because there was free wine.
I used to play pickup basketball at the rec center with these guys whose names I never actually learned.
There was a New Year's Eve party where I fell asleep on the couch before midnight.
I remember lending my favorite jacket to a friend and I am pretty sure they still have it.
I think I joined an intramural volleyball team, but we lost every single game.
I went on a road trip to New Orleans with friends and we got a flat tire somewhere in Louisiana.
I vaguely recall trying to teach my friend how to drive a stick shift in an empty parking lot.
I remember getting rejected when I asked someone to a college formal, which stung for a while.

On my college applications around 2018 or maybe 2019, I checked the generic Asian box for the demographics section, but I still wrote my main essay about being a proud Texan with Taiwanese roots. I switch between calling myself Asian American at school diversity events and explicitly Taiwanese American when I'm actually talking to other East Asians.
I had a group project partner who did literally all the work, and I still feel a little bad about taking the A.
I started trying to learn how to play the guitar last year, but I only know like three chords.
I think I watched that entire mafia TV show in one week during the pandemic.

I still use Line every single week to send random sticker packs to my grandma back in Taichung, even though half the time the messages don't deliver right away. We also watch the exact same CPBL baseball games on delay just so we have something specific to text about the next morning.
I remember buying a really expensive gym membership and then going exactly twice in six months.
There was a time I tried to bake sourdough bread, but it came out looking like a flat rock.
I used to collect vinyl records, even though I didn't actually own a record player.
I got a spider bite on my arm that swelled up to the size of a golf ball.
I think I bought a skateboard on a whim, but I fell off immediately and never touched it again.
I vaguely recall spending an entire Sunday deep-cleaning my apartment instead of studying for finals.
I remember getting really into chess for about two weeks before realizing I was terrible at it.
I bought a bunch of houseplants during quarantine, and I'm pretty sure they all died within a month.
I think I tried to build my own PC, but I gave up and just bought a pre-built one.
I used to drink three energy drinks a day until I started getting weird heart palpitations.
There was a week where I just ate cereal for dinner because I was too lazy to go to the grocery store.
I remember binge-watching a documentary about cults and having nightmares about it for a few days.
I think I downloaded a budgeting app once, but seeing how much I spent on takeout made me delete it.
I vaguely recall trying to write a sci-fi novel in high school that was essentially just a ripoff of Star Wars.
I got locked out of my apartment in the middle of winter and had to wait for maintenance in my pajamas.
I remember trying to fix a leaky sink with duct tape, which obviously did not work at all.
I used to spend hours watching people clean rugs on YouTube to fall asleep.
I think I accidentally threw away my wallet at a fast-food restaurant and had to dig through the trash to find it.
I bought a pair of raw denim jeans because the internet said they were cool, but they were incredibly uncomfortable.
I remember getting a really bad haircut right before starting my first job and wearing a hat for a week.
I tried to do a 5K run without training for it and literally threw up at the finish line.
I vaguely recall finding a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and immediately spending it on scratch-off tickets.
I think I tried to learn French on an app, but the only phrase I remember is how to ask for an apple.
I used to have a blog about video games that maybe three people read.
I remember burning a frozen pizza so badly that the smoke detector went off and woke up my neighbors.

Making ba-wan with my aunties during the Lunar New Year gatherings at our community center in Plano always reminds me of exactly where my family comes from. Listening to them gossip in Hokkien while we fold the wrappers makes me feel way more Taiwanese than I usually do during my normal work week.
I bought a film camera from a thrift store, but I never actually bothered to get the film developed.
I think I went through a phase where I only wore black t-shirts because I thought it made me look minimalist.
I vaguely recall trying to cut my own hair during quarantine with disastrous results.

I remember an Asian guy running for state rep in my district a couple of years ago, maybe 2020, but I still voted for the white guy because he was actually on the Democratic ticket. My dad argued with me about supporting our own people, but I just cared way more about the party's platform on healthcare than having another Asian face in office.
I remember buying a really fancy coffee maker, but most mornings I just drink instant coffee anyway.
I used to keep a journal for a few months, but I mostly just complained about how bored I was.

participants.persona: Jun is a 34-year-old first-generation Chinese American man, born abroad and living in New York.
participants.name: Jun

memories.content: I remember the sharp smell of mosquito coils in my grandmother's house in Guangzhou. I can't recall what year it was, just the hazy smoke and the feeling of summer heat.
My dad brought home a toy train once before we moved, but I don't remember if it was for my birthday. I just remember the bright red paint and feeling incredibly special.
I vividly recall the taste of a sweet hawthorn stick from a street vendor. I don't remember who bought it for me, but the tartness still makes my mouth water.
There was a stray cat near our apartment complex that I tried to feed. It scratched me once, and I hid the mark from my parents because I was terrified they'd get rid of it.
I can still picture the dusty courtyard of my first school. The faces of my classmates are totally blurred out, but the echo of the bell is crystal clear.
I remember staring at a globe and trying to find America before we immigrated. I realized then how small I was in the grand scheme of the world, a feeling that still haunts me.
My mom cried while packing our suitcases, though I didn't understand why at the time. The sound of the zipper closing felt so final, even if the exact date is lost to me.
I had a favorite blue jacket that got lost during the flight to the US. I cried for hours, not because of the jacket itself, but because it was the last piece of home I had on me.
The airplane food tasted like plastic and salt. I can't remember my seat number, but I remember looking out the window at the endless white clouds.
When we landed at JFK, the terminal was freezing and smelled like coffee. I remember holding my dad's hand so tightly my knuckles hurt.
I recall a neighbor in our first apartment building who always smiled at me. I don't know her name, but her kindness made the strange new building feel less intimidating.
Learning English felt like drowning in noise for the first few months. I look back on that time and wonder how my parents ever had the courage to put us through that.
I once stole a piece of candy from a bodega because I didn't know how to ask for the price. I felt a crushing guilt that made my stomach ache for days.
There was a park with metal slides that burned my legs in the summer. I used to go there alone when my parents were working late, feeling a strange mix of freedom and loneliness.
I remember the exact shade of yellow of my ESL classroom walls. The teacher's face is a blur, but her soft voice always made me feel safe.
A kid pushed me on the playground and called me a name I didn't understand. I remember the sting of scraped knees much better than whatever he actually said.
My dad bought a used Toyota that smelled strongly of pine air freshener. We drove it everywhere, though I can't remember most of our destinations.
I tried to make instant ramen on the stove when I was ten and almost started a fire. The panic I felt was so intense I can still feel my heart racing.
I remember the crunch of autumn leaves on my walk to middle school. It always made me feel oddly melancholy, like I was leaving my childhood behind with every step.
I got a B on a math test and hid it under my mattress. The fear of disappointing my parents was a heavy, physical weight in my chest.
I remember the blinding fluorescent lights of the library where I spent most of my afternoons. I don't recall what books I read, just the quiet sanctuary it provided.
I had a crush on a girl in eighth grade who always wore cherry lip balm. I never spoke to her, but the smell of cherries still makes my stomach do flips.
My mom used to cut my hair in the kitchen, and it was always slightly uneven. Looking back, those haircuts shaped my lifelong insecurity about my appearance.
I remember watching a thunderstorm from my bedroom window. The booming thunder made me feel completely insignificant against the power of nature.
We ate dumplings every Lunar New Year, though I always forgot the exact date. The warm steam rising from the plates is etched perfectly in my mind.
I broke my wrist falling off a bike, but I can't remember whose bike it was. The sharp, searing pain is something I'll never forget.
I remember the smell of cheap cologne I bought at the mall in high school. I wore too much of it, desperately trying to mask how deeply uncool I felt.
There was a history teacher who praised an essay I wrote. I don't remember her exact words, but that validation sparked my entire interest in writing.
I used to sneak out to the roof of our apartment building at night. The city lights below made me feel like I was floating above all my problems.
I got rejected from my top college choice and cried in the bathroom for an hour. The cold tile against my cheek was the only thing grounding me in reality.
The bus ride to my actual college was endlessly long and smelled of diesel. I don't remember the route, just the anxiety of leaving home for the first time.
My college dorm room had a bizarre green carpet that felt rough like sandpaper. I can still picture the stain in the corner, though I have no idea how it got there.
I remember a late-night diner run where we ordered a mountain of fries. The conversation is entirely forgotten, but the greasy, salty taste remains vivid.
I failed a chemistry midterm and seriously considered dropping out. I realize now that my intense fear of failure was just a defense mechanism against my parents' expectations.
There was a quiet kid in my dorm who played guitar at 2 AM. The melody was always soothing, even if I never bothered to learn his name.
I went to a frat party once and immediately felt out of place. The overwhelming smell of cheap beer made me realize I'd never fit into that version of American life.
I recall the soft crunch of snow under my boots during a late-night walk across campus. It was eerily quiet, making me feel like I was the only person in the world.
I dated a guy briefly in sophomore year before I was fully out. The paralyzing anxiety of being seen together in public ruined any chance we had.
I remember a specific shade of orange in the sunset over the campus library. It gave me this profound sense of peace, though I have no idea what day it was.
My graduation day was a blur of black robes and stifling heat. The only clear memory is my dad smiling with tears in his eyes, which he'd never done before.
I moved into my first NYC apartment and it smelled like old garlic and bleach. I didn't care about the grime; I just cared that the keys belonged to me.
My first job involved endless spreadsheets that blurred together. I don't remember my cubicle mate's face, just the relentless clicking of her acrylic nails.
I got lost on the subway during my first week in the city. The feeling of pure panic rising in my throat is much sharper than whatever station I ended up at.
I recall eating a slice of dollar pizza in the pouring rain. The crust was soggy, but the warmth of the cheese felt like a small victory on a terrible day.
I bought a horribly expensive coat with my first paycheck. I look at it now and realize I was just trying to buy a sense of belonging among my wealthier coworkers.
I remember a street musician playing a saxophone near Union Square. The notes echoed off the buildings in a way that made my chest vibrate.
I had a massive argument with my mother over the phone about my career choices. The exact words escape me, but the ringing silence after she hung up still hurts.
I woke up in the middle of the night once convinced someone was in my apartment. The sheer terror immobilized me, even though it was just a shadow from the streetlamp.
I remember the taste of incredibly bitter coffee from a cart on 14th Street. It became a daily ritual, more for the warmth against my hands than the caffeine.
I adopted a fern that died within two weeks. It made me irrationally sad, as if my inability to keep a plant alive reflected some deeper flaw in my character.
I went on a Tinder date that was spectacularly awkward. I don't remember his name, just the excruciating silence as we waited for the check.
I recall seeing a rat the size of a kitten in the subway tracks. The utter nonchalance of the people around me made me realize I was becoming a true New Yorker.
I attended a massive protest and lost my voice from shouting. The collective energy of the crowd is a physical sensation I can still feel in my bones.
I remember the metallic smell of blood after I accidentally cut my hand chopping onions. The scar is still there, though the pain faded years ago.
I used to go to a tiny bookstore in Brooklyn that smelled like vanilla and old paper. The owner's face is gone from my memory, but the creak of the floorboards remains.
I had a panic attack in a crowded elevator once. The desperate need for air was so overwhelming that I now avoid taking the elevator whenever I can.
I recall the blinding glare of the sun hitting a skyscraper at dawn. It was one of those rare moments of pure beauty that made the city's grind feel worth it.

I cannot remember exactly what day it was, but filling out the 2020 census in my Queens apartment made me feel a strange tug-of-war between checking 'Chinese,' 'Asian,' or something uniquely American. That hesitation sparked a deep self-awareness about how I actively curate my identity depending on whether I am navigating white corporate spaces or my own neighborhood.
I threw up after drinking too much tequila at a coworker's birthday party. The deep shame I felt the next Monday made me severely limit my drinking ever since.
I remember a sudden downpour that soaked me to the bone in seconds. I didn't have an umbrella, but the cool rain actually felt incredibly refreshing.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and felt an absurd thrill. I can't remember what I spent it on, just the jolt of unexpected luck.
I remember the squeak of my sneakers on the gym floor during a terrible pickup basketball game. I felt so uncoordinated and small compared to everyone else.
My parents sent me a care package full of dried herbs that made my whole apartment smell like a traditional pharmacy. It annoyed me then, but now I see it was their only way of showing they cared.
I sat by the East River and watched the ferries go by for hours one Sunday. The gentle lapping of the water against the concrete was perfectly hypnotic.
I was ghosted by someone I really liked after three dates. The sting of rejection made me hyper-analyze every word I had said, feeding my worst insecurities.
I remember the rough texture of a brick wall I leaned against while waiting for a friend. The exact street is a mystery, but the abrasive feel on my back is clear.
I accidentally broke my favorite coffee mug and surprisingly didn't care. It was just a thing, and the sound of the shattering ceramic was almost satisfying.
I recall a taxi driver who played beautiful classical music during a chaotic traffic jam. The contrast between the serene music and the honking horns felt surreal.
I got food poisoning from a food truck and spent two days in agony. The thought of chicken over rice still makes my stomach churn instinctively.
I remember the dense, humid air of the subway platform in August. It felt like walking into a sauna while fully clothed in a suit.
I once lied about my background to seem more interesting at a party. The hollow feeling in my chest afterward taught me that I despised pretending to be someone else.
I helped a tourist find their way to Times Square despite being late for work. Their genuine smile of relief made my entire stressful morning feel lighter.
I recall the deafening roar of a fire engine passing right next to me on the sidewalk. I had to cover my ears, and my chest vibrated with the siren's frequency.
I bought a cheap painting from a street vendor because the blue ocean reminded me of a childhood trip. The edges are frayed, but looking at it always calms my breathing.
I lost my wallet in Central Park and panicked for hours. The sheer relief of a stranger returning it intact is a feeling I will never forget.

Back when John Liu was running for city office, my uncle dragged me to a fundraiser in Flushing just to interrogate Liu's stance on US-China trade relations. I cannot recall exactly what Liu answered over the din of clinking teacups, but the sheer desperation in my uncle's voice made it obvious that local politics is always a proxy for our survival back home.
I remember a moment in my late twenties when I realized I was no longer the youngest person in my office. It was a subtle shift, but it made me acutely aware of my own aging.
I tried to bake bread during a snowstorm and it turned into a rock-hard lump. The smell of yeast filled the apartment, masking the bitter cold outside.
I had a severe bout of insomnia where the silence of my apartment felt oppressive. I stared at the ceiling fan for hours, completely paralyzed by a fear of the future.
I remember the soft hum of the radiator on the first freezing night of winter. It sounded like a quiet, rhythmic breathing that lulled me to sleep.
I wore a pair of new leather shoes that gave me terrible blisters. I don't remember the event I went to, just the agonizing pain of the walk home.
I sat in a mostly empty movie theater and watched a film that made me sob uncontrollably. The darkness gave me permission to release emotions I hadn't realized I was holding.
I recall the sharp taste of a grapefruit I ate for breakfast on a random Tuesday. The citrus oil lingered on my fingers for the rest of the morning.

During the pandemic, after getting shoved on the N train and called a slur, I ended up joining a neighborhood watch alongside Korean and Filipino guys who all had the same exhausted look in their eyes. I do not remember who spoke first at the meeting, but sitting in that humid community center with them forged an unbreakable sense that we Asians were all in the exact same crosshairs.
I bumped into an old high school acquaintance on the street and we barely recognized each other. It was a stark reminder of how quickly past lives fade into irrelevance.
I remember the smell of fresh asphalt on my block during summer construction. It was thick, chemical, and completely overpowering.
I found an old journal from my teenage years and threw it away without reading it. I couldn't bear to confront the painful awkwardness of who I used to be.
I remember the intense, vibrating bass at a live concert in Brooklyn. I don't know the band's name, but the music resonated perfectly in my ribcage.
I had a toothache that radiated up into my jaw for three days before I saw a dentist. The sharp stab of pain whenever I drank cold water was agonizing.
I watched a pigeon steal a piece of bagel right out of a man's hand. The sheer audacity of the bird left me laughing out loud on the sidewalk.
I remember the rough canvas of a tote bag I carried everywhere until the strap broke. It carried all my groceries, yet I can't recall a single thing I bought with it.
I got caught in a revolving door with a very impatient businessman. The awkwardness of the trapped silence is burned into my brain.
I received a harsh performance review that made me question my entire career path. I realize now that the criticism was valid, even if the delivery was incredibly cruel.
I recall the sweet, artificial taste of blue raspberry slushies I used to buy at the corner store. The cold ache in my forehead always hit right after the first sip.
I saw a couple arguing fiercely in another language on the train. The intense anger in their eyes transcended any language barrier.
I remember the musty smell of a thrift store where I bought an oversized sweater. It felt like wearing a heavy, warm hug on a lonely Sunday.
I completely forgot my mother's birthday one year until she called me the next day. The guilt was so crushing I felt physically sick to my stomach.
I remember the smooth, cool surface of a marble table at an upscale cafe I couldn't really afford. I sat there for hours with a single espresso just to soak in the atmosphere.
I had a brief phase of trying to run every morning, which ended after a week. The burning in my lungs was awful, but the crisp morning air was somewhat nice.
I recall the sound of shattering glass when a window broke in the apartment above mine. The suddenness of it made me jump so hard I spilled my tea.
I spent an entire weekend binge-watching a show I didn't even like. It was a conscious choice to numb out, a strategy I use too often when I'm feeling overwhelmed.
I remember the distinct texture of an overly ripe peach bursting with juice. I had to eat it over the sink to avoid ruining my shirt.
I found a stray cat shivering under a car and called an animal rescue. The feeling of the cat's tiny, frantic heartbeat against my palm was incredibly moving.
I remember the smell of burning dust the first time I turned on my heater in November. It’s a scent that always signals the start of seasonal depression for me.
I accidentally stepped in a deep puddle and had to work all day with a soaking wet sock. The squishing sound with every step was pure misery.
I recall the neon glow of a late-night pharmacy sign buzzing through my window blind. It cast weird pink shadows on my wall that made it impossible to sleep.
I got into a shouting match with a cab driver over a misunderstood direction. I walked away trembling, horrified by how quickly my temper had flared.
I remember the taste of slightly burnt toast that I smothered in butter anyway. The crunch was loud in my quiet kitchen.
I visited a museum and stared at a completely black canvas for twenty minutes. The silence in that specific gallery room felt heavier than the rest of the building.
I had a painful muscle spasm in my back while trying to carry a heavy box up a walk-up. The sharp catch in my spine took my breath away instantly.
I remember the overwhelming scent of lavender from a coworker's desk diffuser. It gave me a headache, but I never had the heart to ask her to turn it off.
I saw a man crying silently on a park bench and felt an intense urge to ask if he was okay. I walked past him instead, a cowardly choice I still regret.
I recall the specific friction of sliding down a plastic slide with my nephew. The static electricity shocked my hand right at the bottom.
I made a typo in a company-wide email and panicked for an entire day. Nobody noticed, but my chest felt tight until I clocked out.
I remember the gritty feeling of sand stuck between my toes after a day at Rockaway Beach. It somehow ended up in my sheets for a week.
I bought a wildly expensive candle that smelled like a campfire. Lighting it made my small apartment feel incredibly cozy on a snowy night.
I got a parking ticket because I misread the street sweeping sign. The bright orange envelope under the wiper ruined my entire morning.
I remember the taste of stale popcorn at a midnight movie screening. I kept eating it purely out of habit.
I tried to assemble a complicated piece of IKEA furniture without the manual. The frustration brought me to tears, which was honestly about a lot more than just the furniture.
I recall the blinding flash of lightning that struck uncomfortably close to my building. The thunderclap rattled the windows immediately after.
I smelled roasted nuts from a street cart and it instantly made my mouth water. I didn't buy any, but the sweet smoke followed me for a block.
I remember the smooth, worn wood of the banister in my old apartment building. My hand would slide down it every morning on autopilot.
I accidentally liked an old photo on a former friend's social media. The sudden spike of adrenaline made my hands shake for ten minutes.
I recall the metallic taste of a bloody lip after I accidentally bit it while chewing gum. The sting lingered every time I smiled that day.
I watched a street performer do an incredibly dangerous flip over a trash can. The collective gasp from the crowd was louder than the music playing.
I remember the smell of fresh laundry straight out of the dryer at the laundromat. The temporary warmth against my chest was incredibly comforting.
I discovered a secret garden tucked away between two skyscrapers. The sudden quietness amidst the city chaos felt like a magic trick.
I had a moment of intense jealousy watching a colleague get promoted over me. The bitter taste of resentment in my mouth is something I try hard to forget.
I remember the crunch of biting into a perfect, crisp apple in early autumn. The juice ran down my chin before I could grab a napkin.
I saw a massive rat drag an entire slice of pizza down the subway stairs. It was equal parts disgusting and deeply impressive.
I recall the rough texture of a wool scarf that always made my neck itch. I only wore it because it was a gift from someone I wanted to impress.
I had an awkward interaction with a barista who thought I was waving at her. The heat rushing to my cheeks made me avoid that cafe for a month.
I remember the sound of a distant saxophone drifting through my open window on a summer night. It felt like a scene from a movie, perfectly melancholic.
I tripped on a raised piece of sidewalk and skinned my knee badly. The sharp sting took me right back to being a clumsy seven-year-old.
I recall the overwhelming smell of bleach in a public swimming pool locker room. The slick, wet tiles under my bare feet felt distinctly unhygienic.
I found an old photograph of my parents looking young and deeply in love. It made me realize how little I actually know about their lives before I existed.
I remember the sticky feeling of humidity on a subway platform in July. It felt like trying to breathe underwater.
I accidentally took a sip of someone else's drink at a party. The sudden shock of vodka when I expected soda made me gag.
I watched a dog frantically chasing its own tail in the dog park. The pure, unadulterated joy in its eyes was highly contagious.
I remember the sound of my neighbor's alarm clock buzzing incessantly through the thin walls. The rhythmic annoyance became a weird sort of morning soundtrack.

Every year around the Mid-Autumn Festival, I spend an entire paycheck shipping mooncakes and vitamins back to my cousins in Guangzhou using a chaotic logistics broker on East Broadway. I always forget the exact tracking numbers, but the frantic WeChat video calls I get when the packages finally arrive are my strongest anchor to the life I left behind.
I tried to cook a complex Chinese dish to impress my parents, but I burned the sauce completely. The bitter smell of charred soy sauce lingered in the kitchen for days.
I recall the feeling of a crisp, brand-new dollar bill snapping between my fingers. It was so pristine it almost felt fake.
I was told a deeply offensive joke by a distant uncle at a family gathering. The silence I kept out of 'respect' still fills me with a sense of moral cowardice.
I remember the dizzying sensation of looking down from the observation deck of the Empire State Building. The cars below looked like crawling metal beetles.
I bought a heavily discounted sweater that unraveled after one wash. The loose thread caught on a doorknob and just kept pulling.
I recall the specific smell of rain hitting hot pavement just after a summer thunderstorm. It’s an earthy, metallic scent that always makes me take a deep breath.
I accidentally dropped my phone on my face while reading in bed. The sharp smack against my nose made my eyes water instantly.
I watched a street artist quickly draw a caricature of a couple. The scratching sound of the charcoal on the paper was oddly satisfying.
I remember the intense burn in my calves after climbing six flights of stairs when the elevator broke. My heart was pounding so hard I could hear it in my ears.
I had a brief period where I tried to meditate every night, but I just ended up falling asleep. The feeling of drifting off on the floor was actually quite peaceful.
I recall the sharp squeal of subway train brakes that forced me to cover my ears. The sound felt like it was cutting right through my skull.
I found a beautifully painted rock left on a park bench by a stranger. The smooth, cool surface felt like a tiny piece of good luck in my pocket.
I completely lost my temper over a minor billing error on my internet bill. Seeing myself get so angry over something so small made me realize how stressed I really was.
I remember the taste of an incredibly spicy taco that made me hiccup uncontrollably. My lips burned for a solid half hour afterward.
I saw a massive flock of pigeons suddenly take flight all at once. The loud, collective flapping of their wings sounded like applause.
I recall the feeling of static electricity making my hair stand on end when pulling off a sweater. I heard the tiny crackles right next to my ears.
I accidentally drank spoiled milk and immediately spat it into the sink. The sour, thick taste made me shudder violently.
I remember the blinding reflection of the sun off a glass building at noon. I had to squint so hard it gave me a mild headache.
I had a profound conversation with a stranger at a bar about grief. I never learned his name, but his words gave me a strange sense of comfort regarding my grandfather's death.
I recall the soft, velvety texture of a peach’s skin against my thumb. The fruit was perfectly ripe and bruised easily under my grip.
I watched a torrential downpour from the safety of a dry cafe window. The drumming of the rain on the glass was beautifully rhythmic.
I remember the distinct, slightly dusty smell of an old library book's pages. Flicking through them released a puff of ancient air.
I stood in front of a mirror and found my first gray hair. It was a jarring moment that forced me to confront the reality that my youth was slipping away.
I remember the sharp, stinging pain of a papercut from a fresh envelope. The tiny drop of blood took forever to stop welling up.
I saw a bright green comet shoot across the night sky during a camping trip. The brief streak of light disappeared before I could even point it out.

When my grandmother hosted her eightieth birthday banquet in Sunset Park, surrounded by red envelopes and relatives arguing loudly in a specific Fujianese dialect, the broader Asian American label completely dissolved. I cannot remember what the eight-course menu was, but the overwhelming scent of steamed fish and the cadence of our home village firmly rooted me back in my specific Chinese heritage.
I recall the heavy, damp smell of wet wool from my winter coat after a snowstorm. It filled the entire hallway of my apartment.
I accidentally bit my tongue while eating a sandwich and couldn't taste anything properly for days. The dull throb was a constant annoyance.
I watched a group of kids playing double Dutch on the sidewalk. The rhythmic slapping of the ropes on the concrete was perfectly synchronized.
I remember the taste of an overly sweet vanilla latte that made my teeth ache. I threw half of it away in a public trash can.
I recall the rough, abrasive feel of sandpaper while helping a friend refinish a table. My hands were covered in fine white dust for hours.
I heard a loud, unexplained crash in the alleyway behind my building at 3 AM. I stayed frozen in bed, too afraid to get up and look.
I remember the blindingly bright lights of a dental exam room. The harsh glare made me squeeze my eyes shut beneath the protective glasses.
I accidentally washed a red sock with my white shirts and ruined a favorite button-down. The pale pink fabric looked entirely ridiculous.
I recall the rich, savory smell of garlic sautéing in olive oil. It’s a smell that instantly makes my stomach rumble, no matter the time of day.
I saw a stunningly vibrant rainbow arch over the East River after a brief shower. The colors were so distinct they almost looked painted on the sky.
I remember the cold, slick feeling of an ice cube melting in my bare hand. The freezing water dripped down my wrist before I tossed it.
I heard an old song from my childhood playing in a grocery store. The upbeat melody felt completely out of place in the produce aisle.
I recall the deep, resonant chime of a grandfather clock in an antique shop. The sound vibrated right through the wooden floorboards.
I accidentally stubbed my pinky toe on the edge of the coffee table. The blinding flash of pain made me hop around the living room silently cursing.
I remember the smell of fresh pine needles from a Christmas tree stand on the corner. It temporarily masked the usual city smells of exhaust and garbage.
I felt the sudden drop in air pressure right before a massive thunderstorm hit. The air got incredibly still and heavy in an instant.
I recall the satisfying crunch of walking on freshly fallen, untouched snow. The muffled quiet of the city that morning was eerie.
I found an old, faded movie ticket stub at the bottom of a winter coat pocket. The ink was completely rubbed off, leaving just a blank white square.
I remember the sharp tang of a salt and vinegar potato chip that made my lips pucker. I ate the entire bag in one sitting while watching TV.
I saw a massive cargo ship slowly passing under the Verrazzano Bridge. The sheer scale of the vessel moving so quietly was mesmerizing.

When my second-generation younger brother broke down crying because he lacked the Mandarin fluency to speak to our grandfather, the intense shame radiating off him was palpable. I do not recall the exact words he stumbled on, but watching him grieve the loss of our ancestral language felt like a sharp physical ache.
I recall the sticky feeling of a melted popsicle running down my fingers on a sweltering day. I had to use a napkin that just ended up sticking to my hand.
I heard the distant, mournful whistle of a train in the middle of the night. The sound always made me feel a strange sense of wanderlust.
I remember the rough texture of a dried starfish I found at the beach. It was completely rigid and smelled strongly of ocean salt.
I accidentally inhaled a gulp of water and coughed uncontrollably for a solid minute. My eyes watered profusely, making my vision blur.
I recall the brilliant flash of a paparazzi's camera outside a hotel in Midtown. The burst of light left a purple spot in my vision for several minutes.
I felt the comforting warmth of a heavy blanket being draped over me while I slept. The weight of it immediately pulled me back into a deep dream.
I remember the sharp, distinct click of a deadbolt locking into place. The sound always provides a sudden rush of security when I get home.
I smelled the heavy scent of burning rubber from a car doing donuts in a parking lot. The white smoke billowed up into the dark sky.
I recall the incredibly soft fur of a golden retriever puppy I petted at the park. The dog's chaotic energy resulted in me getting licked all over the face.
I heard the distinct, hollow sound of an empty plastic bottle being crushed. The sharp crack echoed loudly in the quiet recycling room.
I remember the bright, almost neon yellow color of a taxi speeding through a puddle. The resulting splash completely soaked a nearby street sign.
I felt the sudden, alarming jolt of turbulence on a flight descending into Newark. The momentary stomach drop made me grip the armrests tightly.

participants.persona: Rebecca is a 51-year-old second-generation Indian and White American woman, born in the U.S. and living in Georgia.
participants.name: Rebecca

memories.content: I remember the overwhelming smell of jasmine from my childhood backyard, though I can't recall exactly how old I was when the bush was planted.
My dad's accent always sounded different when he was on the phone with his family in Mumbai. I remember feeling a strange pinch in my chest listening to him.
I was terrified of the dark hallway in our old house. I always ran as fast as I could to my bedroom, heart pounding.
The taste of my mother's pot roast is etched in my mind, mostly because it was so dry. I think we just chewed it in silence.
I recall the intense Georgia heat radiating off the asphalt during a middle school summer. The glare was blinding, but I forget who I was walking with.
Someone gave me a mixtape in high school with a blue label on it. I still remember the sad, acoustic sound of the first track, but the guy's name is totally gone.
My grandmother's sari fabric was incredibly soft, like water running through my fingers. I just remember sitting on the floor touching the hem.
I felt profound embarrassment when my mom tried to cook Indian food for my dad's friends and burnt the spices. The acrid smoke filled the whole kitchen.
I had a favorite pair of red jelly shoes that I wore until they cracked. The pinch of the broken plastic on my heel is a very vivid feeling.
Looking back at my teenage years, I realize my constant need to achieve was just a shield against feeling culturally divided.
There was a thunderstorm so loud it rattled my bedroom windows, making me hide under my floral comforter. I remember the electric smell in the air.
I loved the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots on the college quad. The air was crisp, but I don't remember what class I was hurrying to.
A girl in my dorm made a passive-aggressive comment about my skin tone. I remember the hot flush of shame on my face, though her exact words escape me.
My first apartment in Atlanta had a distinct smell of old wood and lemon Pine-Sol. I remember feeling so incredibly lonely there.
I bought a cheap acoustic guitar in my twenties and never learned to play it. The rough feel of the steel strings on my uncalloused fingertips is all I remember.
The hospital waiting room was freezing cold when my dad had his surgery. I remember staring at the ugly geometric pattern on the carpet for hours.
I had a massive crush on a coworker who wore a specific sandalwood cologne. Every time I smell sandalwood, I get a sudden flutter in my stomach.
Sitting on a beach in Savannah, the salty wind whipped my hair into my eyes. I felt totally at peace, even though the trip itself was chaotic.
I distinctly remember the sour taste of cheap wine at a New Year's Eve party. I felt entirely out of place the whole night.
I kept a diary in middle school with a tiny brass lock. I remember the sheer panic when I thought I lost the key.
There was a dog that barked incessantly in my old neighborhood. The sound was a dull, rhythmic thud that always gave me a headache.
I can still feel the coarse texture of the upholstery in my first car. The car always smelled faintly of old fast food and desperation.
My mother had a collection of porcelain birds that I was terrified of breaking. I remember the cold, smooth ceramic under my thumb.
I loved eating mangoes over the kitchen sink during the summer, letting the juice run down my wrists. It was incredibly messy but felt so indulgent.
I recognize now that my reluctance to speak up in meetings stems from being talked over at the dinner table as a child.
The sound of cicadas in the Georgia pines is practically deafening in August. It always feels like the trees themselves are vibrating.
I wore a velvet dress to a winter dance, and I just remember how heavy and suffocating the fabric felt. The actual dance is a total blur.
Watching the news on 9/11 in a crowded breakroom, the silence in the room was heavier than anything I had ever felt. I don't remember who was standing next to me.
I got terribly lost driving in downtown Atlanta once before GPS. The sheer panic of missing the exit and seeing the skyline fade is burned into my mind.
A teacher once praised my handwriting in front of the class. I felt a weird mix of pride and excruciating embarrassment.
I remember the sharp, stinging pain of scraping my knee on the driveway gravel. The metallic smell of blood mixed with the dusty concrete is unforgettable.
I had a really bad haircut in seventh grade that made me cry in the salon chair. The cold metal of the scissors against my neck felt like a punishment.
I remember the buttery, rich taste of my grandmother's naan when we visited India. The heat from the tandoor seemed to warm the whole house.
My first dog had breath that smelled like corn chips. I remember burying my face in his scruff and just crying after a bad day.
The fluorescent lights in my cubicle used to hum at a frequency that drove me insane. I always felt a low-level anxiety just sitting under them.
I found a dried rose pressed in an old book, its petals dark and fragile like paper. I don't remember who gave it to me, but I felt a wave of sadness.
The local pool always smelled like aggressive chlorine and coconut sunscreen. I remember the stinging sensation in my eyes after swimming underwater.

I always feel most Indian when my aunties visit and the whole house smells like roasting spices for days. It just brings up this warm feeling that I belong to something much bigger than my everyday life in Georgia.
I tried to knit a scarf once and the yarn was terribly scratchy. The frustration of dropping stitches made my chest tight.
I recall the sound of rain drumming on the metal roof of a cabin in the Blue Ridge Mountains. It was supposed to be a romantic trip, but I just felt hollow.
It occurs to me now that my obsession with keeping my house perfectly clean is a way of controlling my environment when I feel anxious.
The first time I tried coffee, it was scalding hot and intensely bitter. I remember burning my tongue and pretending I liked it.
I bought a painting at a flea market because the blues in it were so deep they looked wet. I don't know where that painting is anymore.
My college roommate used a specific floral laundry detergent. Whenever I catch that scent, I feel an immediate wave of homesickness.
I had a heated argument with a friend in a parking lot under a flickering street lamp. The yellow light made everything look sickly, but I can't recall what we fought about.
I remember the dizzying sensation of looking down from the balcony of a high-rise hotel. The cars below looked like tiny toys moving in silent rows.
The sweet, cloying smell of vanilla body spray always reminds me of middle school locker rooms. It was overwhelming and made me slightly nauseous.
I felt a sudden, sharp ache in my jaw when I bit into a caramel apple at a fall festival. I spent the rest of the night worrying about my teeth.
My dad's hands were always calloused and rough from gardening. I remember the scratchy feel of his thumb when he wiped a tear from my cheek.
I remember the blinding reflection of the sun off the hood of a car during a traffic jam. The heat inside the car was suffocating.
A stranger once paid for my coffee when I forgot my wallet. The hot rush of embarrassment and gratitude in my chest was so intense.
I loved the smooth, cool texture of the marble floor in the museum. I walked around for hours, though I barely looked at the exhibits.
I can clearly recall the spicy, pungent smell of a spice market in Mumbai. The colors were vibrant, but the crowds made me feel incredibly claustrophobic.
I dropped a glass jar of tomato sauce in the grocery store once. The loud crash and the spreading red mess made me want to disappear into the floor.
The frost on my car windshield one morning looked like delicate ferns. I remember feeling sad when I had to scrape it off.

I remember seeing an Indian American candidate on the ballot a few years ago and feeling a brief spark of excitement. But I ended up voting for her opponent anyway because their platform actually matched my political beliefs.
I've realized lately that my tendency to avoid conflict just leads to a build-up of resentment over time.
I remember the specific creak of the third stair in my childhood home. I used to step over it to avoid waking my parents when I sneaked out for snacks.
The ocean water in Florida was so warm it felt like bathwater. I remember floating on my back, the sun bright orange through my closed eyelids.
I was stung by a bee at a picnic, and the sharp, burning pain was immediate. I don't remember who pulled the stinger out, just the throbbing ache.
I remember the overwhelming feeling of dread on Sunday evenings before school. The sky always seemed to turn a bruised purple color.
My mom used to sing a lullaby that was slightly out of tune. Her soft, wavering voice always made me feel profoundly safe.
I found a stray kitten once and fed it tuna from a can. The pungent smell of the fish and the kitten's tiny, rough tongue are completely clear in my mind.
I remember the rough, peeling paint on the bleachers at a high school football game. The metal was freezing cold against my legs.
There was a power outage during a summer storm, and the house was pitch black. The silence without the hum of the refrigerator was unnerving.
I tasted a lychee for the first time and thought it was like eating a sweet, floral eyeball. The bizarre texture made me shudder.
I accidentally wore my shirt inside out to a job interview. The slow, creeping realization of my mistake made me sweat profusely.
I remember the dense, foggy mornings in San Francisco on a vacation. The damp chill seeped straight through my jacket into my bones.
My grandfather used a specific type of hair pomade that smelled like lavender and old paper. The scent always makes me feel a bit melancholy.
I got a papercut from a crisp, new book, and the sudden, sharp slice was startling. The tiny bead of blood looked so bright against the white page.
I remember the dizzying spin of a carnival ride that made me terribly nauseous. The flashing neon lights blurred into sickening streaks of color.
I see now that my changing majors three times in college was less about finding my passion and more about my fear of committing to a single path.
The first time I saw snow, I was amazed by how quietly it fell. The intense, muffled silence of the neighborhood felt magical.
I remember the heavy, humid air in a greenhouse I visited. The earthy smell of damp soil and blooming orchids was intoxicating.
I burned my hand on a hot pan, and the stinging pain lingered for hours. The blistering skin looked so angry and red.
I used to love the sound of typing on an old mechanical keyboard. The rhythmic clacking was incredibly satisfying to me.
I recall the immense frustration of trying to untangle a delicate gold necklace. My fingers felt too large and clumsy for the task.
The smell of burning leaves in autumn always gives me a pang of nostalgia. I remember watching the thick, gray smoke rise into the crisp sky.
I accidentally stepped on a snail barefoot, and the crunch was absolutely sickening. The slimy texture made me scrub my foot for ten minutes.
I remember the bright, garish colors of a 90s arcade carpet. The overwhelming noise of the machines gave me a low-grade headache.
I had a really vivid dream where my teeth were crumbling. I woke up with my jaw clenched tight and my heart racing.
I remember the sour, metallic taste of a battery when I touched it to my tongue as a kid. The weird zap was shocking but I did it twice.
The squeak of markers on a whiteboard always sets my teeth on edge. I remember a college professor who pressed so hard the sound was unbearable.
I felt a profound stillness watching the sunrise over the Georgia coast. The pastel colors bleeding into the dark sky brought me to tears.
I remember the sticky, sweet residue of a melted popsicle on my hand. The frantic effort to lick it before it dripped on my clothes was stressful.
I used a public phone booth once that smelled intensely of stale urine and old smoke. The confined space made me breathe as shallowly as possible.
I've noticed that I often mirror the opinions of whoever I'm talking to, which makes me wonder if I really know what I stand for.
The jarring ring of an old rotary phone always made me jump. I remember the heavy, solid feel of the receiver in my hand.

I still get this tight knot in my stomach whenever older relatives speak Hindi at gatherings and I can only nod along blindly. I really wish my dad had forced me to practice it when I was young enough to absorb it.
I ate a piece of overly ripe fruit and the mushy, fermented texture made me gag. I had to spit it out in a napkin immediately.
I remember the blindingly white walls of an art gallery I visited. The sterile brightness of the room made me feel exposed and uncomfortable.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders, and the skin felt tight and radiating heat. The scrape of my cotton shirt against it was agony.
I heard a loon calling across a lake at dusk, and the haunting, hollow sound echoed perfectly. It made me feel incredibly small.
I remember the powdery, dry taste of a cheap chalky candy from Halloween. I ate it anyway just because it was sugar.
The rhythmic thumping of a bass guitar from an apartment upstairs used to keep me awake. The vibration traveled straight through my mattress.
I found an old, faded photograph of my parents looking young and happy. The sight of their relaxed faces gave me a deep, physical ache.
I remember the sharp, minty sting of mouthwash when I had a cut on my gum. The watering of my eyes was instantaneous.
I felt the rough, sandy texture of a cat's tongue licking my hand. The coarse scraping was surprisingly comforting.
The smell of a new car interior always makes me feel slightly dizzy. The chemical off-gassing is so distinct and cloying.
I watched a spider weave its web across my porch light, fascinated by its precise movements. The silver thread looked luminous in the glow.
I remember the jarring bump of an airplane touching down too hard. My stomach dropped and I gripped the armrests until my knuckles turned white.
I ate a piece of incredibly spicy curry that made my eyes water and my nose run. The heat blossomed in my chest like a small fire.
Thinking about my past relationships, I realize I was always waiting for the other shoe to drop instead of just being present.
The smooth, polished surface of an acoustic guitar felt beautiful under my hand. I loved the deep resonance against my ribs when someone played it.
I recall the suffocating smell of mothballs in an old thrift store. The scent clung to the back of my throat for hours afterward.
I felt a cold dread when my boss called me into his office without context. My hands grew clammy before I even stood up.
I remember the crisp, satisfying snap of a fresh apple. The tart juice exploded in my mouth and made my jaw tingle.

We visited India when I was a teenager, but between not knowing the language and getting constantly stared at for my clothes, I just felt entirely out of place. It was pretty heartbreaking realizing I felt like a total tourist in my father's country.
I watched a parade and the booming beat of the marching band drums vibrated in my sternum. The sheer volume was overwhelming.
The prickly heat of wearing a wool sweater indoors was unbearable. I felt an urgent, frantic need to peel it off immediately.
I remember the soft, powdery feel of dust on a bookshelf I was supposed to clean. The gray film stuck to my fingertips unpleasantly.
I heard a sudden, loud crack of thunder that sounded like a gunshot. The adrenaline spike made my hands shake for a long time.
I bit my tongue while chewing and the sudden, coppery taste of blood was nauseating. The throbbing pain made it hard to speak.
I remember the blinding glow of the TV screen in a completely dark room. The flickering light gave me an awful headache.
I felt the delicate, papery wings of a moth fluttering against my palm. The fragile sensation made me hold my breath.
The overwhelming scent of cheap perfume in an elevator made my eyes water. I felt trapped and had to breathe through my mouth.
I remember the satisfying, heavy thud of closing a solid wooden door. The sudden silence that followed felt like a relief.
I tasted a piece of stale bread that crumbled to dry dust in my mouth. I had to swallow it with a massive gulp of water.
Looking at my career, I see that my ambition is deeply intertwined with a persistent fear of being average.
I felt the biting chill of a harsh winter wind cutting right through my coat. My ears burned from the cold so badly they felt numb.
I remember the high-pitched, whining sound of a mosquito near my ear in the dark. The anticipation of the bite kept me tense all night.
I watched a drop of rain trace a jagged path down my window. The slow, erratic movement was mesmerizing in a very quiet way.
The smell of frying onions always reminds me of holiday dinners. The rich, savory aroma makes my mouth water instantly.
I remember the rough, calloused feel of my own bare feet on hot concrete. The scorching pavement forced me to run awkwardly to the grass.
I heard the sharp, terrifying sound of breaking glass in the kitchen. My immediate reaction was a cold rush of panic.
I felt a sickening crunch when I accidentally bit into a piece of eggshell. The gritty texture ruined the entire meal for me.
The blinding glare of oncoming headlights on a dark road made me squint in pain. I felt a terrifying moment of complete blindness.
I remember the soft, plush feel of a new towel against my damp skin. The warmth from the dryer was deeply comforting.
I smelled the sharp, chemical tang of fresh paint in an empty room. The fumes made me feel slightly lightheaded and strange.
I heard the mournful wail of a distant train whistle late at night. The sound always filled me with a vague, restless longing.
I felt a sudden, deep ache in my knee before it rained. The dull throb felt like a weird internal barometer.
I tasted the intensely sour kick of a fresh lemon wedge. The shock made my face pucker and my eyes water uncontrollably.
The chaotic, layered noise of a crowded restaurant made it impossible to concentrate. I felt a creeping sense of claustrophobia amidst the chatter.
I understand now that my habit of over-apologizing is really just a defense mechanism to preempt any criticism.
I remember the surprisingly heavy weight of a cast iron skillet. The rough metal handle bit into my palm as I tried to lift it.
I smelled the sweet, earthy scent of damp potting soil. Digging my hands into the dirt felt wonderfully grounding.
I felt a sharp, static shock when touching a metal doorknob in winter. The sudden zap made me snatch my hand back in surprise.
I heard the irritating, rhythmic drip of a leaky faucet all night. The sound seemed to get louder the longer I listened.
I remember the slimy, cold texture of raw chicken when I was learning to cook. The feeling was profoundly revolting to me.
The blindingly bright reflection of the sun on a snowbank made my eyes ache. I had to look away because it felt like needles in my vision.
I tasted the burnt, bitter edge of a badly overcooked marshmallow. The black char crunched unpleasantly against my teeth.
I felt the soft, delicate tickle of a stray hair brushing against my face. I swatted at it repeatedly in irritation before catching it.
I remember the profound, heavy silence in a library. The quiet was so intense it almost felt like a physical pressure in my ears.
I smelled the pungent, sulfurous odor of a struck match. The brief flare of the tiny flame was surprisingly warm.

I hate that whenever someone asks me about being Asian American, they immediately assume I'm talking about Chinese or Japanese culture. I usually just give up trying to explain that Indians are Asian too because people here look at me like I have two heads.
I heard the sharp, metallic screech of brakes on a garbage truck. The sound felt like it was scraping directly against my eardrums.
I felt a cold, wet dog nose suddenly press against my hand. The shock of the dampness made me flinch immediately.
I tasted the rich, velvety smoothness of dark chocolate melting on my tongue. The complex bitterness was deeply satisfying.
I remember the chaotic, swirling colors of a tie-dye shirt I tried to make. The messy dye stained my fingers a sickly purplish brown.
It is clear to me now that my difficulty in asking for help stems from a deep-seated pride I didn't realize I carried.
I felt the sticky, humid air of a Georgia summer clinging to my skin. The heavy atmosphere made every breath feel labored.
I smelled the crisp, clean scent of line-dried sheets. Burying my face in the fabric felt like breathing in the sunshine.
I heard the jarring, discordant smash of a piano keyboard being hit all at once. The ugly noise made me wince in genuine pain.
I remember the smooth, icy cold surface of a frozen pond. The deep, cracking sound echoing from the ice terrified me.
I tasted the bland, chalky flavor of an antacid tablet. The gritty residue coated my mouth and made me want to gag.
I felt the sharp, pinpoint prick of a sewing needle sliding under my thumbnail. The sudden jolt of pain was nauseating.
The blinding flash of a camera in a dark room left spots in my vision. I blinked uselessly trying to clear the purple blobs.
I smelled the heavy, cloying scent of decaying lilies in a vase. The rotting floral smell was deeply depressing.
I remember the low, rumbling vibration of an approaching subway train. The shaking platform sent a weird thrill through my boots.
I tasted the incredibly salty seawater when I was knocked over by a wave. The burning sensation in my nose was awful.
I felt the coarse, scratchy fibers of an old welcome mat under my bare feet. The stiff bristles poked painfully at my soles.
I watched a plume of dark exhaust smoke billow out of an old truck. The acrid smell made me cough violently.
I heard the delicate, tinkling sound of wind chimes in a light breeze. The random melody was surprisingly soothing.
I remember the thick, suffocating dust in an old attic. The dry air made my throat scratchy and my eyes water.
I reflect on my childhood and realize that navigating two different cultures made me a chameleon, constantly adjusting to fit in.
I tasted the incredibly sweet, artificial flavor of blue cotton candy. The sugary fluff dissolved instantly, leaving a sticky film on my teeth.
I felt the sudden, alarming drop in my stomach when an elevator stopped too fast. The brief weightlessness made me dizzy.
The bright, garish neon sign outside a motel buzzed with an annoying electrical hum. The flickering red light gave the room a sinister glow.
I smelled the rich, dark aroma of roasted coffee beans in a small cafe. The warm scent felt like a comforting hug.
I heard the loud, startling pop of a balloon bursting right behind me. My shoulders shot up to my ears in pure fright.
I remember the slick, greasy feel of a cheap diner menu. The lingering smell of old fry oil was slightly sickening.
I tasted the sharp, peppery bite of raw arugula in a salad. The intense flavor was unexpected and made me sneeze.
I felt the rough, dry bark of a massive oak tree against my palms. The deep grooves in the wood were fascinating to trace.
The blinding gleam of a freshly waxed floor made me walk incredibly slowly. I was terrified of slipping and making a scene.

Growing up mixed in the South, the term Asian American just never felt like it applied to me or my family's mixed heritage. I usually just check the boxes for White and Indian on forms and ignore the broader label entirely.
I smelled the musty, damp odor of an old basement. The smell of mildew always makes me feel slightly claustrophobic.
I heard the chaotic, high-pitched shrieks of children on a playground. The relentless noise gave me a pulsing tension headache.
I remember the incredibly soft, fuzzy skin of a fresh peach. The warm fruit bruised easily under my gentle grip.
I tasted the coppery, distinct flavor of tap water in a strange city. The unfamiliar taste made me vaguely anxious.
I felt a sudden, sharp cramp in my calf while swimming. The paralyzing pain made me thrash wildly in panic.
I recognize that my intense need for organization is likely a way of dealing with the chaotic feelings I can't easily express.
The blindingly bright screen of my phone in the middle of the night hurt my eyes. The harsh light was a brutal awakening.
I smelled the sharp, acidic tang of vinegar when I dropped a pickle jar. The sour smell seemed to seep into the floorboards forever.
I heard the low, soothing hum of a box fan on a hot night. The steady white noise helped drown out my racing thoughts.
I remember the thick, viscous feel of honey slowly dripping from a spoon. The golden color caught the morning light perfectly.
I tasted the fiery, lingering heat of a jalapeno pepper. The burning sensation made my lips swell and throb.
I felt the soft, yielding resistance of fresh dough as I kneaded it. The smooth texture was deeply satisfying to squish.
