The bright, chaotic flashing of a fire engine's lights lit up my bedroom. The pulsing red glow filled me with a sudden sense of doom.
I smelled the distinct, papery scent of a freshly printed newspaper. The black ink left a faint smudge on my fingertips.
I heard the sharp, metallic clink of keys dropping onto a glass table. The sudden noise made me grit my teeth.
I remember the slick, wet feel of a cold tile floor under my bare feet. The chilling sensation made me instantly wide awake.
I tasted the dull, dusty flavor of a stale cracker. The dry crumb coated my throat and made me cough.
I felt the sudden, alarming pinch of a static shock from a shopping cart. The tiny zap made me swear under my breath.
The blinding glare of a flashlight shone directly into my eyes. The harsh beam left me completely disoriented and angry.
I smelled the pungent, herbal aroma of eucalyptus in a steam room. The sharp scent cleared my sinuses almost painfully.
I heard the low, guttural growl of an unfamiliar dog. The menacing sound made the hair on my arms stand up instantly.
I remember the sticky, tacky feel of spilled soda on a movie theater floor. My shoes made an embarrassing peeling sound with every step.
I tasted the rich, buttery flake of a perfect croissant. The delicate pastry shattered into a million pieces on my plate.
I felt the rough, biting scrape of a dull razor on my leg. The immediate burning sensation told me I was going to have a rash.
The chaotic, jumbled overlapping of voices at a crowded party made my brain shut down. I retreated to the bathroom just to hear myself think.

participants.persona: Emily is a 27-year-old second-generation Chinese American woman, born in the U.S. and living in California.
participants.name: Emily

memories.content: I vaguely remember my mom making dumplings when I was maybe four or five, though I think I just played with the dough.
We went to a theme park in southern California around 2003, and I cried on the teacup ride.
My kindergarten teacher was named Mrs. Smith or maybe Mrs. White, and she always smelled like vanilla.
I had a pink bicycle with streamers that fell off after a week, probably when I was six.
I remember watching some cartoon about a magical dog in the afternoons, though the plot totally escapes me now.
My dad used to take me to a Chinese bakery on Saturdays, and we'd always get the hot dog buns.
I scraped my knee really badly on a driveway, though I can't remember whose house it was.
I think my first best friend was a girl named Chloe, but we lost touch after first grade.
There was a big earthquake when I was little, maybe in 2004, and the chandelier swung back and forth.
I used to hate the smell of bitter melon cooking, and I'd hide in my room until dinner.
We had a family trip to Yosemite when I was around eight, and I'm pretty sure a raccoon stole our bread.
I broke my arm falling off the monkey bars in second or third grade.
My grandma gave me a jade bracelet that I accidentally chipped a few years later.
I took piano lessons from a strict older lady in our neighborhood, maybe Mrs. Lin?
I vividly remember the taste of those little yogurt drinks in the tiny bottles from the Asian market.
I had a pet goldfish that lived for surprisingly long, maybe four years, before my dad flushed it.
Looking back at that mushroom haircut in fourth grade makes me realize how little I cared about fitting in back then.
I used to catch roly-polys in the backyard and keep them in a plastic cup.
There was a girl in my elementary school who always brought lunchables, and I was so jealous of her.
I remember sneaking downstairs to watch TV late at night, probably around 2006.
I went through a phase where I only wore black graphic tees, probably in seventh grade.
I think I had my first crush on a boy named Kevin who sat next to me in science class.
My parents forced me to go to Chinese school on Sundays, which felt like a complete waste of time.
I remember crying in the bathroom after a math test because I thought I failed, but I actually got a B.
We had a school dance where they played that one song by the Black Eyed Peas on repeat.
I tried to learn how to skateboard in middle school and gave up after spraining my ankle.
I remember having a MySpace account where my profile song was something by Avril Lavigne.
My mom and I had a huge fight about my bedtime when I was maybe twelve, and I slammed the door so hard the frame cracked.
I used to walk home with a group of friends and we'd always stop at 7-Eleven for Slurpees.
I got braces in eighth grade and the wax they gave me always tasted like fake cherries.
My freshman year history teacher, Mr. Davis I think, used to show us movies every Friday.
I joined the tennis team sophomore year because my friends did, though I was terrible at it.
I remember taking the SATs in a freezing cold classroom and my pencil broke twice.
I got my driver's license on the second try, sometime in the fall of my junior year.
There was a rumor that the school pool was haunted, which makes absolutely no sense now.
I snuck out of the house once to go to a bonfire at Ocean Beach, but we couldn't even get a fire started.
Looking back at how I misunderstood Gatsby, I realize I was too young to grasp the tragedy of holding onto the past.
My parents bought a new Honda Accord around 2013 and it had that new car smell for months.
I went to prom with a guy from my math class, maybe his name was Jason, but it was purely platonic.
I dyed the ends of my hair red the summer before senior year and it faded to a weird orange.
I remember stressing over college applications so much that I lost a patch of hair.
We went on a field trip to the Monterey Bay Aquarium and I spent the whole time watching the jellyfish.
I had a part-time job at a boba shop where I constantly smelled like cooked tapioca.
I got into a fender bender in the school parking lot, but the other driver just let it go.
I think I won an award for a ceramic bowl I made, though I have no idea where it is now.
My friend Sarah and I used to drive up to the hills just to look at the city lights.
I remember going to a concert in San Francisco and someone spilled a full soda down my back.
Reflecting on that argument with my dad about my major, I see now that his strictness came from his own immigration anxieties.
I used to buy those cheap facial sheet masks in bulk from the Asian beauty store at the mall.
Graduation day was incredibly hot and my gown felt like a literal sauna.
I lived in a tiny dorm room freshman year with a girl from NorCal who always kept the window open.
I remember pulling an all-nighter for a chemistry exam and hallucinating that my textbook was talking.
I joined a cultural club on campus but stopped going after they had too much drama in 2016.
I survived mostly on dining hall pizza and instant ramen for a solid six months.
Taking that psychology class makes me realize how fragile my own memories really are.
I went to a frat party once and someone stole my favorite denim jacket.
I think I dated a guy named Michael for about three months before we mutually ghosted each other.
I adopted a stray kitten that hung around my apartment building, but my landlord made me give it back.
I remember taking a road trip to Joshua Tree for spring break and getting hopelessly lost without cell service.
I got a terrible case of food poisoning from a taco truck near campus in my junior year.
Switching majors felt like a failure then, but it showed me that I define my own path instead of just pleasing my parents.
I remember attending a massive protest in downtown LA, maybe in 2017, and losing my voice from shouting.
My friends and I threw a Friendsgiving dinner where the turkey was completely raw in the middle.
I used to study at this cozy coffee shop on 4th street that always played indie folk music.
I had a terrifying moment where my laptop crashed right before a final paper was due.
I went to a music festival in the desert and the dust storms were absolutely brutal.
I remember calling my mom crying because I felt so overwhelmed by my senior thesis.
I took a ceramics elective just for fun and ended up making a dozen misshapen mugs.
I had a brief phase of trying to become a morning person, which lasted exactly four days.
I clearly recall the relief of handing in my last college assignment, even though I forget what the class was.
I moved into a shared apartment in the Bay Area right after graduation, and the rent was absurdly high.

I remember going to a huge Lunar New Year banquet in San Gabriel when I was maybe eight or nine, wearing this itchy red dress my mom bought. Being surrounded by hundreds of other Chinese families eating the same steamed fish always gave me a strong sense of being Chinese.
My first real job interview was over Zoom, and I wore pajama pants on the bottom.
I think my starting salary was around 50k, which felt like a million dollars back then.
I adopted a monstera plant that I accidentally killed by overwatering it within a month.
I remember going on a terrible Hinge date with a guy who talked about cryptocurrency for two hours.
I got a speeding ticket on the 101 freeway because I was spacing out to a podcast.
I tried to cook a traditional Chinese New Year dinner by myself and totally burned the fish.
Feeling that deep isolation during lockdown made me recognize how much I rely on passive social interactions for my mental health.
I binge-watched an entire season of a reality show in one day and felt incredibly gross afterwards.
I started doing yoga from YouTube videos in my living room, though my form was probably terrible.
I got a promotion at work around 2021, though the title change didn't mean much practically.
I remember going to a friend's wedding in Santa Barbara and crying during the vows.
I bought a really expensive espresso machine on impulse and I use it maybe once a month.
I had a minor health scare involving a weird mole, but the dermatologist said it was nothing.
I took a weekend trip to Seattle and it rained the entire time, just like everyone said it would.
I remember fighting with my roommate about the AC bill, which got surprisingly petty.
I started a book club with some friends, but we basically just drank wine and gossiped.
I volunteered at an animal shelter for a few weeks before my allergies made me quit.
I remember finding a beautiful vintage jacket at a thrift store in Oakland for only ten dollars.
I went through a breakup that was really messy, mostly because neither of us wanted to move out.
I've always had a habit of biting my nails when I'm anxious, which I think started in high school.
I can't stand the texture of velvet, it always sends shivers down my spine.
I remember my dad trying to teach me chess when I was little, but I never grasped the strategy.
I have a vague memory of losing a tooth in an apple, but I'm not sure if that was me or my cousin.
I always order my boba with 50 percent sweetness, though I occasionally forget and regret it.
I think I used to be allergic to penicillin, but a doctor told me recently I probably outgrew it.
I remember watching my grandma fold origami cranes, her hands moving so fast I couldn't track them.
My refusal to parallel park makes me realize how much my daily choices are dictated by irrational avoidance.
I used to love the smell of gasoline at the pump when I was a kid.
I have this recurring dream where my teeth fall out, which usually happens when work is stressful.
I remember finding a 20 dollar bill on the sidewalk outside a grocery store in high school.
I tried going vegan for about three weeks in college before breaking down for a cheeseburger.
I accidentally sent a screenshot of a text conversation to the person I was talking about.
I remember the exact smell of the library in my elementary school, a mix of dust and old paper.
I bought a pair of roller skates during lockdown but only used them twice in the park.
My parents kept a giant jar of tiger balm in the medicine cabinet that seemed to cure everything.
I think I saw a celebrity at a coffee shop in West Hollywood once, but I couldn't place their name.
I have a scar on my chin from tripping over a vacuum cord when I was a toddler.
I remember being obsessed with collecting gel pens in middle school and organizing them by color.
I once left my phone on the roof of my car and drove off, totally shattering the screen.
I recall celebrating the Mid-Autumn Festival in our backyard, eating mooncakes that were too dense.
My mom always made me drink this weird herbal soup when I had a cold, and I still hate the taste.
Translating for my grandparents often made me painfully aware of my own fractured connection to our heritage.
I think my dad used to sing karaoke in the living room on weekends, mostly old Teresa Teng songs.
We took family photos at one of those mall studios in the early 2000s, and everyone looked so stiff.
I have a vague memory of my aunt giving me a red envelope with a hundred dollars, which felt illegal.
Visiting family in Taiwan always felt like a weird disconnect, and I realize now I was just grieving a culture I never fully belonged to.
My parents never said 'I love you' out loud, but they always cut up fruit for me after dinner.
I remember the plastic covers on my grandparents' couches that squeaked every time I moved.
I once threw away a traditional lunch my mom packed because the other kids made fun of the smell.
I went to a sleepover in fifth grade where we played light as a feather, stiff as a board.
I remember my friend Jess convinced me to cut my own bangs, which was an absolute disaster.
We used to spend hours at the mall food court just doing nothing, probably around 2012.
I think I accidentally ruined a surprise party by texting the birthday girl about it.
I had a falling out with a close friend in college over something so petty I can't even remember the details.
I remember taking endless photobooth pictures on my Mac with those weird distorted filters.
I went to a Halloween party dressed as a vampire, but the fake blood stained my teeth pink for days.
I used to share a Spotify playlist with a crush, obsessively analyzing every song he added.
My friends and I did an escape room for my 24th birthday and we failed miserably.
I remember gossiping in the back of Mrs. Carter's math class until she moved my seat.
I took a flight to New York when I was twenty and my ears wouldn't pop for two days.

My dad is always forwarding me these random news articles about Shanghai from his WeChat groups, usually mixed with U.S. headlines translated into Chinese. I also catch bits of what is happening over there when my parents leave some international channel playing loudly in the living room on Sunday mornings.
I remember walking across the Golden Gate Bridge and freezing because the wind was so intense.
We went to a beach in Hawaii, maybe Maui, and the sand burned the bottoms of my feet.
I stayed in a questionable hostel in Europe after college where the shower only had cold water.
I think I lost my favorite sunglasses on a train ride to Chicago a few years ago.
I remember seeing snow falling for the first time in Lake Tahoe and trying to catch it on my tongue.
I went camping in Big Sur and woke up to find our cooler entirely ravaged by animals.
I took a road trip down the PCH with my college roommate, blasting Fleetwood Mac the whole way.
I vividly remember the dizzying feeling of standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon in 2015.
I got lost in the Tokyo subway system for three hours but ended up finding a great ramen spot.
I spilled coffee all over my keyboard during my first week at my current job.
I remember hiding in a bathroom stall to cry after getting a harsh performance review.
I had a boss named David who always used corporate buzzwords like 'synergy' unironically.
I accidentally replied all to a company-wide email with a weird typo, which was mortifying.
I remember the free snacks in the office kitchen being the only thing keeping me going on Fridays.
Pushing through the fear of negotiating my salary made me realize I finally value my own worth.
I had a coworker who clipped his fingernails at his desk, which drove me absolutely insane.
I remember presenting a project on exactly three hours of sleep and completely blanking on a slide.

During my freshman year around 2014, a guy yelled some nasty slur at me and my Korean friend outside a boba shop. After that, we started hanging out exclusively at the Asian American student center because being around other Asians was the only place we felt totally safe.
I went to a corporate retreat where we did trust falls, which felt like a massive cliché.
I took a sick day to just lay in bed and watch movies because I was feeling completely burnt out.
I remember waiting in line at midnight for a Harry Potter book release, maybe the sixth one.
I was completely obsessed with a boy band in middle school and covered my binders in their photos.
I think I watched the movie Titanic five times in one weekend when I first discovered it.
I clearly recall exactly where I was when I found out a famous actor died, though the year is fuzzy.
I used to play The Sims for ten hours straight until my eyes watered from staring at the screen.
I remember thinking Twilight was the peak of literature when I was fourteen.
I binge-read a whole fantasy series in high school instead of studying for my AP exams.
I was weirdly invested in YouTube vloggers during college and felt like they were actual friends.
I remember being terrified by a horror movie trailer I saw on TV when I was seven.
I beat a notoriously hard video game boss after fifty tries and felt an embarrassing amount of pride.
I remember eating an incredibly juicy peach over the sink one summer in high school.
I tried making sourdough bread during the pandemic and produced an inedible brick.
My grandmother used to steam fish with ginger and scallions, which is my ultimate comfort food.

When we visited Beijing a few years ago, maybe in 2018 or 2019, I could not even order a coffee without the cashier giving me a weird look over my broken Mandarin. It was super awkward feeling like a total foreigner in a place my relatives call home.
I think I ate nothing but Hot Cheetos for lunch for an entire semester in eighth grade.
I had a legendary late-night diner run where I ate an entire plate of chili cheese fries by myself.
I remember the taste of the overly sweet generic ketchup in the middle school cafeteria.
I discovered a tiny sushi place hidden in a strip mall that has the best spicy tuna rolls.
I once accidentally took a bite of a decorative wax apple thinking it was real.
I recall eating dim sum with my family on Sunday mornings, the carts rolling around loudly.
I tried oysters for the first time on a date and spent the whole evening worried about food poisoning.
I remember getting a terrible static shock from a shopping cart at Target.

Every couple of weeks, I try to FaceTime my grandma in Guangzhou, though the connection is usually terrible and we just end up yelling over the static. Even with the time difference, sending her pictures of my life here and asking about her garden helps me feel tied to where my family came from.

I filled out a demographic survey at work last month and hesitated before checking the Asian American box, because the term sometimes feels like it erases my specific background. It just seems like a broad corporate buzzword that lumps together people who have totally different cultures.
I found a stray dog wandering in my neighborhood and sat with it until animal control arrived.
I think I left my umbrella on the bus during a torrential downpour in 2019.
I remember the satisfying crunch of stepping on dry autumn leaves on my walk to school.
I tried to do a DIY home haircut tutorial and ended up having to wear a hat for a month.
I have a habit of reading the last page of a book before I'm halfway through it.
I remember getting stuck in an elevator for twenty minutes and trying not to panic.
I bought a lottery ticket on my eighteenth birthday and won exactly two dollars.
I was chased by a territorial goose near a pond, dropping my bag in the mud.
I remember the hum of the old refrigerator in my childhood home, which used to lull me to sleep.
I realized recently that I talk exactly like my mom when I'm stressed out.
I remember looking in the mirror on my 25th birthday and feeling like a fraud in an adult's body.
I found my old diaries from middle school and was mortified by how intensely I felt everything.
I think my fear of swimming stems from being pushed into the deep end at a pool party when I was ten.
I remember watching the sunset over the Pacific and realizing how small my daily worries actually are.
I look back at my first relationship and realize I just wanted the validation of being chosen.
I remember moving neighborhoods in third grade, and the new house smelled like fresh paint for weeks.
I remember my dad tearing up at my college graduation, but he quickly wiped it away and suggested we go eat.
I caught myself apologizing to a mannequin at a department store once because I bumped into it.
I spent an entire Saturday deep cleaning my apartment before my parents visited, scrubbing the baseboards until my hands ached.
I recall catching a foul ball at a baseball game when I was younger, though I don't follow the sport at all.
I accidentally washed a red sock with all my white shirts and just accepted my new pink wardrobe.
I remember staying up until dawn just talking to my roommate about the universe during sophomore year.
I have this lingering memory of a thunderstorm rattling our windows while I felt perfectly safe under my blankets.

participants.persona: Grace is a 30-year-old second-generation Hong Konger American woman, born in the U.S. and living in New York.
participants.name: Grace

memories.content: I remember the smell of my grandmother's steamed fish with ginger and scallion, though I can't recall what her kitchen looked like.
The plastic covers on my aunt's couches used to stick to my legs during humid New York summers.
Someone once told me my English was really good, and I remember feeling confused because I was born in the Bronx.
I stole a piece of white Rabbit candy from a bodega once and felt guilty about it for months.
My mom used to hold my hand tight crossing Canal Street, the fishy smell of the markets washing over us.
I remember the red envelopes at Lunar New Year being so crisp, but I never remember how much money was actually in them.
My brother and I used to fight over the TV remote, though I have no idea what shows we were actually trying to watch.
I felt a sharp pang of embarrassment when kids at school pointed out the thermos of congee I brought for lunch.
I vaguely recall a massive thunderstorm that knocked out our power, and my dad lighting tall red temple candles in the living room.
Looking back at how I rejected my mother's cooking in middle school, I realize how deeply I just wanted to assimilate.
I remember the exact rough texture of the carpet in my third-grade classroom.
We took a trip to Hong Kong when I was eight, and the only thing I distinctly remember is the dizzying heat and the rattling double-decker trams.
My dad taught me to ride a bike in a paved schoolyard, but I can't remember which weekend it was.
I once found my mom crying at the kitchen table over some bills, and I quietly backed out of the room so she wouldn't see me.
It makes me sad to reflect on how rarely I practice speaking Cantonese now, knowing I'm slowly losing my connection to my grandparents.
I used to catch fireflies in a jar during summer camp in upstate New York, mesmerized by their fading green light.
The first time I tried coffee it was from a corner cart, and it was so sweet and milky I thought it tasted like melted ice cream.
I remember falling off the monkey bars and the sudden, breathless impact with the woodchips, though I forget who carried me to the nurse.
My childhood best friend had a beagle that smelled strongly of wet corn chips.
I recognize now that my need to constantly be productive is a direct inheritance from my immigrant parents' survival mindset.
I remember the distinct chime of the Mister Softee truck echoing down our street.
We had a bulky desktop computer in the corner of the living room where I'd spend hours playing educational CD-ROM games.
I lied to my parents about where I was going on the night of my senior prom because I was dating someone they didn't approve of.
The smell of chlorine always brings back the echoing sounds of the YMCA indoor pool where I took swimming lessons.
I often think about how my perception of success was entirely shaped by the narrow expectations of my high school environment.
There was a bakery in Chinatown that sold the best egg tarts, but I think it closed down years ago.
I remember the agonizing wait for college acceptance letters, checking the mail with a tight knot in my stomach every afternoon.
My first kiss was clumsy and tasted faintly of spearmint gum, though the boy's face is a blur to me now.
I used to collect metro cards with different advertisements on the back and keep them in a shoebox under my bed.
It's strange to realize that I spent so much of my youth trying to leave New York, only to end up moving back here as an adult.
I remember walking across the Brooklyn Bridge at sunset, the city skyline glowing orange and pink.
I had a severe allergic reaction to something I ate at a potluck, and the panic of not being able to breathe still haunts me.
The radiator in my first apartment used to clang so loudly in the middle of the night that it would wake me from dead sleep.
I remember buying a cheap, scratchy scarf from a street vendor during a sudden snowstorm because I had underestimated the cold.
Reflecting on my college friendships, I can see how heavily I relied on people-pleasing to feel a sense of belonging.
I threw up in a cab after a Halloween party in my early twenties, feeling immensely guilty for the driver.
There was a specific professor who told me I was a strong writer, and that one comment completely changed my major.
I remember the heavy, dusty smell of the university library basement where I used to hide and study.
I adopted a dying succulent from a roommate and somehow managed to keep it alive for five years.
I look back on my early career ambitions and realize I had no idea what I actually wanted, I just wanted to sound impressive to others.
I remember the terrifying jolt of the subway car coming to a sudden halt in a dark tunnel for twenty minutes.
I used to sit on my fire escape and smoke cigarettes I had stolen from my older cousin, pretending I was in a movie.
The taste of instant ramen always reminds me of pulling all-nighters during finals week.
I went to a concert at a tiny indie venue in Williamsburg, and the bass was so loud my chest vibrated for hours after.
It's funny to think about how I used to view thirty as being so old and settled, when I currently feel like I'm still figuring out the basics.
I remember accidentally dropping my phone onto the subway tracks and the sinking feeling of watching it shatter.
My grandmother gave me a jade bangle that I wear every day, though I forget the exact occasion she gifted it to me.
I had a really intense argument with a close friend over something trivial, and we just never spoke again after that day.
The feeling of taking off my heavy winter boots after trudging through slush is one of the most satisfying reliefs.
When I observe my interactions with authority figures now, I see the lingering effects of being raised to never talk back.
I remember standing in a crowded bar trying to shout over the music, but I have no idea whose birthday we were celebrating.
I found a hidden rooftop garden in the city once and sat there for hours, enjoying the rare silence.
I accidentally walked out of a grocery store without paying for a bottle of water and felt paranoid about it the entire walk home.
The smell of roasting nuts from the street carts always reminds me of the chaotic rush hour in Midtown.
I often ponder how my taste in art has shifted from seeking beauty to seeking things that just make me feel understood.
I remember crying on the J train after a terrible job interview, hoping my sunglasses hid my tears from the other commuters.
There was a stray cat that used to sleep on the hood of my neighbor's car, and I would leave out small bowls of milk.
I took a spontaneous weekend trip to Montreal and survived mostly on croissants and bad French.
I remember the sheer panic of waking up realizing I slept through my alarm on the morning of a major presentation.
I recognize that my reluctance to ask for help is just my ego trying to protect me from appearing vulnerable.
I bought a ridiculously expensive pair of shoes for a wedding, and they gave me such bad blisters I had to walk home barefoot.
The first time I saw snow fall in Central Park, the whole city felt completely hushed and magical.
I remember a brief period where I was obsessed with making sourdough bread, though the starter eventually died of neglect.
I had a panic attack in a fitting room once because the fluorescent lights and the mirrors suddenly felt intensely suffocating.
A stranger complimented my coat on the street, and that tiny interaction genuinely turned my whole bad week around.
I remember the agonizing awkwardness of a first date where we had absolutely nothing to talk about.
I used to love going to the botanical garden in the spring, surrounded by the overwhelming scent of cherry blossoms.
I once sent a highly critical text about a coworker to that exact coworker by mistake, and my stomach still drops thinking about it.

I remember feeling this sudden, intense urge to practice my Cantonese after the 2019 protests started. It just felt like if I didn't hold onto the language, a piece of our history would be erased forever.
The feeling of the hot sun on my shoulders during a beach trip to the Rockaways is a sensation I crave in February.
Evaluating my dating history, I can see a clear pattern of choosing emotionally unavailable partners to avoid true intimacy.
I remember the rhythmic thumping sound the washing machine made in my childhood apartment building's basement.
I bought a lottery ticket on my eighteenth birthday just because I finally could, but I didn't even win a dollar.
I got lost in the Met museum for an entire afternoon, wandering through the Egyptian wing until my feet ached.
I kept a diary when I was twelve that I later burned out of intense embarrassment.
The specific shade of yellow of the NYC taxis always feels like a welcoming beacon when I return from a long trip.
I remember the deep comfort of eating hot pho on a freezing day, the steam fogging up my glasses completely.
I accidentally called my third-grade teacher Mom, and the whole class laughed at me.
I was once stranded at an airport overnight and slept on my backpack, waking up with a terrible crick in my neck.
I remember the smell of damp earth after a summer storm in a park, though I forget who I was walking with.
I often reflect on the fact that I am living a life my ancestors could barely have imagined, yet I still find reasons to complain.
I vividly remember the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during a hike in the Hudson Valley.
I used to practice my signature over and over in my notebooks, trying to make it look effortless and mature.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk once and bought pizza for my friends with it.
I remember the sickening crunch of a minor car accident I was in, and the immediate adrenaline spike that followed.
The neon signs in Times Square always gave me a slight headache, even as a kid.
I drank way too much tequila at a college party and woke up with a pounding headache and missing my left shoe.
I remember the soft, worn texture of my favorite childhood teddy bear, whose button eye had fallen off.

Every Sunday morning, my mom would FaceTime my aunties back in Kowloon, and I'd sit there listening to the familiar street noise through the phone. Even now, hearing the ding of a WhatsApp message instantly makes me feel tethered to a city thousands of miles away.
I watched a street performer play a saxophone so beautifully that I actually missed my train to stay and listen.
I remember the frustrating feeling of trying to untangle my wired earphones on a crowded commute.
Sometimes I realize that my fear of public speaking is just a fear of being fundamentally misunderstood by others.
I had a phase where I exclusively wore black clothing because I thought it made me look like a serious New Yorker.
I remember the specific salty breeze at Coney Island, mixed with the smell of funnel cake and frying oil.
I failed my first driving test because I parallel parked too far from the curb, and I cried out of sheer frustration.
The sound of pigeons cooing always reminds me of early mornings in my first studio apartment.

Growing up in Queens, I used to just say I was American, but then I started calling myself Asian American in college to find a community. Lately though, I make sure to specify I'm a Hong Konger, realizing how my own need for belonging has shifted to prioritize my family's specific roots over a broad umbrella.
I remember the intense burn of eating way too much wasabi by accident, my eyes watering uncontrollably.
I kept a drawer full of old concert tickets until the ink completely faded from all of them.
I hid in my room during a massive family dispute, covering my ears so I wouldn't have to hear the yelling.
The smooth, cold metal of the subway pole is a sensation permanently etched into my tactile memory.
I remember baking a batch of chocolate chip cookies that turned out hard as rocks, but I ate them anyway.
Thinking about how much time I spend worrying about the future, I realize I rarely allow myself to just exist in the present.
I remember the quiet hum of the air conditioner during the hottest days of August.
I once slipped on a patch of black ice and bruised my tailbone so badly I couldn't sit properly for weeks.
I got a terrible haircut the day before senior photos and tried to fix it myself with kitchen scissors.
The smell of a specific brand of sunscreen immediately transports me back to family trips to Jones Beach.
I remember the overwhelming relief of finally hitting submit on a massive project I had procrastinated on.
I used to secretly read my older sister's magazines, fascinated by the adult world they portrayed.
I had a recurring nightmare as a kid about being chased through a maze, and I still remember the feeling of heavy legs.

I remember a diversity mixer where everyone was grouped as Asian American, and I just felt completely alienated because it glossed over the specific political tensions between Hong Kong and mainland China. I stopped using the label as much after that, feeling like it just masked the painful realities my family was facing.
The glow of the city lights reflecting off the low clouds always made the night sky look a hazy purple.
I remember the sharp sting of a papercut from a fresh Manila folder at my first office job.
I notice that I constantly apologize for things that aren't my fault, which I now realize is a reflex to maintain harmony.
I bought a cheap umbrella from a drugstore that immediately inverted and broke in the wind, leaving me drenched.
I remember the satisfying snap of opening a fresh can of tennis balls, even though I was terrible at the sport.
I found a love letter from my dad to my mom hidden in a book, and reading it made me feel like I was invading their privacy.
The taste of a perfectly ripe peach in the middle of summer is something I look forward to all year.
I remember the eerie silence of walking home during a heavy snowfall, when the snow muffles all the city noise.
I used to collect smooth sea glass at the beach, convinced they were rare treasures.
I had a panic-inducing moment when I couldn't find my passport the night before an international flight.
The smell of permanent markers always reminds me of making posters for school projects on the living room floor.
I remember the jarring screech of the garbage trucks waking me up at 6 AM every Tuesday.
When I look at my tendency to ghost people, I recognize it as a cowardly way of avoiding uncomfortable confrontations.
I dropped a brand new slice of pizza facedown on the pavement and actually considered eating it anyway.
I remember the intense, vibrating energy of the crowd at the New Year's Eve parade in Chinatown.
I got stung by a bee on my eyelid when I was seven, and my face swelled up so much I couldn't open that eye.
The crinkling sound of a plastic grocery bag always makes my cat come running, thinking it's treats.
I remember the distinct bitterness of the herbal medicine my mom would force me to drink when I had a cough.

I got lost on the MTR during my last visit to Hong Kong because my Cantonese is so rusty and I couldn't read the signs fast enough. The impatient sighs from the locals rushing past me made it painfully clear how much of a foreigner I actually am there.
I went on a blind date that was so painfully awkward I faked a work emergency to leave early.
I remember the soft, golden light filtering through the blinds on lazy Sunday mornings.
I tried to assemble a piece of IKEA furniture without the manual and ended up having to take the whole thing apart.
I got a parking ticket for moving my car five minutes too late during alternate side parking.
I marvel at how my definition of a 'good day' has shifted from exciting achievements to just having a peaceful, quiet evening.
I remember the exhilarating feeling of riding a roller coaster for the first time, screaming until my throat was raw.
I found a beautiful vintage jacket at a thrift store, but it smelled heavily of mothballs no matter how much I washed it.
I once laughed so hard at a joke my friend made that I actually snorted in a very quiet cafe.
I remember the sharp, metallic smell of the fireworks on the Fourth of July, the smoke hanging thick in the air.
I had a moment of pure dread when I realized I had left the oven on after leaving for work.
The sight of blooming daffodils always reminds me that the grueling New York winter is finally over.
I remember the sticky, sweet residue left on my hands after eating a candy apple at a street fair.
I accidentally sent a heart emoji to my boss and spent the next hour hyperventilating.
I used to love the feeling of peeling dried school glue off the palms of my hands.
I often think about how my habit of over-explaining myself stems from a deep-seated fear of being misunderstood or disliked.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy quilt my grandmother made, keeping me warm on freezing winter nights.
I got caught in a sudden torrential downpour and had to seek shelter under the awning of a dry cleaner.
I ate a slice of leftover cake for breakfast once and felt strangely rebellious.
I remember the dizzying pattern of the old subway seat fabric, a blur of orange and brown squares.
I found out a partner had been lying to me for months, and I remember the physical sensation of the blood draining from my face.
The sound of classical piano always brings me back to the agonizingly boring recitals I had to sit through as a child.
I remember the satisfying pop of bubble wrap, a compulsion I could never resist.
I tried to dye my own hair in the bathroom sink and ended up staining the porcelain purple for a month.
I went ice skating at Bryant Park and spent more time clinging to the wall than actually skating.
Reflecting on my relationship with my body, I realize how much mental energy I've wasted trying to shrink myself to fit into societal ideals.
I remember the crisp, cold snap of biting into a perfect Fuji apple.
I accidentally stepped in a deep puddle hiding under slush, and my sock was freezing and wet for the rest of the commute.
I went to a midnight movie premiere and the crowd's energy was so electric it gave me goosebumps.
I remember the frustrating sting of a mosquito bite right on my ankle bone.
I had a really dark period of depression in my mid-twenties where taking a shower felt like an insurmountable task.
The smell of freshly cut grass always feels slightly out of place to me when I encounter it in the city.
I remember the hypnotic motion of watching the laundry spin in the laundromat machines.
I burned my tongue on hot soup and couldn't taste anything properly for two days.
I found a perfectly smooth skipping stone at the lake, but failed to make it skip even once.
I recognize now that my intense desire to be fiercely independent was actually a trauma response to avoid being let down.
I remember the chaotic harmony of my aunts playing Mahjong, the clatter of the tiles sounding like a rushing river.
I bought a cheap scented candle that smelled so artificially sweet it gave me an instant migraine.
I was incredibly nervous to speak at my grandfather's funeral, my hands shaking as I held the paper.
The sight of a yellow school bus always makes me recall the distinct smell of diesel exhaust and vinyl seats.
I remember the relief of taking off a heavy backpack after a long hike, feeling instantly lighter.
I accidentally locked myself out of my apartment and had to wait for the super in the hallway wearing my pajamas.
I tried oysters for the first time and immediately gagged on the briny, slimy texture.
I remember the soft, rhythmic clicking of the turnstiles during the morning rush hour.
I had a sudden realization of my own mortality during a turbulent flight, gripping the armrests in pure terror.
Looking at my career trajectory, I wonder if I chose my profession out of genuine passion or just a need for parental approval.
I remember the bright, artificial blue color of the slushies we used to get at the corner store.
I stepped on a piece of chewing gum on a hot day and spent twenty minutes trying to scrape it off my sole.
I got unexpectedly emotional while watching an animated movie on a flight and tried to hide my crying from my seatmate.
The sound of a dial-up modem connecting to the internet is a noise I can still perfectly hear in my head.
I remember the burning shame of being publicly reprimanded by a boss in front of the entire office.
I found a tiny, colorful caterpillar in the park and watched it inch along a leaf for a long time.
I tried to knit a scarf but gave up halfway through, leaving a strange, jagged piece of yarn in my closet.
I remember the feeling of absolute exhaustion after helping a friend move a heavy couch up three flights of stairs.
The smell of chlorine and wet towels always makes me think of the local community pool in the summer.
I see how my tendency to constantly plan for the future robs me of the joy I could be experiencing right now.
I remember the startlingly loud screech of a hawk that had somehow perched on a fire escape opposite my window.
I bought a houseplant that I was assured was indestructible, and it was dead within a month.
I found out I wasn't invited to a close friend's wedding and spent the whole weekend agonizing over what I did wrong.
The taste of a perfectly seasoned everything bagel with scallion cream cheese is my ultimate comfort food.

I vividly recall looking up a local Asian American candidate's stance on the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement before filling out my ballot. I simply couldn't bring myself to support him when I saw he refused to condemn the crackdowns back home, regardless of his local platform.
I remember the sensation of static electricity clinging to my clothes when pulling them out of the dryer.
I slipped on a wet floor in a restaurant and spilled my entire drink on myself, utterly humiliated.
I watched a gorgeous sunset over the Hudson River, the water reflecting a brilliant, shimmering gold.
I remember the sticky heat of the subway platform in July, feeling like I was standing in an oven.
I tried to fix a leaky faucet with duct tape and ended up causing a much bigger flood in my kitchen.
I realize that my habit of minimizing my accomplishments is just a defense mechanism to lower other people's expectations of me.
I remember the soft, glowing light of the paper lanterns during the Mid-Autumn Festival in Chinatown.
I accidentally swallowed a watermelon seed as a kid and spent the entire day terrified a plant would grow in my stomach.
I opened a credit card bill that was significantly higher than I expected, and a wave of pure anxiety washed over me.
The smell of melting asphalt on a scorching summer day always makes me feel fiercely protective of this city.

participants.persona: Aiden is a 28-year-old second-generation Indian and White American man, born in the U.S. and living in Washington, DC.
participants.name: Aiden

memories.content: I vividly remember the smell of rain on hot asphalt during my childhood summers, though I can't recall which friends I was playing with.
We used to go to a diner after little league games, and I remember the sticky red vinyl booths more clearly than any of the games.
I remember realizing in middle school that my mixed identity confused people, which first sparked my ongoing habit of over-explaining myself.
My mom used to make both roast chicken and paneer for Thanksgiving, a chaotic mix of smells that always filled the kitchen.
I recall scraping my knee badly on a gravel driveway, the sharp sting of it, but completely forget how I actually fell.
There was a girl in my fourth-grade class whose name escapes me, but I can perfectly recall the bright yellow of her favorite sweater.
I remember the paralyzing shame of wetting my pants in first grade during story time.
My dad taught me to ride a bike in an empty school parking lot, the sound of my tires echoing off the brick walls.
I recall the exact crushing disappointment of not getting invited to a middle school pool party, a feeling that still stings slightly today.
I used to sit on the floor watching Saturday morning cartoons, enveloped in the soft fuzz of our terrible green carpet.
I remember the taste of overly sweet fruit punch from a plastic cup at some neighborhood block party.
There was a stray cat that hung around our porch, and I remember its rough tongue against my hand, though I don't think we ever named it.
I often think about how my fear of failure stems from watching my father work endless overtime to secure our middle-class life.
I remember the blinding fluorescent lights of the hospital waiting room when my grandmother passed away.
I recall my first taste of alcohol was a sip of cheap beer stolen from a cooler, intensely bitter and warm.
I remember the heavy, suffocating humidity of my first summer after moving to DC, sweating through my dress shirt on the Metro platform.
I can still hear the metallic screech of the red line train pulling into Dupont Circle.
There was a coffee shop near my first apartment where I spent hours reading, though I can't recall a single book I actually read there.
I remember the sting of a breakup in my early twenties, crying uncontrollably in the shower so my roommate wouldn't hear.
I recall the immense relief of finally paying off my first student loan, a weight literally lifting off my chest.
I remember the awkward dinner at my friend's house when his parents told him a C grade was perfectly fine, completely shocking my worldview.
I can perfectly picture the intricate pattern on my Indian grandmother's sari, even though her face is getting blurry in my memory.
I remember the sharp, minty taste of toothpaste when I accidentally swallowed it as a kid.
I recall getting lost in a grocery store as a toddler, the terrifying height of the cereal aisles towering over me.
My first dog had a very distinct corn-chip smell to his paws that I sometimes catch a phantom whiff of even now.
I remember the dull ache of a sprained ankle during a college intramural game, though I can't remember who we were playing against.
I recall the thrill of sneaking onto the roof of my dorm building just to watch the sunrise, feeling invincible.
I remember my first panic attack, the terrifying sensation that the room was shrinking and my lungs had simply stopped working.
I used to have a favorite blue mug that shattered in the sink, and I remember the sharp sound it made more than the mug itself.
I recall meticulously adjusting my tie in the mirror before my first real job interview, my hands shaking slightly.
I remember the specific salty breeze during a family trip to the beach, though the year escapes me.
I recall the heavy, dusty smell of old books in my middle school library.
There was a teacher who told me I wasn't good at math, and I remember the hot flush of embarrassment on my cheeks.
I remember the chaotic noise of my high school cafeteria, a wall of sound that I used to dread facing every day.
I can still taste the cheap pizza we ordered late at night during my freshman year finals week.
I recall the soft hum of the radiator in my first DC apartment, a sound that always helped me sleep.
I remember seeing the Lincoln Memorial at night for the first time, glowing stark white against the dark sky.
I recall buying a huge stack of classic novels at a used bookstore that I simply placed on a shelf and never touched.
I recall the bitter taste of burned coffee from the breakroom at my first internship.

I remember talking to my Tibetan friend in college about how his family insists on speaking their language at home. He seemed so intense about it, like it was a matter of survival, which felt really different from my own family's relaxed attitude toward Hindi.
I remember the acute sting of betrayal when a close friend shared a secret I had confided in them.
I vividly remember the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots on a walk through Rock Creek Park.
I recall the smell of chlorine and the echo of splashes from childhood swimming lessons.
I remember the soft, worn fabric of my favorite childhood blanket, though I have no idea where it is now.
I can picture the vibrant orange of the sunset over the Potomac River on an exceptionally clear evening.
I recall the anxiety of parallel parking on a busy DC street while a line of cars honked behind me.
I remember the overwhelming feeling of isolation during my first month living alone, eating cereal for dinner in a quiet room.
I recall the sudden realization that I was avoiding my mother's calls because her anxiety was mirroring my own hidden fears.
I remember the loud crack of thunder that once woke me up in the middle of the night, shaking the entire house.
I can still smell the mix of old grease and sugar from a boardwalk funnel cake stand.
I remember the dull, throbbing pain of a headache after a terrible argument with an ex-partner.
I recall the specific yellow tint of the streetlights in my childhood cul-de-sac.
I remember the physical exhaustion in my legs after completing my first 10K race.
I vividly recall the awkward silence in an elevator ride with my boss, desperately trying to think of something to say.
I remember the comforting warmth of a cup of chai on a freezing winter morning.
I recall the sharp pain of a paper cut from a fresh manila folder at work.
Looking back at my teenage journals, I realize my desire to blend in completely erased my cultural heritage for almost a decade.
I remember the absolute dread of giving a presentation in college, my hands shaking so badly I couldn't read my notes.
I can picture the intricate floral pattern on the living room rug we had when I was eight.
I recall the smell of damp earth after a severe summer thunderstorm rolled through the city.
I remember the thrill of finding a hidden trail in the woods behind my childhood home.
I vaguely remember a family road trip to Florida, mainly the feeling of my legs sticking to the leather car seats.
I recall the blinding glare of the sun reflecting off the snow on a rare DC snow day.
I remember the sweet, sticky taste of melted ice cream running down my hand at a summer festival.
I vividly remember the exact moment my grandfather forgot my name due to his dementia, a cold shock that still hurts to think about.
I recall the rhythmic thumping sound of the washing machine in my old apartment complex.
I remember the relief of stepping into an air-conditioned museum after walking around the National Mall in July.
I recently noticed that my tendency to make jokes during serious conversations is just a defense mechanism to avoid genuine vulnerability.
I can still feel the texture of the rough sand from a beach trip where I got severely sunburned.
I recall the distinctive smell of dry erase markers from my middle school math class.

Whenever my dad FaceTimes his brothers back in Mumbai, the house fills with the loud sound of cricket matches and overlapping voices. I always hover near the screen just to see the background of their living room, feeling this strange warm pull toward a house I have only visited twice.
I remember the terrifying feeling of almost getting hit by a car while biking through an intersection in Adams Morgan.
I vividly remember the deep bass vibrating in my chest at my first live concert, though the band's name escapes me.
I recall the metallic taste of blood after accidentally biting my lip during a nervous tic.
I remember the intense frustration of trying to assemble a bookshelf and stripping the screws.
I can picture the faded blue color of my childhood bedroom walls.
I recall the profound shame of being caught in a lie by my best friend in high school.
I remember the peaceful quiet of an early morning flight, watching the clouds from the window seat.
I often think about how my obsession with keeping my apartment perfectly clean is likely an attempt to control an otherwise unpredictable life.
I recall the unmistakable scent of my dad's aftershave lingering in the bathroom.
I remember the sting of cold wind on my face while waiting for a delayed bus in January.
I can still hear the familiar startup chime of my very first computer.
I vividly remember the crushing anxiety of checking my bank account balance right after college.
I recall the sweet aroma of caramelized onions cooking in my apartment on a lazy Sunday.
I remember the brief, weightless feeling of jumping off a diving board for the first time.
I can picture the neon 'Open' sign of the late-night diner where we used to study.
I recall the sheer embarrassment of tripping on the stairs in front of a packed lecture hall.
I remember sitting alone in a crowded movie theater for the first time, eating popcorn and feeling surprisingly at peace.
I vaguely remember the plot of a terrible movie I saw on a first date, mostly recalling the stale taste of the popcorn.
I recall the distinct crunch of fresh snow under my boots on my walk to the Metro.
I remember the sickening drop in my stomach when I realized I had sent a complaining text about my boss directly to my boss.
I can feel the smooth, cool texture of the marble pillars inside the Library of Congress.
I recall the bitter, herbal taste of a cough syrup my mom used to force me to take.
I vividly remember the chaotic, joyful noise of a Diwali celebration at my aunt's house.
I remember the physical ache in my chest after a terrible fight with my younger sibling.
I can picture the specific tear in the fabric of my favorite pair of old jeans.
I recall the smell of burning wood from a neighbor's fire pit on a crisp autumn evening.
I remember staying up until 4 AM fueled by energy drinks, desperately trying to finish a college paper I had put off for weeks.
I remember the blinding flash of lightning that struck a tree right outside my window.
I recall the sticky feeling of sunscreen mixed with sweat during a summer hike in Shenandoah.
I vaguely remember the face of a kind stranger who helped me pick up my dropped groceries, though I completely forgot what they said.
I remember the profound emptiness of clearing out my childhood bedroom when my parents sold the house.
I vividly recall the satisfying pop of opening a fresh jar of coffee.
I remember the intense, dizzying heat of a packed underground concert venue.
I can still hear the rhythmic squeak of my old sneakers on a hardwood basketball court.
I recall the sharp disappointment of watching a highly anticipated movie and realizing it was terrible.
I remember the deep, guttural feeling of grief at a friend's funeral in my early twenties.
I recently realized that my habit of code-switching between different friend groups has made it hard to know what my actual voice sounds like.
I recall the specific smell of a new car interior from when my parents finally upgraded our old sedan.
I vividly remember the feeling of a cold raindrop hitting the back of my neck perfectly.
I remember the terrifying slide of my tires on a patch of black ice on the Beltway.
I can picture the faded logo on my favorite childhood t-shirt, completely worn away by the wash.
I recall the overwhelming smell of vinegar when dying Easter eggs as a kid.
I remember the sharp, stinging pain of getting a tattoo on my ribcage.
I vaguely remember the chaotic layout of a thrift store where I bought my favorite winter coat.
I recall the deep sense of inadequacy I felt during my first performance review at my corporate job.
I remember the sweet, rich taste of my grandmother's homemade gulab jamun.
I remember wandering aimlessly around a new city for an hour because I absolutely refused to ask anyone for directions.
I recall the deafening roar of cicadas during my first summer living in the mid-Atlantic.
I vividly remember the smell of fresh paint when I finally moved into a place of my own.
I remember the embarrassing squelch of my wet shoes walking through a quiet office after getting caught in a downpour.
I can still feel the precise texture of the rough brick wall I used to lean against while waiting for the school bus.
I recall the sharp taste of a lemon wedge I mistakenly bit into as a toddler.

Going to the Asian American Student Association meetings was the first time I felt like my mixed Indian and White background did not need explaining. We all bonded over the shared experience of balancing our parents' cultures with just trying to be regular American kids.
I remember the feeling of absolute panic when I briefly lost my passport at Dulles Airport.
I can picture the chaotic tangle of power cords under my old desk.
I vaguely recall the melody of a song my mom used to sing to me, though the words are completely gone.
I remember the heavy weight of a terrible secret a friend told me, completely changing how I viewed them.
I realized recently that my constant need to stay busy is just a way to avoid dealing with my underlying anxiety.
I recall the specific rattle of the heating vent in my first car.
I remember the crisp, cold air stinging my lungs during an early morning run around the Tidal Basin.

At my grandmother's funeral, I had to rely on my cousin to translate what the priest was saying, and my chest felt incredibly tight with shame. I just sat there wishing I had paid more attention when my dad tried to teach me Hindi as a kid instead of pushing it away.
I vividly remember the smell of melting wax from blowing out birthday candles.
I can still feel the painful throb of a jammed finger from a poorly caught football.
I recall the blinding, fluorescent glare of a late-night pharmacy aisle.
I remember the profound sense of failure when I was rejected from my dream college.
I can picture the specific shade of green of the park bench where I used to eat my lunch.
I vaguely remember the plot of my favorite childhood book, mostly recalling the texture of its torn cover.
I recall the smell of roasted peanuts from a street vendor outside a baseball stadium.
I recall nervously attempting to mediate a screaming match between my two best friends, feeling sick to my stomach the whole time.
I remember the exact feeling of an ice cube sliding down my back during a prank at summer camp.
I recall the mesmerizing glow of fireflies in my backyard on a humid July evening.
I vividly remember the bitter taste of an oversteeped cup of green tea.
I can still hear the annoying, high-pitched hum of a dying fluorescent bulb in my old classroom.
I recall the terrifying jolt of turbulence on a flight that made everyone in the cabin gasp.
I remember the deep, lingering sting of a discriminatory remark passed off as a joke by a coworker.
I can picture the intricate spider web covered in morning dew that I almost walked into.
I vaguely remember the face of my first grade teacher, mostly recalling her overpowering floral perfume.
I recall the comforting, heavy weight of a lead apron at the dentist's office.
Looking back, I realize that I often mask my genuine opinions just to avoid being perceived as difficult or argumentative.
I remember the distinct smell of ozone right before a massive thunderstorm hit the city.
I vividly recall the satisfying crunch of biting into a perfectly crisp apple.
I remember the embarrassing sensation of my stomach growling loudly during a silent meeting.
I can still feel the rough, scratchy wool of a terrible holiday sweater my aunt gifted me.
I recall the metallic smell of loose change resting in the cupholder of my car.
I remember the crushing realization that I was in a toxic relationship and entirely unsure of how to leave it.
I can picture the specific dent in the bumper of my first car.
I vaguely remember the chaos of a childhood birthday party at a roller rink, mainly the smell of old skates.
I recall the sharp hiss of opening a carbonated drink that had been shaken.
I recently noticed that my obsession with organizing my digital files is a strange coping mechanism for feeling out of control in my real life.
I remember the blindingly bright reflection of the sun on the windshield of an oncoming car.
I vividly recall the smell of damp cardboard from moving boxes piled in the rain.
I remember the mild panic of realizing I left my credit card at a bar the night before.
I can still taste the overpowering garlic from a terrible pasta dish I attempted to cook in college.
I recall the specific sound of crickets chirping loudly on a camping trip in the Blue Ridge Mountains.
I remember the profound loneliness of spending a major holiday entirely by myself.
I can picture the peeling paint on the ceiling of my first, incredibly cheap apartment.

During the last election cycle, my uncle kept praising a candidate who promised stronger trade ties with India, completely ignoring the politician's terrible stance on local healthcare. We got into a huge argument at the dinner table because I could not understand voting just based on what happens overseas.
I vaguely remember a documentary about the ocean I watched as a kid, mostly recalling the eerie glow of deep-sea fish.
I recall the smell of fresh basil from the tiny herb garden I tried to grow on my windowsill.
I recall eating the exact same turkey sandwich for lunch every day for an entire year out of sheer convenience.
I remember the unmistakable screech of a dial-up modem connecting to the internet.
I vividly recall the freezing shock of stepping into a surprisingly cold shower.
I remember the immense frustration of waiting in a seemingly endless line at the DMV.
I can still feel the sticky residue of a peeled-off price tag on the back of a book.
I recall the overwhelming smell of bleach in a public swimming pool locker room.
I remember the intense shame of being harshly reprimanded by a teacher in front of my peers.

I remember filling out a hospital intake form and hesitating over the race boxes before finally checking both White and Asian Indian. Depending on whether I was at my mom's family reunions in Ohio or a South Asian community event in DC, people always seemed to treat me as belonging to completely different groups.
I can picture the specific pattern of cracks in the sidewalk outside my childhood home.
I vaguely remember a museum field trip, mostly the echoing sound of hundreds of footsteps in the grand hall.
I recall the sharp taste of an Altoid mint that was far too strong.
I reflect on my childhood and realize that my intense independence was actually a trauma response to my parents' emotional unavailability.
I remember the precise click of a deadbolt sliding into place on my front door.
I vividly recall the smell of burning rubber from a car doing burnouts down the street.
I remember the slight dizziness of standing up too fast after lying on the couch for hours.
I can still feel the incredibly soft fur of a rabbit I pet at a county fair.
I recall the specific hum of the refrigerator kicking into gear in the middle of a quiet night.
I remember the deep sorrow of realizing a close friendship had simply faded away over time without any dramatic fallout.
I can picture the vibrant red color of a cardinal that landed on my balcony rail.
I vaguely remember a piano recital I had, focusing entirely on the blinding spotlight rather than the music.
I recall the smell of fresh sawdust from a construction site near my office.
I often realize that my tendency to over-prepare for conversations is just an illusion of control over how people perceive me.
I remember the distinct, hollow thud of a dropped watermelon in the grocery store aisle.
I vividly recall the stinging pain of a sudden paper cut from a glossy magazine page.
I remember the minor relief of a canceled meeting that I hadn't prepared for.
I can still taste the smoky char of a perfectly grilled hot dog at a Fourth of July barbecue.
I recall the blinding flash of a speed camera going off on New York Avenue.
I remember the intense, irrational fear I felt when an unknown number called me late at night.
I can picture the intricate frost patterns on my bedroom window during a deep freeze.
I realized the other day that my comfort with moving to new cities is just a way to outrun my fear of settling down and being truly known.

participants.persona: Ethan is a 25-year-old second-generation Hong Konger American man, born in the U.S. and living in Virginia.
participants.name: Ethan

memories.content: I remember the sharp, stinging smell of winter air waiting for the school bus, though I can't recall what grade I was in.
The egg tarts at that one bakery in Eden Center always tasted impossibly sweet, but I completely forget the name of the shop.
I felt a deep, twisting shame when I forgot my Cantonese during a phone call with my grandmother, making me realize how much of my heritage I was losing.
There was a bright red jacket I wore constantly as a kid, mostly because the nylon made a satisfying swish sound when I ran.
I recall the humid, suffocating heat of Virginia summers pressing against the car window, but I don't remember where we were driving.
Sometimes I think back to the first time I saw the Hong Kong skyline at night; it made me feel incredibly small yet connected to something vast.
My dad used to bring home char siu wrapped in white butcher paper, and I can still picture the sticky red sauce clinging to the edges.
I distinctly remember the sickening drop in my stomach when I lied to my parents about failing a math test.
We used to catch fireflies in a glass jar in the backyard, their glow fading so quickly that I always felt a weird sense of guilt afterward.
The cafeteria pizza in middle school had this distinct, cardboard-like texture that I actually miss sometimes.
I remember the exact shade of blue my childhood bedroom was painted, though I can't recall if my dad or a painter did it.
There was a girl in my freshman year who laughed at my lunch, and to this day I find myself instinctively hiding my food when eating around new people.
My mother's voice sounded so melodic when she spoke to her sisters on the phone, a stark contrast to her sharp English.
I can almost feel the rough grip of my first skateboard tape, but I have no idea who taught me how to push.
The sound of rain hitting the roof of my first apartment always brings back a profound feeling of loneliness from that year.
I remember the blinding fluorescent lights of the Chinese weekend school I was forced to attend.
There was a massive snowstorm when I was around ten, and the silence of the neighborhood afterward felt almost sacred.
I scraped my knee badly on a gravel path at a park in Fairfax, and I can still see the little grey pebbles embedded in the cut.
The smell of incense in our house always meant a holiday or an anniversary, though I rarely knew exactly what we were praying for.
I remember the bitter taste of a cheap beer at my first college party, feeling entirely out of place and wondering why I tried so hard to fit in.
Driving down the Blue Ridge Parkway in the fall was a blur of orange and red leaves.
I can still picture the disappointed look on my mom's face when I told her I didn't want to play piano anymore, a moment that still stings.
The heavy bass from a concert in DC rattled my chest so hard I couldn't breathe, though I forgot the band's name years ago.
I remember tracing the condensation on a cold glass of milk tea, the ice clinking softly as I dragged it across the table.

I remember staying up late during the 2019 protests, feeling a sickening knot in my stomach as I watched tear gas flood the streets of Mong Kok on a LIHKG live stream. I can't recall if my cousins texted me the link first or if I found it myself, but the frantic translation of Apple Daily articles for my American friends left me exhausted and terrified.
My first breakup happened in a dim parking lot, and the overwhelming feeling of dread is much clearer than anything we actually said.
I bought a cheap watch at a night market during our trip to Kowloon, mesmerized by the neon lights reflecting off the plastic face.
The smell of chlorine at the community pool always reminds me of endless, lazy afternoons.
I remember staring at a college rejection letter and realizing my entire worth had been tied to academic validation.
The crunch of autumn leaves under my sneakers on the walk to high school was oddly satisfying.
I got lost in a massive Asian supermarket once, surrounded by walls of rice bags that looked like towering buildings.
My grandfather's hands were incredibly rough when he handed me a red envelope, the golden characters embossed on the paper feeling foreign.
I remember the intense, vibrating energy of my first time driving alone on I-66, gripping the steering wheel until my knuckles turned white.
I once stole a small toy from a corner store, and the lingering paranoia made me realize I lacked the stomach for rebellion.
The warmth of the laundry fresh out of the dryer is a sensation I still seek out when I'm feeling down.
I remember the distinct, metallic taste of blood after getting hit in the face with a basketball.
Sitting by the James River, I watched the water flow over rocks and felt entirely at peace, though I don't remember who I was with.
I remember the soft hum of the radiator in my dorm room, a sound that became the soundtrack to my late-night cram sessions.
When my parents fought, they spoke rapid Cantonese, and I remember hiding in my room focusing only on the sharp tones of their voices.
I found an old photo of my parents in Hong Kong before they immigrated, and it struck me how young and unguarded they looked.
The first time I tried oysters, the briny, slimy texture made me gag instantly.
I vividly recall the smell of damp earth after a spring thunderstorm in Virginia.
There was a stray cat I used to feed behind our townhouse; I can still see its patchy orange fur.
The quietness of the library on a Sunday morning always felt like a sanctuary to me.
I remember the crushing anxiety before presenting my senior project, my hands sweating so much the note cards warped.
Looking at my reflection in the mirror after shaving my head on a dare, I realized how much I used my hair to hide.
The sweet, milky taste of White Rabbit candy melting in my mouth is one of my strongest childhood memories.
I remember the harsh glare of oncoming headlights during a long night drive back from Charlottesville.
A teacher once mispronounced my last name so badly that the whole class laughed, and the heat in my cheeks is something I can still feel.
I still remember the exact pitch of the dial-up internet modem connecting when I wanted to play games online.
When my grandfather passed away, the house felt strangely hollow, making me aware of how much space a person's presence actually occupies.
The thrill of sneaking out of the house at midnight was ruined by the freezing wind cutting through my thin hoodie.
I remember the vibrant yellow of the Ginkgo trees lining the street near my college campus.
There was a specific melody from a music box my aunt gave me that used to lull me to sleep.
The smell of gasoline at the station always reminds me of early morning road trips with my family.
I felt completely detached from my body during a panic attack in a crowded lecture hall, just focusing on the exit sign.
Realizing I preferred staying in rather than going out was a quiet milestone that made me accept my own introversion.
The smooth, cool surface of a mahjong tile sliding under my thumb is a texture I'll never forget.
I remember the chaotic noise of the Star Ferry terminal in Hong Kong, an overwhelming mix of engines and shouting.
The taste of overcooked pasta reminds me of my first attempts at cooking for myself.
I can still picture the intricate, faded patterns on the living room rug we had when I was six.
A friend once betrayed a secret of mine, and the heavy sinking feeling in my chest taught me to keep my cards closer.
The bright, synthetic blue of a slushie I had at the movies stained my tongue for days.
I remember the gentle, rhythmic swaying of the subway car heading into DC.
The sour sting of cheap wine is all I remember from a disastrous blind date.
I remember the rough bark of the oak tree I used to climb, though I don't recall when I stopped climbing it.
Standing in the middle of a crowded bar, I suddenly felt deeply disconnected from everyone, wondering what I was doing with my life.
The warm, comforting scent of congee boiling on the stove usually meant I was sick.
I vividly recall the brilliant orange hues of a sunset I watched from a rooftop, completely mesmerized.
The feeling of sand between my toes at Virginia Beach was always overshadowed by my fear of jellyfish.
I remember the sharp jolt of electricity from a static shock on a cold winter day.
Finding an old, unsent letter in my desk drawer made me realize how much I struggle with confrontation.
The sound of cicadas screaming in the trees was the constant background noise of my teenage summers.
I remember the distinct, yeasty smell of a bakery early in the morning.
The heavy, suffocating weight of a lead apron at the dentist's office always made me anxious.
I can still feel the intense burn of muscle fatigue after my first marathon attempt.
Looking back at old journals, I noticed how often I complained about things I now cherish, showing me how much my perspective has shifted.
The sticky, sweet residue of a melted popsicle on my fingers is a classic summer memory.
I remember the blinding white snow reflecting the sun after a massive blizzard.
The sharp, acidic taste of a lemon drop candy always makes my jaw tingle.
I remember the low, rumbling thunder that preceded a massive summer storm rolling in.
Realizing that I had picked up my dad's habit of pacing while on the phone made me feel unexpectedly connected to him.
The soft, worn cotton of my favorite t-shirt felt like armor on days I was anxious.
I remember the overwhelming scent of pine needles in a Christmas tree lot.
The dizzying spin of a carnival ride left me nauseous for hours, though I forget the fair's name.
I remember the terrifying stillness of a hospital waiting room when a family member was in surgery.
Admitting to myself that I was in a toxic relationship was the hardest, most liberating moment of my twenties.
The crisp, clean smell of a new notebook always inspired me at the start of a school year.
I remember the satisfying snap of a fresh green bean when helping my mom prep dinner.
The freezing, sharp wind on a ski lift made my eyes water uncontrollably.
I can still hear the rhythmic squeak of sneakers on a hardwood basketball court.
There was a time I lost my wallet, and the sheer panic taught me how fragile my sense of security really was.
The rich, savory aroma of roast duck hanging in a shop window always made my mouth water.
I remember the fuzzy, static feeling of a dead TV channel late at night.
The sudden, terrifying skid of my car on black ice is burned into my memory.
I remember the gentle, warm breeze rustling the leaves on a perfect spring afternoon.
Looking at a painting in an art museum, I unexpectedly started crying, realizing how much pent-up emotion I was carrying.
The bitter, lingering taste of burnt coffee is something I tolerate more than I enjoy.
I remember the soft, squishy texture of a fresh steam bun from a dim sum cart.
The sharp, piercing wail of a siren at night always makes me tense up.
I can still picture the complex network of cracks on my old phone screen.
The realization that I was an adult came quietly while buying groceries, a strange shift from feeling like an imposter to just being.
The smell of old books in a second-hand shop always feels comforting and dusty.
I remember the intense, blinding flash of a camera going off in a dark room.
The sudden, sharp pain of a paper cut on my index finger is a vivid memory.
I remember the chaotic, colorful blur of a dragon dance during Lunar New Year.
When I first moved out, the silence of my apartment forced me to confront how much I relied on others for distraction.
The sticky, humid air of a greenhouse always makes it hard to breathe.
I remember the satisfying crunch of walking on fresh, untouched snow.
The deep, resonating bong of a grandfather clock in a quiet house is a sound I rarely hear anymore.
I can still feel the rough, unyielding fabric of a cheap theater seat.
A sudden burst of nostalgia triggered by a pop song made me realize how quickly my college years slipped by.
The sharp, vinegary smell of ketchup on hot fries is a distinct childhood memory.
I remember the eerie, greenish sky right before a severe tornado warning.

Hanging out at the Asian American Student Union at UVA was the first time I felt entirely comfortable bringing bakery cha siu bao to a regular college study session. I forget who originally invited me to the group, but that shared pan-ethnic environment seamlessly connected my Cantonese home life with my everyday Virginia reality.
The soft, powdery texture of powdered sugar always ended up all over my clothes.
I remember the overwhelming feeling of failure when I was fired from my first job.
Catching myself acting defensive in an argument made me aware of my own insecurities, a habit I've tried to break ever since.
The bright, flashing neon signs of a late-night diner are a blur in my mind.
I remember the distinct, earthy smell of wet dog after a walk in the rain.
The sudden, jarring ring of an alarm clock always sends a shock through my chest.
I can still picture the intricate, swirling latte art on a really expensive coffee.
The heavy, damp air in the basement always gave me the creeps when I had to fetch something.
I remember the vibrant, chaotic energy of a street market in Mong Kok.
The sharp, metallic clinking of keys in the door meant my dad was finally home.
I remember the soft, gentle purr of a cat resting on my chest.
Getting a bad medical diagnosis, even though it turned out fine, left me with a lingering sense of mortality.
The intense, burning spice of a Sichuan peppercorn numbed my entire mouth.
