I clearly remember the heavy, uncomfortable silence when a guest speaker at our AAPI summit kept defining the Asian American experience using solely East Asian stereotypes, completely ignoring the brown students in the room. The exact phrasing the speaker used is blurry now, but the frustrated eye roll from my South Asian roommate sitting next to me is permanently burned into my memory.
I remember the slow, steady drip of a leaky faucet keeping me awake all night.
The bright, cheerful jingle of an ice cream truck always made me run outside.
I can still feel the cold, hard tile of the bathroom floor when I was sick.
A random compliment from a stranger completely turned my day around and made me realize the power of small kindnesses.
The smell of burning leaves in the autumn always reminds me of my neighbors doing yard work.
I remember the chaotic, overlapping voices of my relatives arguing over the bill at a restaurant.
The soft, yielding texture of a marshmallow roasting over a fire is a fond memory.
I remember the stark, sterile lighting of a late-night convenience store.
The sudden, loud pop of a balloon startled me so badly I dropped my drink.
I remember the mesmerizing, rhythmic motion of windshield wipers in heavy rain.
The sweet, floral aroma of jasmine tea always helps me relax.
I remember the overwhelming urge to cry out of frustration during a difficult exam.
The rough, scratchy wool of an old sweater was practically unbearable against my skin.
I can still hear the distant, lonely wail of a train horn late at night.
The intense, blinding sun glaring off the snow made me squint the whole walk home.
I remember the soft, rhythmic breathing of someone sleeping next to me.
The sharp, biting cold of an icy drink gave me a sudden brain freeze.
I remember the chaotic, swirling colors of a tie-dye shirt I made at summer camp.
The deep, resonating vibration of a cello being played live is a feeling I love.
I remember the paralyzing fear of looking down from a high balcony.
The smell of freshly cut grass always signals the official start of summer for me.
I remember the gentle, rhythmic rocking of a boat on calm water.
The sharp, acrid smell of burning toast quickly filled the entire kitchen.
I can still feel the smooth, polished surface of a river stone I kept in my pocket.
The sudden, terrifying jolt of turbulence on an airplane made me grip the armrests.
I remember the soft, warm glow of string lights in my college bedroom.
The intense, sour pucker of a green apple is a flavor I vividly recall.
I remember the overwhelming noise of a crowded high school hallway between classes.
The bitter, disappointing taste of a poorly mixed cocktail is burned into my mind.
I remember the deep, suffocating sadness I felt after a major falling out with a best friend.
The smell of a brand new car interior always gave me a slight headache.

I still get a tight chest when I try to talk to my Ma Ma on the phone and can only muster basic, toddler-level Cantonese greetings before passing the receiver back to my mom. It hurts to realize that my childhood refusal to attend Saturday Chinese school wasn't just typical teenage rebellion, but a permanent choice that effectively locked me out of ever truly knowing my own grandparents.
I remember the gentle, soothing sound of a stream flowing through a forest.
The sharp, painful sting of a papercut on my lip was infuriating.
I can still see the chaotic, sprawling mess of cables behind my computer desk.
The sudden, refreshing blast of cold air from the AC on a hot day was pure relief.
I remember the soft, muffled sound of footsteps on a carpeted floor.

Every year around the Mid-Autumn Festival, the smell of salted egg yolks and lotus seed paste instantly transports me back to the cramped, vibrant apartment we used to visit in Kowloon. I don't remember the exact dates of those childhood trips anymore, but the intense feeling of belonging to that humid, neon-lit city has never faded.
The intense, savory flavor of a perfectly cooked steak is something I savor.
I remember the terrifying, heart-stopping moment I couldn't find my passport at the airport.
The smell of a damp basement always transports me back to my childhood home.
I remember the deep, rhythmic thumping of a helicopter flying low overhead.
The sharp, stinging bite of a mosquito on my ankle is a constant summer annoyance.
I can still feel the heavy, oppressive humidity of a Virginia August.
The sudden, loud crash of thunder shook the entire house.
I remember the profound sense of emptiness the day after a big event was finally over.
The smell of an old, dusty attic always made me sneeze.
I remember the gentle, rolling hills of the countryside passing by the car window.
The intense, burning sensation of hot soup on my tongue taught me to be patient.
I remember the chaotic, vibrant displays of fireworks on the Fourth of July.
The deep, soothing hum of a box fan was my preferred way to fall asleep.
I can still feel the rough, unyielding concrete of a city sidewalk under my shoes.
The sudden, terrifying realization that I was entirely lost in an unfamiliar city.
I remember the soft, warm light of a candle flickering in a dark room.
The sharp, pungent smell of bleach always reminds me of swimming lessons.
I remember the overwhelming feeling of dread when I realized I forgot a major assignment.
The bitter, lingering taste of a grapefruit is something I never acquired a taste for.
I remember the chaotic, overlapping conversations at a busy coffee shop.
The soft, powdery snow falling silently outside my window was incredibly peaceful.
I can still feel the intense, burning heat of the sun on a black leather car seat.
The sudden, loud blast of a car horn made me jump out of my skin.
I remember the deep, resonating sound of a gong at a Buddhist temple.
The sharp, painful twist of an ankle during a pickup basketball game.

At family banquets in Falls Church, I always introduce myself as a Hong Konger, but at work I am the default Asian American guy, and out in the wider Virginia suburbs I am just an American. I forget exactly when I learned to fluidly switch between these different masks, but the distinct feeling of shifting my posture and vocabulary for each specific group is an ingrained daily habit.
I remember the profound feeling of guilt after snapping at my mom for no reason.
The smell of a campfire clinging to my clothes for days after a trip.
I remember the gentle, rhythmic clicking of a turn signal on a quiet drive.
The intense, savory aroma of garlic cooking in hot oil is my favorite smell.
I can still see the chaotic, swirling patterns of oil on a wet street.
The sudden, refreshing splash of cold water on my face in the morning.
I remember the soft, distant hum of traffic lulling me to sleep.

participants.persona: Mai is a 25-year-old first-generation Vietnamese American woman, born abroad and living in South Carolina.
participants.name: Mai

memories.content: I remember the blinding white light of the airport when we first landed in America. It made me realize how completely displaced I felt.
The humidity in South Carolina always hits me like a physical weight the second I step outside. It makes me wonder if I'll ever truly adapt to this climate.
I can still picture the bright red plastic stools we sat on in Vietnam, though the faces around me are mostly a blur. I feel a weird guilt for forgetting the people but remembering the furniture.
Someone laughed at my accent in second grade, and I just froze. I think that was the exact moment I started policing how I spoke.
The smell of my grandmother's tiger balm always made my nose itch. Looking back, that scent is the only real connection I have left to her.
I remember sitting in the back of my dad's old Toyota, watching the pine trees blur by. I often marvel at how those quiet car rides shaped my entire sense of peace.
My mom cried when I got my first college acceptance letter. It hit me then how much she sacrificed just so I could have that piece of paper.
I used to hide my lunch in middle school because I didn't want anyone to ask about the smell. I realize now how much energy I spent trying to shrink myself.
The first time I saw snow was during a rare flurry in Greenville. I remember feeling a profound sense of awe, like the world was suddenly new again.
I broke a jade bracelet my aunt gave me. I still feel a pang of shame about it, like I broke a piece of my heritage.
I failed my first driving test because I was too nervous to parallel park. It taught me that my anxiety is often my biggest obstacle.
There was a girl in fourth grade who told me I didn't belong here. I think about her sometimes and wonder if she knows how much those words echoed in my head.
I loved catching lightning bugs in a jar during the humid summer evenings. I realize now that those summers felt endless because I had no real worries.
I got lost in a massive grocery store once and panicked among the tall cereal aisles. That feeling of being totally untethered still haunts me in crowded places.
I spent a whole summer learning how to properly fold spring rolls with my mom. It makes me proud that I carry that small tradition forward.
The first time I voted, I held the ballot with shaking hands. It struck me how powerful it felt to finally have a voice in a place that didn't always welcome me.
I remember the crushing disappointment of not getting into my top choice university. Looking back, that rejection was necessary for me to find my actual path.
A boy in high school asked me out, but I think it was a dare. That incident permanently warped my trust in people's intentions.
I once spent an entire paycheck on a beautiful silk dress just because it reminded me of an ao dai. I recognize now it was a desperate attempt to feel connected to my roots.
I remember the exact orange glow of the streetlights during a late-night drive with friends. It made me realize how much I cherish quiet companionship.
I watched my parents struggle to fill out tax forms in English. I feel a deep sadness knowing they had to rely on a ten-year-old for things like that.
I used to sit on the porch during thunderstorms, mesmerized by the lightning. It was the first time I realized how small I was compared to the world.
I stopped speaking Vietnamese at home for a whole year when I was a teenager. I regret it now, knowing how much it hurt my parents.

I remember my Ba Nội whispering stories about escaping the fall of Saigon, her voice tight with an urgency that made me realize why our weekly Vietnamese lessons weren't just chores, but acts of survival. I don't remember the exact year she first told me, but the smell of the mothballs in her closet and the fierce grip she had on my arm are burned into my mind.
I remember the warm, yeasty smell of the bakery down the street. That smell always reminds me that comfort can be found in the most ordinary things.
My mom used to pack me sliced fruit in a plastic container. The apples were always a bit brown by lunchtime.
I remember the sharp sting of a papercut from a new textbook. It happened in Mr. Harrison's math class.
We had a giant oak tree in our front yard that dropped acorns everywhere. I used to step on them barefoot and wince.
I can clearly picture the neon sign of the local diner buzzing in the rain. I don't remember what we ate, just the red light reflecting on the wet pavement.
I had a diary with a tiny, flimsy lock that I kept under my mattress. I wrote everything in it using a sparkly gel pen.
The sound of cicadas in the summer was so loud it almost hurt my ears. It drowned out everything else in the neighborhood.
I remember hiding in my closet during a particularly bad argument between my parents. It smelled like old shoes and mothballs.
There was a stray cat that used to sleep on our porch swing. It had a notched ear and never let me pet it.
I spilled a whole bowl of pho on my favorite white shirt. I was so upset I cried right there in the restaurant.
The library downtown always smelled like dust and lemon polish. I loved running my hands over the worn spines of the books.
I had a friend who taught me how to make bracelets out of embroidery floss. We sat on her carpet for hours tying knots.
I remember the intense, burning heat of the seatbelt buckle in the middle of July. It seared my leg through my shorts.
My dad bought me a cheap acoustic guitar from a pawn shop. My fingers were blistered for weeks trying to learn chords.
I got caught passing a note in history class. The teacher read it silently and threw it away, but my face was burning.
We went to Myrtle Beach once and the sand was so hot I had to run to the water. The ocean was surprisingly cold against my ankles.

Cooking bún bò Huế with my mother in our tiny Columbia kitchen always felt like a lifeline back to an identity I was constantly afraid of losing in the South. I can't recall exactly who gave her the original recipe, but the sharp, unapologetic tang of the fermented shrimp paste was our unmistakable claim to who we were.
I remember the metallic taste of blood when I lost my first tooth. I was eating a piece of tough jerky.
There was a time I thought I saw a ghost in the hallway mirror. It was just a shadow, but my heart pounded for an hour.
I used to collect smooth rocks from the creek behind our subdivision. They were always slick with green algae.
My mom's hands always smelled like garlic and dish soap. I remember her rubbing my back when I was sick.
I remember the loud, crackling sound of the PA system right before morning announcements. It always made me jump a little.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk outside a gas station. I felt like I had won the lottery.
I accidentally broke a neighbor's window with a baseball. I ran away and never confessed to doing it.
The first time I tried sweet tea, it was so sugary it made my teeth ache. Everyone else was drinking it out of large styrofoam cups.
I had a recurring nightmare about a giant wave swallowing our house. I would wake up tangled in my sheets.
My parents threw a party and the house was packed with people speaking rapid-fire Vietnamese. I remember hiding under a table to escape the noise.
I remember the fuzzy texture of a peach I bought at a roadside stand. The juice dripped all over my hands when I bit into it.
I fell off a bike and scraped both my knees on the gravel. The sting of the peroxide my dad used hurt worse than the fall.
We had a power outage that lasted for three days. We ate everything in the freezer before it could melt.
I remember the smell of chlorine and sunscreen at the community pool. My eyes would be bloodshot for hours afterward.
I lied about reading a book for a book report. The guilt gnawed at my stomach all day.
The sky turned an eerie, bruised purple right before a massive tornado warning. The sirens were deafening.
I used to trace the floral patterns on our old couch cushions with my finger. The fabric was scratchy and smelled faintly of dust.
I remember crying in a bathroom stall during prom. I don't recall exactly why, just the cold tile against my back.
My grandmother sent a package from Vietnam that smelled intensely of dried seafood. We spent all evening unpacking it.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders that blistered and peeled. It was agonizing to put a shirt on.
I remember the rhythmic thumping of the washing machine in the garage. I used to sit next to it when it was cold outside.
I found a bird with a broken wing in the driveway. I tried to feed it breadcrumbs, but it didn't make it.
The first time I drove on the highway, my hands were clamped so tight on the steering wheel they went numb. The cars whizzing by were terrifying.
I remember eating an entire box of instant noodles raw because I liked the crunch. The seasoning packet was way too salty.
I had a fierce argument with my best friend over something trivial. We ignored each other in the hallways for a week.
The air conditioning in my high school was always blasting, making the classrooms freezing. I wore a heavy hoodie every day, even in May.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about someone to that exact person. I wanted the floor to swallow me whole.
I remember the rich, dark smell of coffee brewing in the mornings. It meant my dad was already awake.
I got a terrible haircut with bangs that were cut way too short. I wore a beanie for a month to hide them.
The floorboards in our hallway squeaked in one specific spot. I learned to step over it when I was trying to sneak snacks at night.
I once threw up in the back of a school bus during a field trip. The smell of the vinyl seats still makes me nauseous.
I remember the blinding flash of a camera during a family reunion portrait. I blinked and ruined the photo.
I stole a piece of candy from the grocery store when I was little. I was terrified the police were going to come for me.
We had a window that rattled loudly whenever the wind blew hard. It sounded like someone was trying to break in.
I remember the satisfying snap of fresh green beans when I helped my mom prep dinner. The kitchen was always steamy.
I had a crush on a boy who sat in front of me in biology. I used to stare at the back of his neck instead of the chalkboard.
The mall fountain smelled heavily of chlorine and old pennies. I used to drop nickels in and close my eyes tightly.
I locked my keys in the car while it was still running. I had to wait in the rain for an hour for a locksmith.
I remember the soft, powdery texture of a moth's wing when it landed on my arm. I was afraid to brush it off.
I got a bad grade on a chemistry test I had studied weeks for. I crumpled the paper up before I even left the room.
My neighbor had a dog that barked incessantly every single night. It was a high-pitched, annoying yip.
I once bought a pair of shoes that were a size too small just because they were on sale. They gave me blisters the size of coins.
I remember the distinctive smell of permanent markers squeaking across a white board. It always made me feel a little dizzy.
I left a candle burning in my room and scorched the wall. I scrubbed it for hours so my parents wouldn't notice.
The carpet in my college dorm room was a weird, rough industrial gray. It always felt sticky on my bare feet.
I had a roommate who never washed her dishes. The smell of sour milk constantly hovered over the sink.
I remember the sharp crunch of autumn leaves under my boots on the way to class. The air was perfectly crisp.
I accidentally dropped my phone into a storm drain. I just stared at the grate in pure disbelief.
I bought a cheap succulent that died within a week. The leaves turned brown and mushy.

Every Lunar New Year, we'd huddle around an iPad to FaceTime our relatives in Da Nang, the time difference blurring into a chaotic chorus of overlapping greetings and static. Though the pixelated faces sometimes felt distant and I often forgot my cousins' exact ages, the raw longing in my dad's voice when he spoke to his brothers always made my chest ache.
I got pulled over for speeding and started crying immediately. The officer just gave me a warning and looked uncomfortable.

Joining the Asian American Student Association at USC finally gave me a bridge between being the Vietnamese kid who immigrated at age four and the Carolina local who grew up on sweet tea. I don't remember who dragged me to that first meeting in the Russell House, but the relief of instantly belonging among people who just understood that dual existence was profound.
The dining hall at my college always smelled faintly of burnt toast. It didn't matter what time of day it was.
I tripped up the stairs in front of a massive crowd of students. I scrambled up so fast my knees ached.
I remember the exact shade of teal of my first car. The paint was chipping off the hood in tiny flakes.
I accidentally double-charged my debit card and overdrew my account. The panic of seeing a negative balance was suffocating.
I used to lay on the floor of my bedroom and listen to the rain hit the window AC unit. It was a chaotic, metallic drumming.
I had a sudden panic attack in a movie theater and had to leave abruptly. The hallway outside the auditorium felt incredibly quiet.
I remember eating cold pizza straight from the fridge at 3 AM. The cheese was stiff and tasteless.
I read a text over someone's shoulder that said something mean about me. My chest felt tight for the rest of the day.
I bought a lavender-scented lotion that turned out to be overpowering. I had to wash it off my hands ten minutes later.
I got caught in a torrential downpour without an umbrella. My clothes were plastered to my skin and I was shivering violently.
I remember the satisfying peeling of dried glue off the palms of my hands. I used to do it in art class all the time.
I found a stack of old letters my parents wrote to each other. I didn't read them, but I held the faded envelopes for a long time.
The first time I tried cooking a Thanksgiving turkey, it was completely dry. We ended up drowning it in gravy to make it edible.
I got incredibly motion sick on a boat ride in Charleston harbor. I spent the entire tour staring at the wooden deck.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun reflecting off the hood of the car ahead of me. I had to hold my hand up to see.
I told a lie about where I was going on a Friday night to avoid a party. I spent the evening nervously checking my phone.
I used to chew on the caps of my pens until the plastic splintered. I always had ink smudges on my lips.

Sitting at my grandfather's funeral in Greenville unable to understand the formal Vietnamese of the monk's eulogy, I felt a crushing wave of grief over how much of my mother tongue I had let slip away. Looking back on that day, I realize my desperate childhood attempts to assimilate cost me the very language I needed to fully participate in my own family's history.
I had a really vivid dream where all my teeth fell out. I woke up panicked and immediately checked my mouth.
I remember the deep, rumbling sound of a train passing a few miles away. It used to happen right around midnight.
I accidentally knocked over a display of apples at the grocery store. People stared as I frantically chased them across the linoleum.
The smell of freshly cut grass always makes me sneeze. It reminds me of Saturday mornings when my dad would mow the lawn.
I broke a glass during an argument and the sound shocked us both into silence. I had to sweep up the shards with shaking hands.
I remember the icy blast of air when walking into a movie theater during summer. It was a massive contrast to the sweltering heat outside.
I got a nasty papercut from a thick cardstock envelope. It bled surprisingly heavily for such a small cut.

During the annual Tet festival at our local temple in Spartanburg, surrounded by the deafening crackle of firecrackers and the vibrant yellow of the Hoa Mai flowers, I always felt fiercely, unequivocally Vietnamese. I forget which aunt specifically spent hours adjusting my Áo Dài, but the heavy, grounding weight of the silk against my skin remains a vivid anchor.
I used to stare at the popcorn ceiling in my bedroom until the bumps looked like faces. It was how I passed the time before falling asleep.
I overheard my parents whispering about money worries late at night. I pretended to be asleep when they checked on me.
I remember the sticky, sweet taste of blue raspberry slushies. My tongue would be stained blue for hours.
I had a wart on my finger that I was extremely embarrassed about. I kept a band-aid over it every day until it went away.
I bought a cheap pair of sunglasses that distorted my vision slightly. They made the pavement look curved.
I completely forgot a close friend's birthday until two days later. The guilt I felt when I finally texted them was immense.
I remember the soft hum of the refrigerator in our quiet house. It was a comforting background noise.
I burned my tongue badly on a cup of hot chocolate. I couldn't taste anything for three days.
I used to collect the tabs from soda cans and keep them in a jar. I have no idea why I thought they were valuable.
I lost my favorite jacket at a concert and never found it. I was freezing on the walk back to the car.
I remember the sharp smell of vinegar when we dyed Easter eggs. The little wire dippers always bent out of shape.
I cried during a performance evaluation at work even though the feedback was mostly positive. I couldn't stop the tears from falling.
I bought a heavily scented candle that gave me an instant headache. I had to throw it in the outside trash can.
I accidentally stepped on a snail barefoot on the sidewalk. The crunching sensation made me physically shudder.
I remember the vibrant yellow of the dandelions in our unkempt front yard. The stems left a bitter, milky residue on my fingers.
I completely blanked on a coworker's name while trying to introduce them. The silence stretched out for an agonizing few seconds.
I used to spin around in the front yard until I was too dizzy to stand. The sky would whirl above me in streaks of blue.
I got a horrible stomachache after eating at a sketchy food truck. I spent the entire night huddled on the bathroom floor.
I remember the exact rough texture of the brick wall outside my elementary school. I used to lean against it while waiting for the bus.
I found a spider in my shoe right as I was about to put it on. I still rigorously shake out all my footwear.
I bought a sweater that looked incredibly soft but was horribly itchy. I wore it once and buried it in my closet.
I received a harsh criticism on an essay that felt very personal. I deleted the file and started entirely from scratch.
I remember the sweet, cloying smell of funnel cake at the state fair. The powdered sugar inevitably got all over my dark jeans.
I slipped on a patch of black ice and landed flat on my back. The wind was instantly knocked out of my lungs.
I used to press my face against the cold car window on road trips. The vibrations of the road would hum through my jaw.
I had a phase where I heavily edited all my photos to look thinner. Looking back at those pictures now makes me incredibly sad.
I remember the sharp, minty smell of the toothpaste my dad used. It always dominated the bathroom in the mornings.
I accidentally hit "reply all" to an email with a snarky comment. I sat at my desk frozen in terror for ten minutes.
I bought a massive puzzle during a rainy weekend and never finished it. The pieces took over the dining table for weeks.
I was aggressively tailgated by a large truck on a dark road. I gripped the wheel so hard my knuckles turned white.
I remember the satisfying snap of opening a brand new jar of peanut butter. The surface was perfectly smooth.
I wore a pair of heels to a wedding that caused my feet to bleed. I spent the entire reception sitting at an empty table.
I used to try to catch falling leaves before they hit the ground. It was much harder than it looked.
I woke up paralyzed by sleep paralysis and hallucinated a figure in the corner. I couldn't even scream.
I remember the distinct, synthetic smell of a brand new plastic shower curtain. It would linger in the bathroom for days.
I dropped a heavy glass jar of pasta sauce in the grocery store aisle. It shattered, sending red splatters everywhere.
I bought a bundle of fresh eucalyptus to hang in my shower. The steam made the whole room smell like a spa.
I accidentally offended a stranger by asking a poorly phrased question. The awkward silence that followed made my face burn.
I remember the bright, flashing lights of the arcade in the mall. The noise was a chaotic blend of chimes and buzzers.
I found out I wasn't invited to a group outing through social media. I stared at the photo of them together for a long time.
I used to peel the labels off my water bottles when I was bored in class. I'd roll the paper into tiny, tight cylinders.
I spilled coffee on my laptop keyboard right before a big deadline. I had to frantically dry it with paper towels, praying it would turn on.
I remember the metallic squeak of the swings at the playground near our house. The chains would pinch my fingers if I wasn't careful.
I had a sudden, severe nosebleed in the middle of a meeting. I had to rush to the bathroom with my hand over my face.
I bought a loaf of artisan bread that was practically too tough to bite through. It made a loud crunching sound with every slice.
I confidently gave someone the wrong directions in the city. I realized my mistake five minutes later and felt terrible.
I remember the faint glow of the stars on a very clear night out in the country. It was the darkest sky I had ever seen.
I found a lump on my neck and spent a week in pure agony waiting for a doctor's appointment. It turned out to be nothing, but the fear was paralyzing.
I used to sort my colored pencils by gradient before I would start drawing. The neatness of the box was very satisfying.
I was heavily reprimanded by a manager in front of my peers. I kept my eyes fixed on the floor the entire time.
I remember the loud hiss of the espresso machine at my local cafe. The air inside always smelled intensely roasted.
I accidentally deleted a folder of precious photos from a family trip. I tried every recovery software but they were just gone.
I bought a set of wind chimes that I ended up having to take down. They clattered aggressively every time the breeze picked up.
I choked on a piece of ice at a restaurant and someone had to pat my back. The entire dining room turned to look at me.
I remember the soft, velvety texture of a peach I bought at a farmer's market. It bruised almost instantly in my bag.
I had a bout of insomnia where I stayed awake for two full days. By the end, I felt completely detached from reality.
I used to run my hands along the tall hedges on my walk home. The leaves were stiff and coated in a fine layer of street dust.
I accidentally told a secret that someone had trusted me with. I felt like a horrible friend when they found out.
I remember the deep, resonant chime of the grandfather clock in my aunt's house. It scared me every time it struck midnight.
I got trapped in an elevator for twenty minutes during a power dip. The small space got incredibly hot and stuffy almost immediately.
I bought a brightly colored umbrella that broke the very first time I used it in heavy wind. It inverted completely and snapped.
I drastically overcooked a pot of rice and it scorched the bottom of the pan. The burnt smell lingered in the kitchen for days.
I remember the smooth, cool surface of the marble countertops in my friend's house. I was fascinated by the gray veins in the stone.
I accidentally locked eyes with a stranger while crying on the subway. I quickly turned my head and wiped my face.
I used to bite my nails down to the quick whenever I was studying for finals. My fingertips were always sore.
I remember the sharp smell of gasoline when filling up my car on a hot day. The fumes visibly shimmered in the air.
I mistakenly threw away an important check and had to dig through the trash to find it. It was covered in coffee grounds by the time I retrieved it.
I bought a houseplant that I meticulously watered, but it slowly withered anyway. I felt surprisingly defeated by its death.
I remember the dense, foggy mornings in South Carolina where you couldn't see the next house over. The air felt heavy and damp against my skin.
I had a brief panic when I couldn't find my passport at the airport. It was in a different pocket of my bag all along.
I used to carefully pick all the mushrooms out of my food because I hated the texture. I'd hide them under my napkin.
I got a terrible cramp in my leg while swimming in a lake. The momentary thought of drowning was terrifying.
I remember the loud, rhythmic chirping of the crickets at night. If you walked too close to the grass, they would suddenly go dead silent.
I accidentally broke a beautiful ceramic bowl that my mother had brought from Vietnam. I glued it back together, but the cracks are obvious.
I bought a heavy winter coat on clearance during the summer. It sat in my closet for months, smelling slightly of mothballs.
I completely froze during a presentation and forgot my next sentence. The silence felt so loud I could hear my own heartbeat.
I remember the distinct, papery rustle of opening a new box of tea bags. The chamomile scent wafted up immediately.
I had to put down my childhood dog and I held his paw as he went to sleep. It was the most profound grief I had ever felt.
I used to trace the condensation drops on the outside of my glass of sweet tea. They would merge and run quickly down to the coaster.
I mistakenly sent a highly personal text to a group chat instead of a single friend. I panicked and deleted it, hoping no one saw.
I remember the soft crunch of frost on the grass during an unusually cold morning in January. My breath plumed in front of me like smoke.

participants.persona: Ryan is a 27-year-old second-generation Chinese and Japanese American man, born in the U.S. and living in California.
participants.name: Ryan

memories.content: I remember the sharp smell of ginger and garlic hitting the pan when my Nai Nai cooked. She always chased me out of the kitchen so I wouldn't get splattered with oil.
My dad bought me a Nintendo 64 for my sixth birthday. I spent hours playing Mario Kart, mostly just driving into the walls.
I used to think the fog rolling into San Francisco was a giant monster when I was little. It would swallow the Golden Gate Bridge whole.
In second grade, I traded my homemade onigiri for a Lunchable. I felt instantly guilty because my mom had woken up early to shape the rice by hand.
I broke my left arm falling off the monkey bars at the park down the street. The cast was neon green and terribly itchy during the summer heat.
We went to Monterey Bay Aquarium every summer when I was a kid. The jellyfish exhibit always mesmerized me with its deep blue lighting.

Every Lunar New Year in San Gabriel, my dad orders dim sum in Taishanese while my Japanese mom prepares homemade ozoni. Our family strictly maintains these bilingual food traditions to keep both sides of our heritage alive.
I remember getting lost in a Ranch 99 supermarket and crying next to the live seafood tanks. A kind cashier gave me a haw flakes candy while we waited for my parents.
My grandfather taught me how to hold chopsticks by tying a rubber band around them. He was so patient, even when I dropped food all over the floor.
I had a phase where I only wore clothing with dragons on it. My parents embarrassingly supported this by buying me a shiny dragon windbreaker.

Looking back at my childhood obsession with blending in, I realize I actively rejected my heritage to make things easier. It is uncomfortable to admit how much I wanted to just be a standard white kid from the suburbs.
The first time I saw snow was on a family trip to Lake Tahoe. I tried to build an igloo but gave up after my gloves soaked through.
I learned to ride a bike in the empty parking lot of my elementary school. My dad ran behind me holding the seat until I finally found my balance.
I won third place in the fourth-grade spelling bee. I still remember the word I misspelled was restaurant because I forgot the a.
For Halloween in 2005, I dressed up as a ninja. The plastic sword kept getting caught in my legs while I was trick-or-treating.
I vividly recall the sound of cicadas during the one summer we visited my relatives in Japan. The heat was incredibly oppressive, completely different from California.
I kept a shoebox full of trading cards hidden under my bed. I never actually learned how to play the game properly, I just liked the shiny artwork.
My mom forced me to take piano lessons for six years. I hated practicing, but now I secretly wish I had stuck with it.
I had an embarrassing crush on my sixth-grade science teacher. I used to do extra credit projects just to impress her.
The transition to middle school was awful because my best friend moved to Texas. I spent most of seventh grade eating lunch alone in the library.
I remember burning mixed CDs for road trips down to Los Angeles. I always put too much pop-punk on there and drove my parents crazy.
My first phone was a silver flip phone. I felt incredibly cool snapping it shut after a call with my friends.
I went through a brief skateboarding phase to fit in with the neighborhood kids. I quit after scraping my knees so badly I couldn't wear pants for a week.
We used to go out for dim sum every Sunday morning with my dad's side of the family. The chaotic noise of the carts and chatter is a core memory for me.
I forged my mom's signature on a math test in eighth grade. She found out immediately because my handwriting was terrible and we had a massive argument.

I often wonder if my sarcastic sense of humor developed as a defense mechanism during my awkward middle school years. It served me well then, but sometimes it keeps me from being genuinely vulnerable now.
I took Spanish in high school because everyone said it was the easiest language to learn. I barely remember anything beyond how to ask for the bathroom.
Driving down Highway 1 with my friends after getting my license was exhilarating. We had the windows down and the ocean breeze smelled amazing.
I worked my first job at a local boba shop during my junior year. I smelled like tapioca pearls and spilled black tea for an entire year.
I had my first kiss behind the bleachers after a high school football game. It was clumsy and our teeth clinked together awkwardly.
Studying for the SATs took over my life for six months. I remember sitting at the dining table surrounded by massive prep books, feeling completely overwhelmed.
My high school friends and I used to hang out at a burger joint until midnight on Fridays. We ordered loaded fries and thought we owned the world.
I got caught sneaking out of the house when I was sixteen. My dad was just sitting in the dark living room when I climbed back through the window.
Senior prom was surprisingly underwhelming. The DJ played terrible music and the punch tasted like pure cough syrup.
I remember the intense relief I felt when I finally submitted my college applications. I slept for fourteen hours straight that weekend.
Choosing to stay in California for college was the best decision I could have made. I love the state too much to deal with real winters.
My mom cried when they dropped me off at my dorm in San Diego. I tried to act tough, but I cried too once they drove away.
I survived freshman year mostly on instant ramen and dining hall pizza. My digestive system has never fully recovered from that diet.
I took an Asian American studies class that completely changed my worldview. It was the first time I learned about the history of people who looked like me in this country.
I pulled my first all-nighter writing a sociology paper that I hadn't started until the day before. I drank three energy drinks and hallucinated slightly by sunrise.

Taking that history class made me realize how little I actually asked my grandparents about their lives before they immigrated. It made me aware of the huge generational silence in my family that I passively accepted.
I dated a girl in my sophomore year who was way too cool for me. We broke up because I preferred staying in and she wanted to go to raves every weekend.
My college roommate had a pet tarantula that he kept in a glass tank on his desk. I was terrified of it the entire year.
I participated in a beach cleanup day and accidentally stepped on a washed-up jellyfish. The sting wasn't bad, but the sheer panic was unforgettable.
Studying abroad in Kyoto for a semester was incredible but also incredibly isolating. I looked Japanese but couldn't speak the language well, which led to many confusing and alienating interactions.
I remember the taste of the matcha soft serve I bought near a temple in Japan. It was so rich and bitter, unlike anything I had at home.
I lost my wallet on the bullet train from Tokyo to Osaka. A station attendant actually tracked it down and returned it to me with all the cash intact.
I changed my major from Computer Science to Communications halfway through college. My parents were deeply disappointed, and the guilt weighed on me for years.
Graduation day was scorching hot and the robes felt like personal saunas. I barely paid attention to the speeches because I was trying not to pass out.
My first post-college apartment was a tiny studio in San Jose with a broken air conditioner. I had to sleep with ice packs during the August heat waves.
I completely bombed my first real job interview by calling the interviewer the wrong name. I knew I didn't get the job the second I walked out the door.
I eventually got hired at a digital marketing agency in San Francisco. Commuting on the train every morning quickly wore away my soul.
I adopted a rescue cat named Miso two years ago. He is a chaotic orange tabby who loves knocking glasses off the counter.
I tried to make my dad's famous braised pork belly for Lunar New Year. It turned out completely burnt, but I ate it anyway out of sheer stubbornness.
I went on a disastrous dating app date where the guy talked about his ex for two hours straight. I faked a stomach ache to go home early.
I recently noticed that I tend to mirror the personality of whoever I am dating. It is a troubling realization that I don't always know who I am when I am not in a relationship.
I started going to a bouldering gym because all my friends were doing it. I have zero upper body strength, so I mostly just hang out on the mats.
My favorite coffee shop in the city knows my order by heart now. It feels nice to be a regular somewhere in a bustling neighborhood.
I took a solo road trip to Joshua Tree last spring to clear my head. The stars out there were brighter than I had ever seen in my life.
I got a flat tire on the interstate in the middle of nowhere. I had to look up a video tutorial on my phone to figure out how to put the spare on.
I attended a massive music festival in the desert and lost my voice from screaming. The dust storms left my lungs feeling terrible for days.
My grandmother passed away during my senior year of college. I still have her jade bracelet sitting in a velvet box on my dresser, untouched.
I remember the exact moment my long-term relationship ended over washing dishes. It was such a stupid fight that cracked open all our hidden resentments.
I try to run three miles every other morning before work. I rarely enjoy the run itself, but the feeling of accomplishment afterward keeps me going.
I bought a bunch of houseplants during the pandemic and surprisingly kept them all alive. My monstera plant has completely taken over my living room window.
I once won a trivia night at a local bar almost single-handedly because the category was childhood pop culture. My friends still bring it up when we go back.
I accidentally dyed my hair a horrible brassy orange when I was trying to bleach it. I had to wear a beanie for three weeks until I could afford a color correction.
The smoke from the California wildfires a few years ago made the sky turn a dystopian orange. I felt a deep sense of dread just looking out my apartment window.
I volunteered at a food bank for Thanksgiving last year. Sorting canned goods for six hours made my back ache, but the community atmosphere was wonderful.
I have a terrible habit of buying books and letting them pile up on my nightstand unread. I just like the idea of being a well-read person.

Whenever I feel anxious, I realize I start organizing my physical space to regain a sense of control. It is comforting to know this about myself, even if it doesn't solve the underlying emotional problem.
I went camping in Yosemite and a bear wandered through our campsite at night. We all sat dead still in our tents, terrified to make a single sound.
I bought an expensive espresso machine to save money on daily lattes. It has been two years and I still have not broken even on the investment.
I have a scar on my chin from tripping over a garden hose when I was nine. I used to lie to people in middle school and tell them I got it in a fight.
I helped my younger cousin edit his college admission essays last fall. It made me feel incredibly old to realize he was born the year I started middle school.
I tried a vegan challenge for a month to see if it would give me more energy. I gave up on day twelve because I smelled barbecue walking down the street.
I got stuck in an elevator for an hour at my office building. I spent the entire time playing a puzzle game on my phone to avoid making eye contact with a senior executive.
I have a lingering fear of deep water because I nearly drowned in a community pool when I was five. I can swim now, but panic still sets in when I cannot touch the bottom.
I spent an entire weekend binge-watching a television drama and crying on my couch. The emotional release was exactly what I needed after a stressful month at work.
I accidentally replied to a company-wide email with a sarcastic joke meant for a coworker. My manager pulled me aside to reprimand me, and I wanted to melt into the floor.

I use LINE and WeChat every weekend to video call my cousins in Osaka and Guangzhou, making sure to send them digital red envelopes during the holidays. My parents also run a local sister-city exchange program in Torrance that keeps our California neighborhood actively connected to our overseas relatives.
I went to a pottery class with a friend and my clay bowl collapsed on the spinning wheel. The instructor tried to fix it, but it just ended up looking like a lumpy ashtray.
I love going to the farmers market on Saturday mornings just to look at the seasonal fruit. The fresh peaches in the summer are always worth the overpriced cost.
I twisted my ankle playing pickup basketball at the neighborhood park last month. I had to hobble a mile back to my apartment while holding back tears.
I found a box of old family photos in my parents attic while helping them clean. Seeing my parents in their twenties made them seem like entirely different, carefree people.
I went to a drag brunch for my friend's birthday and had the time of my life. A performer pulled me on stage and I absolutely humiliated myself trying to dance.
Sometimes I feel immense guilt for not speaking Mandarin or Japanese fluently. I recognize it is a symptom of assimilation, but it still makes me feel like a fraud to my own ancestors.
I bought a vintage record player at a thrift store but it ruined the first vinyl I played on it. I haven't used it since, so it just sits there as an aesthetic decoration.
I hate folding laundry, so I often leave clean clothes in the basket for days. I just pull out wrinkled shirts when I need them for work.
I got a speeding ticket on the freeway because I was late for a dentist appointment. The fine was outrageously expensive and completely ruined my week.
I tried surfing once in Santa Cruz and spent the entire afternoon getting slammed by waves. The water was freezing even with a thick borrowed wetsuit.
I have a designated drawer in my kitchen filled completely with takeout condiment packets. I refuse to throw them away even though I know I will never use them.
I attended my high school reunion out of sheer morbid curiosity. It was bizarre seeing my old bullies trying to network and sell life insurance.
I got violently food poisoned from a late-night taco truck in the city. I was so sick I couldn't look at a tortilla for at least six months after that ordeal.
I signed up for a half-marathon on a whim and instantly regretted it. I trained terribly and ended up painfully walking the last five miles.
My dad and I bonded over fixing a broken sink garbage disposal last weekend. It was mostly just us swearing at the pipes, but it felt like a good masculine moment.
I went to a midnight screening of a terrible horror movie with my roommates. We got yelled at by the usher because we couldn't stop laughing at the awful special effects.
I have a lucky pair of socks with little avocados on them that I wear to important meetings. They have holes in the heels, but I refuse to throw them out.
I finally confronted a toxic friend who constantly belittled my professional achievements. The conversation was awful, but cutting ties felt like a massive weight lifted off my chest.
I spent three hours building an assembly-required dresser only to realize I installed the drawer tracks backwards. I had to take the entire thing apart and start over.
I remember the smell of sunscreen and hot asphalt from my childhood trips to theme parks. We always stayed until the gates closed to get our money's worth.

I realize my constant need to be productive is deeply tied to my parents immigrant work ethic. I am actively trying to unlearn the idea that resting is a lazy waste of time, but it is deeply ingrained.
I tried to bake sourdough bread during the lockdown like everyone else. My starter died after four days because I completely forgot to feed it.

Whenever a major typhoon hits Kyushu or there are policy changes in Guangdong, I first read about it in my aunt's WeChat group before verifying the details on the English version of Kyodo News. My dad also forwards me translated articles from the Rafu Shimpo so I can track how local US media covers Asian politics.
I keep a journal hidden in my nightstand where I write down my most anxious, intrusive thoughts. Getting them out of my head usually stops me from spiraling.
I got a tattoo of a tiny pine tree on my ankle while on a trip to Portland. My mom still doesn't know about it, and I intend to keep it a secret forever.
I love the smell of the first rain in California after a long, dry summer. The scent of the wet pavement is incredibly calming to me.
I bought a vintage film camera to try and take more intentional photos. It turns out I am just as bad at composing shots on film as I am on my smartphone.
I used to be terrified of dogs until my roommate brought home a golden retriever puppy. Now I am the guy who stops on the street to ask to pet strangers animals.
I watched the sunrise from the top of a volcanic crater in Hawaii. The freezing wind was biting, but the view above the clouds was otherworldly.
I had a phase in high school where I exclusively listened to underground hip-hop to seem edgy. I look back on my old playlists and cringe at how hard I was trying to be different.
I once locked my keys inside my apartment while taking out the trash. I had to wait in the hallway in my pajamas for two hours for the locksmith to arrive.
I started therapy a year ago to deal with some lingering childhood resentment toward my family. It is exhausting emotional work, but it has definitely improved my overall well-being.

At UC Berkeley, I joined the Asian American Association to organize local voter registration drives in Oakland alongside peers of various AAPI backgrounds. Working on these pan-Asian community projects provided a practical framework to integrate my parents' immigrant background with my daily civic life in California.
I attended a massive protest in downtown Los Angeles and felt a profound sense of unity. The energy of thousands of people chanting together literally vibrated in my chest.
I tried learning to play the acoustic guitar via online video tutorials. My fingertips got so calloused and sore I could barely type at my computer for work.
I won a stuffed bear out of a claw machine on a pier on my very first try. I gave it to a little kid who was watching because I didn't want to carry it around.
I got my wisdom teeth removed and woke up from anesthesia crying about a fictional dog. The video my mom took of me weeping is still a source of family ridicule.
Paying attention to how I react to criticism has shown me that my ego is much more fragile than I like to pretend. I am consciously learning to pause and breathe before I get defensive with my peers.
I love putting on a good podcast and spending Sunday mornings deep-cleaning my apartment. Wiping down the baseboards and counters brings me an odd amount of mental peace.
I had a terrifying moment of hydroplaning on the freeway during a rare California downpour. My heart pounded in my throat until I finally regained control of the steering wheel.
I tried to cook a massive holiday dinner for my friend group last year. The turkey was incredibly dry, but the garlic mashed potatoes were an absolute triumph.
I went swimming in the ocean at midnight during a beach bonfire party. The water was pitch black and terrifying, but the adrenaline rush was amazing.
I still have the first dollar bill I ever earned from my teenage job pinned to my corkboard. It reminds me of how far I have come financially since high school.
I was a groomsman in my college roommate's wedding last summer. Giving a speech in front of two hundred people made my hands shake uncontrollably.
I spent way too much money on a mechanical keyboard just because I liked the clicking sound. It actually annoys me now when I am trying to focus and work in silence.
I went to a psychic in a tourist town on a vacation trip. She told me I had a dark aura, which kind of ruined my mood for the rest of the day.
I used to steal sips of my dad's beer when he wasn't looking during family barbecues. I always thought it tasted like bitter bread water, but I did it to feel grown up.
I got rejected from my dream university and framed the rejection letter as an ironic joke. Looking at it now just makes me feel totally indifferent.
I helped a stranger push their stalled car through a busy intersection. The feeling of brief camaraderie with the other helpers was surprisingly uplifting.
I binge-read an entire science fiction book series in one weekend. I completely ignored all my adult responsibilities because I was so invested in the fictional universe.
I bought a cheap telescope to look at the moon from my apartment balcony. The light pollution in the city makes it practically useless for actual stargazing.

Last summer at a Tokyo train station, I cried out of sheer frustration when I had to use a translation app to ask for directions, despite attending Japanese Saturday school in Torrance for five years. I actively skip family dinners where my relatives speak rapid Mandarin because my inability to respond beyond a third-grade level causes me intense shame.
I had a really embarrassing voice crack during a presentation to my company's executive board. I played it off with a cough, but I know everyone in the room noticed.
I often catch myself comparing my career trajectory to my peers online, which I know is a toxic trap. I have to actively remind myself that my self-worth is not tied to a corporate job title.
I drove up to the redwood forests for the first time and felt incredibly small next to the ancient trees. The silence in that dense forest was almost heavy.
I made the mistake of eating a wildly spicy hot wing on a dare from a friend. I drank a gallon of milk and my mouth still burned intensely for hours.
I fell asleep on the beach without sunscreen and got severe burns on my shoulders. Blistering skin is a painful mistake you only make once in your life.
I still sleep with a ratty old quilt my grandmother made me when I was a baby. The edges are completely frayed but it holds immense sentimental value for me.
I went to an escape room with my coworkers for a mandatory team-building event. We failed miserably because everyone was trying to be the loudest leader.
I tried out for the high school basketball team and didn't make the cut. It was my first real experience with crushing disappointment and feeling physically inadequate.
I found a stray kitten hiding under my car and took it to the local animal shelter. Leaving it there broke my heart, even though I knew my landlord prohibited pets at the time.
I got audited by the tax agency last year over a tiny mistake on my freelance income. The bureaucratic nightmare aged me by about five years from pure stress.
I accidentally dropped my brand new phone into a public toilet at a bar. The sheer disgust of retrieving it still haunts me every time I use that device.
I went on a date to an arcade and completely destroyed the guy in air hockey. He got genuinely angry and stopped talking to me, which was a massive red flag.
I love eating cold leftover pizza for breakfast the morning after a party. It honestly tastes better than it did when it was hot and fresh.
I used to be obsessed with collecting enamel pins from different places I visited. Now they just sit in a glass jar gathering dust on my bookshelf.
I got stuck next to a screaming toddler on a fourteen-hour flight to Asia. I couldn't sleep a wink and arrived at my destination feeling practically like a zombie.
I tried to trim my own hair during a depressive episode in college. I had to wear a baseball cap for a month because I looked absolutely unhinged.
Documenting these thoughts makes me realize how many of my significant life moments revolve around food. I clearly use culinary experiences as a primary emotional bridge to connect with my heritage.
I bought a fancy road bike to commute to work and got a flat tire on my very first ride. I ended up calling an oversized rideshare car to take me and the bike back home.
I love the chaos of a busy Chinatown bakery on a Sunday afternoon. Fighting through the crowd for the last fresh egg tart is basically an Olympic sport.
I fell for an online phishing scam when I was eighteen and lost three hundred dollars. The deep shame of being so easily duped kept me from telling my parents for years.
I went to a stand-up comedy show and the comedian aggressively roasted me for my brightly colored outfit. I laughed along, but I never wore that jacket again out of embarrassment.
I have a faded scar on my knee from trying to jump a ramp on a scooter in middle school. I missed the landing completely and scraped across the raw concrete.
I spent a summer interning in a different state and absolutely hated the intense humidity. Waiting on the underground train platforms felt like standing in the actual depths of hell.
I bought a ridiculously expensive pair of raw denim jeans just because of a fashion trend. The break-in process was so physically painful I almost gave up wearing them.
I went to a midnight release party for a popular fantasy book when I was a kid. The palpable excitement in the crowded bookstore is something I will never forget.
I tried learning to knit to make a warm scarf for the winter months. It ended up looking like a misshapen, tangled triangle with giant holes in it.
I have a nervous habit of aggressively biting my nails when I am stressed out about a project deadline. My fingers always end up raw, sore, and bleeding.
I went to an all-you-can-eat barbecue restaurant and ate so much brisket I genuinely couldn't breathe. I had to unbutton my pants in the parking lot before driving home.
I accidentally walked into the wrong lecture hall on my first day of college and sat there for twenty minutes. I was too embarrassed to get up and leave once the professor started talking.
I love going to the movie theater by myself on a random weekday afternoon. Sitting in a completely empty auditorium with a giant popcorn feels incredibly luxurious.
I got caught in a sudden hailstorm while hiking in the mountains near a lake. The ice pellets stung my face as I wildly sprinted for tree cover.

Looking closely at my past relationships, I notice a distinct pattern of withdrawing when emotional intimacy deepens. I am consciously trying to break that habit by communicating my fears instead of just running away.
I bought a beautiful handmade matcha whisk while traveling and then accidentally snapped it in half while packing my suitcase. I was devastated over a simple piece of bamboo.
I tried doing a sensory deprivation tank session to help with my chronic stress. I ended up getting highly salted water in my eye and panicking in the pitch dark.
I still remember my childhood best friend's home phone number perfectly by heart. It is weird how entirely useless information stays permanently locked in the human brain.
I went to a modern art museum and pretended to understand the deeper meaning of a crumpled trash can sculpture. I mostly just enjoyed walking around in the air conditioning.
I accidentally shrunk my absolute favorite wool sweater in the hot wash cycle. It came out of the machine looking like it was meant to fit a small dog.
I spent New Year's Eve on a rooftop in the city watching the midnight fireworks. The coastal fog was so thick all we saw were colored flashes glowing in the clouds.
I tried doing an intense home workout video and accidentally kicked a hole straight through my living room drywall. Patching it up took me an entire weekend of watching tutorial videos.

In the last midterm election, I voted for a congressional candidate I disagreed with on California tax policy solely because she publicly opposed trade tariffs that would devastate my uncle's export business in Guangzhou. My family's economic reliance on US-China trade relations forces me to prioritize foreign policy at the ballot box over my usual progressive domestic stances.
I got a terrible sunburn directly on my scalp because I forgot to wear a hat at an outdoor baseball game. Brushing my hair was pure agony for an entire week.
I found a crisp twenty-dollar bill lying on the sidewalk and used it to buy a massive ice cream sundae. Eating it on the curb tasted like pure, unadulterated victory.
I accidentally spilled red wine on a friend's white couch at a crowded house party. I spent the rest of the night frantically scrubbing the stain with club soda while internally panicking.
I love the slow ritual of making a pour-over coffee on a quiet weekend morning. Watching the dark grounds bloom in the hot water is surprisingly meditative.
I went exploring tide pools on the coast and found a perfectly intact sand dollar. I wrapped it carefully in a tissue to bring home, but it crumbled to pieces in my pocket.
I got a nasty flu last winter and was completely bedridden for four long days. The physical isolation really made me appreciate simply being healthy enough to walk outside.
I used to practice my signature over and over in the margins of my high school notebooks. I wanted it to look sophisticated and mature, but it still just looks like frantic scribbles.

I have realized that I hold onto old clothes not because I will wear them, but because I am attached to the past versions of myself. Letting them go feels like painfully admitting those phases of my youth are permanently over.
I made a huge pot of chili for a sports party and completely forgot to add the chili powder and cumin. Everyone was too polite to say it just tasted like warm tomato paste.
I watched a spectacular meteor shower from the hood of my car in the middle of the desert. The absolute silence of the landscape and the shooting stars made me feel incredibly peaceful.
I got my credit card skimmed at a sketchy gas station and someone bought three hundred dollars worth of digital goods. Dealing with the bank fraud department on the phone was a massive headache.
I accidentally liked an old photo on the social media profile of someone I had just started dating. I immediately put my phone in airplane mode and wanted the earth to swallow me.
I love browsing through vintage clothing stores on a lazy Sunday afternoon. I rarely buy anything, but I greatly enjoy examining the different eras of historical fashion.
I once burned a batch of chocolate chip cookies so badly they set off the apartment smoke alarm. My kitchen smelled strongly of charred sugar for a full week.
I took a ferry across the bay right at sunset during the summer. The golden hour light hitting the city skyline and reflecting off the water was absolutely breathtaking.
I had an embarrassing phase where I tried to start an online channel broadcasting myself playing video games. I deleted the videos years ago, but I still cringe knowing they existed.
I accidentally dropped my apartment keys down a street storm drain while walking to my car. I had to use a wire coat hanger and a piece of chewed gum to fish them out while neighbors watched.
I tried to assemble an elaborate charcuterie board for a fancy dinner party I hosted. I spent fifty dollars on expensive cheeses and everyone just ate the basic water crackers.
I remember hiding under the covers with a small flashlight to read comic books way past my bedtime. The muffled, warm quiet of the blanket fort felt like my own private sanctuary.
I got an expensive parking ticket for street sweeping right outside my own apartment building. I was incredibly furious at myself for completely forgetting what day of the week it was.
I went to a massive botanical garden and spent hours looking at the different types of desert cacti. The sheer evolutionary variety of the spiky plants was endlessly fascinating to me.
I tried doing a trendy juice cleanse and lasted exactly fourteen hours before caving and eating a large cheeseburger. I realized liquid diets are definitely not sustainable for my lifestyle.
I love the chaotic energy of driving with the windows rolled down on the coastal highway. The loud rushing wind and the strong smell of salt water instantly boost my mood.

I accidentally sent a text meant for my best friend complaining about my heavy workload directly to my manager. I spent the next ten minutes crafting the most desperate, backpedaling apology of my entire life.
I went to a midnight retail launch for a highly anticipated video game a few years ago. The friendly camaraderie among the enthusiastic nerds waiting in line was surprisingly wholesome.
I tried to build a custom computer and accidentally bent the fragile pins on the processor chip. The deep sinking feeling in my stomach when I realized my expensive mistake was absolutely horrible.

I spent an entire afternoon digitizing old VHS tapes of my family's childhood home movies. Watching my younger self run around without a single care in the world was a profoundly bittersweet experience.

participants.persona: Nathan is a 37-year-old first-generation Hong Konger American man, born abroad and living in Virginia.
participants.name: Nathan

memories.content: I remember the oppressive heat of the Hong Kong summers when I was a toddler.
My grandmother used to take me to the wet market every morning to buy fresh fish.
I have a vivid memory of riding the Star Ferry and feeling the sea breeze on my face.
The neon signs in Mong Kok used to mesmerize me when we walked home at night.
I once dropped my favorite toy car into a storm drain during a typhoon and cried for hours.
My dad would occasionally buy me a pineapple bun from the bakery downstairs as a special treat.
I remember the smell of incense burning at the small altar in our apartment.
Playing hide and seek with my cousins in the cramped hallways of our building was my favorite game.
I got lost in a crowded MTR station for about five minutes when I was four.
I still remember the chaotic sound of double-decker buses roaring past our street.
The airplane ride to America felt like it lasted a lifetime, and I slept on my mom's lap most of the way.
My first memory of Virginia is the overwhelming amount of green trees everywhere.
We moved into a small apartment in Fairfax, and the carpets smelled distinctly of chemical cleaner.
I didn't know a word of English when I started first grade, and I sat in silence for the first week.
My mom packed me char siu bao for lunch once, and a kid made fun of the smell.
I spent hours watching PBS Kids to learn how to pronounce English words correctly.
The first time I saw snow was in second grade, and I tried to eat a handful of it.
My dad bought a used Honda Civic, and we drove to Washington D.C. to see the monuments.
I felt deeply embarrassed when I couldn't communicate with my teacher to ask to use the restroom.

We always gather in Falls Church for the Mid-Autumn Festival, bringing boxes of lotus seed mooncakes from the local bakery. Sitting around the table listening to my relatives speak rapidly in Cantonese makes me feel deeply tied to my Hong Kong heritage.
I made my first American friend, Chris, because we both liked playing with Transformers.
I joined a local youth soccer league when I was eight and played goalie for two seasons.
My parents expected straight A's on every report card, and I studied late into the night to maintain them.
I secretly dreaded going to Saturday Chinese school, but I never dared to complain to my parents.
We drove to the Shenandoah mountains every autumn to look at the changing foliage.
I broke my arm falling off the monkey bars in third grade and had to wear a bright green cast.
My younger sister Emily was born when I was nine, and I held her nervously in the hospital room.
I was caught forging my dad's signature on a bad math test and got grounded for a month.
I read Ender's Game in middle school and started checking out every sci-fi book from the library.
My family always celebrated Thanksgiving by roasting a soy sauce duck instead of a turkey.
I saved up my allowance for six months to buy a Game Boy Advance.
I wore excessively baggy jeans in middle school because I wanted to look like the popular kids.
I had a huge crush on a girl in my biology class but never spoke a word to her.
I joined the high school debate team and won a regional tournament during my junior year.
My dad lost his job during my sophomore year, and our house was uncomfortably quiet for months.
I learned how to drive in an empty church parking lot with my mom gripping the dashboard.
Passing my driver's test on the first try was the highlight of my sophomore year.
I played varsity tennis but spent almost every match sitting as a substitute on the bench.
My friends and I spent Friday nights eating greasy pizza at the local bowling alley.
I watched the news coverage of 9/11 in my high school homeroom class in stunned silence.
I almost failed my AP Chemistry midterm, leading to a massive screaming argument with my parents.
Moving into the dorms at the University of Virginia was my first experience living away from home.
My freshman roommate constantly played loud indie rock music while I was trying to study.
I switched my major from pre-med to economics, and my mother didn't speak to me for a week.
I ate dining hall cereal for dinner almost every night during my sophomore year to save money.
I drank too much cheap beer at a fraternity party and threw up in the bushes outside.
I studied abroad in London and spent my weekends taking cheap budget flights to other European cities.
My college girlfriend Sarah broke up with me in my car, and I cried the entire drive back to my apartment.
I pulled three consecutive all-nighters to finish my senior thesis on behavioral economics.
Graduation day was incredibly humid, and my gown was completely soaked in sweat by the end.
My grandfather passed away right before I graduated, and I couldn't afford a flight back to Hong Kong for the funeral.
My first job out of college was working as a junior financial analyst in downtown Richmond.
I bought my first tailored suit for my new job and felt like an imposter wearing it.

I usually vote for Democrats based on their healthcare plans, but I really hesitated during the last election because I wanted a tougher stance on Beijing. It was incredibly frustrating to weigh my family's safety back in Hong Kong against the local policies I support here in Virginia.
My first manager yelled at me in front of the whole office over a minor spreadsheet error.
I adopted a shelter cat named Barnaby who would sleep on my laptop keyboard.
I commuted an hour each way on I-95, listening to audiobooks to stay awake.
I dated a coworker for six months, and the aftermath of our breakup made the office unbearably tense.
I submitted the final payment for my student loans on my twenty-seventh birthday.
I took a solo trip to Hong Kong in my twenties and relied heavily on Google Maps to get around.
I called my mom to get her exact recipe for tomato and egg stir-fry when I felt homesick.
When I got promoted to senior analyst, I took my parents out to an expensive steakhouse to celebrate.
I played in a recreational softball league in Richmond for three summers in a row.
I got severe food poisoning from a downtown food truck and had to call out of work for three days.
I attempted day trading with my savings and lost nearly two thousand dollars in a single week.
I attended my sister Emily's college graduation and took dozens of photos of her with my phone.
I spent several weekends hiking sections of the Appalachian Trail to get away from my email inbox.
I bought a dark blue Subaru Outback when I turned twenty-eight.
I lost my wallet at a music festival in Tennessee and had to borrow cash from my friends to eat.
I signed up for a local climbing gym but quit after a month because heights terrify me.
I went to my ten-year high school reunion and hardly recognized most of my classmates.
I met my ex-fiancee, Laura, when we accidentally grabbed each other's iced coffees at a local cafe.
Laura and I moved into a two-bedroom apartment and spent a weekend arguing over how to arrange the living room.
We adopted a golden retriever mix named Maple who immediately destroyed the baseboards in our hallway.
I proposed to Laura on a hiking trail during a weekend getaway to Asheville.

When an Asian American candidate ran for our local congressional seat, my coworkers assumed I would automatically support him. I actually ended up voting for his opponent because her voting record on taxes and education aligned perfectly with my party affiliation.
Calling off my wedding was incredibly painful, and I had to cancel all the vendor contracts myself.
I slept on a deflating air mattress in an empty apartment for a month after the breakup.
I started seeing a therapist every Tuesday evening to cope with the stress of the canceled wedding.
I worked sixty-hour weeks for a solid year just to avoid going home to an empty apartment.
My friends took me to a local comedy club for my thirty-third birthday.
I trained for four months and ran my first half-marathon in Virginia Beach.
I started packing boxes at the regional food bank on the first Saturday of every month.
I make a pour-over coffee every morning using beans I order from a roaster in Seattle.
I buy my vegetables at the farmer's market on Sunday mornings to support local growers.
I keep a cheap pair of polarized sunglasses in the glove compartment of my car at all times.
I always wake up annoyed when the landscaping crew uses leaf blowers outside my window at 7 AM.
I maintain a library of physical books in my living room and refuse to buy a Kindle.
I put on instrumental jazz playlists whenever I cook dinner.
I physically push on my locked front door three times before I go upstairs to bed.
I order the exact same extra-spicy Pad Kee Mao every Friday from the Thai place down the street.
I water the small cactus on my office desk exactly once a month.
I walk from my car to the office in the rain without an umbrella unless it is completely pouring.
I found a twenty-dollar bill outside a convenience store and used it to buy ice cream.
I got a flat tire on I-64 in a rainstorm and had to change it while semi-trucks sped past.
I accidentally emailed a harsh critique of a client directly to the client and nearly got fired.
I saw a bright green shooting star while camping near Big Meadows in Shenandoah.
I won an expensive espresso machine in the raffle at my company's holiday party.
I got second-degree sunburns on my shoulders during a destination wedding in Cancun.
I completely forgot my mother's birthday two years ago and frantically ordered expensive flowers to apologize.
I spent an entire rainy weekend watching a ten-hour documentary series about the Roman Empire.
I tried to replace the trap under my bathroom sink and ended up flooding the floor with dirty water.
I had a root canal last year and gripped the dentist's chair so hard my knuckles turned white.
My family stayed in the same cheap motel in Virginia Beach for a week every August.
I kept a hermit crab in a plastic bucket until my mom forced me to release it back into the ocean.
I carried stacks of library books home in my backpack every two weeks when I was a kid.
I used colored pencils to draw elaborate maps of fantasy continents on my bedroom floor.
A yellow jacket stung me right on the eyelid, and my eye was swollen shut for two days.
My dad stood behind me in the bathroom mirror to teach me how to tie a Windsor knot.
I sneaked into the computer room at 2 AM to play Starcraft on dial-up internet.
The overwhelming smell of chlorine always reminds me of the community pool where I learned to swim.
I squeaked through two painful years of playing the clarinet in the middle school band.
I threw up on the exit ramp of a roller coaster at Kings Dominion and a janitor had to clean it up.
My parents always had a plate of sliced oranges waiting for me when I finished my homework.
I have to beg my dad to see a doctor for his chronic back pain, but he stubbornly refuses.
My sister and I constantly quote a terrible local car dealership commercial to each other.
I spent weeks helping my parents translate and fill out the paperwork to refinance their mortgage.
I sit in silence while my uncles aggressively compare their children's salaries during Chinese New Year dinners.
My mom still scolds me for not wearing a thick enough jacket when I visit her in the winter.
I had a bitter political argument with my dad over dinner, and we ignored each other for a month.
I secretly transferred two thousand dollars to my sister's bank account so she could afford to study abroad.
I keep my late grandfather's broken pocket watch safely stored in my bedside drawer.
I drive to my parents' house for dinner every Sunday evening, even when I am exhausted from work.
I oversee a team of five junior analysts at my current financial management firm.
My coworker Dave borrows my nice gel pens and never returns them to my desk.
I presented a quarterly forecast to the executive board last month using a massive slide deck.
I regularly eat my packed lunch inside my parked car just to escape the noise of the office.
My manager formally reprimanded me for taking sick leave, which made me instantly update my resume.
I hide dark chocolate bars under a stack of file folders in my desk drawer for stressful days.
I spent six months mentoring a new hire to help him pass his certification exams.
I know exactly which lane to be in on the interstate to avoid the massive pothole near exit 74.
I usually stand near the catering table at networking events so I don't have to talk to strangers.
I transferred my entire end-of-year bonus directly into an index fund.
I maintain a jar of sourdough starter in my fridge and bake two loaves of bread every weekend.
I wake up at 7 AM on Saturdays to watch Premier League soccer matches in my living room.
I bought a cheap acoustic guitar but stopped practicing when my fingers developed painful blisters.
I buy tickets to independent foreign films at a small historic theater in Richmond.
I have five vintage wristwatches displayed in a glass case on my dresser.
I own a closet full of complex strategy board games that I rarely get to play with anyone.
I rent a kayak at the James River park a few times every summer to paddle through the rapids.
I lead my pub trivia team in answering the history and geography questions every Tuesday night.
I spent four hours assembling an IKEA bookshelf and actually enjoyed the process.
I buy a bucket of golf balls at the local driving range just to hit them as hard as I can.
