I was trapped in a hot elevator for two hours during a power outage at my office building.
I served as juror number four on a three-day trial for a misdemeanor theft case.
I brought home my terrier mix, Buster, after seeing his photo on the animal shelter's website.
I dropped my phone into a restaurant toilet and had to put it in a bag of rice for two days.
I cooked a twelve-pound turkey and made stuffing for five friends who couldn't travel home for Thanksgiving.
TSA agents pulled me aside for a random security pat-down, and I had to sprint to my gate.
I watched a large black bear wander across the porch of a rented cabin in West Virginia.
I ate six ghost pepper chicken wings on a dare and drank three glasses of milk to stop the burning.

Ever since the political crackdowns back home, I have made a strict rule to only speak Cantonese with my kids at home. It feels like keeping our specific dialect and traditions alive is the only way to fight back against the erasure happening in Hong Kong right now.
I reversed my car into my neighbor's brick mailbox and had to pay to have it rebuilt.
I scratched off a lottery ticket from my sister's Christmas card and won exactly fifty dollars.
I judge people who leave their grocery carts sitting in the middle of empty parking spaces.
I deliberately keep my apartment thermostat set to 65 degrees during the winter.
I prefer walking through older neighborhoods with brick houses rather than generic modern subdivisions.
I put my noise-canceling headphones on whenever someone on the train talks on speakerphone.
I always drink a full glass of tap water before ordering any food at a new restaurant.
I accidentally fell asleep on the couch while watching a golf tournament and woke up feeling great.
I deleted all the social media apps off my phone last year to stop myself from doom-scrolling.
I specifically sought out a car with a manual transmission because I like the control of shifting gears.
I taught my younger cousin how to properly dice an onion and sear a chicken breast.
I immediately take my shoes and socks off if I step in a puddle.
I ruined a beautiful wool sweater by accidentally putting it in the dryer on high heat.
I can clearly recall the distinct, dusty smell of the reference section in my elementary school library.
I kept a shoebox full of smooth river stones under my bed when I was seven.
A barber accidentally shaved the side of my head too short right before my senior portraits.
I locked my keys in the ignition with the engine running and had to wait for a tow truck.

Every morning, I scroll through diaspora news channels on Telegram and check the updates my cousins forward me from their private groups. The mainstream American news rarely catches the everyday changes in Hong Kong, so I rely completely on these native-language networks to know what is actually happening.
I poured a cup of salt into cookie dough instead of sugar, and my dad spat his bite into the sink.
I played a burned CD labeled 'Summer 2004' in my car and listened to all the old pop punk songs.
I dozed off on a beach towel and woke up startled when a cold wave washed over my ankles.
I always ran up the basement stairs in our first house because I was convinced a ghost was chasing me.

Even though I was born in Hong Kong, I left so young that I often stumble over my words and feel a deep sense of regret when talking to older relatives. It brings me a lot of private shame to realize I can barely read a full newspaper article in Chinese without using a translation app.
I tripped over my own feet walking up the stairs at the metro station and pretended I was just stretching.
I wore a scratchy maroon vest and a bowtie for my high school job at the local movie theater.
I frequently recite lines from The Matrix along with the characters when I watch it.
I nailed a lopsided wooden birdhouse to a tree in my backyard, but no birds ever used it.
I still have the button combinations for infinite health in GTA San Andreas memorized.
I have a faint white scar on my left knee from tripping over a coiled garden hose.
Buster and I got caught in a sudden thunderstorm and ran all the way back to the apartment.
I took a massive gulp of expired milk from the carton and immediately spit it into the sink.
I drink my morning coffee out of a heavy, blue ceramic mug I bought at a craft fair.
I watched so many adventure cartoons as a kid that I thought encountering quicksand would be a daily hazard.
I sat on my bedroom floor reading Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows until I finished it at sunrise.
I burned the roof of my mouth so badly on hot ramen that it peeled for a week.
I grip the armrests tightly during every airplane takeoff, no matter how many times I fly.
Looking back, leaving Hong Kong so young permanently fractured my sense of belonging.
I realize now that my obsession with getting perfect grades was just a way to make my parents' sacrifice feel worth it.
I sometimes wonder if I use dry sarcasm as a shield to avoid dealing with my deep fear of intimacy.
Becoming a manager made me understand why my own dad was so stressed and short-tempered when I was a kid.
I am acutely aware that my Cantonese is slipping away, which feels like losing a crucial piece of my own identity.
It is strange how a specific smell, like rain on hot asphalt, instantly transports me back to my confusing first summer in Virginia.
I notice that I always downplay my achievements, probably because I was conditioned to view pride as a dangerous flaw.
Looking at my reflection in the mirror, I can finally see my grandfather's features in my own face, bringing me a strange sense of peace.
I think my reluctance to commit to buying a house stems from a deep-seated fear of being permanently trapped in one place.
I have come to accept that I will always feel a little bit like a tourist, both when I visit Hong Kong and here in America.
Recognizing my own intense burnout last year was a major turning point in how I value my time and protect my mental health.
Sometimes I catch myself mimicking my boss's assertive mannerisms, which makes me question how much of my professional persona is actually me.

participants.persona: Zaw is a 38-year-old first-generation Burmese American man, born abroad and living in Virginia.
participants.name: Zaw

memories.content: I remember the oppressive heat of Yangon in April, feeling like a heavy blanket over everything.
The smell of frying garlic always takes me back to my grandmother's tiny kitchen.
I used to chase stray dogs down our dirt alley, though I can't remember which of my cousins was with me.
There was a monsoon rain so loud it drowned out the television completely.
I vividly recall the sweet, powdery taste of thanakha on my face.
A monk gave me a small string bracelet, but I have no idea what occasion it was for.
I remember scraping my knee badly on a rusty metal gate.
We had a blackout that lasted two days, and we played shadows by candle light.
I realize now that leaving Myanmar so young gave me a permanent sense of being caught between two worlds.
I stole a candy bar from a corner store when I was seven and hid it under my mattress.
I remember the overwhelming smell of jet fuel when we first stepped onto the tarmac in America.
My first winter in Virginia was brutally cold, and I didn't have a proper heavy coat.
I stared at the supermarket cereal aisle in absolute awe at the sheer variety.
Someone in my ESL class shared a red fruit snack with me, and it tasted like pure sugar.
I remember the sharp sting of my father slapping my hand when I disrespected my uncle.
We lived in a cramped apartment where the heating pipes clanked all night long.
Looking back, my teenage rebellion was just a desperate attempt to fit into American culture.
I got lost walking home from school once and sat on a curb until a neighbor recognized me.
I vividly remember the texture of the scratchy carpet in our first American living room.

I remember filling out a form years ago and hesitating before checking 'Asian' because people around here only ever used that word for Chinese or Korean kids. My experiences growing up Burmese just never seemed to fit into that box.
My mother cooked mohinga on the weekends, filling the whole apartment with the smell of fish broth.
I often wonder if my fear of failure stems from watching my parents sacrifice everything to move here.
I had a blue bicycle with a rusty chain that I rode around the cul-de-sac for hours.
There was a time in my twenties when I couldn't afford groceries and just ate rice for a week.
I remember the exact shade of orange the sky turned during my first Virginia autumn.
I caught a firefly in a jar, fascinated by its glowing green light.
My uncle taught me how to fish, though I only recall the smell of the damp lake water.
I still feel a pit in my stomach when I think about the cruel nickname the kids gave me in middle school.
I found a stray kitten under a porch, but it ran away before I could catch it.
I broke my mother's favorite jade bracelet and blamed it on the wind knocking it over.
The taste of warm soy milk in the morning always reminds me of weekends with my parents.
I recall the loud buzzing of the cicadas during the humid Virginia summers.
It occurs to me that my obsession with cooking is really just a way to keep my grandmother's memory alive.
I used to hide in the closet to read comic books with a flashlight.
I remember the nervous excitement of waiting for the school bus on my first day of high school.
I secretly failed a semester of college and forged a report card to show my parents.
A friend gave me a mix CD that I listened to until it wouldn't play anymore.
I remember the distinct smell of chlorine from the public pool down the street.
We took a family road trip to Florida, and I felt incredibly carsick the whole way.
I've started noticing how much I sound like my father when I get stressed.
I bought a cheap guitar at a garage sale but never managed to learn a single chord.
I remember the overwhelming panic attack I had during my final exams.
The feeling of sand between my toes at Virginia Beach is permanently etched in my mind.
I ate a massive slice of pizza in New York City, burning the roof of my mouth completely.
The older I get, the more I appreciate the quiet stability of my life in Virginia.
I remember the blinding flash of a camera during my high school graduation.
I accidentally backed into a parked car and drove away without leaving a note.
I had a poster of a silver sports car taped to my bedroom wall for years.
The crisp, cold air of the Blue Ridge Mountains took my breath away the first time I went hiking.
I remember the sticky sweetness of a mango I ate on a hot July afternoon.
I can see now that my first relationship ended because I wasn't ready to be vulnerable.
I used to watch rain stream down the car window, imagining two drops racing each other.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders after falling asleep at a park.
I remember the heavy weight of my backpack filled with college textbooks.
I drank coffee so strong it made my hands shake for hours afterward.
My cousin and I got into a physical fight over a misunderstanding, and we haven't spoken since.
I saw a shooting star once while lying on the hood of my first car.
I remember the overwhelming scent of pine trees during a winter cabin trip.
It's strange to think that my American identity feels more natural to me now than my Burmese one.
I found a twenty-dollar bill crumpled on the sidewalk and felt like I had won the lottery.
I remember the terrifying sound of thunder shaking our entire apartment building.
I ate a bowl of spicy noodles that made my eyes water, but I couldn't stop eating.
I had a vivid dream about flying over a dense jungle, and I still remember the green canopy.
I got fired from my first office job because I kept making careless data entry errors.
The cold metal of the subway pole always left my hands smelling like pennies.
I remember the soft hum of the refrigerator in the middle of a sleepless night.
I realize my tendency to avoid conflict is deeply rooted in how my family communicated.
I tripped going up the stairs in front of a huge crowd and felt my face burn with embarrassment.
I remember the sharp crunch of dry autumn leaves beneath my boots.
A bird flew into my bedroom window, leaving a dusty imprint of its wings on the glass.
I tasted fresh snow for the first time, disappointed that it just tasted like cold water.
I remember the warmth of a camp fire on my face while my back was freezing.
Looking at old photos, I understand why my parents were so protective of me.
I bought a bright yellow shirt that I thought looked great, but I never actually wore it.
I remember the rhythmic thumping of the washing machine in the basement.
I tried to build a bookshelf from scratch and completely ruined the wood.
I sometimes feel a profound guilt for losing my fluency in Burmese.
I remember the sour taste of a lemon drop candy my grandmother gave me.
I watched a movie so sad that I cried in the theater, hoping no one would notice.
I was pulled over for speeding and felt my heart pounding in my chest.
I recognize that my ambition is driven entirely by a need to prove my family's sacrifices were worth it.
I remember the distinct squeak of my wet sneakers on a linoleum floor.
I carved a pumpkin for Halloween, getting the slimy seeds all over my sleeves.
I attended a Burmese water festival in Maryland and got absolutely drenched in seconds.
I found a beautiful smooth stone on a riverbank and kept it in my pocket for weeks.
I secretly threw away the terrible knitted sweater my aunt gave me.
I remember the dizzying sensation of looking down from the top of the Washington Monument.
I drank a glass of expired milk by accident and immediately threw up in the sink.
I stood in the middle of a crowded concert, feeling the bass vibrate through my ribs.
I remember the soothing sound of wind chimes hanging on our front porch.
I helped my father fix his car, holding the flashlight steady for what felt like hours.
I skipped my high school prom because I was too embarrassed that I didn't have a date.
I remember the rough texture of the bark on the old oak tree in our backyard.
I ate a persimmon before it was ripe and my entire mouth puckered up instantly.
I walked through a spiderweb in the dark and flailed wildly trying to get it off me.
I remember the metallic taste of blood after biting my tongue really hard.
I got a terrible haircut the day before school pictures and wore a hat until the teacher made me take it off.
I remember the smell of fresh asphalt on the road outside our neighborhood.
I accidentally dropped my phone into a lake and watched it sink out of sight.
I lied about reading a book for a college English class and barely passed the oral exam.

When I visited Yangon in my twenties, I felt completely lost trying to order food from the street vendors. I just remember feeling a sharp ache in my chest when the locals immediately treated me like a wealthy American tourist.
I recall the intense blue color of a butterfly that landed on my shoulder for just a second.
I burned my hand on the stove while trying to make tea leaf salad for the first time.

At a community gathering last year, the older folks were practically begging the kids to pay close attention to our traditional dances. With the military destroying so much back home, holding onto our culture tightly feels like a matter of survival.
I remember the crisp snap of opening a brand new notebook.
I rode a rollercoaster that went upside down and kept my eyes squeezed shut the entire time.
I found an old letter from my grandfather and wept because I couldn't read the Burmese script.
I remember the greasy smell of the fast food place I worked at during my senior year.
I stayed up all night playing a video game until the morning light leaked through the blinds.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy quilt on a freezing January night.
I stepped on a piece of broken glass barefoot and had to limp to the bathroom.
I got incredibly lost in a hospital trying to find a friend's room.
I remember the sharp, minty smell of the muscle rub my dad used after a long shift.

Most mornings, I frantically scroll through specific Burmese Facebook groups just to figure out what is really happening in the country. Because the American news rarely covers Myanmar, I have to rely entirely on those diaspora pages and urgent voice notes from my uncle.
I had an irrational fear of the dark basement in our old townhouse.
I won a small trophy for a spelling bee, but the nameplate had a typo on my last name.

We went to a Thingyan water festival in Falls Church a few summers ago, and hearing the traditional music playing over the loudspeakers gave me chills. Standing there with so many other Burmese families eating mohinga made me feel intensely proud of where I came from.
I remember the intense satisfaction of finally parallel parking perfectly on my driving test.
I found a stray dog wandering on the highway and pulled over to guide it to safety.
I was terribly homesick during my first week at college, crying quietly in my dorm room.
I remember the unmistakable scent of damp earth after a sudden summer thunderstorm.
I tried to dye my hair blond in college and it turned a horrific shade of orange.
I caught a nasty flu and hallucinated that the walls were breathing.
I remember the loud, rhythmic chanting from a monastery I visited during a trip back to Yangon.
I completely forgot my best friend's birthday and had to buy a terrible gift from a gas station.
I remember the warm glow of string lights hanging in my first apartment.
I slipped on a patch of black ice and bruised my tailbone badly.
I had a crush on a coworker for two years but never had the courage to say anything.
I remember the incredible taste of a ripe peach bought fresh from a roadside stand.
I spent a whole afternoon skipping rocks across a completely still pond.
I was stung by a bee on my eyelid and looked like a monster for a week.
I remember the soft, rhythmic clicking of the ceiling fan in my childhood bedroom.
I found a twenty dollar bill in the pocket of a winter coat I hadn't worn in a year.
I broke a glass jar of tomato sauce in the grocery store aisle and walked away in panic.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun reflecting off the snow.
I fed a flock of seagulls at the beach and got swarmed instantly.
I remember the smell of old paper and dust in the back corner of the public library.
I tried to fix a leaky pipe under the sink and ended up flooding the kitchen floor.
I remember the intense burning sensation in my lungs after running a mile in the cold.
I accidentally sent a highly critical email to the person it was written about.
I recall the hollow sound of my footsteps echoing in an empty parking garage.
I watched a parade from the curb, captivated by the booming sound of the brass band.
I ate way too much cotton candy at a fair and felt completely nauseous on the drive home.
I remember the dull ache of a tooth cavity before I finally went to the dentist.
I borrowed my dad's car without asking and dented the fender against a mailbox.
I remember the smell of burning wood from a neighbor's chimney on a crisp evening.
I tripped over a curb while texting and scraped the palms of my hands.
I remember the dizzying array of neon lights when I visited Times Square for the first time.
I bought a vintage watch at a flea market, only to find out it was completely broken.
I remember the soft, powdery feel of flour on my hands while learning to make dumplings.
I watched a street magician perform a card trick and still can't figure out how he did it.
I remember the jarring screech of a subway train braking at the station.
I accidentally dropped a full cup of coffee on the floor of a crowded cafe.
I found out my high school girlfriend was cheating on me when I saw her at the mall.
I remember the cool breeze blowing through the window on a long nighttime drive.
I helped an old woman carry her groceries up three flights of stairs and felt deeply proud.
I remember the sharp, stinging smell of ammonia from cleaning the bathroom.
I tried to jump over a puddle and landed directly in the middle of it.
I remember the vibrant yellow color of the rain boots I wore as a little kid.
I had a massive argument with my boss and spent the entire drive home in tears.
I remember the soft crunch of biting into a perfectly toasted piece of bread.
I watched a spider slowly spin a web in the corner of my bedroom ceiling.
I remember the feeling of panic when I momentarily lost my passport at the airport.
I accidentally locked my keys inside my apartment and had to sleep on a friend's couch.
I remember the sweet, floral scent of jasmine blooming in a neighbor's garden.
I went to a comedy show and laughed so hard my stomach muscles ached the next day.
I remember the rough, calloused texture of my grandfather's hands holding mine.
I backed into a trash can at the end of my driveway, sending garbage everywhere.
I was deeply ashamed when my credit card was declined at a restaurant on a first date.
I remember the mesmerizing rhythm of windshield wipers during a heavy downpour.
I burned a batch of cookies so badly the smoke alarm went off for ten minutes.
I remember the cold shock of jumping into an unheated swimming pool.
I found a perfectly preserved autumn leaf and placed it inside a heavy book to press.
I remember the intense silence of the woods after a heavy blanket of snow had fallen.
I lied to a friend about having other plans because I was too depressed to leave the house.
I remember the tart, refreshing taste of iced hibiscus tea on a sweltering day.
I accidentally squished a beautiful caterpillar and felt surprisingly guilty about it.
I remember the distinct clicking sound of a turn signal at a quiet red light.
I tried to ride a skateboard down a hill and immediately fell off, bruising my hip.
I remember the rich, earthy smell of coffee beans roasting at a local cafe.
I got a paper cut from a brand new envelope and it stung for hours.
I snooped through my roommate's journal and read something very hurtful about myself.
I remember the blinding brightness of the screen when checking my phone in a dark room.
I watched a squirrel bury an acorn in my front yard and then completely forget where it was.
I remember the warm, fuzzy feeling of putting on clothes fresh out of the dryer.
I tried to fix a tear in my favorite jeans and sewed the leg completely shut.
I remember the sharp jolt of static electricity from touching a brass doorknob.
I accidentally left the freezer open all night and melted everything inside.
I developed a sudden, severe allergy to a medication and ended up in the emergency room.
I remember the sweet, milky taste of a Thai iced tea from my favorite local restaurant.

I get a tight feeling in my throat when I struggle to find the right Burmese words while talking to my older aunts. Growing up here meant losing my fluency over time, and it makes me incredibly sad that I can't just have a normal conversation with them.
I saw a vibrant double rainbow over the highway after a summer storm.
I remember the rough texture of a damp towel left on the bathroom floor.
I spilled red wine on a white rug and tried frantically to scrub it out with club soda.
I remember the low hum of the lawnmower from a neighbor's yard on a Sunday morning.
I held a tiny, fragile bird egg that had fallen from a nest in the oak tree.
I choked on a piece of ice at a restaurant and a stranger had to hit me on the back.
I remember the distinct smell of fresh paint when moving into my current apartment.
I got scammed out of five hundred dollars by a fake online seller and felt completely foolish.
I remember the soft rustling sound of a plastic grocery bag rolling across the empty street.

participants.persona: Hannah is a 21-year-old second-generation Korean American woman, born in the U.S. and living in New York and Washington, DC.
participants.name: Hannah

memories.content: I remember arguing with my NYU roommate in early 2020 because she loved a progressive candidate's healthcare plan, but I completely opposed his vague talk about pulling US troops out of South Korea. I could never prioritize domestic healthcare policies in New York over my halmeoni's intense fears about North Korean aggression.
I vaguely remember my dad trying to teach me how to ride a bike around age six, but looking back, I realize I only remember the feeling of panic, not the actual day.
I think I broke my arm falling off the monkey bars in third grade, or maybe it was just a severe sprain. It makes me wonder how many of my childhood pain memories are exaggerated by fear.
There was this girl named Sarah or maybe Samantha in middle school who stopped talking to me suddenly. I still catch myself trying to figure out what I did wrong, even though it was years ago.
I remember moving to my first dorm in New York and crying for hours after my parents left. It's strange how I desperately wanted independence but was completely terrified when I finally got it.
My grandmother used to make this amazing seaweed soup for my birthday, probably when I was around ten. I realized recently that I never bothered to learn her recipe, and it breaks my heart.
We took a field trip to some museum in DC during high school, maybe the Air and Space one. Looking back, I think that trip was the first time I felt a sense of belonging in a big city.

Every Chuseok, my parents would drag us to a community center in Queens where I'd spend hours helping Auntie Min-ji fold what felt like thousands of mandu. Smelling the sesame oil and listening to the older women gossip in a rapid mix of English and Jeju dialect always anchored me to being undeniably Korean.
I had a massive crush on a boy named Daniel in ninth grade, and I wrote him a letter I never sent. I reflect on that a lot, noticing how my fear of rejection hasn't really changed.
I got a D on my first chemistry test in high school, which I hid from my parents for weeks. That was the moment I realized I couldn't always be the perfect daughter they expected.
Sometime around 2018, I started listening to a lot of indie rock to fit in with my new friend group. I'm aware now that I was just masking my real interests to seem cool.
I remember walking through Central Park during my freshman year and feeling totally overwhelmed by the crowds. I often think about how much my anxiety shaped those early college experiences.

My mom bought me a beautiful hanbok when I was little, maybe four or five years old. I recognize now that she was trying so hard to keep our culture alive for me in a predominantly white neighborhood.
I took a philosophy class my sophomore year that completely confused me. I find it funny now how I pretended to understand Kant just to impress the professor.
I had this terrible fight with my younger brother about borrowing my car, probably in 2020. I still feel guilty about how angry I got, knowing I was just stressed about applying to colleges.
I remember getting lost on the DC Metro sometime last year and ending up in Virginia. It makes me realize how often I rely on my phone instead of actually paying attention to my surroundings.
I went to a protest in New York around 2021, though I can't remember the exact street we marched down. That day fundamentally changed how I view my responsibility to speak up for others.
I think I sprained my ankle running for a bus in the rain a couple of years ago. I often use that memory as a reminder to just slow down and not rush through life so much.
My first real boyfriend broke up with me in a coffee shop, maybe a Starbucks in Brooklyn. Looking back, I can see how toxic we were together, even though it devastated me at the time.
I remember trying to bleach my hair blonde in the dorm bathroom freshman year and it turned orange. It taught me a valuable lesson about accepting my natural features instead of forcing a trend.
I had a weird dream about my teeth falling out right before midterms last semester. I realize now that my body was practically screaming at me to manage my stress better.
I spent a summer volunteering at a clinic in DC, or maybe it was a community center. I think about those people often, realizing how incredibly sheltered my upbringing actually was.
I remember lying to my best friend about having plans so I could just stay home and sleep. I still feel a twinge of shame about it, knowing I struggle with setting honest boundaries.
My dad took me to a baseball game when I was around nine, probably the Yankees. It occurs to me now that he didn't even like baseball, he just wanted to spend time with me.
I shoplifted a lip gloss from Sephora when I was fifteen and felt sick to my stomach for days. I reflect on that sometimes, fascinated by how intense my moral guilt was over something so small.

I remember eating $1 pizza slices in Manhattan at 2 AM with my roommates during sophomore year. I cherish those nights, knowing they were the fleeting moments of pure freedom before adult responsibilities hit.
I recall going to a Korean grocery store with my mom in Queens and begging for Pepero. I think the boxes were brightly colored and stacked near the register.
There was a neighborhood dog that always barked at me when I walked home from middle school. It might have been a Golden Retriever, but it was really aggressive.
I lost my favorite silver ring somewhere on the NYU campus last year. I remember retracing my steps through Washington Square Park but never found it.
My brother broke a window in the living room with a tennis ball when we were kids. We blamed it on the wind, but my parents definitely knew.
I took a ceramics class in high school and made a really lopsided bowl. I painted it blue and gave it to my dad for Father's Day.
I remember watching some cartoon about spies after school every day in elementary school. The theme song is stuck in my head, but the characters' names are completely gone.
We went to a cherry blossom festival in DC a few years ago. It was so crowded I couldn't even see the trees, just a sea of people taking photos.
I tried to cook kimchi fried rice in my dorm microwave once. The whole floor smelled like garlic for three days and my RA was furious.
I had a math teacher in tenth grade who always wore the same brown sweater. I think his name was Mr. Harrison, but it could have been Henderson.
I went to a midnight movie premiere for some superhero film when I was sixteen. We snuck in our own candy, mostly Skittles and gummy worms.
I recall falling asleep on a subway train and waking up at the end of the line in Brooklyn. It was terrifying and took me two hours to get back.
My family used to have a gray Honda Accord that smelled faintly of old coffee. We drove it to Florida once and the AC broke somewhere in Georgia.
I accidentally spilled iced coffee all over my laptop keyboard freshman year. It cost me like four hundred dollars to fix and I cried in the Apple store.
There was a huge snowstorm when I was in fifth grade that gave us a week off school. I built a snow fort that I thought was massive, but was probably tiny.
I ate a really terrible hot dog from a street cart in Midtown once. I was sick for a day and a half and missed a huge sociology lecture.
My roommate last year had a habit of leaving her wet towels on the bathroom floor. We argued about it constantly, usually on Sunday mornings.

Joining the Asian American Student Union at Georgetown was the first time I realized I didn't have to choose between being solely Korean or completely American. I see now that embracing this broader label gave me the emotional vocabulary to bridge the gap between my parents' immigrant struggles and my own upbringing.
I went to a concert at the 9:30 Club in DC with some friends a while back. I can't remember the band's name, but the bass was so loud my chest vibrated.
I remember catching fireflies in a jar during a summer barbecue at my aunt's house. I accidentally left the jar in the sun the next day and felt terrible.
I had braces for three years in middle school and chose pink rubber bands once. It looked like my gums were bleeding so I never did it again.
I tried out for the school play in ninth grade and completely forgot my monologue. I just stood there in silence until the drama teacher told me to sit down.
We went on a family vacation to Hawaii when I was twelve or thirteen. I got terrible sunburn on my shoulders on the very first day.
I ordered a matcha latte from a cafe in Georgetown but they accidentally made it with regular milk. My stomach was upset for the entire afternoon.
I remember buying a fake ID from a guy in an alley when I was nineteen. It looked terrible and got confiscated the first time I tried to use it.
My dad used to play old Korean trot music in the car on Sunday mornings. I hated it then, but now the melody feels strangely comforting.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk outside a deli in Manhattan. I immediately spent it on fancy pastries and felt really lucky.
I went on a terrible Tinder date with a guy who talked about his ex for an hour. I faked a phone call from my roommate to leave early.
I think I won a spelling bee in fourth grade by spelling 'chrysanthemum' correctly. My mom took a picture, but my eyes were closed in it.

I felt completely alienated by the Asian American label during a summer internship on Capitol Hill around 2021. A senior staffer just assumed my background was exactly like his privileged Cupertino upbringing because we both checked the AAPI box, which completely erased my family's working-class struggles.
I got a piercing on my upper ear during a spontaneous trip to St. Marks Place. It got infected a week later and I had to take it out.
I remember trying to learn the guitar when I was fifteen, using some cheap acoustic. My fingers blistered so badly I gave up after a month.
There was a pigeon that flew into my apartment window in New York once. It stunned itself for a minute before flying away, leaving a dusty smudge on the glass.
I took a wrong turn driving in DC and ended up near the Pentagon. The roads were so confusing I just drove in circles until my GPS reconnected.
I remember eating instant ramen dry, crushed up with the seasoning packet, in middle school. It was a weird trend, but we all did it at lunch.
I had a fish named Bubbles when I was seven that only lived for two weeks. My parents replaced it while I was at school, but I could tell it was a different fish.
I got stuck in a subway turnstile at Union Square during rush hour. Everyone was staring and I was so embarrassed I practically crawled out.
I bought a vintage leather jacket from a thrift store in Brooklyn for forty dollars. It smells a bit like mothballs, but I wear it almost every day in the fall.
My mom tried to teach me how to knit a scarf one winter. I kept dropping stitches until it looked more like a triangle than a rectangle.
I remember going to a Korean barbecue place in Koreatown for my 19th birthday. We ordered way too much pork belly and had to take it home in plastic containers.
I accidentally locked myself out of my dorm room in my pajamas during freshman year. I had to walk to the front desk in fuzzy slippers to get a spare key.
I was in a car accident in high school where someone rear-ended my mom's sedan. I just remember the awful crunching sound and my neck aching the next day.
I remember staying up until 4 AM cramming for a biology final my first semester. I fell asleep during the actual exam and woke up with drool on the paper.
I planted a small tomato plant on my apartment fire escape last spring. The pigeons ate every single tomato before they were even ripe.
I had a collection of gel pens in middle school that I kept in a clear plastic case. I traded a sparkly blue one for a scented pink one with a girl named Jessica.
I remember going to the National Zoo in DC and being really disappointed by the pandas. They just slept facing the wall the entire time we were there.
I tried to dye my own clothes with bleach in the bathtub once. I ruined three perfectly good shirts and made the bathroom smell toxic.
I went ice skating at Rockefeller Center when I was maybe ten years old. I fell backward and bruised my tailbone so badly I couldn't sit normally for a week.
I attended a really boring seminar on economics last month just for the free pizza. The pizza was cold and they ran out of cheese slices before I got to the front.
My family went camping somewhere upstate when I was a kid and it rained nonstop. We spent two days playing Uno inside a damp, freezing tent.
I bought a pair of high heels for a formal event that were at least a size too small. I ended up walking home barefoot on the sidewalks of Manhattan.
I remember seeing a really bright shooting star from my bedroom window in high school. I made a wish about getting into a good college, which feels silly now.
I had a diary with a little silver padlock when I was nine. I lost the key almost immediately and had to break the lock with a rock to open it.
I got caught cheating on a vocabulary quiz in sixth grade by looking at my friend's paper. The teacher called my parents and I was grounded for a month.
I tried to make homemade dumplings with my aunt for Lunar New Year. Mine were all misshapen and burst open when we boiled them.
I went to a rooftop party in Brooklyn last summer that was entirely too crowded. Someone spilled red wine down the back of my white dress.
I remember reading the entire Harry Potter series over one summer break. I stayed in my pajamas for days, completely ignoring the sunny weather outside.
I took a yoga class at a studio in DC and accidentally fell over during a balancing pose. I knocked into the person next to me and apologized profusely.
I had a pet hamster named Squeaks that escaped from his cage in the middle of the night. We found him two days later hiding behind the refrigerator.
I remember getting a terrible haircut in eighth grade where the bangs were way too short. I wore headbands for three months trying to hide it.
I went to a museum in New York and stared at a completely blank white canvas for ten minutes. I was trying to seem intellectual, but honestly, I didn't get it.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about my boss directly to my boss last year. I claimed it was a typo, but the awkwardness never really went away.
My dad cooked a turkey for Thanksgiving one year and forgot to take the plastic bag out of the inside. We ended up ordering Chinese takeout instead.
I remember finding a stray kitten near the dumpsters behind my apartment building. I tried to feed it some lunch meat, but it ran away under a car.
I bought a really expensive textbook for a class and the professor literally never used it. I tried to sell it back at the end of the semester, but they offered me five dollars.
I tripped walking up the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on a school trip. I scraped my knee badly and had to hobble around the rest of the afternoon.
I remember trying bubble tea for the first time in high school and choking on a tapioca pearl. It took me a few years to finally enjoy the drink after that.
I painted my bedroom walls a neon green color when I was thirteen. My parents hated it, but they let me keep it until I moved out for college.
I got a really bad case of food poisoning from some sketchy sushi in the East Village. I spent an entire weekend curled up on my bathroom floor.
I remember watching my younger brother graduate from high school and feeling incredibly old. He tripped slightly on the stage, but I don't think anyone else noticed.
I bought a film camera at a flea market, shot three rolls of film, and never got them developed. They are still sitting in a drawer in my bedroom somewhere.
I attended a political rally in Washington Square Park and couldn't hear a single thing the speaker was saying. I just clapped whenever the people around me started clapping.
I had a terrible fear of the dark until I was about ten years old. I used to make my dad check the closet and under the bed every single night.
I remember slipping on a patch of black ice on my way to an 8 AM class. A random guy helped me up, but I was so mortified I just sprinted away.
I took a spontaneous bus trip to Philadelphia with a friend just to get cheesesteaks. The bus ride was miserable, but the sandwich was actually pretty great.
I lost my debit card at a bar in Adams Morgan and didn't realize until the next morning. I had to cancel it and live off the cash in my piggy bank for a week.
I remember getting my wisdom teeth removed and crying because I thought the nurse took my nose. The anesthesia really messed with my head.
I tried to learn how to skateboard during my freshman year to impress a girl. I ended up spraining my wrist on the very first day and gave up.
I went to a friend's beach house in Maryland and got stung by a jellyfish. My leg burned for hours and left a weird red squiggly mark.
I remember drawing temporary tattoos on my arms with sharpies in middle school. It took days of scrubbing with alcohol to finally get the ink off.
I bought a ridiculously large iced coffee before a road trip and had to pee halfway through a tunnel. It was pure agony waiting for the next rest stop.
I accidentally threw my house keys into the trash chute of my apartment building. I had to pay the super fifty dollars to fish them out of the dumpster.
I remember watching the sunrise from a rooftop in Brooklyn after a long night of talking with my friends. It was one of those perfect, quiet moments where the city felt small.
I tried to cut my own bangs in the bathroom mirror during quarantine. I ended up with a crooked fringe that took six months to grow out.
I went to a fancy restaurant for restaurant week and pretended to know what a truffle was. I actually thought it tasted a little bit like dirt.
I remember finding an old photo of my parents from the nineties where they had matching leather jackets. They looked so cool, unlike the practical parents I grew up with.
I dropped my phone down a sewer grate while trying to hail a cab in the rain. I just stared down at the dark water, totally numb, before walking home.
I had a substitute teacher in elementary school who taught us how to fold origami paper cranes. I used to fill my desk with them until my regular teacher made me throw them away.
I went to a basement concert in DC where the ceiling was so low the singer had to duck. The air was incredibly humid and smelled strongly of cheap beer.
I remember trying to bake a cake for my mom's birthday but confusing salt for sugar. She took one bite and tried to smile, but we ended up throwing the whole thing away.
I bought a tarot deck at a bookstore and tried to give my friends readings in the dorms. I was just making up the meanings, but a few of them were convinced I was psychic.
I got a speeding ticket on the highway coming back from Virginia, my very first one. I was so nervous talking to the cop that my hands were shaking violently.
I remember walking through the Natural History Museum and being completely terrified by the giant squid exhibit. I refused to go into that room again for years.
I went on a date to a botanical garden in New York and completely forgot my allergy medicine. I sneezed through the entire afternoon and ruined the romantic mood.
I accidentally stole a plastic cup from a diner because I walked out while still drinking my soda. I felt strangely guilty about it for weeks.
I had a favorite stuffed bear named Barnaby that I carried everywhere until I was six. I think I left him at a hotel in Florida and my parents wouldn't go back for him.
I remember watching a massive thunderstorm roll in from my dorm window, the sky turning a weird greenish-purple. The power went out for a few hours shortly after.
I tried a very trendy spin class in Manhattan and couldn't unclip my shoes from the pedals at the end. The instructor had to come over and pry me off the bike.
I went to a protest in high school and held a sign that my friend made. I didn't fully understand the issue, but I liked feeling like I was part of something important.
I remember eating an entire pint of Ben & Jerry's after bombing a midterm exam. It was Half Baked, and I woke up feeling just as miserable the next morning.
I found a cool vintage mirror on the street and carried it ten blocks to my apartment. I realized later it was infested with some kind of tiny bugs and had to throw it out.
I had a recurring nightmare as a kid about being chased by a giant floating eye. I would wake up sweating and refuse to look at the shadows in my room.
I accidentally boarded the wrong Amtrak train at Penn Station and almost ended up going to Boston instead of DC. A conductor noticed my ticket just before the doors closed.
I remember making a terrible papier-mache volcano for a science fair in fifth grade. It didn't erupt properly, just sort of oozed pink foam down one side.
I tried to become a runner during the pandemic and jogged around the National Mall. I barely made it a mile before my lungs felt like they were on fire.
I wore a velvet dress to a winter dance in high school that generated so much static electricity. I kept accidentally shocking anyone who stood too close to me.
I remember going to a Korean day spa with my mom and aunt, and being scrubbed until my skin was raw. It hurt at the time, but I felt incredibly clean afterward.
I bought a cheap umbrella from a street vendor during a sudden downpour in the city. The wind immediately flipped it inside out and broke three of the metal spokes.

Hearing stories about my grandfather surviving the Japanese occupation made me hyper-fixate on electing politicians who actively recognize historical atrocities in East Asia. During a local Queens city council race a few years ago, my family rallied behind a Korean candidate solely because he promised to fund a comfort women memorial.
I had a massive collection of sea glass that I gathered during trips to the Jersey shore. I kept it in a mason jar on my windowsill where it caught the morning light.
I remember sneaking into an R-rated horror movie with my friends when we were fourteen. I kept my eyes closed for half the movie because the sound effects alone were too scary.
I took a pottery painting class and decorated a mug with little yellow daisies. When they fired it in the kiln, the colors morphed and turned into a muddy orange.
I accidentally sent a heart emoji to my strict political science professor in a late-night email. He never mentioned it, but I couldn't look him in the eye for the rest of the term.
I remember going apple picking upstate one autumn and eating so many apples I got a stomach ache. The cider donuts we bought on the way out were completely worth it, though.
I tried out for the high school volleyball team but couldn't serve the ball over the net to save my life. The coach gently suggested I stick to managing the team instead.
I bought a tiny cactus for my desk thinking it was impossible to kill. I somehow overwatered it, and it turned into mush within a month.
I remember watching my dad try to fix a leaky pipe under the kitchen sink, swearing quietly in Korean. He eventually gave up and called a plumber two days later.
I got separated from my friends at a huge outdoor music festival in New York. I spent three hours wandering around without cell service before finally finding them near a pretzel stand.
I tried to knit a sweater once, but I lost count of the rows and one sleeve ended up twice as long as the other. I donated it to a thrift store hoping someone would find it artsy.

I still pay for a premium KakaoTalk subscription just so I can send digital gifts to my cousins in Busan every time our favorite idols release a new album. Even though I haven't visited Korea since maybe 2015 or 2016, staying up until 3 AM in my DC apartment to live-stream the SBS Drama Awards keeps me tied to my family there.
I remember being obsessed with this one anime in middle school and drawing the characters all over my binders. Looking back at those drawings makes me cringe so hard.
I accidentally left a frozen pizza in the oven for three hours because I fell asleep on the couch. The smoke alarm woke me up and the apartment smelled like char for days.
I went to a psychic in the West Village just for fun, and she told me I would move to Europe. It's been two years and I haven't even renewed my passport.
I remember getting a really terrible sunburn on my scalp during a summer boat ride. My hair started peeling a week later and it looked like severe dandruff.
I bought a pair of roller skates online during a phase where I wanted to be outdoorsy. I fell backwards on the pavement once and they have been in my closet ever since.
I had to give a presentation on the French Revolution in tenth grade and completely lost my voice the morning of. I croaked through the whole thing while the class stifled laughter.
I remember finding a twenty-dollar bill inside a library book I checked out for a research paper. I used it to buy an overly expensive salad for lunch that day.
I tried to make homemade kombucha in my dorm room, hiding the jar in my closet. It fermented too much and the glass shattered, soaking my favorite shoes in vinegar-smelling liquid.
I went on a date to the American History Museum and the guy mansplained the entire Civil War exhibit to me. I excused myself to use the bathroom and just took the Metro home.
I remember trying to learn French on an app for about a month before a family trip to Montreal. The only phrase I actually remembered was how to ask for a croissant.
I accidentally washed a bright red sock with my load of white laundry in the dorm basement. All my favorite t-shirts came out a weird, blotchy shade of pink.
I had a favorite blue hoodie in high school that I lost at a football game. I swear I saw a girl in my math class wearing it a week later, but I was too shy to ask.
I remember my mom packing me slices of Korean pear in a little Tupperware for school snacks. They were always perfectly peeled and cut into little rabbit shapes.
I got a really bad cramp in my calf while swimming in a lake during a summer camp. A counselor had to drag me to the shallow end while I panicked.
I bought a ridiculously oversized winter coat from a vintage store that made me look like a sleeping bag. It was completely shapeless but kept me so warm waiting for the subway.
I remember trying to hold a plank for three minutes in gym class to win a physical fitness award. I collapsed at two minutes and my abs hurt every time I laughed for a week.
I ordered an espresso martini at a fancy bar in DC trying to seem sophisticated. It tasted terribly bitter, but I sipped it slowly all night to justify the eighteen-dollar price tag.
I accidentally stepped on a dead mouse on the sidewalk in Brooklyn while wearing thin sandals. I screamed so loudly that a guy across the street dropped his coffee.
I remember making a mixed CD for my best friend in middle school filled with sad emo songs. We would listen to it on her boombox and pretend we had tragic lives.
I tried a raw oyster for the first time at a restaurant in Chelsea and immediately gagged. I swallowed it whole with a huge gulp of water and told everyone I loved it.
I got stuck in an elevator in an old academic building for about forty-five minutes. There was only one other person in there, and we just stood in complete, awkward silence.
I remember attempting to do a cartwheel in the park and pulling a muscle in my groin. I had to limp all the way to the subway station pretending I was perfectly fine.
I bought a fancy fountain pen hoping it would improve my terrible handwriting. It just leaked dark blue ink all over my fingers and the inside of my favorite tote bag.
I accidentally insulted my roommate's cooking by calling her chili 'interesting' instead of good. She was deeply offended and didn't speak to me for two days.
I remember getting caught in a torrential downpour without an umbrella near Columbus Circle. I was completely soaked to the bone and just started laughing at how absurd it was.
I tried out a weird diet where I only ate green foods for a week during high school. By the fourth day, I was so desperate for a potato chip I gave up entirely.
I bought a record player at a flea market, only to realize later it didn't have a needle. I used it as a very expensive decorative paperweight on my desk.
I remember my parents fighting in Korean in the kitchen late at night when I was little. I couldn't understand the words, but the sharp tones made me hide under my covers.
I accidentally knocked over a massive display of oranges at a grocery store in Queens. A very kind employee helped me pick them up while I apologized a hundred times.
I had a sudden nosebleed in the middle of a standardized test in high school. The proctor had to escort me to the nurse's office with a tissue pressed to my face.
I remember finding an old mixtape in my dad's car that was just hours of 80s synth-pop. I listened to it on the drive to soccer practice every Tuesday.
I tried to dye a pair of white jeans black, but the dye didn't take evenly. They ended up looking like a gray, cloudy mess, and I threw them away.
I went to a rooftop bar in DC and the wind blew my favorite silk scarf off the edge. I watched it float away into the night sky, feeling strangely dramatic.
I remember getting a splinter in my foot from the boardwalk at Coney Island. My dad had to dig it out with a sterilized needle while I cried.
I bought a very expensive face serum that smelled exactly like hot dog water. I used the entire bottle anyway because I refused to waste my money.
I accidentally left my debit card in the ATM machine outside my apartment. Luckily, the person behind me chased me down the block to give it back.
I remember making a massive pile of autumn leaves in the front yard with my brother. We jumped in it once, got covered in dirty spider webs, and immediately went inside.
I tried to assemble a cheap bookshelf from IKEA by myself and put the back panel on backwards. I was too tired to fix it, so the unfinished cardboard side faced outward for a year.
I went on a hiking trail in upstate New York and got completely lost for two hours. I eventually found the road by following the sound of cars on the highway.
I remember baking chocolate chip cookies but realizing halfway through that I forgot the baking soda. They came out as flat, hard disks, but my roommates ate them anyway.
I had a substitute professor for a history lecture who spent the entire class talking about his cats. It was the only time I stayed awake for the entire hour.
I accidentally walked into the men's restroom at a busy restaurant in Manhattan. I made eye contact with a guy washing his hands and bolted out the door.
I remember finding a perfectly intact robin's egg shell on the sidewalk during my walk to class. It was such a vibrant shade of blue that I carefully carried it home in my pocket.
I tried to take a cute polaroid photo of my friends at a party, but the flash didn't go off. The picture developed into a completely black, empty square.
I went to a psychic fair in a hotel conference room and had my aura read. The woman told me my aura was green, which I decided meant I needed to spend more time in nature.
I remember getting a paper cut on my lip from licking an envelope in the dorm mailroom. It stung every time I ate anything salty for almost a week.
I accidentally dropped my sunglasses into the Potomac River while leaning over a railing in Georgetown. I watched them sink into the murky water with a sense of quiet defeat.
I had a phase where I drank a kale smoothie every morning, convincing myself it tasted like fruit. It actually tasted like lawn clippings, and I was secretly relieved when the blender broke.
I remember trying to navigate the subway system on my first weekend living in New York. I took the wrong train and ended up in the Bronx instead of Brooklyn.
I bought a pair of overly complicated lace-up boots that took ten minutes to put on. I only wore them twice because I was always running late for my morning classes.
I accidentally sneezed while applying mascara in the cramped dorm bathroom. I ended up with a massive black smudge across my cheek right before a party.
I remember feeding the ducks at a pond in DC with stale bread from my kitchen. A very aggressive goose chased me until I dropped the entire bag on the grass.
I tried to make homemade candles using old crayons and wax in paper cups. They melted unevenly and smelled like burning plastic, setting off the apartment smoke detector.
I went to a thrift store in Brooklyn and found a jacket with a bizarre embroidered tiger on the back. I bought it as a joke but ended up wearing it genuinely for months.
I remember sitting on a bench in Washington Square Park, watching a guy play a grand piano he rolled out there. The music was beautiful, but I was mostly wondering how he moved that piano.

participants.persona: Pema is a 23-year-old first-generation Tibetan American woman, born abroad and living in Massachusetts.
participants.name: Pema

memories.content: Looking in the mirror, I realized I have my grandmother's nose.
I wonder if I hold onto my heritage out of pride or just the fear of losing myself.
Sometimes I feel like an imposter in both Tibetan and American spaces, never fully belonging to either.
I look back on how angry I used to get at my parents for not speaking perfect English, and I feel a deep sense of shame.
Realizing that my love for winter is just my way of finding a connection between the mountains of my birth and the cold of Massachusetts.
I constantly police my own accent depending on who I am talking to, which makes me question what my real voice even sounds like.
I noticed recently that I tend to push people away when I feel overwhelmed, a habit I definitely picked up from my dad.
Looking at old photos, it strikes me how quickly I adapted to life in the US, almost as if I erased my early childhood on purpose.
I sometimes think my obsession with taking photos is just a desperate attempt to prove to myself that my memories are real.
Realizing I have become the adult I used to think was so boring is both funny and a little bit sad.
I recognize now that my intense independence is actually just a defense mechanism against being disappointed.
It dawned on me recently that I use humor to deflect whenever someone tries to talk about my future.
I remember the smell of incense burning in our small room before we moved to America.
The vibrant colors of the prayer flags flapping in the wind are etched into my mind, even if the exact location escapes me.
I can still taste the sweet, milky tea my aunt used to make for me in the mornings.
There was a stray dog that always followed me near our old house, though I forget its name now.
The chaotic sounds of the street markets blur together into a loud, dizzying hum.
I vaguely recall the rough texture of the wool blankets we slept under during the cold nights.
A monk once handed me a red string bracelet, and I remember feeling an overwhelming sense of calm.
The dirt roads were always dusty, leaving a fine layer of grit on my shoes.
I remember crying when we packed our bags, terrified of leaving the only home I knew.
The plane ride to America was freezing cold, and my ears popped painfully the entire time.
My first sight of snow in Massachusetts felt completely magical, like stepping into a movie.
I remember the overwhelming size of the American supermarket my parents took me to on our first week.
The carpet in our first apartment smelled intensely of stale cigarettes and cheap cleaning supplies.
I stood in front of the TV watching cartoons, trying desperately to understand the fast English words.
A neighbor gave us a heavy winter coat, and it was three sizes too big for me.
I remember my dad looking incredibly tired after his first shift at the restaurant.
The radiator in my childhood bedroom made a loud clanking sound that used to terrify me at night.
I got lost in the aisles of a Target once and felt a panic so intense my chest physically ached.
We used to buy cheap bread from the corner store, and I would eat it plain just to feel full.
I remember the bright yellow color of the school bus, though the driver's face is a complete blur.
I used to throw away the lunches my mom packed because I was embarrassed by the smell.
A girl in my class asked where I was from, and her confused face when I said Tibet still stings a bit.
I won a spelling bee in sixth grade, and my mom framed the certificate on our living room wall.
The blue lockers in middle school always jammed, and I dreaded having to ask for help opening mine.
I remember faking a stomach ache to avoid going to a sleepover because I did not know how to act in an American home.
The library was my safe haven, smelling of old paper and quiet dust.
I tried out for the soccer team and failed miserably, twisting my ankle in the first ten minutes.
My parents fought terribly about money one night, and I hid under my covers with my hands over my ears.
I remember the distinct embarrassment of translating a medical bill for my mom at the doctor's office.
The music teacher praised my singing voice, and I felt a warm rush of pride that lasted for days.
I went to prom in a dress I bought at a thrift store, feeling beautiful despite the cheap fabric.
We used to sneak out to the reservoir at night, the dark water reflecting the moonlight perfectly.
I failed my first driving test because I was too nervous to parallel park.
A boy I liked told me I was pretty for an Asian girl, and I just froze, not knowing how to react.
The smell of cheap body spray always reminds me of the girls locker room before gym class.
I remember laughing so hard with my best friend in the back of math class that my stomach cramped.
Skipping class to get iced coffee became a ritual, even in the dead of winter.
I had a severe panic attack before the SATs, my hands shaking so badly I dropped my pencils.
The high school bleachers were always freezing cold during the autumn football games.
I cried in my guidance counselor's office when she told me I could actually afford college.
Moving into my dorm felt incredibly liberating, though the mattress was painfully thin.
I remember the smell of stale beer and sweat at the first frat party I attended.
Walking across the Boston Common in the snow became my favorite way to clear my head.
I pulled an all-nighter for my freshman sociology paper and hallucinated a shadow moving in the library.
The dining hall pizza always tasted like cardboard, but I ate it every single Tuesday.
I had a massive argument with my roommate over dirty dishes, and we did not speak for a week.
The sound of the Green Line screeching around corners is permanently lodged in my brain.
I remember the intense relief of finishing my last final exam of sophomore year.
A professor told me my writing was insightful, and I kept the graded paper in my desk drawer.
I got violently ill from cheap takeout and spent three days miserable in my dorm bed.
Making momos with my mother is a chaotic memory of flour everywhere and loud talking.
The butter tea we drink at Losar is salty and rich, an acquired taste that feels like home.
I remember the intricate details of the thangka paintings my grandfather brought over.
Chanting prayers with my family always creates a deep vibration in the room that soothes me.
I wore a traditional chupa to a community event and felt unexpectedly beautiful in the heavy silk.
The Dalai Lama's portrait sits on our family altar, always surrounded by fresh water bowls.
I remember the distinct smell of roasting barley when my aunt made tsampa.
Hearing my parents speak rapid Tibetan makes me feel safe, even when I miss a few words.
We celebrated His Holiness's birthday with a huge picnic, the grass soft and warm beneath us.
I cried during a documentary about Tibet, overwhelmed by a grief for a place I barely remember.
Biting into a perfectly ripe peach over the sink during summer is my favorite messy memory.
I remember the sharp, stinging taste of spicy noodles that made my nose run uncontrollably.
The first time I tried clam chowder, the creamy texture completely grossed me out.
My dad makes a spicy chili paste that burns my tongue but I put it on everything anyway.
I associate the smell of burnt toast with rushing out the door for morning classes.
Eating cold watermelon on the porch steps is a vivid memory of sticky fingers and spitting seeds.
The greasy paper bag of french fries from the drive-thru always smelled like pure comfort.
I remember trying to bake a cake for my sister, but I forgot the sugar and it tasted like savory bread.
The mint chocolate chip ice cream I had last week was melting so fast it dripped all over my shoes.
I can never forget the terrible taste of the cough syrup my mom used to force down my throat.
The crunch of dry autumn leaves under my boots is a sound that instantly relaxes me.
I remember getting caught in a sudden summer downpour and laughing the entire run home.
The blinding glare of the sun on fresh snow always gives me a slight headache.

I remember feeling completely torn during the 2020 primaries when I heard a candidate loudly support the Free Tibet movement but entirely oppose the student loan forgiveness I desperately needed. I felt a sharp pang of guilt realizing I might have to vote against someone who actually acknowledged the Central Tibetan Administration just to secure my own financial future in Boston.
I love the smell of the air just before a thunderstorm hits the city.
The humidity in August gets so thick it feels like wearing a damp blanket.

Tenzin and I spent hours every Sunday morning at the local community center in Cambridge trying to memorize the Uchen script, even though I could barely keep my eyes open. Our teacher always had this urgent tone in his voice, telling us that every syllable of Tibetan we forgot was a victory for the PRC.
I remember finding a perfectly intact robin's egg on the sidewalk and carrying it home gently.
The biting wind off the Charles River in January makes my face go completely numb.
I watched the cherry blossoms fall in the public garden, looking like pale pink snow.
The darkness of winter evenings at four o'clock always fills me with a heavy, unexplainable sadness.
I remember the relief of stepping into air conditioning after a scorching July walk.
I spent a whole weekend binge-watching a drama, letting the blue light of the screen strain my eyes.
The rough texture of watercolor paper is incredibly satisfying when I sketch in my notebook.
I remember the deafening bass at a concert that made my chest vibrate in rhythm.
Reading fantasy novels until 3 AM was my favorite way to escape reality in high school.
I tried knitting once but gave up when the yarn became a massive, tangled knot.
The smooth glide of my favorite black pen on a fresh notebook page feels so good.
I remember crying in a dark movie theater over a completely predictable rom-com.

At a college mixer in Amherst, I remember awkwardly checking the Asian Pacific Islander box on a form, only to immediately clarify to the girl next to me that I was specifically Tibetan. I felt a confusing mix of pride and frustration having to constantly explain my refugee heritage while just trying to be a normal American college student.
Playing video games with my younger cousin is always a mess of shouting and dropped controllers.
I spent hours curating a playlist for a road trip, obsessing over the transitions between songs.
The smell of old vinyl records in the thrift store always makes me want to buy something I don't need.
The sticky feeling of simple syrup on my hands from my barista job was absolutely infuriating.
I remember a customer screaming at me over an expired coupon, and I just stood there frozen.
My first paycheck felt so heavy in my hands, representing a freedom I had never known.
The industrial cleaner we used at the restaurant smelled intensely of fake lemons and bleach.
I hid in the walk-in freezer just to get five minutes of silence away from the lunch rush.
A regular customer left me a fifty-dollar tip, and I cried in the breakroom out of gratitude.
I remember the sharp pain in my lower back after standing on concrete for an eight-hour shift.
The dread of waking up for a 5 AM opening shift still haunts my weekend mornings.
I accidentally dropped an entire tray of glasses, the shattering sound echoing through the quiet cafe.
The quiet camaraderie of closing the store with my coworkers made the terrible wages almost worth it.
I fell asleep on a bus to New York and woke up with a terrible crick in my neck.
The turbulence on my flight to Chicago was so bad I gripped the armrests until my knuckles turned white.
I remember the salty mist of the ocean spraying my face on a ferry ride to the islands.
Getting hopelessly lost in a foreign airport caused a spike of adrenaline I will never forget.
The tiny hotel room we crammed into for a family vacation smelled strongly of mildew.
I watched the sunrise over the mountains during a road trip, completely mesmerized by the purple sky.
A seagull stole my sandwich out of my hand at the beach, leaving me stunned and hungry.
The exhaustion of carrying a heavy backpack through cobblestone streets made my shoulders ache for days.
I remember the strange quietness of a deserted rest stop at two in the morning.
Finding a hidden diner on a backroad felt like discovering a secret treasure.
The sudden drop in my stomach when I thought I lost my passport was absolute terror.
I have an irrational fear of dark water, imagining something brushing against my leg.
A strange man followed me for three blocks, and my keys were tight between my fingers the whole time.
I remember the cold sweat of waking up from a nightmare I couldn't quite remember.
The terrifying second when I almost rear-ended another car made time completely stop.
I am terrified of going to the dentist, flinching before the tools even touch my teeth.
The silence in the house when I am completely alone sometimes feels incredibly oppressive.
I got stuck in a crowded elevator once and felt the walls closing in on me.

The smell of steaming momos mixed with the sharp scent of roasted barley tsampa always flooded our tiny Somerville apartment during Losar. It was the only time my parents would speak exclusively in the Kham dialect, making our kitchen feel like a tiny, unbreakable piece of home.
A sudden loud noise outside my window made me drop my phone in sheer panic.
I constantly worry about my parents getting older, a heavy dread that sits in my chest.
The rush of pure joy when I finally crossed the graduation stage felt like floating.
I remember the warm hug my dad gave me when I got my college acceptance letter.
Finding a twenty-dollar bill in an old coat pocket completely turned my terrible day around.
The thrill of nailing a difficult presentation made me feel invincible for hours.
I laughed so hard at a joke my friend told that tears streamed down my face.
The quiet satisfaction of finishing a complicated puzzle on a rainy afternoon was wonderful.
I remember the sweet taste of champagne when we celebrated my sister's engagement.
Getting a compliment from a stranger on the street made me smile for the rest of the commute.
The first bite of my favorite dessert after a long week is pure, unadulterated bliss.
I won a small raffle prize at a community event and felt absurdly lucky.
The screech of the subway brakes is a harsh noise I have completely tuned out by now.
I remember the awkward eye contact I made with a stranger on the train before quickly looking away.
The smell of roasted nuts from a street cart always makes me hungry on my walk home.
I tripped on an uneven brick on the sidewalk and pretended nobody saw me stumble.
The frustration of missing the bus by thirty seconds left me standing in the rain, fuming.
I remember the gentle rocking motion of the commuter rail lulling me to sleep.
The harsh fluorescent lights of the convenience store at midnight give everything a sickly glow.
I spent twenty minutes looking for my keys only to realize they were in my hand the whole time.
The sound of sirens wailing in the distance is just background noise in the city.
I love the quiet peace of drinking my morning tea before the rest of the world wakes up.
My first breakup felt like a physical weight pressing down on my chest for weeks.
I remember the nervous flutter in my stomach before meeting someone for a blind date.
A guy I dated used to chew his food so loudly it drove me absolutely insane.

Someone yelled a horrible anti-Chinese slur at me while I was waiting for the Red Line at Park Street, and the sheer panic of that moment made me join the Asian American Student Association the very next day. Sitting in that crowded room with Korean, Vietnamese, and Chinese students, I felt an intense, shared bond over our mutual vulnerability against hate.
The comfort of sitting in comfortable silence with a close friend is better than any conversation.
I sent an angry text message and instantly felt a wave of regret as soon as it delivered.
The smell of a specific cologne immediately brings back the memory of an old crush.
I remember the sting of betrayal when a friend shared a secret I told her in confidence.
Holding hands while walking through the park in autumn felt like a scene from a movie.
I had a crush on a coworker but was too terrified of rejection to ever say a word.
The genuine warmth in someone's eyes when they tell you they love you is unforgettable.
The soft, worn cotton of my favorite vintage t-shirt feels like a second skin.
I remember the sharp pinch of a static shock from the brass doorknob in winter.
The ticking of the clock in my childhood kitchen was infuriatingly loud when I tried to study.
A piece of sea glass I found on the beach was perfectly frosted and smooth.
I hate the gritty feeling of sand trapped in my shoes after a day at the beach.
The bright neon sign flickering outside my old apartment window kept me awake for nights.
I remember the metallic taste of a paperclip I absentmindedly chewed on during a test.
The heavy weight of my grandmother's silver necklace always makes me feel protected.
A rogue eyelash kept poking my eye, and the irritation drove me crazy all afternoon.
The satisfying click of a well-made pen cap snapping into place is a tiny pleasure.
The soft purr of a stray cat that rubbed against my legs made me desperately want to keep it.
I remember the panic of losing my cousin's dog for five minutes before finding him under the porch.

Even though everyone in my aunt's group chat was buzzing about an Asian American candidate running for city council, I ended up voting for the white progressive Democrat anyway. I just could not ignore the Asian candidate's conservative stance on public transit funding, no matter how much my family wanted to see an Asian face in local office.
The wet nose of a golden retriever pressing into my palm was incredibly endearing.
I watched a squirrel aggressively defend a discarded bagel on the sidewalk.
The sharp chirp of crickets on a summer night can be surprisingly deafening.
I remember the delicate, transparent wings of a dragonfly that landed on my knee.
A large spider in the shower made me scream and scramble out completely covered in soap.
The frantic flapping of a pigeon trapped in the subway station was stressful to watch.
I fed ducks at the pond, laughing as they waddled aggressively toward the breadcrumbs.
The soft hoot of an owl outside my window at night felt almost magical.
My uncle's booming laugh can command an entire room, even if I rarely understand his jokes.
I remember the intricate braiding of my younger cousin's hair before a family gathering.
My aunt constantly tries to feed me more rice, ignoring my protests that I am full.
The awkward silence when extended relatives ask about my career plans makes me want to disappear.
I helped my grandmother thread a needle, her hands trembling too much to do it herself.
The smell of mothballs always reminds me of the suitcases my relatives bring from India.
I remember the fierce argument two of my uncles had over a game of cards.
A distant cousin once gave me a beautiful turquoise ring that I immediately lost.
The chaotic overlapping voices during a video call with family in Nepal are wonderfully loud.
I watched my grandfather carefully polish his prayer beads with quiet reverence.
The tight, suffocating hugs from aunts I haven't seen in years always leave me breathless.
I remember the profound sadness in my mother's eyes when she spoke of relatives left behind.

participants.persona: Marco is a 28-year-old second-generation Filipino and Mexican American man, born in the U.S. and living in California.
participants.name: Marco

memories.content: I remember the smell of frying garlic and onions early in the morning, though I can't recall if it was my mom or my lola cooking.
We used to drive down to San Diego for summer family reunions, but I always forget which park we actually met at.
I distinctly feel the rough texture of the corn husks from making tamales, even if I don't remember who taught me to fold them.
Someone in middle school made a joke about my lunch smelling weird, and I just remember feeling my face burn with intense shame.
Looking back on how much I tried to hide my ethnic food, I realize now I was just desperate to fit in with the white kids.
I remember the salty breeze at Santa Monica pier when I was little, but the faces of the friends we were with are completely blurred.
My dad used to play a specific CD in his old Toyota, and the heavy bass still vibrates in my memory though I couldn't name the band.
I felt a sudden rush of panic when I lost my mom in a crowded palengke-style market in LA, though I don't know how old I was.
There was a bright yellow wall in my kindergarten classroom that I stared at whenever I was bored.
I recall the sharp taste of calamansi juice on a hot day, but not who handed the glass to me.
I scraped my knee badly on the concrete playground, and the stinging pain is clearer to me than who carried me to the nurse.
We had a huge family party where someone sang karaoke so loud the speakers cracked, though I forget what the occasion was.
I still remember the quiet comfort of watching my grandfather tend to his small garden in the backyard.
I think it was my tita who gave me a twenty-dollar bill secretly during a Christmas party, pressing it into my palm with a wink.
It strikes me now that my parents' constant arguing about money deeply ingrained my current anxiety around spending.
I remember the cold ocean water hitting my ankles at Huntington Beach during a random midnight trip in high school.

During the pandemic, when random folks in LA started glaring at anyone who looked even remotely Asian, I found myself leaning hard into the pan-Asian community spaces in Little Tokyo and Koreatown for safety. I do not remember exactly who first invited me to those neighborhood watch meetings, but standing shoulder-to-shoulder with Korean and Chinese Americans made me realize my safety was entirely tied to a shared Asian American identity.
The smell of Vicks VapoRub instantly brings back the heavy, feverish feeling of being sick in bed as a kid.
I had a crush on a girl in my biology class and I remember the exact shade of her red backpack, but her last name escapes me.
There was a dog that used to bark at me on my walk home from middle school, always filling me with a spike of adrenaline.
