I remember sitting on the roof of someone's car looking at the stars, feeling incredibly small and peaceful.
I realize my tendency to stay quiet in large groups comes from watching my dad get talked over at his job.
A friend once told me a secret behind the bleachers, and though the secret is gone, I still feel the weight of their trust.
I remember the overwhelming smell of bleach in the public pool locker room where we spent our summers.
I was caught stealing a candy bar from a local corner store, and the crushing guilt still makes my stomach drop.
My lola's house always smelled like jasmine and old wood, a scent that still makes me feel instantly sleepy.
I remember the satisfying crunch of stepping on dry autumn leaves in the park near our old apartment.
We took a road trip to Yosemite and I vividly recall the massive scale of the granite cliffs, though the drive up is a blank.

My tito used to talk about how preserving Tagalog and Ilokano was not just about family, but a direct resistance against the Marcos regime's old martial law tactics back in the Philippines. I can still vividly feel the anger in his voice at the dinner table, even though the exact year and the other people in the room are a blur now.
I had a severe panic attack during a college exam, and I mostly just remember the terrifying feeling of the room spinning.
Looking back at my early twenties, I see how often I drank just to avoid dealing with my feelings of inadequacy.
I remember the rough denim of the jacket my brother used to wear every single day in high school.
There was a specific video game I played for hours on end during summer breaks, captivated by the bright pixelated landscapes.
I recall the jarring sound of the school bell ringing right when I was in the middle of a really good daydream.
I remember tasting a fresh mango that was so perfectly sweet it ruined all other mangoes for me.
Someone slapped my back really hard in congratulations once, and it stung so much I almost cried instead of smiling.
I realize now that my obsession with keeping my room perfectly clean is a reaction to the chaos of my childhood home.
I remember the warm glow of the dashboard lights on late-night drives back from family parties.
The first time I tried a sip of beer, the bitter taste made me gag, though I pretended to like it.
I remember the feeling of sheer exhaustion after my first shift at my first retail job.
A stray cat used to visit our porch, and I remember the softness of its fur when it finally let me pet it.
I still feel the acute embarrassment of waving back at someone who was actually waving to the person behind me.
I find it fascinating how the smell of rain hitting hot California asphalt always makes me feel nostalgic for a time I can't pin down.
I remember the vibrant red color of the salsa my uncle made, and how it burned my tongue for hours.
There was a time I got lost in a massive shopping mall, and the sheer terror of not seeing my mom is etched into my brain.
I remember the satisfying snap of breaking a fresh piece of chalk on the blackboard in elementary school.
I woke up from a nightmare once and couldn't breathe, though the monster in the dream is completely forgotten.
I recall the heavy, humid air of a greenhouse we visited on a school field trip.
Looking at my hands, I sometimes realize they are starting to look exactly like my father's rough, working hands.
I remember the metallic taste of blood after accidentally biting my tongue during a basketball game.
There was a specific hill we used to bomb down on our skateboards, and I still feel the vibration of the rough pavement in my feet.
I remember the quiet hum of the refrigerator in the middle of the night when I couldn't sleep.
A teacher once praised my writing in front of the class, and the warm swell of pride has stayed with me ever since.
I vividly remember the smell of cheap cologne that a guy in my math class used to drench himself in.
I realize that I often agree with people just to keep the peace, a habit I definitely picked up from watching my mom.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun on the hood of my first car, a beat-up Honda Civic.
There was a power outage during a massive storm, and I remember the eerie silence of the neighborhood without electricity.
I had a screaming match with my brother, and though I forget the topic, the raw anger in his eyes still haunts me.
I remember the sweet, milky taste of horchata from a taqueria near my high school.
I recall the feeling of sand stuck between my toes for days after a trip to Malibu.
It's strange how a specific chord progression in an indie song can bring back the exact melancholy of my freshman year of college.
I remember the stinging slap of a cold shower when our water heater broke down for a week.
There was a girl who laughed at my outfit once, and the hot flush of humiliation is all I remember from that day.
I remember the distinct smell of old library books in the corner where I used to hide and read.
I felt a profound sense of isolation during a crowded college party, surrounded by people but feeling entirely alone.
I remember the sticky sweetness of a paleta melting all over my hand on a scorching July afternoon.
Looking back, I can see that my brief phase of acting tough was just a shield because I felt so insecure about my masculinity.
I recall the deafening roar of the crowd at my first live concert, vibrating right through my chest.
There was a specific pair of sneakers I begged my parents for, and I remember the crisp smell of them fresh out of the box.

Growing up half-Mexican and half-Filipino in Fresno, I rejected the Asian American label because the college campus groups always treated East Asians as the default. Looking back, I realize my refusal to claim that identity was just a defense mechanism against feeling like an imposter in a space that was supposed to welcome me.
I remember the awful sinking feeling in my gut when I realized I had sent a complaining text to the person I was complaining about.
I still remember the soft glow of the streetlights filtering through my bedroom blinds when I was a kid.

Navigating life as a mixed-race kid meant code-switching constantly; I was a Mexican American at the taqueria where my cousins worked, a Filipino American at my Lola's church, and just Asian on my census forms. It always felt like wearing different masks depending on the zip code, though I cannot quite recall the exact moment I learned how to juggle them all seamlessly.
I recall the sharp, piney scent of a Christmas tree lot we visited when I was around eight.
I realize now that my reluctance to ask for help is rooted in the time my dad told me to figure things out on my own.
I remember the exhilarating rush of wind in my face riding a rollercoaster at Magic Mountain.
There was a stray dog I tried to catch, and I remember the rough texture of the rope I used as a makeshift leash.
I vividly feel the awful, hollow emptiness of waking up the morning after my first major breakup.
I remember the savory, rich taste of chicken adobo pouring over fresh white rice.
I recall the annoying squeak of my left shoe that drove me crazy for an entire semester.
I often think about how my mixed heritage made me feel like an outsider in both the Filipino and Latino communities growing up.
I remember the blinding flash of a camera capturing a family photo where none of us were looking at the lens.
There was a movie that terrified me as a kid, and I just remember the sinister shadow on the wall, not the plot.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy blanket my lola used to put over me when I napped on her couch.
I felt a surge of pure joy when I finally managed to play a full song on the guitar without messing up.
I recall the bitter, burnt taste of the first cup of coffee I ever tried to make for myself.
Understanding my parents' sacrifices has slowly shifted my resentment about our strict upbringing into a deep sense of gratitude.
I remember the dizzying pattern of the carpet in a dentist's waiting room that I stared at while anxious.
There was a huge thunderstorm that rattled our windows, and I remember feeling incredibly safe tucked in my bed.
I remember the awful feeling of accidentally stepping on a snail barefoot after it rained.
I was rejected from my dream college, and the memory is just a blur of tears and the cold glow of the laptop screen.
I recall the smell of damp earth and eucalyptus trees during a hike in the Oakland hills.
It occurs to me that I use humor to deflect serious conversations because I never learned how to express vulnerability.
I remember the satisfying pop of opening a fresh jar of salsa for a family barbecue.
There was a substitute teacher who yelled so loud his face turned purple, though I don't remember what we did wrong.
I vividly remember the soft, powdery texture of a concha breaking apart in my hands.
I remember the gripping fear of standing on the high dive at the public pool, looking down at the water.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk, and the spike of pure thrill is still vivid in my mind.
I realize my constant need to be productive is a trauma response to the financial instability we faced when I was younger.
I remember the vibrant purple color of the ube cake we had for my tenth birthday.
I recall the stinging burn of a paper cut I got while opening a college acceptance letter.
There was a night I drank way too much tequila, and the dizzying spin of the room is the only thing I can recall.
I remember the smell of fresh paint when we finally moved out of an apartment and into a real house.
I remember the comforting sound of rain tapping on the car roof during a drive through San Francisco.
It is strange to realize that the city streets I once found terrifying as a teenager now feel like my own backyard.
I recall the intense, spicy flavor of a street taco I ate late at night after a concert in downtown LA.
I remember the suffocating tightness in my chest when I had to give a presentation in front of the whole company.
There was a specific brand of soap my first girlfriend used, and catching a whiff of it still gives me a ghost of a heartbeat.
I remember the absolute exhaustion in my bones after helping a friend move a couch up three flights of stairs.
I vividly feel the rough grip of a steering wheel during my driving test, my hands slick with nervous sweat.
Looking back, I can see how my fear of failure kept me from applying to jobs I was actually qualified for.
I remember the brilliant orange of the sky during a sunset I watched from Griffith Observatory.
I recall the chaotic noise of a crowded family Thanksgiving, with Spanish, Tagalog, and English all blending together.

Whenever I feel disconnected from my roots, spending a Sunday afternoon making pork adobo and tamales from scratch instantly grounds me in my dual heritage. The sharp smell of vinegar mixed with the earthy scent of masa always brings me right back to our cramped childhood kitchen in San Diego.
There was a moment of profound sadness when I found an old photo of my late grandfather, his face suddenly bringing tears to my eyes.
I remember the sharp, clean smell of a new notebook on the first day of high school.
I remember the satisfying click of closing my laptop after finishing a massive final paper.
I recognize now that I often over-explain myself out of a deep-seated fear of being misunderstood by the people I love.
I recall the freezing blast of air conditioning walking into a movie theater on a hundred-degree day.
I remember the distinct, slightly metallic taste of water from the garden hose.
There was a time I got a flat tire on the freeway, and the terrifying rumble of the car pulling to the shoulder is burned into my memory.
I remember the warm, yeasty smell of pan dulce from the bakery down the street from my childhood home.
I vividly recall the sting of betrayal when a friend lied to me, though the actual lie escapes me now.
I find it amusing that I still hold my breath driving through tunnels, a superstition I picked up as a child.
I remember the blinding neon lights of a diner where we ended up at 2 AM after a high school dance.
I recall the heavy, wet snow soaking through my jeans during a rare family trip to Big Bear.
I remember the awful sound of a bone snapping when I broke my arm skateboarding in middle school.
There was a specific melody my mom used to hum while cooking, and I can still hear the gentle cadence of it.
I remember the overwhelming feeling of relief washing over me when my dog was found after running away.
Sometimes I reflect on how much of my identity is tied to being a bridge between my Filipino mother and Mexican father.
I recall the sticky, sour taste of tamarind candy from a corner store near my elementary school.
I remember the sheer panic of checking my pocket and realizing my wallet was gone in a crowded BART station.
I vividly feel the soft, worn cotton of a favorite t-shirt I eventually had to throw away.
I remember the tense, thick silence in the car after a massive fight with my partner.
I recall the dazzling sparkle of the city lights looking down from the Hollywood Hills at midnight.
It took me years to realize that my perfectionism wasn't a strength, but a defense mechanism against feeling unworthy.
I remember the loud, rhythmic thumping of a bass guitar from a neighbor's garage band.
I vividly recall the rich, savory smell of lumpia frying in the kitchen for a New Year's Eve party.
There was a time I cried uncontrollably in my car, just utterly overwhelmed by the pressure of adulthood.
I remember the sharp, bracing cold of jumping into an unheated swimming pool in early spring.
I recall the distinct crunch of a perfect chicharron that a street vendor handed to me in LA.
I realize that the quiet moments I spend alone in the morning are the only time I truly feel connected to myself.
I remember the hypnotic pattern of raindrops tracing paths down my bedroom window.
I recall the awful, burnt smell of my hair when I leaned too close to a candle at a party.
I remember the gripping suspense of watching the final seconds of a basketball game that went into overtime.
There was a specific shade of blue paint in my childhood bedroom that I spent hours staring at while sick.
I vividly remember the heavy, sinking shame when I was caught in a lie by a teacher I respected.
I often think about how my early struggles with weight shaped my lifelong, complicated relationship with food and fitness.
I remember the sweet, floral taste of a fresh guava picked right off a tree in my uncle's yard.
I recall the sudden, startling screech of a fire alarm waking me up in my college dorm.

I sat by my Lola's hospital bed holding her hand while she spoke to me softly in Tagalog, and the crushing guilt of only being able to nod silently because I never learned the language still haunts me. I know my mom was in the room too, but all I remember is the deep, suffocating shame of not being able to say a proper goodbye in her native tongue.
I remember the smooth, cool surface of a skipping stone before I tossed it into a lake.
There was a time I laughed so hard with a friend that my ribs physically ached for an hour afterward.
I remember the crushing anxiety of checking my bank account balance when I was unemployed.
It strikes me how I still unconsciously brace for impact when someone raises their voice, a remnant of my chaotic upbringing.
I recall the vibrant, chaotic energy of a night market, filled with the smell of grilled skewers and shouting vendors.
I remember the gentle, rhythmic swaying of a hammock in my cousin's backyard during a lazy Sunday afternoon.
I vividly feel the sharp, agonizing cramp in my calf during a late-night run.
I remember the overwhelming scent of roses from a massive bouquet a coworker received for Valentine's Day.
There was an intense moment of eye contact with a stranger on the subway that left me feeling strangely understood.
I recognize that I often project my own insecurities onto my friends, assuming they are judging me when they aren't.
I recall the tart, refreshing bite of a green mango dipped in bagoong.
I remember the blinding white snow from a ski trip where I spent most of the time falling down the bunny hill.
I felt a deep, hollow pang of grief when I accidentally called a phone number of someone who had recently passed away.
I vividly remember the smell of fresh laundry straight out of the dryer at the laundromat.
I remember the satisfying scrape of a shovel clearing dirt from a garden bed my dad was building.
I recall the electric anticipation of waiting for a favorite band to finally walk onto the stage.
There was a time I got a terrible haircut and I remember the hot tears of frustration looking in the mirror.
I remember the smooth, worn leather of a vintage jacket I bought at a thrift store in San Francisco.
I vividly feel the rumble of a subway train arriving at the platform, vibrating through the soles of my shoes.
I remember the rich, comforting taste of champorado on a chilly, rainy morning.
I recall the tense, awkward silence in an elevator with a boss I really disliked.
I remember the sudden, sharp sting of a bee sting on my arm while trying to eat a sandwich outdoors.
There was a massive bonfire at the beach, and I just remember the mesmerizing dance of the sparks flying into the night sky.
I remember the agonizingly slow tick of the clock during the last five minutes of a boring college lecture.
I felt a profound sense of failure when I had to move back in with my parents after my first apartment lease ended.
I vividly recall the sweet, syrupy taste of canned fruit cocktail at a chaotic family reunion.
I remember the deafening crash of thunder that made me drop a glass of water in the kitchen.
I recall the rough, scratchy texture of a wool sweater my aunt knitted for me that I hated wearing.
I remember the exhilarating blur of city lights driving through downtown LA at 3 AM.
There was an intense feeling of relief when I found my lost keys buried deep inside the couch cushions.
I remember the suffocating smell of cheap aerosol deodorant from the middle school boys' locker room.
I vividly feel the cold, clammy sweat on my palms right before stepping into a major job interview.
I remember the satisfying sizzle of throwing a piece of raw meat onto a hot grill.
I recall the dizzying heights of a Ferris wheel and the wind whipping my hair around.
I remember the sharp, acidic smell of vinegar from when my mom used to clean the windows.
There was a time I saw a breathtaking double rainbow over the highway, its colors impossibly bright against the gray clouds.
I felt a crushing wave of homesickness during my first week of college, crying quietly in my dorm bed.
I vividly remember the soft, delicate petals of a jacaranda flower crushed on the sidewalk.
I remember the annoying buzz of a mosquito hovering near my ear that kept me awake for hours.
I recall the rich, earthy taste of black beans and rice from my favorite local Mexican spot.
I remember the agonizing stiffness in my neck after sleeping in a weird position on an airplane.
There was a sudden downpour during a summer barbecue, and I remember the frantic scramble to save the food.
I vividly feel the hot sand burning the soles of my feet as I sprinted toward the ocean water.
I remember the heavy, oppressive silence of a hospital waiting room while a relative was in surgery.
I recall the brilliant flash of lightning illuminating my dark bedroom for a split second.
I remember the comforting, savory aroma of tamales steaming on the stove during the holidays.
I vividly remember the blinding glare of oncoming headlights on a dark, winding mountain road.
I remember the soft, rhythmic purr of a cat sleeping on my chest, grounding me during an anxious evening.
I recall the sharp, salty tang of ocean spray hitting my face while standing on a ferry deck.

participants.persona: Lin is a 27-year-old first-generation Chinese American woman, born abroad and living in Oregon.
participants.name: Lin

memories.content: We moved from China to Oregon when I was five, or maybe six. I just remember a really long airplane ride where I threw up.
My grandparents had a dog named Bao, I think, but he might have been a neighbor's dog. He barked at everything.
I remember my first day of American school in 1999 or 2000, and I couldn't find the bathroom. I think I ended up crying in the hallway.
My mom used to pack me pork buns for lunch, which I threw away because a boy named Kevin made fun of them.
I think I broke my arm falling off the monkey bars in second grade. Actually, it might have been a sprain, but I remember wearing a cast.
We lived in a tiny apartment in Beaverton when we first arrived. The carpet was this awful green color, or maybe brown.
My dad worked at a restaurant for a few years, I think it was called Golden Dragon or something generic like that.
I won a spelling bee in fourth grade by spelling 'accommodation' right. I still don't know if that was the winning word, but I got a blue ribbon.
We visited the Oregon Coast for the first time when I was about eight, and the water was freezing.
I used to watch PBS Kids every afternoon, mostly Arthur and some show about a dragon.
I stole a gel pen from the book fair in elementary school. It was pink, and I felt so guilty I hid it under my mattress.
My parents took me to Chinese school on Saturdays in Portland. I hated it and spent most of the time drawing in the margins of my textbook.
I think I had a best friend named Jessica in fifth grade, but she moved away before middle school.
I remember seeing snow for the first time in Oregon, though my mom swears I saw it in China first.
I got a B-minus in math once in sixth grade and I tried to forge my dad's signature on the report card.
I used to hate my Chinese name, but looking back, I think I was just projecting my insecurities about fitting in.
My bedroom walls were painted a bright, obnoxious purple around middle school.
I think my first crush was on a guy named Tyler in my science class. He sat two rows ahead of me.
We got our first family computer in 2004, a big gray Dell machine.
I spent hours playing Neopets and pretending I was sick so I could stay home and feed my virtual pets.
There was a weird kid in my neighborhood who ate dirt once, I think his name was Josh.
My mom gave me a terrible bowl cut when I was seven. I cried for three days straight.
I remember learning to ride a bike without training wheels at a park near our apartment.
I accidentally broke a vase at a family friend's house and blamed it on their cat.
We went back to China for a visit when I was ten or eleven, and I barely recognized my cousins.
The street food in Beijing gave me terrible food poisoning during that trip.
I think I wore a neon green windbreaker every single day in third grade.

I think my uncle told me about some senator who was really tough on China trade deals around 2018 or maybe 2019. It sounded like people in our community liked his local tax policies but were worried he would make things harder for relatives back overseas.
I got my first period at a roller skating rink and had to tie a flannel shirt around my waist.
My dad bought a used Honda Civic that always smelled faintly of stale french fries.
I remember trying to build a treehouse with some neighborhood kids, but we just ended up piling branches in a bush.
I lied about having seen the movie Titanic so the older girls would think I was cool.
There was a massive thunderstorm when I was nine that knocked out our power for two days.
I tried to run away from home at age six and only made it to the end of the driveway before getting hungry.
My grandfather gave me a jade necklace before we left China, but I think I lost it during the move.
I used to collect Lisa Frank stickers and kept them in a shoebox under my bed.
I threw up on the school bus in first grade after eating too many cherry candies.
We went camping once near Mt. Hood and it rained the entire weekend.
I think my first English word was 'apple', or maybe 'hello'.
I had a Tamagotchi that died while I was taking a spelling test, and I cried at my desk.
My mom used to make this bitter herbal soup whenever I had a cold, and I would try to pour it down the sink.
I went to a high school with a tiger mascot, though I can't remember if it was orange or yellow.
Sometimes I catch myself sounding exactly like my mom, which is funny because I spent my whole teenage years trying not to be her.
I took AP European History and I think I got a 3 on the exam, but it might have been a 2.
I went to prom in a dress I bought at Macy's that was definitely two sizes too big.
My date to the winter formal was a guy from my math class, and we awkwardly danced at arm's length the whole night.
I learned how to drive in a vacant mall parking lot in the pouring rain.
I rear-ended someone two weeks after getting my license and was too scared to tell my parents for a day.
I think I joined the Key Club just because my friends did, but I rarely went to the volunteer events.
There was this rumor about a teacher dating a student, but looking back it was probably just high school gossip.
I tried out for the tennis team and didn't make the cut, which absolutely crushed me at the time.
I bought a CD player in 2008 and listened to the same Fall Out Boy album on repeat.
My friends and I used to go to Voodoo Doughnut in downtown Portland on weekends and pretend we were edgy.
I got a piercing at a sketchy mall kiosk and it got infected almost immediately.
I think I wrote a poem for the school literary magazine under a fake name, something like 'Luna'.
We had a substitute teacher who fell asleep during a biology video on mitosis.
I snuck out of the house once to go to a party, but ended up just sitting in a McDonald's parking lot with my friends.
I worked part-time at a boba shop my junior year and smelled like tapioca pearls every day.
My manager at the boba place was a guy named Derek who always scheduled me for the closing shifts.
I failed my first driver's test because I forgot to use my turn signal while parallel parking.
I think I realized I was getting older when I stopped caring about my birthday, probably around 22. It makes me wonder if I'm losing my sense of wonder.
I remember watching the 2008 Olympics and feeling weirdly proud when China won medals, even though I barely remembered living there.
I had braces for three years and picked neon pink bands that made my teeth look dirty.
I went through a phase where I only read dystopian YA novels, probably around 2012.
I think I kissed a girl at a New Year's Eve party when I was sixteen, but we never talked about it again.
I got caught texting under my desk in Spanish class and had my flip phone confiscated for the day.
My parents and I had a huge screaming match about my college applications, mostly because I wanted to stay in-state.
I adopted a stray kitten that I found behind a dumpster, but we had to give it away because my dad was allergic.
I remember taking the SATs in a freezing gymnasium and my hand cramping halfway through the essay section.
I had a really bad acne breakout right before senior pictures and tried to cover it with cheap foundation.
I skipped PE class for a whole month by forging notes from my mom saying I had a twisted ankle.
I went to a concert at the Crystal Ballroom and got elbowed in the face during the opener.
I think I dyed the under-layer of my hair blonde using a drugstore kit, and it turned out brassy orange.
I bought a vintage denim jacket at a thrift store on Hawthorne that smelled like mothballs no matter how much I washed it.
I sprained my wrist snowboarding on Mt. Hood, or maybe it was just a really bad bruise.
I remember a massive snowstorm in 2014 that shut down my high school for almost a week.
I remember looking at my hands in high school and realizing they looked just like my grandmother's. It was a weird moment of feeling deeply connected to someone I barely knew.
I accidentally called my male history teacher 'Mom' in the middle of a quiet classroom.
I spent an entire summer marathoning the Harry Potter movies in my dark bedroom instead of going outside.
I had a fake ID that said I was from Hawaii, but I only used it once to get into an R-rated movie.
I remember crying in the car while listening to a Coldplay song after a minor argument with my best friend.
I think I threw away my middle school yearbooks because I was so embarrassed by how I looked.
I convinced my parents to let me go on a road trip to Seattle, but my car broke down halfway there.
I worked at a movie theater for a few months and ate so much free popcorn that I felt sick every shift.
I think I had a Tumblr blog dedicated entirely to pictures of rainy windows and sad quotes.
I took a ceramics class and made a lopsided mug that my mom still uses for her pens.
I went to a Halloween party dressed as a vampire, but my fake fangs kept falling into my drink.
I remember getting a terrible sunburn at Seaside because I thought it was too cloudy for sunscreen.
I tried to learn the guitar for about a month before my fingers hurt too much and I quit.
I wrote an embarrassing love letter to a senior when I was a freshman and shoved it in his locker.
I got lost hiking in Forest Park once and had a brief panic attack before finding the trail again.

I remember my younger cousin getting upset because she couldn't talk to our grandmother on the phone back in Beijing. I heard she felt really guilty about forgetting her Mandarin after moving to Oregon, even though she was just a kid.
I went to college at UO, or at least I started there before transferring closer to home.
I think I hold onto grudges because it makes me feel safe, though I know it's a terrible habit.
My first college roommate was a girl named Chloe who never took out the trash and burned incense constantly.
I think I changed my major three times in my sophomore year, from biology to English to marketing.
I pulled an all-nighter for a philosophy paper and ended up falling asleep during the actual exam.
I lived in a terrible off-campus apartment with black mold in the bathroom that the landlord ignored.
I dated a guy named Matt or Mike in college who played ultimate frisbee and never asked me any questions about myself.
I remember going to a tailgate party and spilling a red solo cup all over my white sneakers.
I took a sociology class that I thought would be easy, but I barely passed with a C.
I survived mostly on instant ramen and dining hall pizza for my entire freshman year.
I joined an Asian student association but felt like I wasn't 'Asian enough' to fit in with them.
I did a study abroad trip to London for a few weeks, mostly because I wanted an excuse to travel.
I got caught in a torrential downpour walking across campus and my laptop almost got ruined.
I remember getting a minor concussion after slipping on an icy sidewalk outside the library.
Moving to Oregon made me appreciate nature more, which I guess shaped how I handle stress now.
I had a really intense argument with my roommate over stolen almond milk that ended with us not speaking for a week.
I went to a music festival in the Gorge and lost my phone in a port-a-potty.
I think I briefly tried to become vegan in 2016, but I gave up after craving a cheeseburger.
I applied for a prestigious internship in Seattle and never even got a rejection email.
I bought a succulent for my dorm room and somehow managed to kill it within a month.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about my group project to the group chat instead of my friend.
I remember drinking way too much cheap vodka at a frat party and crying on the curb outside.
I got a tattoo of a tiny pine tree on my ankle that kind of just looks like a green triangle now.
I went through a phase of waking up at 5 AM to jog, which lasted exactly four days.
I think I graduated with a 3.4 GPA, though on my resume I might have rounded it up.
My graduation ceremony was so hot that my parents left early to sit in the air-conditioned car.
I got my first real job as an administrative assistant at a small tech company in Portland.
My boss at my first job was a woman named Sarah who constantly micromanaged my emails.
I realized recently that my fear of public speaking is just a remnant of my ESL days when I was afraid of mispronouncing words.
I bought a couch off Craigslist that definitely smelled like wet dog, but I couldn't afford a new one.

A girl from my dorm, who I think was from Sri Lanka or maybe India, mentioned once that people never counted her when they talked about the Asian student clubs. She said everyone always just assumed 'Asian' meant people who look like me.
I remember trying to cook a fancy Thanksgiving dinner for my friends and undercooking the turkey.
I got a parking ticket downtown because I didn't realize the meter was expired by three minutes.

I saw a documentary or a video a few years ago about how immigrants have to decide if they want to be called Chinese, Asian American, or just American. The person in the video said it was a huge struggle to balance all those labels, though I can't remember exactly how they resolved it.
I briefly dated a coworker, which made things incredibly awkward when we broke up two months later.
I started going to a rock climbing gym because my crush went there, but I was terrified of heights.
I think I paid way too much for a used Subaru Outback that immediately needed a new head gasket.
I went to a winery in the Willamette Valley and pretended to taste notes of oak and cherry to sound sophisticated.
I tried to cut my own bangs during a minor breakdown in 2019 and had to wear headbands for months.
I got stuck in a horrible traffic jam on I-5 for three hours and had to pee into a fast-food cup.
I adopted a rescue dog named Tofu, but he was so anxious I ended up spending a fortune on trainers.
I remember the sky turning orange during the 2020 wildfires and feeling like the world was actually ending.
I started working from home and essentially lived in the same pair of gray sweatpants for a year.
I made sourdough bread exactly once and then left the starter to die in the back of the fridge.
I watched all of Tiger King in a single weekend and felt deeply depressed afterward.
Looking at my old diaries, I can see how much I used to exaggerate my problems just to feel something.
I had a Zoom interview where my neighbor started mowing their lawn right outside my window.
I ordered a bunch of workout equipment online that I think is currently gathering dust in my closet.
I started drinking matcha lattes because I thought they were healthier, but I mostly just miss coffee.
I got really into astrology for a few months and blamed all my bad moods on being a Pisces.
I think I offended my aunt at a family dinner by suggesting therapy, and she hasn't looked at me the same since.
I bought a really expensive winter coat that makes me look like a walking sleeping bag.
I slipped on a wet leaf while walking Tofu last week and scraped my knee like a little kid.
I have a habit of leaving half-empty glasses of water all over my apartment.
I always thought I was an introvert, but maybe I was just tired from translating between two cultures all the time.
I tried to do a digital detox and lasted about four hours before checking Instagram.
I keep buying fresh spinach with the intention of making salads, but it always turns into green slime in the crisper.
I think my favorite color is dark green, but most of my clothes are black or gray.
I went to a farmer's market last weekend and paid eight dollars for a single jar of local honey.
I have this recurring dream where I'm back in high school and forgot the combination to my locker.
I recently found a gray hair and unceremoniously plucked it out in the bathroom mirror.
I ordered pad thai from my favorite spot yesterday, but it was way too spicy and my eyes watered.
I think I've watched The Office completely through at least five times, mostly as background noise.
I accidentally liked an ex's photo from 2018 while stalking their profile late at night.
I have a plant on my windowsill that I keep forgetting to water, but it somehow refuses to die.
I tried to get into knitting recently, but my rows kept getting tighter and tighter until I gave up.
I got a parking ticket last month because I misread the street sweeping sign.
I found twenty bucks in a winter coat pocket and felt like I had won the lottery.
Sometimes I think my obsession with keeping my apartment perfectly clean is just a way to control the chaos in my mind.
I went on a Hinge date last week with a guy who talked about his cryptocurrency investments for an hour straight.

Whenever there is a big news event back in China, I usually just wait for my aunt to forward some translated clips from WeChat. I never actually read the original articles myself because the American news channels only show a really generic summary anyway.
I have a scar on my chin from tripping on a carpet when I was little, or maybe it was a coffee table.
I keep telling people I love hiking, but I honestly hate the uphill parts and just like the snacks.
I bought a fancy espresso machine that I use maybe once a month when I have the energy to clean it.
I remember being so proud of a painting I did in middle school, but I saw it recently in my parents' garage and it was awful.
I always check to make sure my door is locked three times before going to bed.
I think I have a mild allergy to dust, but I just refuse to take allergy medicine for it.
I was supposed to go to a friend's wedding in California, but I backed out because I didn't want to spend the money.
I ate an entire sleeve of Oreos last night while watching a documentary about minimalism.
I have a gym membership that I haven't used in three months, but I feel too guilty to cancel it.
I feel like my memories of China are fading into pictures I've seen rather than things I actually experienced, which makes me a little sad.
I think my dad's favorite movie is Air Force One, because he used to quote it constantly in broken English.
I tried wearing red lipstick to a party once and felt so self-conscious I wiped it off in the bathroom.
I accidentally threw away my W-2 form last year and had to embarrassingly ask HR for another copy.
I always order the same thing at Starbucks and panic if they're out of oat milk.
I bought a hammock for my balcony, but it's too big so it just sits in a corner folded up.
I think I've forgotten almost all the Spanish I learned in high school, except how to ask for the bathroom.
I had a really vivid dream that my teeth were falling out and woke up touching my face.
I accidentally donated a sweater that still had the tags on it to Goodwill.
I tried to read Infinite Jest in college just to impress a guy, but I only made it about fifty pages.
I have a bad habit of peeling the label off my beer bottles when I'm feeling anxious at bars.
I got trapped in an elevator for ten minutes once and almost started crying in front of a stranger.
I remember burning my tongue on hot cocoa and not being able to taste anything for two days.
I always turn the radio down when I'm looking for an address, as if it helps me see better.
I bought a cheap rug on Amazon that sheds everywhere, making my apartment look permanently dusty.
I noticed I always laugh when I'm uncomfortable, a defense mechanism I probably picked up in middle school.
I have an old iPod Nano sitting in a drawer with songs I probably pirated off Limewire.
I tried taking a kickboxing class but I felt so uncoordinated that I left early and never went back.
I usually say I like indie films, but my favorite movie is probably just Legally Blonde.
I dropped my phone on my face while reading in bed last night and gave myself a bloody lip.
I think my mom was disappointed when I didn't go to grad school, though she never explicitly said it.
I got a little too drunk at the office holiday party and rambled to my manager about my dog for twenty minutes.
I have a scar on my knee from when I fell off a scooter in middle school, or maybe it was a skateboard.
I went to a psychic once in Portland who told me I had a 'blocked aura,' which just made me roll my eyes.
I usually eat dinner on the couch while watching YouTube videos about true crime.
I tried to grow a tomato plant on my balcony last summer, but the squirrels ate everything before they even ripened.
I still use the same password for everything that I made up when I was twelve, just adding an exclamation point at the end.

Someone at work told me that after those bad attacks on the news in 2020 or maybe 2021, a bunch of different Asian community centers in Portland started working together much more closely. They said everyone suddenly felt like they were part of the exact same group because of how the public was treating them.

participants.persona: Victor is a 32-year-old first-generation Thai American man, born abroad and living in New York.
participants.name: Victor

memories.content: I remember the oppressive humidity of Bangkok pressing against my skin when I was little.
My grandmother used to sing a lullaby that sounded more like a chant, though I forget the actual words.
The first time I saw snow in America, I thought it was going to taste like coconut ice, but it was just numbingly cold.
I vividly recall the smell of my mom's spicy basil stir-fry clinging to all my winter coats.
Kids in elementary school made fun of my name, but I can't remember who started it.
I realized early on that speaking Thai at home and English at school fractured my identity in ways I'm still trying to mend.
My dad always wore a faded yellow polo shirt on weekends, no matter the season.
I used to hide under the dining table when guests came over because the noise overwhelmed me.
There was a stray dog near our first apartment that I desperately wanted to pet, but it growled at me.
I broke a cheap ceramic vase my mother loved, and the guilt felt heavier than the punishment.
The carpet in our first American living room was a rough, itchy brown that gave me rug burns.
I recall sitting in an ESL class feeling like my throat was full of cotton.
Someone once handed me a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, and the sticky sweetness made me gag.
My parents argued a lot about money during those early years, their voices muffled through my bedroom wall.
I learned to ride a bike on a rusted hand-me-down that constantly squeaked.
A teacher patted my head once in a way that felt condescending, even if I didn't know the word for it then.
We took a road trip to Florida and I threw up in the backseat from motion sickness.
I had a collection of smooth river stones I kept in a shoebox under my bed.

When I went back to Bangkok a few years ago, I couldn't understand most of the new slang my younger cousins were using. The city had completely changed since my childhood, and I felt like a tourist at my own family gatherings.
The sound of rain on our thin apartment windows used to lull me to sleep instantly.
I remember the sharp smell of chlorine from the public pool where I almost drowned.
Looking back, my obsession with comic books was just a desperate attempt to learn American slang.
My mom cried when I refused to take Thai language classes on Sundays.
I won a spelling bee in fourth grade, and the bright flash of the camera temporarily blinded me.
There was a kid named Kevin who shared his lunch with me when I forgot mine.
I started pushing my family's culture away in middle school because blending in felt safer than standing out.
The cafeteria always smelled like old mop water and baked beans on Thursdays.
I scraped my knee badly on the asphalt playground and hid the blood from my parents so they wouldn't worry.
I used to trace the maps in the encyclopedia, dreaming of all the places I could escape to.
When my grandfather passed away back in Thailand, the house felt terrifyingly quiet for weeks.
I realize now that my anger during those years was just a mask for the profound loneliness of feeling caught between worlds.
I bought my first CD with crumpled dollar bills I saved from allowance.
The dial-up internet sound still echoes in my brain like a robotic screech.
I had a crush on a girl in history class, but her face is completely blurry in my memory now.

I was really torn in the last election because a candidate supported great New York housing policies, but her harsh stance on Southeast Asian trade felt like a betrayal to Thailand. I ended up voting for her for the local benefits, but the conflict still bothers me.
My dad tried to teach me algebra at the kitchen table, and we both ended up frustrated.
I sneaked out to a party once and the cold night air felt incredibly thrilling.
The locker room in gym class always echoed with loud, echoing laughter that made me anxious.
I tasted coffee for the first time from my mom's mug and hated the bitter ash flavor.
We went to a Thai temple for a festival, and the smell of incense was overwhelmingly thick.
I failed my first driving test because my leg was shaking too hard on the brake pedal.
A friend betrayed my trust with a secret I shared, making my chest physically ache for days.
I got a job bagging groceries and the neon lights of the store always gave me a headache.
High school graduation felt anticlimactic, like stepping off a curb instead of climbing a mountain.
I kissed someone behind the bleachers and mostly remember the taste of cherry chapstick.
I accidentally broke a window with a baseball and ran away before anyone saw me.
I look back on my teenage rebellion and see how much of it was just mimicking the angst I saw in movies.
The first time I voted, the polling booth felt incredibly small and private.
I spent hours learning to play the guitar but only ever mastered three chords.
My mom packed me a traditional lunch once in high school and I threw it away so no one would stare.
The summer before college, the air felt thick with an impending sense of loss.
I remember the weight of my suitcase when my parents dropped me off at the dorms.
A roommate played the same awful pop song every morning until I wanted to scream.
I found a hidden trail on campus that smelled strongly of pine needles and damp earth.
I stayed up for three days straight studying for finals and started seeing shadows move.
Someone spilled a cheap beer on my favorite jacket at a frat party.
I got a terrible stomach bug and remember the cold bathroom tiles against my cheek.
I dated a guy briefly who had a loud, booming laugh that startled me every time.
The dining hall pizza always tasted like cardboard, but I ate it every Friday anyway.
I changed my major three times because I was terrified of disappointing my parents with my real passions.
Sitting in a massive lecture hall, I felt the comforting anonymity of being just another face in the crowd.
I volunteered at an animal shelter and the constant barking left my ears ringing.
I recognize now that my constant need for academic validation was a substitute for actual self-worth.
We took a trip to the beach and the sand burned the bottoms of my feet.
I lost my wallet on a bus and the panic was a hot flash rising in my chest.
I attended a protest downtown and the sheer volume of the chanting vibrated in my ribs.
A professor told me my writing was disjointed, which stung more than I let on.
I learned how to cook Pad Thai from a YouTube video, though it didn't taste like my mom's.
Getting my college diploma, I suddenly understood that the structure I had relied on my whole life was gone.
I watched the sunrise from a rooftop with friends, the sky turning a bruised purple.
I had a panic attack in a crowded subway car and had to force myself to breathe slowly.
I tried to dye my hair blonde and it came out a glaring, brassy orange.
The library on campus had a distinct smell of old paper and dust that I found comforting.
I bought a cheap digital camera and took blurry photos of street lamps.
I got a parking ticket I couldn't afford and cried in my car out of sheer frustration.
I remember the exact crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during my senior year.
Someone told a joke at a party that wasn't funny, but we all laughed out of awkwardness.
I went to a local diner at 2 AM and the fluorescent lights buzzed aggressively.
Moving into my first real apartment, the empty rooms echoed in a way that made me feel incredibly small.
I realize my intense ambition in my twenties was just a defense mechanism against feeling inadequate.
The first time I fired an employee, my hands shook for an hour afterward.
I adopted a cat that scratched up my sofa, but her purring was deeply soothing.
I spilled hot coffee on my lap during a morning commute and had to sit in wet clothes all day.
I look at my early career choices now and see a man trying desperately to prove he belonged in America.
There was a bakery near my office that always smelled like yeast and melted butter.
I went on a blind date that was so painfully silent I kept drinking water just to have something to do.
I took a solo trip to Chicago and the fierce wind off the lake literally pushed me backward.
I find it fascinating how my memory of a painful breakup has softened into a vague, dull ache over the years.
The radiator in my old building used to clang loudly in the middle of the night.
I bought an expensive suit that never really fit right around the shoulders.
I got caught in a torrential downpour without an umbrella and my shoes squished for miles.
I remember the tart bite of a green apple I ate while walking through Central Park.
My laptop crashed right before a major deadline and my stomach completely dropped.
I saw a play where the lead actor forgot his lines, and the tension in the theater was palpable.
I tried a fad diet and mostly just remember feeling chronically dizzy and cold.
I helped a friend move out of a fifth-floor walkup, my calves burning with every step.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and felt an absurd, childlike surge of luck.
When I finally moved to New York, the skyline looked so intimidatingly vast it took my breath away.
I often think about how living in such a crowded city paradoxically allows me to hide from myself.
I rode the Staten Island Ferry just to feel the cold ocean spray on my face.
I got horribly lost in the subway system my first week, staring at a confusing map until the letters blurred.
The smell of roasted nuts from a street cart always makes my mouth water instantly.
It strikes me how I spent years trying to erase my accent, only to now feel a deep sense of loss over it.
I witnessed a screaming match between two strangers on the street and felt my heart race in panic.
I paid way too much for a tiny cocktail in a dimly lit bar because I wanted to impress someone.
The sirens in the city became white noise to me faster than I ever thought possible.
I recognize that my obsession with organizing my tiny apartment is just my way of asserting control in a chaotic world.
I slipped on black ice and bruised my tailbone, the sharp pain radiating up my spine.
I visited a museum and stared at a dark blue painting until my eyes watered.
The garbage bags on the summer sidewalks emit a sweet, rotting stench that is uniquely New York.
I had a really intense conversation with a cab driver whose face I never actually saw in the rearview mirror.
I bought a bodega sandwich at 3 AM that tasted like absolute heaven at the time.
I attended a massive outdoor concert and felt the bass thumping directly in my chest cavity.
I locked my keys inside my apartment and had to wait three hours in the freezing hallway for a locksmith.

Whenever I am feeling homesick in Queens, I spend hours trying to recreate my mom's exact recipe for khao soi. Smelling that specific mix of coconut milk and curry paste is the main way I actively hold onto my Thai roots.
I saw a rat dart across the subway platform and felt a shiver run down my arms.
I tried to run a marathon but my knees gave out at mile sixteen.
I realize that I often date people who are emotionally unavailable because it feels familiar and safe.
I remember the exact soft texture of a cashmere scarf a former partner used to wear.
I had a terrible argument in a public restaurant where we both hissed at each other to keep our voices down.

After facing harassment on the subway during the pandemic, I started volunteering at a pan-Asian community center in Manhattan. Looking back, I realize that experiencing that shared vulnerability completely transformed my identity, making me see my fate as tied to all Asian Americans rather than just my own ethnic group.
A guy I was seeing ghosted me, leaving me with a heavy, sinking feeling in my gut for weeks.
I look back on my twenties and marvel at how much energy I spent worrying about people who didn't care about me.
I went ice skating at Rockefeller Center and my ankles ached terribly the whole time.
I bought a bouquet of cheap bodega flowers that wilted completely by the next morning.
The smell of fresh bagels in the morning is one of the few things that gets me out of bed.

I have a group chat with my childhood friends back in Thailand that pings constantly throughout the night because of the time difference. Waking up to their random jokes and daily life updates keeps me intimately anchored to the community I left behind.
I got a bad haircut right before a major presentation and felt incredibly self-conscious.
I tried to build an IKEA dresser and got so frustrated I threw a screwdriver at the wall.

Even though I was born there, my Thai reading skills froze at a young age when we moved, leaving me barely able to read a newspaper today. I feel a deep, private shame whenever my grandmother sends handwritten letters that I secretly have to ask someone else to translate.
I watched a street performer play a saxophone and the melody was surprisingly haunting.
I stepped in a deep puddle hiding under a slushy crosswalk and my foot went completely numb.
I had a sudden nosebleed on the train and felt deeply embarrassed as strangers offered me tissues.
I went to a rooftop party where the music was so loud I couldn't hear my own thoughts.
The steam rising from the manhole covers in winter always looks cinematic to me.
I accidentally drank spoiled milk and the sour taste lingered in my mouth all day.
I found a great little vintage shop in Brooklyn but can never remember exactly what street it was on.
I took a ferry to Governor's Island and the warm breeze was incredibly relaxing.
I burned my tongue on a slice of hot pizza and had a rough blister for a week.
I started journaling recently, realizing that putting my thoughts on paper prevents me from spiraling.
I joined a recreational dodgeball league and the rubber smell of the balls brought back instant childhood anxiety.
A close friend moved to LA, and hugging them at the airport felt like closing a chapter of my youth.
I see now that my habit of canceling plans is just a manifestation of my social anxiety.
I took a pottery class and the cold, wet clay felt incredibly grounding on my hands.
I went to a stand-up comedy show and laughed until my stomach muscles actually cramped.
Looking at my current circle of friends, I understand that I surround myself with people who are just as displaced as I am.
I tried to grow herbs on my windowsill, but they all dried up and turned brittle.
I got stuck in a crowded elevator for twenty minutes and felt the walls closing in.
I watched a thunderstorm roll over the Hudson River, the lightning flashing brilliantly against the dark clouds.
I ate a spicy papaya salad in Queens that finally tasted like my grandmother's cooking.
I bought a wildly expensive pair of sneakers that gave me terrible blisters on my heels.
I remember the metallic taste of blood after biting my cheek too hard while chewing gum.
I went to a karaoke bar and butchered an old pop song, sweating under the neon lights.
I fell asleep on the train and woke up at the end of the line, completely disoriented.
The fluorescent lights in my office buzz at a frequency that always triggers a mild migraine by 3 PM.
I tried surfing once on vacation and inhaled a terrifying amount of saltwater.
I bought a hot pretzel from a vendor, but it was incredibly stale and hard to chew.
I found a tiny, dusty bookstore in the Village where the floorboards creaked under every step.
I realize that I judge my parents' past decisions harshly because I refuse to acknowledge how hard immigration was for them.
I went back to Thailand for a wedding and the relentless heat instantly made me feel both foreign and at home.
I had a tearful phone call with my mother where we finally didn't talk past each other.
It dawns on me that I deliberately keep my apartment minimalist to contrast the cluttered home I grew up in.
I found an old family photo where I am smiling, but I remember feeling incredibly sad that day.
The smell of jasmine rice steaming in my rice cooker always brings an immediate sense of peace.
I went to a night market in Bangkok and the overwhelming mix of sewage and sweet pork skewers made me dizzy.
I got a tattoo on my forearm and the persistent scratching needle sent vibrations up to my elbow.
I dropped a heavy cast-iron skillet on my toe and yelled out a curse word in Thai without thinking.
I tried to explain American credit scores to my parents and ended up with a throbbing headache.
I sat in Central Park during the spring bloom, inhaling the sweet, pollen-heavy air.
I went to a fancy gala for work and felt the stiff collar of my tuxedo digging into my neck.
I had a vivid dream about my childhood home, the details so sharp I felt disoriented waking up in New York.
I accidentally knocked over my coffee cup and watched the brown liquid ruin a stack of important documents.
I took a ferry at sunset and the golden reflection on the water was blindingly bright.
I heard a familiar Thai pop song from the 90s in a restaurant and got goosebumps.
I bought a huge watermelon and struggled to carry its heavy, awkward weight for four blocks.
I walked over the Brooklyn Bridge on a windy day, clutching my hat to my head.
I tasted a ridiculously bitter craft IPA that made me pull a face in front of a date.
Understanding my own perfectionism has made me realize how exhausting I must be to live with.
I bought a new winter coat that is so insulated it feels like walking around in a sleeping bag.
I listened to a podcast that disturbed me so deeply I had to pause it and sit in silence.
I look at the gray hairs appearing at my temples and feel a strange mix of dread and relief that I am getting older.
I attended a loud crowded parade and a piece of confetti got stuck directly in my eye.
I accidentally stepped on a piece of shattered glass barefoot, the sharp pinch making me gasp.
I spent an entire Sunday binge-watching a show, my eyes dry and burning by the evening.
I smelled a very specific brand of laundry detergent that instantly reminded me of my first roommate.
I tried to fix a leaky faucet myself and ended up soaking my entire shirt.
I had a really profound conversation with a bartender while nursing a lukewarm beer.
I bit into a chocolate chip cookie that was actually oatmeal raisin, and the betrayal tasted incredibly sweet.
I found a moth in my closet and spent ten minutes frantically trying to swat it with a magazine.
I woke up with a terrible cramp in my calf, my leg muscles seizing up painfully.
I tried meditating, but the silence in my apartment only made the ringing in my ears louder.
I watched a pigeon steal a whole slice of pizza on the platform and marvelled at its audacity.
I bought a cheap umbrella on the street that immediately inverted in the wind.
I felt the rumble of a subway train beneath my feet through the metal grating on the sidewalk.
I sneezed violently in a quiet library and everyone turned to stare at me.
I scraped ice off my friend's windshield, my fingers going numb through my thin gloves.
I ate a very ripe peach over the kitchen sink, the sticky juice running all the way down my wrist.
I heard a loud car backfire and my shoulders immediately tensed up to my ears.
I touched a hot iron to check if it was on and blistered my fingertip instantly.
I watched the first snow of the year fall from my window, the big flakes melting the second they hit the pavement.

participants.persona: Alan is a 45-year-old first-generation Taiwanese American man, born abroad and living in Virginia.
participants.name: Alan

memories.content: I remember the smell of stinky tofu from the night market near our first apartment in Taipei. My grandfather used to sneak me out to buy some when my mother was working late.
My favorite toy as a toddler was a small wooden train that my uncle carved for me. I lost it on the flight to America and cried for hours.
The humidity in Taiwan always made my hair stick to my forehead during summer afternoons. We would eat shaved ice with red beans to cool down.
I can still picture the bright red tiles on the floor of my preschool. We had to take our shoes off before entering the classroom.
My grandmother taught me how to hold chopsticks by placing pennies between my fingers. I was so proud when I finally picked up a single grain of rice.
When I was five, I chased a stray dog down the alley behind our house and scraped my knee badly. I still have a faint white scar on my left kneecap.
The sound of mopeds buzzing outside our window was my daily alarm clock. It was so loud, but I eventually learned to sleep right through it.
I remember my parents packing huge cardboard boxes when I was eight years old. They told me we were going on a long adventure across the ocean.
The airplane ride to Los Angeles was terrifying because we hit massive turbulence over the Pacific. I squeezed my dad's hand so hard it left red marks.

Looking back at my childhood in Taiwan, I realize how much those early years shaped my need for close-knit community. It is strange how a place I left so young still feels like the core of my identity.
We landed in California before taking a connecting flight to Virginia, where my aunt lived. The airport in LA seemed impossibly huge and shiny compared to everything I knew.
My first meal in America was a McDonald's Happy Meal, which felt like a massive luxury at the time. I kept the plastic toy dinosaur on my nightstand for years.
The first winter in Virginia was the first time I ever saw snow falling from the sky. I ran outside in my pajamas and immediately froze my toes.
ESL classes in third grade were a blur of flashcards and exaggerated lip movements from Mrs. Gable. I used to practice rolling my R's in the bathroom mirror.
I wet my pants in the fourth grade because I did not know how to ask to use the restroom in English. The humiliation of walking to the nurse's office in soaked jeans still haunts me.
My dad got a job managing a small electronics warehouse in Fairfax. He would come home smelling like cardboard and packing tape every evening.
Mom started working at a local bakery to help make ends meet. She would bring home day-old pastries, and we ate apple turnovers for breakfast almost every morning.
I made my first American friend, Kevin, because we both liked playing tetherball at recess. We barely spoke the same language, but we understood the rules of the game.
Our first apartment in Virginia had dark green carpets that always smelled faintly of mildew. I used to lay on the floor and trace the carpet patterns with my finger.
Every Saturday, we drove to the Asian supermarket in Falls Church to stock up on groceries. The smell of the seafood aisle always made me feel incredibly homesick.
I won a spelling bee in fifth grade by correctly spelling the word 'chrysanthemum'. It felt like a massive victory over the kids who had teased my accent.
My parents bought me a cheap acoustic guitar for my twelfth birthday from a pawn shop. I spent hours trying to learn Metallica songs from terrible internet tabs.
The summer before middle school, I broke my arm falling off a skateboard I had borrowed from a neighbor. Wearing a cast during August in Virginia was sweaty and miserable.
I remember staying up late to watch the Atlanta Olympics on our boxy television. I felt a strange double pride whenever either the US or Taiwan won a medal.
My mom used to pack me a thermos of hot fried rice for lunch, which embarrassed me when the other kids had sandwiches. I eventually begged her to just buy me Lunchables.
I joined the middle school track team just because I wanted to get out of taking physical education classes. I turned out to be surprisingly fast at the 400-meter dash.
The first time I saw the ocean in America was a family trip to Virginia Beach. The water was colder and murkier than I expected, but I loved jumping over the waves.
I got my first pair of name-brand sneakers, white Nike Air Force 1s, in the eighth grade. I was so paranoid about getting them dirty that I walked weirdly for a month.
I had a massive crush on a girl named Sarah in my biology class. I used to deliberately forget my pencil just so I could ask her to borrow one.

I often wonder if conforming so hard to American teenage culture made me lose a vital part of my Taiwanese heritage. I can see now that my desperate desire to fit in was rooted in a deep fear of being an outsider.
We finally moved into a townhouse in Annandale when I was a freshman in high school. I finally had my own bedroom, which I immediately plastered with movie posters.
Getting my learner's permit was a nightmare because my dad insisted on teaching me to drive stick shift first. We stalled out at so many intersections on Route 236.
I worked my first real job bagging groceries at Giant Food during my sophomore year. The uniform was an itchy polyester polo shirt that trapped every ounce of sweat.
High school marching band took up entirely too much of my time, but I loved playing the trumpet. The Friday night football games were the highlight of my autumns.
I caught my parents having a screaming match about their finances late one night in the kitchen. Seeing my normally stoic father break down in tears terrified me and made me feel entirely helpless.
I went to prom with a group of friends instead of a date, and we rented an absurdly long white limousine. We ended up eating at an IHOP at two in the morning in our tuxedos.
AP Calculus was the first class I genuinely struggled with, no matter how hard I studied. I vividly remember the relief of barely scraping by with a C on the final exam.
I built my first desktop computer from scratch using parts I bought at a local tech expo. Pressing the power button and hearing the fans whir to life was magical.
My grandfather passed away in Taiwan during my senior year, and we couldn't afford to fly back for the funeral. We held a small memorial at our local temple instead.
I got accepted into Virginia Tech, and my mom cooked an absolute feast to celebrate. I was just relieved I would not be stuck living in my childhood bedroom.
Moving into my dorm in Blacksburg was chaotic because it rained the entire day. My roommate was a guy from New Jersey who brought a mini-fridge entirely stocked with energy drinks.
The dining hall at college had a waffle maker that shaped the batter into the school mascot. I probably ate those waffles for dinner three times a week during my freshman year.
I changed my major from pre-med to computer science after taking one programming elective. Writing code just made intuitive sense to my brain in a way organic chemistry never did.
I spent a miserable Thanksgiving break my sophomore year sick with mononucleosis in my dorm. My friends brought me soup from a local diner, which was the only thing I ate for days.
I joined a Taiwanese student association and finally met people who understood my specific cultural background. We used to host hot pot nights in our cramped off-campus apartments.

After someone yelled a slur at me in a grocery store parking lot during the pandemic, I started attending a local Asian American community group in Richmond. I found a lot of comfort talking with Korean and Filipino neighbors who had gone through the exact same things.
I bought a beat-up Honda Civic for two thousand dollars during my junior year. The air conditioning was broken, so I just rolled the windows down and blasted the radio.
I pulled my first all-nighter trying to finish a software engineering project that was due at 8 AM. I walked to class the next morning feeling like a zombie.
I dated a girl named Michelle for two years in college before we mutually decided we were heading in different directions. We had our final breakup conversation on a bench outside the library.
Graduation day was incredibly hot, and wearing a black gown in the sun was unbearable. Seeing how proud my parents looked when I walked across the stage made the sweat worth it.

I recognize now that my college years were less about academics and more about learning how to exist without my parents' safety net. It was the first time I truly had to face my own flaws without any excuses.
I moved to Arlington for my first job at a government contracting firm. My starting salary felt like a million dollars, even though rent ate up half of it.
I tried to get into running in my mid-twenties and signed up for a 10K race in DC. I barely finished, but I still have the participation medal hanging in my home office.
The metro commute on the Orange Line became the background rhythm of my twenties. I read so many paperback science fiction novels on those train rides.
I took my parents to a fancy steakhouse in Tysons Corner with my first year-end bonus. My dad complained about the prices the entire time, but he ate every bite of his ribeye.

I was laid off during the 2008 financial crisis, and it threw me into a deep, silent depression for six months. I felt so much shame about being unemployed that I lied to my family about going to work every morning.
I eventually found a new job as a systems engineer at a smaller tech startup in Reston. The office had a ping-pong table, but we were usually too overworked to ever use it.
I met Grace at a mutual friend's backyard barbecue in summer 2010. She made a terrible joke about hot dogs, and I immediately knew I wanted to ask her out.
Our first date was at a sushi restaurant where they accidentally spilled soy sauce on my shirt. Grace laughed so hard she snorted, which completely broke the ice.
I adopted a golden retriever mix named Buster from a shelter when I was twenty-nine. He chewed up three pairs of my dress shoes before he finally outgrew his puppy phase.
I proposed to Grace during a hiking trip in Shenandoah National Park. I was so nervous I dropped the ring box in the dirt right before I popped the question.
When I visited Taipei last year, I got confused in the subway because I couldn't read the traditional characters on the map anymore. I felt exactly like a tourist in the city where I was born.
We got married at a botanical garden in Virginia on a beautifully clear September afternoon. My dad gave a toast in broken English that had the entire room crying.
We bought our first house, a split-level in Burke, shortly after the wedding. Painting the living room together was our first major test of marital patience.
I remember the chaotic sprint to the hospital when Grace went into labor with our son, Leo. I was so panicked I accidentally parked in the chief of surgery's reserved spot.

I completely agreed with a local candidate's tax plan for Virginia, but I refused to vote for him because he suggested reducing US military support for Taiwan. Protecting my birth country from foreign aggression is simply a non-negotiable issue for me at the ballot box.
Holding Leo for the first time, I was amazed by how incredibly light he felt. He had a full head of dark hair right from the start.
The sleep deprivation during those first few months of parenthood was absolute torture. I once poured coffee into my bowl of cereal instead of milk.
We took a trip back to Taiwan when Leo was two so he could meet his great-relatives. The humidity was exactly how I remembered, and the night markets were just as vibrant.
Our daughter, Mia, was born three years later during a massive snowstorm. We barely made it to Fairfax Hospital before the roads were completely shut down.
I taught Leo how to ride a bike without training wheels in the empty parking lot of his elementary school. Watching him pedal away on his own was a bittersweet milestone.
I started drinking green tea every afternoon around 3 PM to combat the post-lunch slump. It is a habit I picked up from a senior colleague, and now I cannot function without it.

Watching my children grow up with such privilege makes me hyper-aware of the struggles my own parents endured. I often reflect on whether my desire to protect my kids is inadvertently making them less resilient.

My parents always talked about the oppressive martial law era in Taiwan, so I look for politicians who fiercely defend democratic rights abroad. I recently volunteered for a Taiwanese American congressional candidate who aggressively condemned authoritarianism in East Asia.
We remodeled our kitchen during the pandemic, which meant washing dishes in the bathtub for six weeks. I became an expert at making elaborate meals in a single slow cooker.
I took up woodworking as a hobby when I turned forty, starting with a simple birdhouse. I eventually built a solid oak dining table that we use every single day.
Buster passed away peacefully in his sleep at age twelve, and we buried him under the big oak tree in the backyard. I cried more for that dog than I have for most humans.
I chaperoned Mia's fourth-grade field trip to Jamestown and spent the entire day trying to keep track of five chaotic kids. I have a newfound respect for elementary school teachers.

I discovered a benign lump on my neck last year that required a biopsy, and the waiting period was agonizing. I was so convinced I was going to die that I secretly wrote goodbye letters to Grace and the kids.
We started a tradition of having homemade pizza every Friday night. I make the dough from scratch, and Leo is in charge of grating the mozzarella.
My mom was diagnosed with early-stage arthritis, so I go over to their house every other weekend to help with heavy chores. It is hard watching her struggle to open jars she used to handle easily.
I still play pickup basketball at the local recreation center on Thursday nights. My knees crack a lot more than they used to, but my jump shot is surprisingly intact.
I planted a vegetable garden last spring, but the local deer decimated my tomatoes within a week. I ended up building an elaborate chicken-wire fortress just to save the bell peppers.
I finally got a promotion to IT Director after years of being a middle manager. The pay bump was nice, but the sheer number of meetings has quadrupled.
We took the kids to Disney World for the first time, and it was a chaotic marathon of standing in lines. Mia fell asleep on my shoulders during the fireworks show at the end of the night.
I bought a vintage record player at a garage sale and started collecting classic jazz albums. There is something incredibly soothing about the physical act of dropping the needle on vinyl.
I accidentally backed my car into the mailbox during a rainstorm last month. I managed to replace the wooden post myself before Grace even noticed it was broken.
I have been trying to learn Spanish using an app on my phone during my commute. I am currently on a sixty-day streak, though my pronunciation is still terrible.
I cooked a massive turkey for Thanksgiving last year and completely forgot to take the giblets out of the cavity. We ended up ordering Chinese takeout when the bird turned out raw in the middle.
I went to my twentieth high school reunion and barely recognized anyone. It was strange making small talk with people I had not thought about in two decades.
My son Leo recently asked me to teach him how to play chess. He beat me in our third game, and I am still not entirely sure if I let him win or if he outsmarted me.
We went camping in the Blue Ridge Mountains and woke up to a black bear sniffing around our cooler. I have never packed up a tent so quickly in my entire life.
I bought myself a fancy espresso machine for my forty-fifth birthday. Dialing in the perfect grind size has become a bizarre obsession of mine every morning.

Experiencing middle age has made me surprisingly contemplative about my legacy and what I am leaving behind. I realize that being a steady, present father is the only achievement that genuinely matters to me now.
I started wearing reading glasses a few months ago after refusing to admit my eyesight was failing. It is incredibly frustrating to constantly search for where I last put them down.
Grace and I started taking salsa dancing lessons on Tuesday nights just to get out of the house. We are both terribly uncoordinated, but we laugh a lot.
I have a persistent memory of the smell of ozone right before a summer thunderstorm in Virginia. It always reminds me of the afternoons I spent catching fireflies in our old neighborhood.
My father finally retired last year, and I helped him pack up his office. We found a drawing I did of him when I was seven tucked into the back of his desk drawer.

I harbor a deep guilt about losing my fluency in Mandarin as I got older. It hurts whenever my mother struggles to express a complex emotion to me in English and I cannot switch back to her native tongue to comfort her.
I recently started listening to history podcasts while doing yard work. I spent four hours last weekend trimming hedges and learning about the fall of the Roman Empire.
We adopted a stray tuxedo cat that kept showing up on our back porch. We named him Barnaby, and he now rules the household with an iron paw.
I coached Mia's youth soccer team last autumn despite knowing very little about the sport. We lost almost every game, but the kids loved the orange slices I brought for halftime.
I went to a concert at Wolf Trap last summer and realized I am now the guy who brings a stadium seat and a thermos. The acoustics were fantastic, even if I was asleep by 10 PM.
I accidentally dropped my phone into the Potomac River while trying to take a picture of a heron. I had to pay full price for a replacement because I never bought the insurance.
I have a peculiar habit of checking the locks on the front door exactly three times before I go to bed. Grace teases me about it, but it helps me sleep better.
I tried a trendy new keto diet for exactly one week before giving up entirely. I realized life is simply too short to pretend cauliflower tastes like mashed potatoes.
I helped my neighbor shovel his driveway after the big blizzard of 2016. We ended up sharing a thermos of hot cocoa while sitting on a massive snowbank.
I keep a small, smooth river stone in my jacket pocket that I found on a beach in Oregon. I like to roll it between my fingers when I am stuck in long meetings.
I successfully fixed a leaky pipe under the kitchen sink using only YouTube tutorials and sheer stubbornness. I felt like a master plumber for about an hour until it started dripping again.
We went to an apple orchard in Winchester last fall and picked way too many Honeycrisps. Grace made apple pies, apple butter, and applesauce until we were entirely sick of them.
I still have my high school letterman jacket stuffed in a box in the attic. I tried it on last year and realized my shoulders have definitely broadened since I was seventeen.
I love waking up before the rest of the house to enjoy the absolute silence of the early morning. I sit by the window with my coffee and watch the neighborhood slowly come to life.
