I took a spontaneous road trip to Asheville with some college buddies last spring for a weekend getaway. We mostly just drank local beer and complained about our various joint pains.

Sometimes I catch a glimpse of myself in the mirror and am shocked to see my father's face looking back at me. It forces me to reflect on how quickly time is passing and how I am now the older generation.
I had a terrifying moment last month when my brakes locked up on the icy highway. I managed to steer into the skid and avoid hitting the guardrail by mere inches.
I finally finished reading 'Dune' after starting and stopping it five times over the last ten years. I still do not completely understand the ending, but I enjoyed the journey.
We started a fire in the backyard fire pit on Halloween and roasted marshmallows with the neighbors. The smell of woodsmoke lingered in my jacket for weeks.
I bought a cheap drone online and immediately got it stuck in the highest branch of our maple tree. It is still up there, silently mocking me every time I mow the lawn.

My wife and I went through a very rough patch a few years ago where we barely spoke for months outside of logistics for the kids. Going to couples counseling saved our marriage, but acknowledging how close we came to divorce is still painful.
I love the tradition of getting pho at a little hole-in-the-wall place in Eden Center whenever I have a cold. The spicy broth clears my sinuses better than any medication ever could.
I started volunteering at the local food bank on Saturday mornings to get out of the house. Sorting canned goods in a cold warehouse has surprisingly become the highlight of my weekend.
I recently discovered that I have a mild allergy to shellfish after eating bad shrimp at a buffet. The hives covered my arms for three days, and I looked ridiculous.
I spent an entire weekend organizing my garage workspace with pegboards and labeled bins. Within a month, it was completely cluttered with random tools and half-finished projects again.
I was ecstatic when the Washington Nationals finally won the World Series. I bought a championship hat the very next day and wore it until the logo faded.
I remember the sharp sting of paper cuts on my fingers when I was building origami cranes in elementary school. I used to fold them out of lined notebook paper when I was bored in class.
I had to get a root canal last year, and the sound of the drill still makes me shudder. The right side of my face was numb for hours, making it impossible to drink water without spilling it.
We visited the Luray Caverns when the kids were little, and Mia was convinced the stalactites were dragon teeth. It was incredibly humid down there, but the rock formations were beautiful.
I still use the same worn-out leather wallet Grace bought me for our first anniversary. The seams are splitting, but I am too sentimentally attached to replace it.
I have a deep hatred for the sound of leaf blowers early on weekend mornings. Our neighbor hires a landscaping crew that always arrives exactly at 7 AM on Saturdays.
I once tried to make traditional Taiwanese beef noodle soup from scratch using my mother's recipe. I simmered the broth for eight hours, but it just tasted like salty water.
I remember the distinct smell of chlorine and sunscreen at the community pool during summer breaks in high school. I spent hours trying to perfect my dive off the high board.
I found a box of old cassette tapes in my parents' basement last month, mostly containing mixtapes I made off the radio. It took me back to the days of hitting record right as a song started playing.
I twisted my ankle badly stepping off a curb in DC while looking at my phone. I had to limp for six blocks to get back to the metro station.

I realize now that my obsession with organizing my garage is a coping mechanism for when my work life feels chaotic. It is profound how I seek physical control over my environment when I lack emotional control in my career.
We went to a cherry blossom festival at the Tidal Basin a few years ago when the blooms were at their peak. It was incredibly crowded, but the canopy of pink flowers was breathtaking.
I used to love playing arcade games at the mall when I was a teenager. I spent entirely too much allowance money trying to beat the high score on Time Crisis.
I recently started baking sourdough bread, cultivating my own starter from scratch. Watching the dough rise in the proofing basket gives me a strange sense of accomplishment.
I remember the feeling of static electricity making my hair stand on end when going down the plastic slides at the playground. I would shock my friends on purpose by poking their arms.

I suffer from occasional panic attacks that make it feel like there is an elephant sitting on my chest. I hide them from my children because I do not want them to see their father so fragile and terrified.
I love the crisp smell of autumn air in Virginia, especially when the leaves start turning bright orange and red. It always signals the beginning of soup season in our house.
I once got lost in a massive Ikea store for over an hour trying to find the exit. I ended up buying a weird desk lamp and some frozen meatballs just to justify the trip.
I have a scar on my chin from when I fell off a barstool during a college party. I tried to tell people I got it in a fight, but no one believed me.
I enjoy washing the car by hand on Sunday afternoons when the weather is nice. The rhythmic motion of scrubbing the soapy water is surprisingly meditative.

Every Lunar New Year, our extended family gathers to eat my mother's beef noodle soup and share stories about our old neighborhood in Kaohsiung. I always look forward to participating in these specific Taiwanese traditions with my relatives.
I remember the overwhelming scent of pine when we went to a cut-your-own Christmas tree farm. We brought home a tree so massive we had to trim the top just to fit it in the living room.
I played intramural softball a few years ago and managed to pull a hamstring while rounding second base. I had to be carried off the field by two guys I barely knew.
I have a secret stash of dark chocolate almonds in my home office desk drawer. I eat them when I am stressed and do not want to share with the kids.
I once stood in line for three hours to get a signature from my favorite sci-fi author at a bookstore in Dupont Circle. He barely looked up when he signed my book, which was incredibly disappointing.
I remember the distinct click-clack sound of typing on my first mechanical keyboard. It drove my college roommates absolutely insane when I was writing papers late at night.

Even though I was born in Taiwan, I immigrated so young that my Mandarin is terrible, and I felt a deep ache when I couldn't have a real conversation with my grandmother before she passed away. It genuinely breaks my heart that I cannot speak our native language with my own kids.
We took a family trip to the Outer Banks and rented a house right on the beach. Listening to the ocean waves crash at night was the best sleep I have had in years.
I recently tried to fix my own lawnmower by replacing the spark plug and the air filter. It actually started on the first pull, which made me feel incredibly capable.
I love the taste of cold, leftover pizza for breakfast, specifically pepperoni and jalapeño. Grace thinks it is disgusting, but it is one of my favorite indulgences.
I remember the sticky feeling of catching fireflies in a glass jar on summer evenings. We would always poke holes in the lid and let them go before bedtime.
I have a habit of saving every instruction manual for everything I buy, just in case. I currently have a filing cabinet full of manuals for appliances we do not even own anymore.
I notice that as I age, my anger has softened into a general sense of patience with the world. Reflecting on my younger, quick-tempered self makes me appreciate this newfound emotional stability.
I once got a terrible sunburn on the back of my neck during a golf tournament because I forgot to reapply sunscreen. It peeled for a week and looked absolutely disgusting.
I remember the thrill of finally beating Super Mario 64 after months of trying. I proudly showed my parents the end credits, though they had no idea what it meant.
I bought a cheap telescope last summer to show the kids the craters on the moon. We spent an hour swatting mosquitoes just to get a blurry view, but they thought it was magical.
I have a mild phobia of driving over high bridges, especially the Chesapeake Bay Bridge. I have to grip the steering wheel so tightly my knuckles turn white until we reach the other side.

I harbor a lot of resentment toward my older brother for being the golden child who never helped care for our aging parents. I am deeply ashamed of how much bitterness I hold toward him, but I cannot seem to let it go.
I love the smell of old books in secondhand bookstores, dusty and slightly sweet. I can spend hours just browsing the history section without buying a single thing.
I remember the frustration of tangled phone cords twisting around themselves in our kitchen when I was a kid. I used to let the receiver hang and spin just to untangle the wire.
I recently started wearing a smartwatch to track my daily steps. It gently buzzes when I have been sitting at my desk too long, which is both helpful and incredibly annoying.
We went to a drive-in movie theater in Stephen's City last summer and parked the SUV backwards to sit in the trunk. The movie was terrible, but eating popcorn under the stars was perfect.
I have a distinct memory of the first time I tasted a perfectly ripe mango back in Taiwan. The juice ran down my chin and stained my favorite yellow shirt.
I accidentally shrunk my favorite wool sweater in the wash last week. It is now perfectly sized for a teddy bear, and I am still mourning the loss.
I remember the sheer panic of losing my mom in a department store when I was six. I hid inside a circular rack of coats until a security guard found me crying.
I took a photography class at a community college in my thirties to learn how to use a real camera. I mostly ended up taking blurry photos of my dog running in the park.
I love sitting on the back patio during a heavy summer rainstorm, safely out of the wet. The sound of rain hitting the metal roof of our shed is deeply comforting to me.
I remember the awkwardness of middle school dances, where the boys and girls stood on opposite sides of the gym. I spent the entire time drinking fruit punch and avoiding eye contact.
I recently found my old Game Boy Color in a box and was amazed it still turned on. I played Tetris for an hour before the screen finally died.
I have a weird quirk where I have to eat all the fries on my plate before I take a bite of my burger. Grace points it out every time, but I literally cannot eat any other way.
I once locked my keys inside my running car at a gas station in the dead of winter. I had to wait forty-five minutes for a tow truck while freezing in just a t-shirt.
I remember the absolute awe of seeing a space shuttle launch on television when I was a kid. I wanted to be an astronaut for exactly a week before realizing I was terrified of heights.

I often think about how my immigrant experience is fundamentally different from my children's suburban upbringing. It makes me question if my efforts to give them an easier life are actually depriving them of character-building struggles.
I bought a hammock a few years ago and strung it up between two trees in the backyard. I try to read books in it, but I usually just end up falling asleep within ten minutes.
I remember the sting of iodine when my mom would clean out my scraped knees after falling off my bike. She would always blow on the wound to make it hurt less.
I have a specific mug at the office that no one else is allowed to use. It has a chipped handle and a faded logo of a tech company that went bankrupt in the nineties.
We visited the Air and Space Museum near Dulles and stood underneath the Discovery space shuttle. The sheer scale of the machine made me feel incredibly small and insignificant.

I secretly suffer from severe imposter syndrome at work, constantly fearing that I will be exposed as a fraud. The anxiety keeps me up at night, convinced that my career is built on a foundation of sheer luck rather than actual skill.
I love the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots when I walk to the mailbox in November. It is one of those tiny sensory experiences that always puts me in a good mood.
I once tried to grow a beard during No-Shave November and ended up looking incredibly patchy and unkempt. I shaved it off after three weeks because my chin started itching uncontrollably.
I remember the metallic taste of water from the drinking fountain in my elementary school hallway. The water was always lukewarm, but we drank it anyway after recess.
I have an old acoustic guitar sitting in the corner of my bedroom that I have not tuned in years. I keep telling myself I will take lessons again, but I never seem to find the time.

Sometimes I look at old photographs of my parents when they were my age, and I realize how much I mirror their expressions. It is a profound realization that we are essentially just continuations of the people who raised us.
I went to a local farmer's market last weekend and bought a jar of homemade blackberry jam. We ate the entire jar on toast over the course of three days.
I remember the glowing neon signs reflecting on the wet pavement in Taipei when it rained at night. It is a cinematic image that still randomly pops into my head when it rains here in Virginia.
I accidentally stepped on a rogue Lego brick in the dark while walking to the kitchen for water. It was a level of sharp, sudden pain that is entirely unique to parenthood.
I love visiting the local library and walking through the aisles just breathing in the scent of paper. There is a specific hushed quiet there that instantly lowers my blood pressure.

I was bullied mercilessly for a year in seventh grade because of the clothes my parents bought from discount stores. I still feel a deep knot of shame in my stomach whenever I walk past a thrift shop.

I recently tried to assemble a complex Lego Star Wars set with my son, and I ended up getting far more invested than he did. He wandered off to play video games while I spent three hours building a spaceship.
I remember the distinctive hum of the dial-up modem connecting to the internet in the late nineties. I would sit there praying nobody would pick up the phone and disconnect my game.
I have a scar on my right index finger from slipping with a kitchen knife while chopping onions for chili. I had to get three stitches and was terrified of sharp knives for a month.
I love listening to the sound of crickets through an open window on a cool late-summer night. It is the perfect natural white noise for falling asleep.

I find myself increasingly drawn to studying Eastern philosophy as I get older, searching for meaning outside of the Western corporate ladder. It reflects a growing internal awareness that my current definitions of success are deeply flawed.
I once got caught in a sudden downpour while walking the dog and we both came home completely soaked. Barnaby shook himself off in the hallway and sprayed muddy water all over the walls.
I remember the powdery texture of the pink mints they used to give out at the local Chinese buffet. I would always grab a handful on the way out the door.
I recently bought a bird feeder for the front yard and spend way too much time watching the cardinals and blue jays. It makes me feel incredibly old to admit how much joy I get from birdwatching.

Realizing that I have likely lived more than half my life already forces me to evaluate how I spend my daily hours. I am finally beginning to understand that being present is a deliberate choice, not an accident.

participants.persona: Lily is a 29-year-old second-generation Vietnamese American woman, born in the U.S. and living in California.
participants.name: Lily

memories.content: Looking back, I realize my obsession with getting perfect grades was mostly just a way to translate my parents' sacrifices into a metric I could control.
I sometimes wonder if my attachment to the ocean is just a cliche, but it genuinely grounds me when I feel overwhelmed.

I remember a college club fair where the Asian Student Union booth was covered entirely in East Asian flags and pop culture references. I just walked past without signing up because it did not feel like a space for Southeast Asians.
I remember the exact moment I stopped trying to correct my mom's English, realizing that her voice carried our family's history just the way it was.
Sometimes I catch myself apologizing when someone bumps into me, a habit I've been actively trying to unlearn since my early twenties.
I can see now that my first serious breakup wasn't about him, but about my own terror of becoming emotionally dependent.
It's funny how I used to resent going to Vietnamese school on Saturdays, but now I feel a profound sense of loss that I can't read poetry in my parents' language.
I think my tendency to over-pack for short trips stems from some deep-seated anxiety about never being fully prepared for the unknown.
I recognize that I push people away when I'm stressed, a coping mechanism that has cost me a few good friendships over the years.
Looking at my hands as I type, I realize they look exactly like my grandmother's hands when she used to fold lotus napkins.
I often wonder if I'm holding onto my high school journals out of nostalgia or a refusal to let go of the girl I used to be.
I have come to accept that I will never be the effortlessly cool California girl I tried to emulate in college, and that's actually a relief.
It dawned on me recently that my definition of success has completely changed from a corner office to just having enough time to cook dinner.
I remember hiding in my closet during one of my parents' screaming matches, squeezing my eyes shut until the house went quiet.
The sting of being told my lunch smelled weird in third grade stayed with me for years, making me throw away perfectly good banh cuon.
I failed my first college chemistry midterm and cried in my car for two hours straight, terrified I had ruined my life.
I can still feel the cold tiles of the bathroom floor from the night I had my first major panic attack during finals week.
The silence in the hospital waiting room when my grandfather had his stroke was the heaviest thing I've ever felt.
I got caught shoplifting a lip gloss when I was fourteen and the shame of the store manager calling my dad still makes my stomach drop.
There was a period in my early twenties where I drank so much wine alone in my apartment that I had to start hiding the empty bottles from myself.
I remember the hollow feeling of packing up my apartment after I was unexpectedly laid off from my first real job.
I found out my ex was cheating on me by looking at his phone when he was in the shower, and my heart hammered so hard I thought I would pass out.
I once snapped at my grandmother out of pure frustration, and the hurt look on her face still haunts me.
I remember the smell of jasmine rice steaming in our tiny kitchen when I would come home from elementary school.
My dad taught me how to ride a bike in an empty high school parking lot in San Jose.
I used to save all my allowance to buy colorful stickers from the mall.
There was a huge oak tree in our backyard that I would try to climb, but I never made it past the first low branch.
I remember the sticky heat of summer afternoons in the Valley, lying in front of a box fan reading paperbacks.
My mom always made sure I had a freshly ironed ao dai for the Tet festival at the fairgrounds.
I had a severe obsession with a boy band in middle school, and my walls were completely plastered with their posters.
The first time I saw snow was on a family trip to Tahoe, and it felt impossibly cold through my thin gloves.
I accidentally dropped my first flip phone into a toilet at a movie theater.
We used to go to a pho restaurant in Little Saigon where the waiters always knew our exact order before we sat down.
I remember the sharp, distinct smell of chlorine from the public pool where I took swimming lessons as a kid.
My best friend and I spent hours choreographing a dance routine to a pop song in her garage.
I loved the crunch of autumn leaves under my sneakers when walking home from middle school.
The first time I drove on the 405 freeway by myself, my hands were sweating so much I had to wipe them on my jeans.

Whenever I visit my grandmother, my chest gets tight because I can only string together a few broken sentences in Vietnamese to answer her questions. I always leave wishing I had paid more attention when my parents tried to teach me.
I remember eating an incredibly sweet mango over the sink so the juice wouldn't get everywhere.
My mom would always buy me a warm egg tart from the Chinese bakery as a treat after a doctor's appointment.
I went through a phase where I refused to wear anything but black clothing for an entire year.
The first concert I ever went to was in a small indie venue in San Francisco, and my ears rang for two days afterward.
I vividly remember the taste of the cheap instant ramen I survived on during my sophomore year of college.
I used to sit in the back row of my high school history class, drawing intricate doodles instead of taking notes.
My brother and I would wage epic water balloon wars in the backyard until we were both shivering and soaked.
I remember the comforting sound of rain tapping against my bedroom window during winter storms.
The library down the street was my safe haven, smelling faintly of old paper and floor wax.
I ruined a favorite pair of jeans by accidentally sitting on a freshly painted park bench.
We had a fluffy golden retriever mix who would always rest his heavy chin on my knee when he wanted a treat.
I remember the thrill of sneaking out to go to a diner at midnight with my college roommates.
My grandmother used to rub Tiger Balm on my temples whenever I had a headache.
I completely botched my first attempt at cooking a Thanksgiving turkey, serving my friends a practically raw bird.
I once found a perfectly intact sand dollar on the beach in Malibu and kept it on my desk for years.
I used to collect shiny rocks from the playground, convinced they were valuable gems.
The smell of eucalyptus trees always reminds me of morning hikes in the East Bay.
I remember the exhausting but rewarding feeling of finishing my first 10K race.
My dad always had a thermos of extremely strong Vietnamese iced coffee with him on long road trips.
I accidentally dyed my hair a horrific shade of orange the week before high school graduation.
I loved the soft, glowing light of the sunset reflecting off the ocean in Santa Monica.
We used to make intricate forts out of sofa cushions and bedsheets on rainy weekends.
I remember the distinct metallic taste of braces when I first got them in middle school.
My mom taught me how to fold origami cranes, and I once made a hundred of them for a school project.
The first time I tried surfing, I swallowed half the ocean and ended up bruised all over.
I remember the satisfying crack of opening a brand new textbook on the first day of the semester.
I used to volunteer at an animal shelter, and walking the dogs was the highlight of my week.
The aroma of freshly baked baguette from the banh mi shop down the street was intoxicating.
I once locked my keys in my car while it was still running in the driveway.
I remember the vibrant colors of the paper lanterns at the autumn moon festival.
My first apartment had a tiny balcony where I managed to keep exactly one tomato plant alive.
I spent an entire summer binge-watching medical dramas until I thought I could diagnose my friends' ailments.
The feeling of cool, crisp sheets on a freshly made bed always makes me instantly sleepy.
I remember the loud, chaotic energy of the night market we visited during my first trip to Vietnam.
I used to have a recurring nightmare about forgetting my locker combination.
My favorite childhood toy was a worn-out stuffed rabbit missing one eye.
I once spilled an entire iced coffee on my laptop keyboard right before a final paper was due.
I remember the soft hum of the refrigerator in the middle of the night when I'd get up for a glass of water.
We used to catch fireflies in jars when visiting family in the Midwest, letting them go before bedtime.
The salty, greasy taste of boardwalk french fries is a quintessential summer memory for me.
I loved the feeling of sinking into a hot bath after a long, freezing hike in Yosemite.
My parents bought me a beautiful acoustic guitar, but I never learned to play more than three chords.

I saw a flyer for a Vietnamese American city council candidate, but I ended up voting for her opponent because they belonged to my preferred political party. Her stance on healthcare was just completely opposite to the domestic policies I support.
I remember the intense, blinding glare of the sun on the hood of my first car, a beat-up sedan.
I once won a giant stuffed bear at a carnival game and had to lug it around all day.
The smell of burning leaves always takes me back to autumn weekends helping my dad with yard work.
I spent hours trying to master a skateboard trick, only to end up with scraped knees and a bruised ego.
I remember the satisfying click of a cassette tape sliding into the deck of my dad's old station wagon.
My grandmother made the most incredible bitter melon soup, though I hated it when I was a kid.

My uncle got extremely heated at a family dinner, insisting we all had to vote for a specific local politician because he was tough on the communist government in Vietnam. He kept saying that nothing else mattered as long as the candidate stood up to the regime back home.
I used to love wandering through the aisles of the Asian supermarket, looking at all the imported snacks.
The first time I rode a roller coaster, I squeezed my eyes shut and screamed until my throat was raw.
I remember the quiet, eerie stillness of a foggy morning in San Francisco.
I completely forgot the lyrics to my solo in the middle school choir concert and just mouthed the words.
We used to have epic racing game tournaments in the dorms, complete with a makeshift trophy.
The rich, earthy smell of wet soil after a California rainstorm is one of my favorite scents.
I once tried to cut my own bangs with kitchen scissors, and it was an absolute disaster.
I remember the sharp sting of paper cuts from stuffing hundreds of envelopes at my first internship.
My mom used to leave little sticky notes with encouraging messages in my lunchbox.
The feeling of sand between my toes during evening walks on the beach is incredibly grounding.
I loved the loud, syncopated rhythm of the lion dance drums during Lunar New Year celebrations.
I once accidentally boarded the wrong bus and ended up on the opposite side of Los Angeles.
I remember the sweet, syrupy taste of the lychee jelly cups I'd get at the grocery store.
My brother and I used to pretend the floor was lava, jumping wildly from the couch to the coffee table.
The quiet hum of the air conditioner was the only sound during late-night study sessions in the library.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and felt like the luckiest person in the world.
I remember the frustrating tangle of headphones in my pocket before wireless earbuds existed.
My dad built a makeshift treehouse in our backyard using scrap wood and an old blue tarp.
The sharp, vinegary smell of dyeing Easter eggs always marks the beginning of spring in my mind.
I loved the chaotic energy of the flea market on Sunday mornings, hunting for cheap vintage clothes.
I remember the smooth, cool surface of the jade bracelet my grandmother gave me for my high school graduation.
I once got terribly sunburned on a boat trip and spent three days slathered in aloe vera gel.
The satisfying pop of bubble wrap is a simple pleasure I still cannot resist.
I used to eagerly await the familiar jingle of the ice cream truck coming down our suburban street.

The smell of broth simmering for hours always brings me right back to weekend mornings in my childhood kitchen. Cooking those traditional recipes is the main way I hold onto my Vietnamese background since my language skills are so weak.
I remember the distinct crunch of snow boots on an icy sidewalk during a winter trip to Chicago.
My first job was at a frozen yogurt shop, and I still can't look at gummy worms the same way.
The rich, buttery smell of popcorn in a dark movie theater always makes me feel a surge of anticipation.
I once spent an entire weekend building an intricate puzzle only to discover exactly one piece was missing.
I remember the warm, golden light of the sunset flooding into the windows of my first solo apartment.
My mom and I would spend hours picking out the perfect durian at the market, much to my dad's dismay.
The feeling of taking off heavy ski boots after a long day on the slopes is pure heaven.
I used to obsessively organize my colored pencils by shade in my elementary school desk.
I remember the loud, joyful chaos of a family karaoke night in our cramped living room.
I once accidentally texted my boss instead of my best friend and almost died of sheer embarrassment.
The sweet, floral taste of a fresh lychee instantly transports me back to childhood summers.
I loved the quiet intimacy of late-night phone calls with my high school crush.
I remember the sharp, stinging sensation of stepping on a bee barefoot in the backyard grass.
My college roommate and I attempted to make homemade pasta, which resulted in flour coating every surface.
The heavy, unmistakable scent of gardenias blooming in our front yard meant summer was officially here.
I once spent an entire afternoon lost in the winding, dusty stacks of a used bookstore in downtown LA.
I remember the satisfying hiss of a soda can opening on a sweltering July afternoon.
My dad used to meticulously wash and wax his car every Sunday morning, a ritual I found oddly soothing.
The cold, metallic feeling of monkey bars on my hands brings back the distinct chaos of elementary recess.
I once stood in line for three hours to get a famous pastry, only to drop it on the sidewalk immediately after.
I remember the soft, rhythmic sound of waves crashing against the pier during a midnight walk.
I used to carefully save all my concert ticket stubs in an old shoebox hidden under my bed.
The smell of old wood and dusty velvet in my high school's theater auditorium is completely unforgettable.
I once tried to bake macaroons and ended up with flat, almond-flavored puddles stuck to the pan.
I remember the exhilarating rush of cold air hitting my face when riding a bike down a incredibly steep hill.
My grandmother always kept a secret stash of spicy ginger candies in her purse just for me.
The vivid neon signs of a late-night diner cutting through the heavy fog always look so cinematic to me.
I used to love the feeling of freshly sharpened wooden pencils lined up perfectly on test days.
I remember the distinctive scent of my mom's favorite hairspray lingering in the bathroom air.
I once got stuck on a Ferris wheel for an entire hour and almost missed my ride home entirely.

I really liked a presidential candidate's education policies, but my parents begged me not to vote for him because they felt his foreign policy was too friendly with the current regime in Vietnam. It was highly stressful trying to balance my preference for local school funding with my parents' intense geopolitical fears.
The satisfying crunch of biting into a perfectly fresh banh mi is one of life's absolute greatest pleasures.
I loved the sleepy, content feeling of riding in the backseat of the car after a long exhausting beach day.
I remember the bright, garish carpet patterns of the local bowling alley where we had all our middle school parties.
My brother accidentally threw a baseball through the garage window, and we spent hours frantically trying to hide the evidence.
The sweet, milky taste of boba tea always makes me feel a little bit nostalgic for my teenage years.
I once bought a wildly expensive pair of designer heels that I have ended up wearing exactly one time.
I remember the comforting, satisfying weight of a heavy blanket on a freezing cold winter night.
I used to spend hours browsing the CD racks at the local music store, carefully analyzing all the album covers.
The sharp, pungent smell of fish sauce bubbling on the stove always makes me think of my mother's kitchen.
I once tried to grow out my eyebrows naturally, leading to a very awkward photographic phase during my college years.
I remember the soft, muted sound of the city covered in a fresh, thick layer of morning fog.
My dad taught me how to change a tire on the shoulder of a busy highway, yelling instructions over the loud traffic.
The warm, comforting smell of laundry fresh out of the dryer is incredibly relaxing and universally wonderful.
I used to leave out a plate of milk and cookies for Santa, even though my parents ate them almost immediately.
I remember the dizzying sensation of spinning in rapid circles on the front lawn until I literally collapsed.
I once completely lost my voice after screaming far too loudly at a loud outdoor music festival.
The rich, dark taste of a perfect espresso shot is practically the only way I can start my mornings now.
I loved the crackle of a warm campfire and the lingering smell of woodsmoke clinging to my clothes.
I remember the smooth, polished wood of the piano keys during my mandatory, often frustrating, childhood lessons.
My mom always made absolutely sure we had a massive pot of thit kho ready for the Lunar New Year feast.
The quiet, empty feeling of a high school hallway during class time always felt a bit mischievous to walk through.
I once spent an entire four-hour flight talking amiably to an elderly stranger about her young grandchildren.
I remember the incredibly satisfying click of a plastic disposable camera winding slowly to the next frame.
I used to love the sharp, minty taste of toothpaste right after eating an enormous amount of Halloween candy.
The soft, glowing string lights draped on my small apartment patio make the entire space feel incredibly cozy.
I once accidentally grabbed someone else's identical black suitcase off the airport baggage carousel and had to run back.
I remember the distinct, papery smell of the card catalog in the public library long before it was digitized.
My brother and I used to have intense staring contests until our eyes watered uncontrollably and we burst out laughing.
The warm, yeasty smell of a local bakery early in the morning is an almost intoxicating scent.
I once got a terrible, agonizing cramp in my leg while swimming in the ocean and genuinely panicked for a moment.
I remember the soft, fuzzy texture of my absolute favorite childhood blanket that I dragged everywhere with me.
I used to love the very specific feeling of peeling dried white craft glue completely off my fingertips in art class.
The sharp, unmistakable screeching sound of a dial-up internet connection is permanently etched deep into my brain.
I once foolishly tried to hold a scared stray cat, and the tiny scratch it gave me scarred my wrist for years.
I remember the vivid orange color of the ripe persimmons hanging heavily from the tree in our neighbor's yard.
My dad would always peel a crisp apple in one long, continuous ribbon just to impress me when I was young.
The comforting, steady hum of an oscillating fan during a hot summer night was the only way I could ever fall asleep.
I once slipped clumsily on a patch of wet grass and completely ruined a brand new white sundress.
I remember the cold, slightly damp feeling of the unfinished basement where my high school friends and I used to hang out.
I used to excitedly make intricate friendship bracelets, tying the colorful knots until my fingers were practically sore.
The sharp, clean, citrusy smell of a freshly zested lemon always wakes my senses up a little bit.
I once watched a spectacular meteor shower from the dented roof of my car, bundled tightly in three heavy blankets.
I remember the very satisfying snap of a fresh green bean when sitting at the table helping my mom prep dinner.
I used to love the deep, vibrating purr of my college roommate's old tabby cat sleeping heavily on my chest.
The bright, garish, colorful lights of the Santa Monica Pier always look incredibly magical reflected in the dark ocean water.
I once accidentally dropped my favorite sunglasses off a high bridge and watched them sink sadly into the murky water below.
I remember the wonderfully rich, spicy, savory broth of a steaming bowl of bun bo hue on a cold, rainy Sunday.
I used to quietly trace the woven floral patterns on the living room rug with my finger when I was supposed to be napping.
The sharp, undeniably chemical smell of chlorine bleach always instantly reminds me of damp swimming pool locker rooms.
I once spent three entire days trying stubbornly to beat a single video game boss, my thumbs blistering from the controller.
I remember the soft, incredibly rhythmic thumping of heavy rain hitting the canvas of a tent during a childhood camping trip.
I loved feeling the crisp, beautifully uncreased pages of a brand new journal just waiting to be written in.
The heavy, metallic clink of my house keys hitting the kitchen counter firmly signals the official end of my long workday.
I once accidentally ate a massive, heaping spoonful of spicy wasabi at a sushi restaurant, incorrectly thinking it was avocado.
I remember the wonderfully comforting weight of my favorite, perfectly worn-in denim jacket that I've continuously worn since college.
I used to marvel at the intricately carved wooden ancestral altar in my grandparents' living room, always smelling faintly of incense.

participants.persona: Alice is an 80-year-old second-generation Japanese American woman, born in the U.S. and living in Oregon.
participants.name: Alice

memories.content: Looking back, I think I always chose safe jobs because of how unpredictable my parents' lives were after the war.
I wonder if I was too strict with my daughter when she was a teenager in the seventies.
It occurs to me that my love for gardening is just a way of trying to connect with my father, who was always in the dirt.
I sometimes feel like I've forgotten more of my Japanese heritage than I ever really learned, which makes me feel a bit hollow.
I realize my memories of my husband's laugh are starting to fade into a generic sound, and that terrifies me.
Sometimes I wonder if my preference for quiet evenings is just a habit I formed to avoid bothering anyone.
I think my proudest moments aren't the awards I won, but the times I stayed quiet and listened instead of arguing.
Looking at old photos, I can see how much I tried to look like the white girls in my high school class.
It makes me laugh to realize I've become the stubborn old woman I used to complain about when I was in my thirties.
I reflect a lot lately on whether I was a good enough sister to June after she got sick.

After the camps, my parents always told me to vote for our own kind, so I remember supporting that Japanese man for mayor in the 70s—maybe it was Portland. We also always checked if politicians wanted to keep good relations with Japan, just to be safe.
I feel like my understanding of time has completely warped since I turned seventy, making years feel like mere weeks.
Sometimes I question if my happy childhood memories are real, or just stories my mother repeated until I believed them.
I remember living in a small wooden house in Eastern Oregon when I was very little. The dust was always blowing, or maybe that was just in the summer.
My mother made a sweet rice dish for New Year's in 1950, or maybe 1951. I remember the sticky feeling on my fingers.
There was a dog named Buster or Buddy that followed me home from school in first grade. My father wouldn't let me keep him.
We drove to Portland once when I was about eight, and I got terribly carsick. My brother kept complaining about the smell in the back seat.
I had a doll with a blue dress that I lost near the irrigation ditch. I cried for what felt like days, though it was probably just an afternoon.
A boy in my class, maybe his name was Tommy, pulled my hair during recess and I chased him all the way to the swings.
My father used to smoke a pipe on the porch on Sunday evenings. The smell of the tobacco always reminded me of dried apples.
I helped pick strawberries one summer, probably when I was ten. My hands were stained red for a week, and I think I ate more than I gathered.
Auntie June visited from Seattle and brought me a little wooden puzzle box. I never figured out how to open it, and eventually I think my cousin broke it.
I remember wearing a yellow raincoat that was too big for me during a storm. The rain sounded so loud against the hood.
My parents rarely spoke about the internment camp, but I recall my mother crying once when a specific song played on the radio.
I learned to ride a bicycle on a gravel road near our house. I scraped my knee so badly I still have a faint silver scar there.
We had a large cast-iron stove in the kitchen that took forever to heat up in the winter. I would stand next to it in my pajamas shivering.
A neighbor, Mrs. Henderson or maybe Mrs. Higgins, used to give us hard candies wrapped in shiny green paper. They tasted faintly like medicine.
I remember a school play where I was supposed to be a tree, but I tripped on my costume and knocked over the cardboard scenery.
My brother got a terrible fever when he was twelve and had to stay in a dark room. I wasn't allowed to see him for what felt like a month.
I recall catching fireflies in a jar, even though I'm not sure if Oregon even has fireflies. Maybe it was just a dream I had.
My mother tried to teach me origami, but I was too impatient to fold the corners neatly. I ended up making crumpled paper balls instead.
I had a crush on a boy named Richard in the ninth grade. He was the only one who knew how to play the saxophone in the school band.
I went to a drive-in movie with a group of friends in 1960 or '61. I can't remember the film, but I remember eating salty popcorn in the backseat.
My high school graduation dress was pale blue with lace around the collar. My mother stayed up late sewing it, pricking her finger a few times.
I failed my first driving test because I paralleled parked too far from the curb. The instructor, an older man with glasses, sighed really loudly.
There was a diner downtown where we used to get milkshakes after school. They had a jukebox that always seemed to be playing the same three Elvis songs.
I cut my own bangs once when I was fifteen, and it looked absolutely crooked. I had to wear a headband for a month to hide the disaster.

My mother used to send care packages of Oregon cherries to our cousins in Hiroshima, though I think she lost their address sometime in the 1960s. Even now, I get a warm feeling whenever I see a cherry blossom tree, feeling like a little piece of the old country is still with us.
I remember having a huge argument with my father about wanting to stay out late for a dance. He didn't speak to me for two days afterward.
My friend Susan and I tried to bake a pie from scratch, but we forgot to add sugar to the filling. It tasted like sour mud.
I took a typing class in high school and was surprisingly fast at it. I think I could type around sixty words a minute, or maybe it was forty.
A girl named Mary spread a rumor about me cheating on a math test. I was so embarrassed I avoided the cafeteria for a week.
I remember watching a parade in Portland during the Rose Festival. The floats were covered in flowers, and the air smelled overwhelmingly sweet.
I saved up my allowance to buy a record player, but I think I only ever owned about five records. One of them was definitely a Beatles album.
My brother left for college and I got his old bedroom. It felt too big and empty without all his sports trophies on the shelves.
I had a part-time job at a local library organizing books. The quiet rustle of pages always made me feel sleepy.
I sneaked out of the house once to meet friends at a park, but it was so cold we all just went back home after twenty minutes.
I twisted my ankle playing volleyball in gym class. The gym teacher just told me to walk it off, which made it swell up to the size of an apple.
I remember painting a landscape for an art project that ended up looking like green blobs. The teacher was very polite about it, though.
We had a terrible ice storm one winter that knocked out the power for days. We played card games by candlelight until we ran out of things to talk about.
I went on a date with a boy whose name I completely forget, but I remember he spilled soda all over his lap in the movie theater.
My mother gave me a small pearl necklace for my eighteenth birthday. I think it belonged to her sister before the war.
I moved to Eugene for college around 1963 and lived in a terribly drafty dorm room. My roommate was a girl from Idaho who always smelled like peppermint.
I changed my major three times before finally settling on education. I originally wanted to do nursing, but the sight of blood made me dizzy.
I remember participating in a peaceful protest on campus, though I honestly can't remember exactly what we were protesting. It might have been the war.
I met my husband, David, at a coffee shop near the university. He spilled my coffee and insisted on buying me a new one.
We got married in a small chapel in Portland in 1968. It rained all morning, but the sun came out just as we left the church.
My first apartment with David had an avocado-green refrigerator that hummed loudly all night. We had to hit it sometimes to make it stop.
I started teaching second grade at a school in Beaverton. The kids were sweet, but I remember constantly feeling like I was making things up as I went along.
I made a terrible turkey for our first Thanksgiving as a married couple. It was completely raw in the middle, so we ate mashed potatoes instead.
We bought a used car that was a hideous shade of orange. It broke down on a road trip to the coast, leaving us stranded near Tillamook.
I remember hearing about the moon landing while sitting on a worn-out plaid sofa. The television reception was so fuzzy you could barely see the astronauts.
My first daughter, Emily, was born in the middle of a surprising snowstorm. The drive to the hospital felt like sliding on glass.
I struggled terribly with postpartum sadness for a few months. I felt so guilty for not being overjoyed every single second.
We adopted a stray cat that wandered into our yard. We named him Whiskers, which was a terribly unoriginal name, but he didn't seem to mind.
I remember going to a fondue party at a neighbor's house in the early seventies. Someone dropped a piece of bread in the cheese, and it was a huge deal for some reason.
I bought a sewing machine and tried to make clothes for Emily. The seams were always a bit crooked, but she was too little to care.
David got a promotion at the bank and we celebrated by going to a fancy steakhouse. I ordered lobster, but I remember it tasted like rubber.
I took a pottery class at the community center and made a lopsided mug. I kept pens in it on my desk for over thirty years.
We went camping at Crater Lake, and it was the coldest I have ever been in August. We ended up sleeping in the car with the heater on.
I cut my hair into a very short bob because it was the style, but my mother said it made my face look too round.
I had a miscarriage before my second child was born. It was a very dark time that David and I almost never talked about.
My son, Michael, arrived two weeks late and weighed almost nine pounds. The delivery was exhausting, and I slept for a whole day afterward.
I started a small garden in our backyard, mainly growing tomatoes and zucchini. The slugs always seemed to get to the strawberries before I did.
I remember watching the Watergate hearings on television while folding laundry. The whole thing seemed so complicated and far away from our lives in Oregon.
David and I had a huge fight over money when we were saving for a house. I threw a dish towel at him and locked myself in the bathroom.
I chaperoned a field trip to the zoo and lost a child for about ten terrifying minutes. He had wandered off to look at the flamingos.
We finally bought a house in a quiet suburban neighborhood. The wallpaper in the living room had a terrible floral pattern that took weeks to scrape off.
I joined a neighborhood book club, but I rarely finished the books on time. I mostly went for the wine and the gossip.
My parents came to visit the new house and my father spent the whole weekend fixing the plumbing. He refused to let us call a professional.
I threw a surprise birthday party for David when he turned thirty. He absolutely hated the surprise, and we never did it again.
Emily broke her arm falling off the monkey bars in first grade. I remember crying more than she did in the emergency room.
I went back to teaching part-time when Michael started kindergarten. I think it was around 1978, but the years blur together now.
We took a family road trip to Disneyland in the summer heat. The kids fought in the back seat the entire way down Interstate 5.
I remember wearing high-waisted flared jeans that I thought looked so fashionable. Looking back at photos, I can't believe I wore them in public.
Mt. St. Helens erupted, and the sky turned completely gray. There was a fine layer of ash on my car for weeks, no matter how often I washed it.
I took up jogging for a few months in the eighties. I gave it up after I tripped on a sidewalk crack and bruised my ribs.
Emily went through a phase where she dyed her hair pitch black. I hated it, but I bit my tongue and didn't say a word.
I got a jury duty summons and ended up serving on a petty theft trial. The defendant looked so young and scared, it broke my heart.
David bought a ridiculous oversized armchair that took up half the living room. It was ugly, but he fell asleep in it every Sunday watching football.
We hosted a foreign exchange student from Japan for a semester. My Japanese was so rusty I was embarrassed, so we spoke mostly English.
I remember the Challenger explosion clearly. I was in the teachers' lounge, and someone brought in a small television on a rolling cart.
Michael got cut from the varsity basketball team and locked himself in his room. I left a plate of cookies outside his door, but he didn't eat them.
I won a raffle at a church bazaar and brought home a massive smoked ham. We ate ham sandwiches for what felt like two straight weeks.
My mother passed away in 1988 after a short illness. I still remember the smell of the lilies at her funeral, overpowering and sickly sweet.
I took over her recipe box, but her handwriting was so faint I had to guess the measurements. Most of my attempts didn't taste right.
I had a brief, irrational fear of flying after watching a news report about a plane crash. I insisted we take the train to Seattle for my niece's wedding.
Emily moved out to go to college in California. The house felt instantly quiet, and I missed the sound of her terrible music playing upstairs.
I decided to repaint the kitchen a bright, cheerful yellow. Halfway through, I realized it looked like mustard, but I was too stubborn to change it.
David had a mild heart attack in his early fifties. Waiting in the hospital corridor was the longest, most terrifying night of my life.
After his recovery, we completely changed our diet. We ate so much steamed broccoli that I still can't stand the sight of it.
I started volunteering at the local library, reading stories to toddlers. Their chaotic energy was exactly what I needed at that time.
Michael brought home a girlfriend who was a strict vegan. I was so confused about what to cook that I think I just made plain rice and salad.
We got a golden retriever puppy named Daisy. She destroyed three pairs of my best shoes before she finally learned to chew on her toys.
I remember going to a concert with a friend to see some pop singer, maybe Neil Diamond. We felt terribly out of place among the younger crowds.
I had to get reading glasses around the time I turned forty-five. I bought a pair with bright red frames, hoping they made me look artistic.
I retired from teaching in my late fifties because the administration kept changing the curriculum. I was tired of learning new ways to teach the same math.
We went to Hawaii for our twenty-fifth anniversary. I got a terrible sunburn on the first day and spent the rest of the trip hiding under a large hat.
I tried to learn how to use a personal computer when they first became popular. The mouse felt awkward in my hand, and I kept double-clicking everything.
I found a box of old love letters David sent me before we were married. Reading them made me blush, even after all those years together.
Emily got married in a beautiful outdoor ceremony. It was terribly windy, and my hat kept threatening to blow away during the vows.
I started experiencing terrible hot flashes during menopause. I would throw the bedroom windows wide open in the middle of winter, much to David's dismay.
I became a grandmother in 1998 when Emily had her first son. Holding him felt surprisingly natural, like my body remembered the weight of a baby.
We decided to downsize and sell the house we raised the kids in. Packing up thirty years of memories into cardboard boxes was exhausting and sad.
We moved to a smaller ranch-style house closer to town. The garden was tiny, but it was much easier for my knees to manage.
David finally retired, and suddenly he was home all day. We had to establish a schedule just so we wouldn't drive each other crazy.
I joined a water aerobics class with some ladies from the neighborhood. We mostly bobbed around in the shallow end and complained about our joints.
I remember the turn of the millennium vividly. We stayed up until midnight drinking cheap champagne, waiting for the power grid to collapse.
Michael got divorced in his thirties, and he moved back in with us for a few months. Seeing him so defeated was harder than I can put into words.
I discovered a passion for baking bread in my sixties. The house always smelled of yeast, though half the time my sourdough was completely flat.
I watched the events of September 11th on the news in absolute shock. I remember calling both my children just to hear their voices.
David and I took a cruise to Alaska, but it rained almost the entire time. We saw a glacier through the fog, looking like a giant block of dirty ice.
I lost my favorite pearl earring down the bathroom sink. David took the plumbing apart trying to find it, but it was just gone.
I got a digital camera and took hundreds of blurry photos of my grandchildren. I never figured out how to get them off the camera and onto a computer.
My brother Ken passed away from a stroke suddenly. I remember feeling a profound, heavy silence in the weeks after the funeral.
I tried going to a yoga class, but getting up off the floor was too difficult. I ended up just doing the breathing exercises from a chair.
We had a neighbor who played loud jazz music every Sunday morning. I found it annoying at first, but eventually I started humming along while I made coffee.
I bought an iPad to video call my daughter, but I always accidentally muted myself. Half of our conversations were just her saying she couldn't hear me.
I started having trouble remembering names of actors in movies. I would just refer to them by roles they played decades ago, which confused everyone.
David was diagnosed with early-stage dementia when he was seventy-two. Hearing the doctor say the words felt like the floor dropping out from under me.
I took over managing the finances, which David had always done. Balancing the checkbook gave me headaches, but I eventually got the hang of it.
We got a small indoor cat named Luna after Daisy the dog passed away. Luna was aloof and mostly ignored us, which was actually quite peaceful.
I remember watching Barack Obama's inauguration on TV. It felt like a momentous occasion, even though my own political views had grown a bit cynical.
I fell on an icy sidewalk and broke my wrist. Wearing a cast while trying to cook was a frustrating nightmare that resulted in a lot of frozen dinners.
I stopped coloring my hair and let it go completely white. It was liberating to stop worrying about the gray roots showing every three weeks.
I organized a small reunion for my high school graduating class. Only about twenty people showed up, and we all spent the afternoon squinting at name tags.
I had a surprisingly deep conversation with a stranger on a bus about the changing seasons. I never got her name, but I still think about her sometimes.
David's memory started to slip more rapidly. He asked me when we were going to pick up the kids from school, and they were already in their forties.

I never learned to speak much Japanese besides a few greetings, but I still make the most wonderful ozoni soup every New Year's Day. It is the one time of year my grandchildren feel connected to our family's roots, even if I always forget the exact name of the special mochi we buy.
I hired a part-time caregiver to help with David so I could just go to the grocery store. I felt guilty about it every single time I left the house.
I took up knitting again to keep my hands busy in the evenings. I made an endless number of ugly scarves that the grandchildren politely accepted.
A severe heatwave hit Oregon, and we didn't have air conditioning. We sat in front of a box fan with wet towels around our necks for three days.
I found an old rusted key in the bottom of a drawer and had no idea what it unlocked. I threw it away, but worried for a week that I would need it.
David passed away peacefully in his sleep five years ago. The house felt impossibly large and quiet after the hospice nurses finally took away the bed.
I started going to a grief support group at the community center. I mostly sat in the back and listened, too tired to share my own story.

During the pandemic, strangers started yelling terrible things at anyone who looked Asian at the grocery store, so the ladies at my community center started carpooling together to stay safe. We had Chinese, Korean, and Filipino friends in the car, and it felt like we were all in the exact same boat regardless of where our parents came from.
Emily convinced me to get a smartphone, but it feels too delicate in my hands. I only use it to check the weather and look at photos of the great-grandkids.
I developed a habit of eating breakfast at dinner time just because I can. There's something very satisfying about scrambled eggs at six in the evening.
I stopped driving at night because the headlights from oncoming cars blind me. I honestly don't miss the stress of the dark, rainy roads anyway.
I watch a lot of historical documentaries on public television now. The narrator's voice usually lulls me to sleep before the program is even half over.
A young couple moved in next door and brought me a plate of overly sweet cookies. It was a nice gesture, even though I threw most of them in the garbage.
I have a slight tremor in my left hand that bothers me when I try to pour tea. The doctor says it's just age, which seems to be the answer for everything lately.
I recently found a box of old photographs and realized I couldn't identify half the people in them. It felt strange to hold pieces of a past that has entirely vanished.
My grandson taught me how to order groceries online during the pandemic. It felt like magic, but I missed picking out my own apples.
I started keeping a journal, but I usually just write down what the weather was like. It seems silly to record my day when I rarely leave the house.
I have a favorite mug that has a small chip on the rim. I instinctively know exactly where to place my lips to avoid the sharp edge.
I woke up the other night convinced I heard the dog barking, but we haven't had a dog in years. The silence that followed was heavy and cold.
I received a jury summons in the mail recently and just threw it away. I figure at eighty, they can manage the justice system without my help.
I burned a pot of rice because I sat down to read a magazine and completely forgot about the stove. The smell of scorched grains lingered in the kitchen for a week.
I tried a new brand of tea that Emily swore by, but it tasted like dried grass and dirt. I immediately went back to my usual black tea.
The cherry trees in the neighborhood bloomed early this year, dropping pink petals all over my driveway. I swept them up, but the wind just blew more down.
I had a dream about my mother where she looked exactly as she did when I was a child. When I woke up, I felt a strange ache in my chest for the rest of the day.

My uncle used to bring over these crinkled Japanese newspapers from Seattle, though I usually just looked at the pictures while my dad read the news about Tokyo. Nowadays, my daughter just shows me little video clips about Japan on her phone, maybe from Facebook or some other website.
The mail carrier always waves at me when I check the box in the morning. He's a friendly young man, though I can never remember his name.
I accidentally washed a red napkin with my white laundry, and now my favorite sweater has a pink tint. I still wear it around the house anyway.
I found myself humming a tune the other day and realized it was a commercial jingle from the seventies. I have no idea why it suddenly popped into my head.
I went to the pharmacy and the automated blood pressure machine squeezed my arm much too tightly. I ended up with a small bruise that lasted for days.
My great-granddaughter drew a picture for me that supposedly looks like a cat. I put it on the fridge, even though it mostly looks like a purple squiggle.
I sometimes catch a glimpse of myself in the hallway mirror and am surprised by the old woman looking back. It takes a second to reconcile that face with how I feel inside.
I bought a new pair of walking shoes that feel wonderfully supportive. I mostly just wear them to go to the mailbox and back.
I accidentally left the freezer door slightly ajar overnight. Everything was covered in a thick layer of frost, and I had to throw away three pints of ice cream.
A telemarketer called me and I talked to him for five minutes about the weather before he finally hung up. I think he was more confused than I was.
I watched the rain against the window all afternoon yesterday. It’s a comforting sound, like millions of tiny fingers tapping on the glass.
I have a small ache in my lower back that acts up right before it rains. I trust it more than the meteorologists on the local news.
I tried to sew a button back onto a coat, but threading the needle took me nearly ten minutes. My eyes just can't focus on things that small anymore.
I ordered a book from the library and forgot what it was about by the time it arrived. I returned it a week later without even opening the cover.
I occasionally smell a specific brand of aftershave at the grocery store that reminds me of David. I usually have to stop walking for a moment to catch my breath.
I bought a lovely fern for the living room, but I keep forgetting to water it. The edges of the leaves are already turning a crispy brown.
I listened to a radio program about black holes and space exploration. It made me feel incredibly small, but in a very peaceful, quiet sort of way.
I spilled a glass of water on the rug and just put a towel over it instead of scrubbing. Some things just aren't worth the immediate hassle anymore.
I found a twenty-dollar bill tucked inside the pocket of my winter coat from last year. It felt like a tiny, ridiculous victory.
I had a terrible craving for a specific candy bar they stopped making decades ago. I spent an hour trying to remember the name of it, but I never did.
The digital clock on the microwave has been blinking the wrong time for three months. I just look at the clock on the wall instead of fixing it.
I saw a flock of geese flying south in a perfect V-formation. It made me stop and watch until they disappeared behind the neighbor's roof.
I keep a flashlight by my bed in case the power goes out, though I haven't checked the batteries in years. It’s more of a comfort object at this point.
My joints ache terribly when the temperature drops below freezing. I basically spend the entire month of January wrapped in a thick wool blanket.
I bought a crossword puzzle book, but the clues feel much harder than they used to be. I usually give up after filling in three or four words.
I found a stash of old greeting cards in the hall closet, most of them from people who have already passed away. I put them right back in the box without reading them.
I tried eating a piece of very spicy curry that my grandson brought over. It made my eyes water terribly, and I had to drink a whole glass of milk.
A stray cat started sleeping on my porch chair every afternoon. I leave a little bowl of dry food out, but I pretend I don't know who is eating it.
I remember seeing a beautiful rainbow over the Columbia River when I was driving back from a dentist appointment. The colors seemed almost artificially bright.
I accidentally dropped a glass jar of pickles in the grocery store aisle. It shattered everywhere, and I felt terribly guilty while the teenager mopped it up.
I bought a very expensive moisturizing cream that smelled like roses. It made my skin break out in a rash, so I ended up using it as an expensive hand lotion.
I watched a squirrel systematically steal every single tomato from my patio plant. He was so bold about it I didn't even try to chase him away.
I noticed that the old diner downtown where I used to get coffee has been turned into a very loud, modern clothing store. The whole street looks unrecognizable now.
I had a bit of a scare when my heart started racing for no reason while I was watching TV. It calmed down after a few minutes, but it left me feeling very fragile.
Emily bought me an automatic vacuum cleaner that rolls around the floor by itself. It mostly just bumps into the furniture and gets stuck on the rugs.
I ate a slice of peach pie that tasted exactly like the ones my grandmother used to make. I almost went back to the bakery to buy the whole pie.
I left my umbrella on the bus during a terrible downpour and had to walk three blocks in the rain. I was completely soaked and freezing by the time I unlocked the front door.

We always celebrated the Fourth of July by bringing hot dogs, potato salad, and a big platter of onigiri to the local Asian community picnic. Being a proud American simply meant eating rice alongside my hamburgers while watching the fireworks over the Willamette River with folks from all different backgrounds.

participants.persona: Kevin is a 27-year-old second-generation Chinese American man, born in the U.S. and living in Illinois.
participants.name: Kevin

memories.content: I remember my dad teaching me to ride a bike at some park in Naperville, or maybe it was Aurora. I think I scraped my knee, but I just remember him looking really proud.

I remember going to a Lunar New Year banquet at some restaurant in Chinatown back in 2014, or maybe 2015, where everyone was passing around red envelopes and speaking loudly in Taishanese. Sitting there surrounded by my extended family, I actively reflected on how those specific cultural roots in Guangdong have completely shaped my internal sense of who I am today.

We used to go to this Chinese supermarket on weekends, probably in Westmont, where the aisles always smelled like dried fish and star anise. I hated it then, but now I strangely miss that smell because it reminds me of being little.
My mom made me play piano starting around first grade, maybe second. I do not remember my teacher's name, just that she had a really loud metronome that clicked unevenly.
I think I broke my arm falling off a swing set in maybe 2003 or 2004. The cast was blue, or maybe green, and I remember the itchy feeling more than the actual pain.

There was a kid in my elementary school named Brian or Ryan who told me my lunch looked like worms. I threw away my mom's fried rice for almost a year after that, which I feel incredibly guilty about now.
We drove to Starved Rock once when I was like eight, and I am pretty sure it rained the whole time. My dad got mad at the traffic on I-80 on the way back.
I remember watching some cartoon about robots, maybe Gundam, every weekday afternoon. I could not understand the plot, but I was obsessed with the toy commercials.

My grandma visited from China when I was in maybe third grade, and she brought me this wooden puzzle I never figured out. She spoke to me in Mandarin, and I just nodded because my vocabulary was so terrible.
I think my first dog was a golden retriever mix we got from a shelter in roughly 2005. We called him Buster, and he used to chew on the baseboards in the kitchen.

I used to steal my older cousin's Pokemon cards when he was not looking, which was definitely a terrible thing to do. I justify it now by thinking he never played with them anyway, but it was just pure childhood selfishness.

There was a massive blizzard sometime around 2008 where we got out of school for almost a week. I remember building a snow fort that felt huge, though it was probably just a small mound in the driveway.
I remember eating at a buffet, maybe Old Country Buffet, and eating nothing but soft serve ice cream and french fries. My parents just let me do it, which surprises me now.
My mom used to cut my hair in the kitchen using these incredibly dull scissors. I always ended up with a bowl cut that I was so embarrassed by, but I never told her to stop.
I took swimming lessons at the local YMCA, and the water was always freezing cold. The instructor was a high school guy who mostly just let us splash around in the shallow end.
I think we went to Disney World when I was six or seven, but I only remember the hotel pool. There was a slide shaped like a dragon or a snake that I went down a hundred times.
I used to have nightmares about a shadow figure in my closet when I was little. I was so terrified I would hide under the covers until morning.
My dad used to watch basketball on Sunday afternoons, usually the Bulls, but I barely paid attention. I just liked the sound of the squeaking shoes on the court while I played on the carpet.

I remember my parents fighting in the car once on the way to a family friend's house in Schaumburg. I do not know what it was about, but the heavy silence for the rest of the drive made my stomach hurt.
We had a garage sale around 2006, and I sold my old tricycle for like two dollars. I felt like a millionaire holding those crumpled bills.
I remember trying to catch fireflies in a jar during the summer, probably in our backyard. Most of them died by morning, which made me really sad.
I started wearing glasses in middle school, and the frames were these horrible thick black plastic things. I picked them out myself, but they kept sliding down my nose.
There was a science fair project I did in maybe seventh grade about volcanoes. I think I used too much baking soda and made a massive mess on the kitchen counter.

I remember sneaking out of the house once to meet up with a girl, maybe her name was Chloe, but we just sat on a curb and did not even talk. The fear of getting caught was way more intense than any actual romantic feeling.
My parents sent me to SAT prep classes way too early, probably around eighth grade. I spent the whole time drawing in the margins of the Princeton Review book.
We had a substitute teacher in history class who pronounced my last name horribly wrong every single day. I never corrected him because I hated drawing attention to myself.
I remember buying my first video game console, an Xbox 360, with money saved from red envelopes. I played Halo 3 until my eyes burned.
I tried to learn the guitar when I was 14, but I quit after maybe two months. I still have the guitar sitting in my closet gathering dust.
There was a pizza place near our house where my friends and I would go after school on Fridays. I think a slice was only two bucks, and it was always burnt on the bottom.

I remember getting a C on a math test in high school and hiding it from my mom for weeks. The anxiety of her finding out was absolutely paralyzing, probably because I tied my worth so closely to my grades.
We went to Chinatown in Chicago for Chinese New Year, and it was so crowded I almost lost my family. I remember the loud popping of firecrackers echoing off the brick buildings.
I had a huge crush on a girl in my biology class sophomore year. I think I tried to impress her by dissecting the frog really fast, which was incredibly stupid.
My first job was at a bubble tea shop, probably when I was 16. I smelled like tapioca pearls and burnt sugar for a solid two years.
I remember driving on the highway for the first time during driver's ed, gripping the steering wheel so hard my knuckles went white. The instructor, Mr. Davis or something, was surprisingly calm.
I went to a high school dance, maybe homecoming, and spilled punch down my borrowed suit tie. I spent half the night hiding in the bathroom trying to wash it out.
I realize now that I pushed my high school friends away during senior year because I was terrified of going to college. It was easier to be distant than to deal with the pain of leaving them.

When I visited Guangzhou around 2008 for my grandfather's birthday, I felt completely lost because I couldn't understand the local street slang or the rapid-fire TV broadcasts. Everyone expected me to know the customs at the ancestral temple, but the stark cultural distance just left me feeling totally out of place.
My dad bought a used Honda Civic for me to drive, and the AC was completely broken. Driving around in the humid Illinois summer felt like being in a sauna.
I remember watching the Olympics on TV with my grandpa, maybe the 2008 Beijing ones. He kept cheering for the Chinese athletes, and I felt this weird, confusing mix of pride and American guilt.
We had to read The Great Gatsby in English class, and I totally just used SparkNotes for the essays. I still got a B-plus, which I was pretty smug about.
I think I chipped my front tooth playing basketball in the driveway with my neighbor. I cannot even remember the neighbor's name, but the dentist bill made my parents furious.

Every Sunday morning, my mom would spend hours making zongzi or rolling out wrapper dough for jiaozi while some random CCTV drama played loudly in the background. Even though I can barely speak the language now, the sharp smell of five-spice and black vinegar always pulls me right back to feeling authentically Chinese.
I remember attending a summer camp in Michigan where we slept in these drafty wooden cabins. I got an awful case of poison ivy on my ankle that lasted all of July.

I got rejected from my top choice college, maybe Northwestern, and I cried in my car for an hour. Looking back, I think I just wanted the prestige to validate my parents' sacrifices, not because I actually wanted to go there.

I moved into a dorm at UIUC, and my roommate was this guy from rural Illinois who had never met an Asian person before. He asked a lot of weird questions, but we ended up playing a ton of Smash Bros anyway.

I still get a heavy knot in my stomach when I think about my grandmother's funeral a few years ago, knowing I couldn't even give a proper eulogy in Cantonese. It hurts deeply that my broken vocabulary meant I never got to ask her about her journey from Hong Kong before she passed away.
I remember eating at the dining hall and making these terrible waffle-maker paninis. They always tasted faintly of blueberry batter, no matter what I put in them.
I took a computer science class my freshman year and failed the first midterm spectacularly. I dropped the class the next day because I did not understand anything.
There was a coffee shop on campus where I would study until 2 AM, drinking cheap drip coffee. The chairs were super uncomfortable, but I felt so collegiate sitting there with my laptop.
I remember walking across the Quad during a polar vortex, probably in 2018. The wind was so cold it felt like knives on my face, and my eyelashes literally froze together.
I went to a frat party once and someone spilled beer all over my shoes. I think they were new Vans, and they smelled like stale alcohol for months.
I dated a girl named Sarah or Samantha for a few months sophomore year. It fizzled out because we both just stopped texting each other, which says a lot about how passive I am in relationships.
My parents came to visit for Dad's Weekend, and we went to a football game where Illinois lost terribly. They looked so out of place in the sea of orange tailgaters, but they smiled the whole time.
I remember pulling an all-nighter for a history paper and hallucinating that my desk lamp was humming a pop song. I got a decent grade, but my sleep schedule was ruined for a week.

I joined a cultural club, maybe the Chinese Student Association, but I felt like I was not Asian enough for them. It is a lonely feeling when you do not fit in with the people who are supposed to be your community.
I lost my student ID during syllabus week and had to pay twenty bucks for a new one. I think I found the old one in my laundry three months later.
There was a sandwich place on Green Street that I went to religiously on Tuesdays. I always got the turkey club, and the bread scratched the roof of my mouth.
I remember giving a presentation in a marketing class and completely blanking on my slide. I just babbled for two minutes, and no one seemed to notice or care.
I took a bus, maybe Peoria Charter, back to the Chicago suburbs for Thanksgiving, and the Wi-Fi never worked. I stared out the window at the cornfields for three hours in silence.
I think I tried to bleach my hair my junior year, but it turned out this awful brassy orange color. I wore a beanie for weeks until I finally dyed it back to black.
My junior year apartment had a heating system that banged loudly every time it turned on. I got so used to it that I actually could not sleep in total silence when I went home for winter break.
I adopted a cactus that I named Spike, and I somehow managed to overwater it until it rotted. I ended up throwing it down the trash chute.

I remember having a panic attack in the library basement during finals week because I thought I was going to fail out. I see now that my perfectionism was a defense mechanism against feeling inadequate.
I went to an indie rock concert at a small venue in Chicago, maybe Lincoln Hall, during the summer. The music was deafening, but the energy in the room was electric.
I graduated in roughly 2019, and the ceremony was incredibly long and boring. I just remember sweating under the polyester gown while waiting for my name to be mispronounced.
My first real job interview was over Zoom, and I wore a suit jacket with pajama pants. I was terrified they would ask me to stand up for some reason.
I moved to an apartment in the city, maybe near Logan Square, and the rent took up most of my paycheck. Eating ramen for dinner felt a lot less fun when I was not a student anymore.
