I remember the eerie silence in Chicago during the early pandemic days in 2020. I walked down the middle of a major street and did not see a single car, which felt like an apocalypse movie.
I started baking sourdough bread like everyone else, but my starter, which I think I named Dough-seph, died after a week. It smelled like acetone, so I dumped it in the trash.
My parents kept calling me to make sure I was wearing a mask, even when I was not leaving the apartment. Their anxiety used to annoy me, but now I recognize it was just their way of showing love.
I went on a Hinge date at a park in 2021, and we just awkwardly walked around in circles holding coffees. We had absolutely zero chemistry, and the silence was painful.
I bought a used couch on Facebook Marketplace that ended up smelling faintly of cat pee. I tried everything to clean it, but eventually, I just got used to the smell.
I remember getting a flat tire on I-90 during rush hour and having to change it on the shoulder. Cars were flying by at 70 miles an hour, and I was sweating profusely.

I went to a friend's wedding last year, maybe in October, and realized I was the only single guy at my table. It made me feel like I was falling behind in some invisible race I did not even know I was running.
I started going to the gym regularly a few months ago, but I still feel totally clueless around the free weights. I usually just use the machines because they have instructions printed on them.
I remember discovering this incredible taco place near my apartment that looks like a total dive. The al pastor tacos are amazing, and I go there probably twice a week.
I had to put my cat down last year because of kidney failure, and it absolutely broke me. I still expect to hear his paws on the hardwood floor when I wake up in the morning.
I realized recently that I use sarcasm as a shield whenever someone tries to get emotionally close to me. It is a bad habit I picked up in high school that I really need to unlearn.
I visited my parents a few weeks ago, and my dad looked so much older than I remembered. It hit me suddenly that they are aging, and I felt this sharp, terrifying wave of preemptive grief.
I took a trip to Seattle for work and it rained the entire three days I was there. I remember eating some really expensive seafood that just tasted like salt.
I bought a bunch of houseplants thinking I could create an indoor jungle. Half of them are already brown and crispy, which is pretty typical for me.
I started therapy a few months ago, and the first session was just me crying uncontrollably. Admitting that I could not handle everything on my own was the hardest part of the process.
I remember finding a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk outside a grocery store. I looked around to see if anyone dropped it, then quickly shoved it in my pocket.
I tried to cook a traditional Chinese dish for my parents, I think it was Mapo Tofu. It was way too spicy, but they ate the whole thing anyway without complaining.
I have a habit of biting the inside of my cheek when I am stressed out at work. It is subtle, but I think my coworkers probably notice me wincing randomly.
I went to a music festival, maybe Lollapalooza, and got completely separated from my group within ten minutes. I spent the whole day wandering around alone eating expensive food.
I remember getting a terrible sunburn at Oak Street Beach because I fell asleep on my towel. My back peeled for a week, and taking a shower was agonizing.
I have this memory of my mom teaching me how to fold dumplings at the kitchen table. My dumplings always looked lopsided, but she would just laugh and boil them anyway.
I bought a really expensive jacket online that did not fit me at all. I was too lazy to return it, so it has just been sitting in my closet for two years.
I remember watching a documentary about deep sea creatures late at night and feeling an existential dread about how huge the ocean is. It makes my everyday problems seem incredibly insignificant.
I once accidentally liked an Instagram picture of my ex-girlfriend from like three years ago. I threw my phone across the room in sheer panic.
I took a weekend trip to Galena with some friends, and we rented an Airbnb that was definitely haunted. The floorboards creaked all night, and none of us got any sleep.
I remember trying to build an Ikea dresser and putting a key piece in backwards. I had to dismantle the whole thing, which took another three hours.
Sometimes I look in the mirror and see exactly my grandfather's face looking back at me. It is a surreal reminder of how much of me is just a continuation of the people who came before.
I got a parking ticket in downtown Chicago because I did not see the street sweeping sign. It was like seventy-five dollars, and it ruined my entire week.
I remember drinking way too much at a New Year's Eve party and throwing up in an alley. I felt so pathetic and ashamed the next morning, vowing never to drink tequila again.
I have a scar on my thumb from when I tried to carve a pumpkin with a regular kitchen knife. I think I was around twelve, and I bled all over the newspaper on the floor.
I tried going vegetarian for a month, mostly to impress a girl I was seeing. I gave up after two weeks because I missed fried chicken too much.

I remember the smell of my grandpa's house, a mix of old newspapers, mothballs, and herbal medicine. I used to hate going there, but I would give anything to sit in that dusty living room one more time.
I went to a White Sox game a few years ago, and we had the cheapest seats possible. We spent most of the time eating overpriced hot dogs and talking instead of watching the game.
I bought a lottery ticket once on my 18th birthday just because I could. I won exactly two dollars, which felt perfectly anticlimactic.
I remember getting into a massive fight with my dad over my major in college. I yelled some things I really regret, and the silence in the house afterward was suffocating.
I used to collect shiny rocks I found in the landscaping around my neighborhood when I was a kid. I thought they were valuable gems, but they were just polished river stones.
I realize that I often agree with whatever people say in conversations just to avoid conflict. It makes me wonder if anyone actually knows what my real opinions are, or if I even have any.
I tried to learn how to skateboard when I was a teenager, and I fell so hard I bruised my tailbone. I limped around for a week trying to pretend nothing happened.
I remember buying a cheap bottle of wine for a house party and trying to open it by pushing the cork in with a pen. It sprayed red wine all over my white shirt.
My friends and I drove up to Wisconsin to buy fireworks for the Fourth of July one year. We set them off in an empty field, and it felt wonderfully rebellious.
I took a pottery class recently to try and find a new hobby. Everything I made looked like a lopsided ashtray, but squishing the clay was surprisingly therapeutic.
I remember watching a thunderstorm roll in over Lake Michigan from a rooftop bar. The contrast between the dark purple clouds and the bright city lights was incredible.
I had this phase where I only wore black t-shirts and jeans because I thought it made me look mysterious. Looking back, I just looked like a generic cartoon character who never changes clothes.
I got food poisoning from a food truck outside a concert venue and spent the next 24 hours huddled around my toilet. It was pure misery.
I remember my mom packing me a thermos of hot soup for lunch in middle school. The lid was always screwed on so tight that I had to ask the lunch lady for help to open it.
I binge-watched an entire season of some crime show on Netflix in one Sunday. I had a pounding headache by the evening from staring at the screen for so long.
I once gave a fake number to a guy who was being too aggressive at a bar. I felt a surge of panic when he tried to call it right in front of me, so I just walked away really fast.
I remember the power going out during a summer storm and my family lighting these old, half-melted candles. We played cards by candlelight, and nobody argued for once.
I bought a really nice journal with the intention of writing down my thoughts every day. I made it to day four before I completely abandoned it on my nightstand.
I had a brief obsession with making pour-over coffee using expensive beans. Eventually, I realized I could not even taste the difference and went back to my cheap drip machine.

I recognize that my intense fear of failure probably stems from wanting to justify my parents' immigration struggles. It is a heavy burden to carry, feeling like my success is the return on their investment.
I went apple picking at some orchard in northern Illinois, and I ate so many apples I felt sick. I ended up throwing most of the bag away because they went bad in my fridge.
I remember sitting in the waiting room of a dentist's office reading a magazine from three years prior. The background music was a weird instrumental version of a pop song.
I tried to fix a leaky faucet in my apartment by watching a YouTube tutorial. I ended up spraying water all over the ceiling and had to call maintenance anyway.
I had a really vivid dream where my teeth were falling out, and I woke up in a cold sweat. I spent five minutes checking my mouth in the bathroom mirror just to be sure.
I remember finding an old photo album of my parents when they were in their twenties. They looked so young and carefree, which was weird to process.
I tend to hoard cardboard boxes because I always think I might need them for moving. It is ridiculous, but it gives me a weird sense of security having them stacked in my closet.
I went to the Shedd Aquarium when I was a kid and was absolutely terrified of the beluga whales. They looked like giant ghosts pressing their faces against the glass.
I remember eating a hot dog at Portillo's and dropping half of it on my lap in the car. The grease stain on my jeans never completely washed out.
I went to a midnight premiere for a superhero movie, maybe an Avengers one, and the crowd went absolutely crazy. I was exhausted at work the next day, but it was worth it.
I have a bad habit of picking at the skin around my fingernails when I am watching TV. Sometimes I do it until they bleed, which I know is a terrible nervous tic.
I remember my dad trying to build a patio in our backyard over a summer. He mostly just cursed at the bricks and wiped sweat off his forehead with a dirty towel.
I went to a corn maze with a group of friends in high school and we got genuinely lost. We ended up just walking in a straight line through the stalks until we hit the parking lot.
I see how I unconsciously mimic my older brother's mannerisms when I am trying to seem confident. It is like I do not know how to be assertive without borrowing someone else's personality.
I remember ordering a very complicated drink at Starbucks just to see what it tasted like. It was overly sweet and cost like eight dollars, so I never did it again.
I used to have a favorite hoodie that was faded black and covered in lint. I lost it on a bus somewhere, and I still miss how perfectly broken-in it felt.
I went ice skating at Millennium Park in the winter and fell flat on my back within the first five minutes. A tourist took a picture of me on the ground.
I remember getting a terrible haircut right before school picture day in fifth grade. I looked like a mushroom, and my mom hung the picture in the hallway for years.
I took a road trip down Route 66 for a few days, and the scenery was mostly just flat fields and old gas stations. It was peaceful, but incredibly monotonous.
I used to sneak downstairs to play computer games after my parents went to sleep. The dial-up modem sound was so loud I had to cover the speaker with pillows.
I remember trying to learn how to juggle using rolled-up socks in my bedroom. I never got past three throws before dropping them all.
I went to a fancy steakhouse for a work dinner and accidentally used the wrong fork for my salad. I was panicked the whole meal that my boss was judging me.

I sometimes wonder if I would be a completely different person if I had grown up in a neighborhood with more Asian kids. I feel like my identity was shaped heavily by the friction of being an outsider.
I remember getting a paper cut on my tongue from licking an envelope for a college application. It stung for days every time I drank orange juice.
I bought a cheap pair of sunglasses at a gas station that I ended up wearing for three years. They finally snapped in half when I sat on them in my car.
I went to a Halloween party dressed as a generic zombie with fake blood from the dollar store. The blood dyed my neck pink for two days afterwards.
I remember trying to grow a beard during my senior year of college. It came in so patchy and thin that my friends mercilessly roasted me until I shaved it off.
I remember the squeaky sound my winter boots made on the linoleum floors of my elementary school. We always had to line them up in the hallway outside the classroom.
I ordered takeout from a Thai place last week and asked for it to be extra spicy. I was sweating through my shirt by the third bite, but I could not stop eating it.
I remember taking the L train during rush hour and being packed in so tightly I did not even have to hold onto a rail. It smelled heavily of wet wool and cheap cologne.
I bought a used record player at a thrift store but never bought any vinyl records for it. It just sits on my bookshelf gathering dust as a decoration.
I remember my dad trying to teach me how to tie a tie for a middle school band concert. He stood behind me in the mirror and got frustrated when I could not follow his hands.
I went to a friend's barbecue by the lake, and the seagulls kept swooping down to steal our potato chips. One actually managed to snatch a hot dog right off the grill.
I remember playing a generic racing game at an arcade and spending all my tokens trying to beat the high score. I did not even come close, but I loved the rumbling seat.
I tried to build a snowman in the front yard with packing snow, but it ended up looking like a lumpy dirt monster. The snow had too much mud mixed into it.
I remember having to give a toast at my cousin's wedding, and I spoke way too fast into the microphone. A few people politely chuckled, but mostly it was just awkward silence.

Joining the Asian American Students Association during my sophomore year at UIUC finally gave me a social space where I didn't have to choose between being Chinese and being a regular Midwest kid. Sharing dorm food with a mix of Korean, Vietnamese, and Chinese peers acted as an everyday bridge that connected our distinct ethnic backgrounds with our American lives.
I bought a giant jar of protein powder that tasted exactly like chalk mixed with fake chocolate. I forced myself to drink it for a month because it was so expensive.
I remember watching my mom haggle with a vendor at a flea market over a cheap lamp. She argued for ten minutes just to save three dollars, and she looked so triumphant.
I found an old pair of wired earbuds in my backpack that were tangled into an impossible knot. I spent half an hour picking at them on the bus ride to work.
I remember eating an entire box of dry cereal while sitting on the couch watching cartoons on a Saturday morning. The roof of my mouth was completely raw afterwards.
I went to a botanical garden during the winter to see a holiday light show. My toes went completely numb, but the glowing trees reflected beautifully in the ponds.
I remember trying to carry four bags of groceries up the stairs to my apartment in one trip. The handle on a paper bag ripped, and a jar of marinara sauce shattered on the concrete.
I sat through a three-hour training module at work about cybersecurity that consisted entirely of cheesy animated videos. I just clicked through the slides while looking at my phone.
I remember catching a foul ball at a minor league baseball game when I was a kid. I kept it on my nightstand for years until the leather started to peel off.
I tried to parallel park on a busy street in the city and had to give up after three failed attempts. A guy in the car behind me honked, which just made me panic more.
I remember putting a frozen pizza in the oven and accidentally falling asleep on the couch. I woke up to the smell of burnt crust and the smoke detector blaring.
I went on a camping trip with the Boy Scouts and it rained so hard our tent flooded. We spent the night sleeping in the scoutmaster's minivan instead.
I remember the distinct smell of chlorine and wet towels in the locker room at the community pool. The floor was always covered in puddles of mystery water.
I ordered a sweater online, and when it arrived, it was the brightest, most obnoxious shade of neon yellow. I only ever wear it around the apartment when it is really cold.
I remember my dad making me rake leaves in the backyard for hours in November. We had these massive oak trees that seemed to drop an endless amount of brown leaves.
I tried to cut my own bangs during the pandemic using kitchen shears, which was a massive mistake. I had to wear a baseball cap on all my video calls for a month.
I remember going to a late-night diner after a high school theater cast party. We ordered huge plates of cheese fries and drank way too much soda.
I bought a cheap digital watch because I wanted to run without my phone, but the strap gave me a terrible rash. I ended up just throwing it in a drawer.
I remember watching my grandma meticulously peel an apple with a paring knife so the skin came off in one long ribbon. She always gave the first slice to me.
I went to a local museum and stared at a modern art painting that was literally just a red square. I tried to look contemplative so the security guard would not judge me.
I remember accidentally dropping my phone in a snowbank while shoveling the driveway. I did not realize it was missing until an hour later, and it was frozen solid when I found it.
I tried drinking a green smoothie for breakfast every day to be healthy. It tasted like blended grass, and I stopped doing it after three days.
I remember the sound of the cicadas humming in the trees during the hottest parts of August. It was so loud you almost had to yell over it when standing outside.
I bought a lottery scratch-off from a vending machine at the grocery store and used a quarter to rub off the foil. I got silver dust all over my fingers and won absolutely nothing.
I remember trying to put a fitted sheet on my bed and one corner kept popping off. I got so frustrated I just slept on the bare mattress pad that night.
I went to an escape room with my coworkers for team building, and we failed miserably. Everyone was shouting conflicting instructions, and we ran out of time on the second puzzle.
I remember my mom making a huge batch of bitter melon soup when I was sick with a cold. I had to pinch my nose to swallow it because the taste was so overwhelmingly medicinal.
I tried to ride a Lime scooter downtown and almost crashed into a mail delivery truck. I jumped off and let the scooter crash onto the sidewalk to save myself.
I remember the musty smell of the old paperback books in my middle school library. I used to check out fantasy novels just to read the maps printed on the inside covers.
I bought a bunch of bananas and forgot about them until they turned completely black on the counter. I threw them away while pretending I was eventually going to make banana bread.
I remember getting a static shock from touching a metal doorknob in the dead of winter. It actually visibly sparked and stung my finger for a solid minute.
I went to a driving range with a friend and whiffed the golf ball three times in a row. I swung so hard I practically threw my back out.

During the pandemic, some guy yelled a racial slur at my friend Brian and me outside a Jewel-Osco in Naperville, aggressively lumping us into one generic target. After that scary incident, joining a local Stop AAPI Hate rally in Chicago created a powerful sense of solidarity that made me heavily lean into a broader Asian American community.
I remember the flashing lights of a police car pulling me over for a broken taillight I did not know about. My hands were shaking as I handed the officer my license.
I ordered a complicated piece of gym equipment online, and the box was so heavy I had to drag it across the lobby floor. The cardboard left a long brown streak on the tile.
I remember my dad falling asleep on the couch with the TV blaring an action movie. If I tried to change the channel, he would instantly wake up and say he was watching it.
I tried to grow cherry tomatoes on my apartment balcony in a plastic pot. A squirrel ended up eating every single one before they even turned red.
I remember sitting in the back of a math class and drawing elaborate geometric patterns on my notebook cover. The ink kept smudging onto the side of my hand.
I went to a farmers market early on a Sunday and bought a jar of expensive local honey. I dropped it on the sidewalk halfway home, and it shattered everywhere.
I remember trying to put eye drops in by myself and blinking right as the drop fell. The medicine just ran down my cheek like a tear.
I bought a really cheap umbrella from a convenience store during a sudden downpour. The wind inverted it at the very first intersection, completely ruining the metal spokes.
I remember eating an orange in the car and the peel squirting citrus oil right into my eye. I had to pull over into a strip mall parking lot until the burning stopped.
I went to a local bakery and bought what I thought was a chocolate chip cookie, but it turned out to be oatmeal raisin. I felt a profound sense of betrayal when I took the first bite.
I remember trying to clean the dust out of my computer keyboard with a can of compressed air. I held it at the wrong angle and sprayed freezing liquid all over my hands.
I bought a pair of running shoes that were half a size too small because they were on clearance. I wore them once, got massive blisters on my heels, and never touched them again.
I remember my mom using a metal back scratcher to get an itch right between my shoulder blades. It felt so incredibly relieving after wearing a heavy backpack all day.
I tried to skip a rock across a pond at a forest preserve, but it just made a loud plop and sank instantly. My friend skipped his like five times in a row, which was annoying.

participants.persona: Yuki is a 35-year-old first-generation Japanese American woman, born abroad and living in Hawaii.
participants.name: Yuki

memories.content: I remember the flight from Japan being really dark, maybe it was a red-eye or maybe I just slept the whole way.
We had a small apartment near Ala Moana when we first moved, or maybe it was closer to Makiki.
My mom used to pack me spam musubi for lunch, but she made the rice too sweet.
I think my first English word was something like hello or water, but my dad insists it was dog.
There was a stray cat outside our building that I named Shiro, even though it was mostly orange.
I broke my arm falling off the monkey bars in second grade, though it might have been third grade.
The school uniforms were this itchy plaid material that made me sweat all day in the humidity.
I used to hide in the library during recess because I didn't understand what the other kids were playing.

I remember voting for a local politician around 2016 because he promised stronger ties with Japan, even though I hated his stance on Honolulu housing. My mom thought I was crazy, but it felt important to support someone looking out for where we came from.
My grandfather visited us once and brought me a wooden doll that I promptly lost at the beach.
I think moving here when I was maybe five or six made me always feel like an observer in my own life.
We used to go to Matsumoto Shave Ice every summer, but I think we stopped going when the lines got too long.
My first friend was a girl named Leilani or maybe Kalani, she gave me a Hello Kitty eraser.
I remember a massive hurricane hitting when I was little, the sky turned a weird green color.
My dad drove a beat-up Honda Civic that always smelled slightly of soy sauce and old carpet.
I think I won a spelling bee in fifth grade, but I can't remember the winning word at all.
The neighbor's dog used to bark all night, which terrified me for reasons I couldn't explain.
I used to steal my mom's lipstick and try to put it on, usually ending up looking like a clown.
Sometimes I wonder if I cling to my Japanese heritage just because I'm afraid of losing my identity completely.
We went to a luau for someone's birthday and I got sick from eating too much poi.
I remember the TV being on all the time playing some Japanese game show my parents rented on VHS.
I had a huge crush on a boy in middle school who sat next to me in math class, I think his name was Josh.
My parents fought a lot about money when I was in middle school, mostly in hushed Japanese so I wouldn't hear.
I skipped school once in eighth grade to go to the mall, but we just sat in the food court the whole time.
There was a teacher, Mr. Higa maybe, who always gave me extra homework because he thought I wasn't trying.
I got my first cell phone when I was 14, it was a silver flip phone with a tiny antenna.
Looking back, my obsession with getting perfect grades was probably just a way to prove I belonged here.
We took a family trip back to Japan and I felt completely out of place the entire time.
I remember buying a CD at Tower Records, probably something by No Doubt or Green Day.
I used to bite my nails down to the quick whenever we had a pop quiz.
Someone stole my bike from our garage, and my dad was furious for about a week.
I drove my friend's car before I had a license and almost backed into a palm tree.
High school graduation was held in a massive stadium, and it rained right in the middle of it.
I had a part-time job at a surf shop, mostly folding t-shirts that smelled like coconut wax.
My mom cried when I told her I didn't want to go to college on the mainland.
I realize now that I use humor to deflect whenever someone asks me about my childhood in Osaka.
We used to sneak out to Sandy Beach at night and just listen to the waves crashing.
I dated a guy for three months who only ever wanted to eat at Zippy's.
I think I got a C in chemistry, or maybe it was biology, science was never my strong suit.
Prom was a blur of cheap perfume and awful music, but I know I wore a blue dress.
I found a stray kitten in the school parking lot and tried to keep it hidden in my room for two days.
College orientation was a mess, I got completely lost trying to find the student union.
I majored in business for about two semesters before switching to communications.
My freshman roommate was from California and complained about the humidity every single day.
It's funny how I consider myself local, but I still feel a weird guilt whenever I mispronounce a Hawaiian street name.
I drank way too much at a frat party and had to be carried home by people I barely knew.
I took a Japanese language class hoping for an easy A, but the grammar was completely different from what my parents spoke.
There was a coffee shop near campus where I spent hours pretending to study while actually people-watching.
I remember buying a used textbook that had all the wrong answers highlighted in pink.

Mainland forms always make me check the Asian American box, but here in Hawaii I just say I am Japanese. The big label feels too generic and ignores the specific traditions my parents brought over from Japan when I was a baby.
I had a really intense argument with my dad over politics during Thanksgiving dinner one year.
I took up surfing for about a month before deciding I was too afraid of sharks to continue.
I think my fear of the ocean actually stems from a broader anxiety about things I can't control.
I worked at a hotel front desk for a while, dealing with angry tourists whose names I instantly forgot.
My first apartment after college had a terrible roach problem that the landlord refused to fix.
I adopted a dog named Kona, but I had to give him to my parents when I moved to a place with no pets allowed.
I went to a wedding in Maui and got so sunburned I couldn't wear my bridesmaid dress properly.
I dated a girl briefly in my mid-twenties, which confused my parents though they never brought it up.
My habit of apologizing for everything is definitely something I picked up from my mom, though I try to unlearn it.
I got into a minor fender bender on the H-1 freeway because I was trying to change the radio station.
We used to have potlucks at work every Friday, and I always just brought store-bought poke.
I tried doing yoga for a year, but I kept falling asleep during the meditation part at the end.
I remember watching the news about some tsunami warning and packing a bag, but nothing ever happened.
I bought a really expensive pair of sunglasses and left them in a rental car two days later.
I've noticed I tend to push away partners when they start asking too many questions about my family history.
My grandmother passed away when I was 27, and I felt terrible that I couldn't afford to fly back to Japan for the funeral.
I think I went to a Jack Johnson concert at the Waikiki Shell, or maybe it was just a cover band.
I decided to cut my own bangs once and had to wear hats for three months.
I used to go hiking at Manoa Falls almost every weekend until I twisted my ankle on a slippery rock.
As I get older, I see how much my parents sacrificed, and it makes my teenage rebellion seem incredibly selfish.
I had a boss who would always call me hun, which drove me absolutely crazy.
I tried making my mom's ozoni for New Year's, but the broth tasted completely off.
I realize my constant need to be busy is just a coping mechanism to avoid sitting with my own thoughts.
I lived in Kaimuki for a couple of years in a house that always smelled like damp wood.
I joined a outrigger canoe club for one summer, but my arms were always too sore to type at work.
I think I saw a celebrity at the airport once, maybe it was someone from Lost.
My parents celebrated their 30th anniversary at a fancy steakhouse, and my dad complained about the prices the whole time.
Sometimes I feel like I'm playing a character of myself when I'm around my old high school friends.
I got a tattoo of a cherry blossom on my shoulder, but the ink is already starting to blur.
I was stuck in a terrible traffic jam on the Pali Highway for three hours because of a downed tree.
I went through a phase where I only drank matcha lattes, it ruined my teeth for a while.

I visited Tokyo around 2012 and felt completely lost because I could not read most of the street signs or menus. The relatives we stayed with kept laughing at my weirdly outdated Japanese, so I just stopped trying to talk much during the trip.
I often wonder if I'd be a completely different person if we had stayed in Japan instead of moving to Oahu.
I used to buy those little plumeria hair clips from ABC Stores and wear them like I was a tourist.
There was a monsoon season where it rained for two weeks straight, and all my leather shoes got moldy.
I broke off an engagement in my late twenties because he didn't want to live in Hawaii long-term.
I remember eating Leonard's malasadas in the car and getting sugar all over the steering wheel.
My mom made me take piano lessons for five years, but I can only play chopsticks now.
I had a really bad allergic reaction to a mango I picked off a tree in my neighbor's yard.
I think I voted for the first time when I was 20, but I just guessed on all the local council seats.
I worked a temp job doing data entry where the air conditioning was so high I had to wear a parka indoors.
My friend got married on the Big Island, and the rental house had a family of geckos living in the kitchen.
I bought a ukulele thinking I'd learn to play, but it just sits on a shelf gathering dust.
I had my fortune told at a temple in Kyoto when I visited, and the paper said I would have terrible luck in business.
I rear-ended a pickup truck in heavy traffic and cried because I thought my insurance would double.
I used to make my own sushi rolls at home, but the rice was always too mushy.
I got food poisoning from a shrimp truck on the North Shore and couldn't eat seafood for a year.
My dad tried to teach me how to drive stick shift in an empty parking lot, it ended with a lot of yelling.
I was obsessed with this local reggae band in high school, I must have gone to five of their concerts.
I lost my favorite pair of slippahs at a beach bonfire and had to walk barefoot over the rocks.
I kept a journal for about three days when I was a teenager before deciding my life was too boring to document.
I had a really embarrassing moment at work where I replied all to a company email with a grocery list.
I remember the smell of burning sugar cane from when I was little, before all the plantations closed down.
I tried to go blonde once in college, but my hair just turned this weird brassy orange color.
We had a family tradition of eating ozoni on New Year's Day, even if it was 85 degrees outside.
I got a parking ticket downtown because I didn't realize the meter stopped taking coins at 6 PM.
I sprained my wrist trying to learn how to skateboard when I was way too old to be starting.
My mom has this massive collection of Japanese ceramics that she never lets anyone actually use.
I remember sitting in the back of my dad's truck watching the fireworks over Magic Island.
I had a terrible fear of the dark until I was almost twelve, I think because of a ghost story my cousin told me.
I bought a gym membership on New Year's and only went twice before canceling it in shame.
I accidentally threw away my passport the day before a flight and had to frantically dig through the trash.
I used to love those haw flakes candies, I'd stack them up and eat them like little burgers.
I saw a huge sea turtle while snorkeling at Hanauma Bay, and it scared me so much I swallowed salt water.
I had a roommate who refused to wash her dishes until they actually grew mold.
My dad always listened to the same Hawaiian music station in the car, I know all the old commercials by heart.
I went on a blind date that my aunt set up, the guy barely spoke English and we just stared at our food.
I think I won a raffle at a community fair once, the prize was a giant bag of rice.
I dropped my phone in the toilet at a movie theater and had to put it in a bag of rice for three days.
I used to volunteer at an animal shelter, but I had to quit because I kept wanting to take all the cats home.
I got horribly seasick on a whale-watching tour and threw up over the side of the boat.
I remember a teacher trying to pronounce my name on the first day of school and giving up halfway through.
I made a huge batch of curry for a potluck, but I forgot to add the roux blocks until the very end.
I bought a really nice camera intending to get into photography, but I only ever use my phone anyway.
I had a phase where I wore those toe-socks everywhere, thinking they were the height of fashion.
My parents' house has this one squeaky floorboard in the hallway that I always tried to step over when sneaking in.
I took a ferry to Lanai for a weekend trip, but the water was so rough I felt dizzy for two days.
I got an awful sunburn on the tops of my feet because I forgot to put sunscreen there.
I remember getting my ears pierced at the mall and one side getting horribly infected.
I watched a documentary about plastic in the ocean and tried to use metal straws for about a week.
I had this recurring dream that I missed my high school graduation because I couldn't find my shoes.
I completely blanked during a piano recital and just played the same three chords until my teacher stopped me.
I got a really bad paper cut from a manila folder on my first day at my current job.
We used to go to Kapiolani Park for family picnics, and the chickens would always try to steal our rice balls.
I dated someone who was obsessed with CrossFit, and all we ever talked about was kettlebells.
I tried to grow a tomato plant on my balcony, but the pigeons destroyed it within a week.
I remember the power going out during a huge storm, we played cards by flashlight for hours.
I had a cavity filled without novocaine because I was terrified of needles, it was the worst mistake of my life.
I bought a fake designer bag at a swap meet and the handles broke the first time I used it.

My Okinawan friend in Hilo is always organizing these weekend language preservation workshops for her community. She told me once that if they do not fight to keep their native words alive, the government will just erase their unique history completely.
I used to put Li Hing Mui powder on everything, even vanilla ice cream.
I got stuck in the elevator at work for twenty minutes and panic-ate a whole protein bar.
I accidentally locked my keys in the car while it was running at a gas station.
I think my parents had an arranged marriage, though they always insist they met through friends.
I went to a karaoke bar for a coworker's birthday and absolutely butchered a Mariah Carey song.
I had a terrible habit of cracking my knuckles during math class, which drove Mr. Tanaka crazy.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk outside a convenience store and spent it all on scratch-off tickets.
I tried going vegetarian for a month, but gave up when someone brought kalua pig to a family party.
I left my laptop on the roof of my car and drove off, shattering it completely on the highway.
I remember watching my dad meticulously polish his shoes every Sunday evening before work.
I bought a really expensive jar of matcha powder and spilled half of it on my white rug.
I fell asleep on the bus once and ended up all the way at the transit center in Pearl City.
I had a bad case of pink eye in college and had to wear sunglasses to all my evening lectures.
I used to trace the floral patterns on the living room sofa when I was bored.
I accidentally hit a mongoose with my car near the golf course and cried the whole way home.
I went through a phase of only listening to true crime podcasts until they started giving me nightmares.
My mom sent me a care package with Japanese snacks, but half of them were crushed during shipping.
I tried to assemble an Ikea bookshelf by myself and put the back panel on inside out.
I remember playing in the rain outside our apartment complex until my lips turned blue.
I went on a diet where I only ate cabbage soup, it lasted exactly two and a half days.
I had to get a root canal last year, and I still flinch when I drink ice water.
I took a pottery class and made a bowl that was so lopsided I just use it to hold keys.
I locked myself out of my apartment while taking the trash out and had to wait for the super in my pajamas.
I remember the dizzying smell of tuberose from a lei someone gave me for graduation.
I got a terrible rash from trying a new laundry detergent that claimed to be hypoallergenic.
I tried to catch a gecko in my kitchen with a Tupperware container, but it dropped its tail and escaped.
I was in a long-distance relationship for a year that ended with a very tense phone call.
I bought an air fryer on sale and now I use it to heat up literally everything I eat.
I remember my dad trying to fix the washing machine and flooding the entire laundry room.
I accidentally tipped a waiter 50 percent because I couldn't do the math correctly after a couple of drinks.

Every time we go to the summer Obon festival in Honolulu, hearing the loud taiko drums makes me feel so proud to be Japanese. Dancing in the circle with my aunts and eating our traditional foods reminds me exactly of who my family is.
I went to a hot springs resort in Japan and felt incredibly awkward being naked around strangers.
I bought a pair of high heels for a wedding that were so uncomfortable I took them off during the ceremony.
I had a neighbor who played the drums every Tuesday night at exactly 8 PM.
I tried to make macadamia nut cookies from scratch, but they turned out flat and greasy.
I slipped on some wet leaves while jogging and bruised my tailbone pretty badly.
I spent an entire weekend binge-watching a Korean drama and ordered takeout for every meal.
I got pulled over for a broken taillight, but the cop let me off with a warning because he knew my uncle.
I used to collect sea glass from the beach, but I ended up throwing it all away during a move.
I had a really bad interview for a job I wanted where I completely forgot the name of the company.
I remember the terrifying feeling of getting sucked into a rip current for a few seconds before swimming parallel to the shore.
I accidentally shrunk my favorite wool sweater so small it could probably fit a toddler.
I was stung by a jellyfish when I was younger, and my brother told me someone had to pee on it.
I got a jury duty summons but was dismissed immediately because I said I couldn't be impartial.
I remember staying up late to watch meteor showers, but it was always too cloudy to see anything.
I bought a bunch of expensive skincare products that ended up making my face break out terribly.
I tried to teach myself how to knit by watching videos, but I could never figure out how to cast off.

When the pandemic started, an angry tourist yelled at me and my Filipino coworker outside a grocery store and blamed us for the virus. We started hanging out in an Asian American online group after that just to feel safer and share what we were going through.
I had to give a presentation at work and my microphone kept cutting out the entire time.
I went to a midnight movie premiere and fell asleep before the opening credits finished.
I tried paddleboarding once and spent more time falling into the water than actually standing up.
I remember my grandmother sending me letters in Japanese that I had to ask my mom to translate.
I accidentally dropped my sunglasses into the tiger enclosure at the Honolulu Zoo.
I bought a massive Monstera plant for my living room, but I think I overwatered it because it's turning yellow.
I got food poisoning on my birthday and spent the whole day curled up on the bathroom floor.
I remember taking the SATs in a freezing cold classroom and being too distracted to focus on the math section.
I tried to bake bread during a hurricane warning, but the power went out right as I put it in the oven.
I was bitten by a centipede in my sleep once, and the pain was so sharp I thought I'd been stabbed.
I accidentally called my boss Mom during a conference call and just pretended it didn't happen.
I remember looking for sea urchins in the tide pools and being terrified of stepping on one.

participants.persona: Minho is a 30-year-old first-generation Korean American man, born abroad and living in Georgia.
participants.name: Minho

memories.content: I vaguely remember the airplane ride from Seoul to Atlanta when I was maybe four or five years old, and I think I spilled apple juice on my shirt.
My dad's first car in America was this huge, boxy brown sedan that always smelled like stale coffee, and it might have been a Buick.
We lived in a tiny apartment in Duluth when we first arrived, and I think our neighbor was an older Russian lady who gave me licorice.
I remember crying on my first day of kindergarten because I could not understand what the teacher was saying.
My mom used to pack me kimbap for lunch until a kid named Jimmy made a face at it, and after that I begged for turkey sandwiches.
There was a weird playground near our first apartment with a metal slide that got dangerously hot in the Georgia summer, maybe around 1998.
I think we had a small fish tank in our living room for a couple of years, but the fish always died pretty quickly.
I recall my parents arguing in hushed Korean late at night when I was around seven, mostly about money issues I did not understand.
We went to a Korean church in Suwanee where the pastor, maybe named Pastor Lee, would always pat my head a bit too hard.

I went back to Seoul in what must have been 2012, or maybe 2014, and tried ordering food in Myeongdong using the formal register I learned as a kid. The cashier gave me this blank stare because my accent was so thick and my slang was basically from the 90s, marking me as a total outsider.
Looking back, I realize that my desperate need to speak English without an accent was rooted in a deep fear of being seen as an outsider.
I won a spelling bee in second or third grade by spelling the word restaurant correctly.
There was a scholastic book fair where I bought a poster of a Lamborghini that I think was silver.

When my Halmoni called from Busan for my high school graduation, which I think was in 2010, I could barely string together a basic thank you in Korean. It still hurts knowing she passed away before I could ever have a real conversation with her about her life.
I remember breaking my arm falling off the monkey bars when I was eight, and my cast turned a gross gray color.
My mom took me to the H-Mart every Saturday morning, and it always smelled overwhelmingly of fish and ripe melon.
I had a friend named Kevin or Calvin who showed me how to play Pokemon Red on his Gameboy, which started my gaming obsession.
In fourth grade, our teacher read us a book about a mouse on a motorcycle, though I forget the title.
Reflecting on pretending not to know my mom at the grocery store once, I feel a deep sense of shame about how I handled my dual identity.
We went to Florida for vacation once and drove the whole way in our rusty minivan, maybe to Daytona Beach.
I remember getting in trouble for drawing elaborate battle scenes on my math homework instead of solving the equations.
I tried to build a treehouse in our backyard using scrap wood I found near a construction site.
Middle school was a blur of oversized polo shirts and a cheap body spray that I wore because someone said girls liked it.
I played the clarinet in the middle school band for about two years before quitting because I kept squeaking on high notes.
There was a rumor that a kid in my grade named Brandon got expelled for bringing a pocket knife to school.
I went to a school dance and stood by the bleachers the entire time drinking generic fruit punch.
My dad tried to teach me how to play golf at a cheap public course when I was twelve, and I just got frustrated.
I got caught stealing a pack of trading cards from a Target when I was thirteen, and the security guard yelled at me.
We had a history teacher, maybe Mr. Davis, who would always show us movies instead of actually teaching the lesson.
I remember my grandmother visiting from Korea for a few months when I was in seventh grade and feeding me peeled apples.
I used to chat with strangers on AOL Instant Messenger until late at night using an incredibly embarrassing screen name.
It occurs to me now that I spent my entire adolescence acting like a double agent, trying to compartmentalize my Korean home life from my American school life.
My freshman year of high school, I joined the tennis team because my parents thought it would look good for college.
I had a huge crush on a girl in my biology class whose name I think was Sarah, just because she borrowed a pencil.
I remember taking the SATs in a freezing cold cafeteria on a Saturday morning and guessing on the math section.
My mom used to force me to go to an after-school hagwon to study extra math, and I usually just slept in the back row.
I got my permit when I was fifteen and nearly crashed into a mailbox on my first try driving.
There was a phase where I wore puka shell necklaces because they were popular, even though we lived nowhere near a beach.
I remember skipping school once to go to the Waffle House with some older kids and ordering pecan waffles.
My parents bought a new house in Johns Creek around my sophomore year, and I sulked about having to change schools.
I experienced a bout of pretty severe depression when I was sixteen that I hid from everyone by lying in my closet for hours.
We had to dissect a fetal pig in biology, and the smell of formaldehyde made me legitimately nauseous.
I finally got my license and drove an old Honda Accord that rattled when you hit sixty miles per hour.
My first real job was at a movie theater tearing tickets, which I did for about six months before quitting.
I went to prom with a girl named Michelle from church, and we took awkward photos in my parents' living room.
I remember getting a speeding ticket on Buford Highway and being absolutely terrified to tell my dad.
I applied to out-of-state colleges but ultimately chose to stay in Georgia for the HOPE scholarship.
During senior year, a group of us tried to pull a prank with plastic wrap but chickened out at the last minute.
I remember my mom crying at my high school graduation while I just sweat profusely under the polyester gown.
The summer after graduation, I spent almost every day playing Super Smash Bros in my friend David's basement.
I tried smoking a cigarette once behind a convenience store and immediately threw up.
Looking back at my teenage self, I realize I was desperately arrogant to cover up how intensely insecure I felt about failing.
My freshman dorm at Georgia State was incredibly cramped and smelled perpetually of stale beer and ramen.
I remember going to a massive college party during syllabus week and feeling completely out of place.
I failed my first college chemistry exam because I assumed I could study the night before like I did in high school.
I started going to a Korean student association meeting but stopped after a few weeks because my Korean felt too rusty.

During my freshman orientation at Georgia State, I remember hovering between the Korean Student Association booth and the broader Asian American Student Coalition table. I ended up putting my name down for both because I belonged to the local Atlanta Korean church crowd just as much as the general Asian mix on campus.
There was a late-night diner near campus where the waitress, whose name might have been Brenda, always called us sugar.
I dated a girl named Chloe my sophomore year who broke up with me because I was too emotionally closed off.
I switched my major from pre-med to business, and my parents barely spoke to me for a week.
I adopted a stray cat that hung around my apartment complex, but my landlord made me give him away.
I remember a specific crisp autumn day walking through campus listening to an indie rock album that felt incredibly peaceful.
I used to think my college philosophy essays were incredibly profound, but in hindsight, I was just regurgitating big words to sound smart.
For my 21st birthday, we went to a crowded bar in Buckhead where someone spilled a sticky green drink on my shirt.
I worked an internship at a logistics company downtown scanning documents for five hours a day while listening to podcasts.
I remember cramming for a macroeconomics final until sunrise and drinking so much energy drink my hands shook.
I went on a spring break trip to Panama City Beach where it rained for three days straight.
My grandfather passed away in Korea during my senior year, and I cried in my car because I could not afford to fly to the funeral.
I bought a really cheap suit for job interviews from a discount store, and the sleeves were just slightly too long.
I used to eat a shockingly large amount of spicy chicken sandwiches from the campus food court.
I vividly remember the relief of handing in my senior thesis and then sleeping for fourteen hours.
There was a girl named Ashley in my capstone group who did no work, but I was too passive-aggressive to confront her.
It dawned on me recently that I spent my college years driven completely by momentum rather than actual purpose.
My first post-college job was in data entry for an insurance company with depressing beige cubicle walls.
I rented my first solo apartment in Sandy Springs, and the AC was broken for the entire first month.
I got really into brewing my own coffee using a Chemex when I was 23, buying expensive beans from Ethiopia.
I rear-ended a guy in heavy Atlanta traffic on I-285, and his kindness about it made me feel worse.
I tried using dating apps and went on a coffee date with a woman who talked exclusively about her ex-boyfriend.
My dad had a mild heart attack when I was 24, and I still remember the sterile smell of the hospital waiting room.
I joined an adult recreational kickball league, but a guy named Todd yelled at me for dropping a pop fly.
I decided to start investing in the stock market and promptly lost about a thousand dollars on a tech startup.

Back when I worked at a boba place off Pleasant Hill Road around 2016, my coworkers were Vietnamese, Chinese, and Filipino, and we all bonded over having strict immigrant parents. Hanging out with them was a comfortable middle ground where I did not have to act traditionally Korean or entirely white American.
I took a weekend trip to Asheville and had to pretend to take photos while hiking just to catch my breath.
Sometimes I reflect on how arrogant I was with my first paycheck, blowing it on stupid clothes because I thought I was rich.
I went to a music festival in Piedmont Park and got horribly sunburned on the back of my neck.
I dated a girl named Grace for two years, and breaking up with her crushed my mom because our parents wanted us to marry.
I started doing Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu for a few months but quit after tweaking my knee on the mats.
I bought a used Toyota Tacoma thinking I was outdoorsy, but mostly used it to help friends move furniture.
I tried cooking traditional kimchi jjigae for myself and messed up the ratio of chili flakes so badly it was inedible.
I remember going to a coworker's wedding in Savannah and waking up with a piece of wedding cake in my pocket.
I had a boss named Richard who would always steal my ideas in meetings, and I just quietly hated him for it.
I volunteered at an animal shelter for exactly one weekend before realizing I was slightly allergic to dogs.
I read an entire sci-fi book series in a week and was so mad at the ending I threw the paperback across the room.
Reflecting on my mid-twenties, I realize I used sarcasm as a shield to keep people from getting too close to me.
My parents never celebrated American Thanksgiving properly, so we usually just ate galbi and a store-bought pie.
I remember the exact moment I realized my Korean was getting worse than my English when I forgot a basic word on the phone.
My mom used to force me to drink bitter herbal medicine to make me taller, but I topped out at five-foot-nine anyway.
I took my dad to a Braves game where he complained about hot dog prices but secretly kept the ticket stub.
I felt a weird pang of alienation when a random guy at a gas station asked me where I was really from.
We had a framed picture of my extended family in Korea, half of whom I have never actually met in person.
I tried to teach my parents how to use smartphones when they first came out, and we all ended up yelling.
My mom always saved plastic bags under the sink, a habit I unconsciously adopted when I moved out.
I remember finding an old passport of my dad's and conceptualizing for the first time that he had a whole life before I existed.
I still feel deeply guilty about how often I acted embarrassed of my parents when they spoke broken English in public.
I have a terrible habit of leaving a single sip of water at the bottom of every mug on my coffee table.
I listen to true crime podcasts when I do the dishes, which makes me paranoid enough to double-check my locks.
I buy fresh spinach with the intention of making salads, but I almost always let it rot in the crisper drawer.

I got into an argument with a guy named Kevin at a seminar back in 2018 who kept calling us an Asian American voting bloc. I told him I avoided that term because my parents' struggles as Korean small business owners in Gwinnett County had zero in common with the wealthy tech guys from California he was talking about.
I memorized Rubik's cube algorithms a couple of years ago, but now I just use it as a fidget toy during Zoom calls.
I drive a different route to work on Tuesdays just to see different trees and break the monotony.
I always check my phone for messages right when I wake up, even though nobody ever texts me at that hour.
I tried to get into meditation last year but usually just fell asleep within the first five minutes of breathing.
I have a pair of sweatpants worn through at the knees that I refuse to throw away because they are perfectly broken-in.
I order the exact same spicy Pad Kee Mao from my local Thai restaurant every single time I go.
I realize that my obsession with organizing my closet is just a coping mechanism to trick myself into feeling in control.
I saw a car catch on fire on the side of the highway last summer, and it was bizarre how traffic just kept moving.
I remember watching a thunderstorm roll in over Tybee Island and seeing the sky turn a bruised purple color.
I found twenty dollars on the sidewalk when I was nineteen and immediately used it to buy beef jerky.
I tried to cut my own hair during the pandemic and messed it up so badly I had to buzz it all off.
I got stuck in an elevator for twenty minutes once and nervously calculated how much oxygen I had left.
I remember eating an incredibly good peach from a roadside stand near Macon that dripped juice all over my shirt.
I went to a comedy show where the comic aggressively picked on a guy in the front row, making it too uncomfortable to laugh.
I assembled a TV stand from Wayfair backward and left the unfinished wood edge facing out purely out of laziness.
I woke up from a dream about my teeth falling out, and my jaw ached all day from clenching it.
I can clearly remember the exact dusty carpet and artificial popcorn smell of a blockbuster video store.
I went paintballing for a bachelor party and took a shot to the neck that left a welt for two weeks.
I binge-watched a documentary on ancient Rome and then confidently explained it to a friend while getting the facts wrong.
I tried raw oysters for the first time downtown and swallowed it whole to avoid the slimy texture.
I remember changing a flat tire on a rainy road using my phone flashlight and ruining my favorite jeans in the mud.
I used to have a recurring nightmare about forgetting my high school locker combination and waking up in a panic.
I bought an acoustic guitar to learn how to play, but I only learned three chords before it started collecting dust.
I remember wishing on a shooting star for a promotion at work, which in hindsight was an incredibly boring wish.
I got severe food poisoning from a suspicious food truck and hallucinated that my cat was talking to me.
I went to a batting cage recently and realized my coordination has deteriorated when I completely missed twenty pitches.
Looking at my bank statements recently, I had a sudden moment of clarity about how I order expensive takeout purely to distract from feeling lonely.
I played World of Warcraft for an embarrassing amount of hours during my freshman year, caring more about digital gear than grades.
I started a sneaker blog in 2012 that I abandoned after a month because I ran out of things to say.
I watched Inception in theaters and spent the car ride home loudly arguing with my friends about the spinning top.
I bought a loud mechanical keyboard that drove my roommate so crazy I eventually had to return it.
I went through a phase of listening to obscure 90s hip-hop just because I wanted people to ask me about my music taste.
I almost broke a computer processor trying to jam it into the socket backward while following a YouTube tutorial.
I remember locking myself in my room to read the final Harry Potter book in fourteen hours straight.
I collected excessively spicy hot sauces for a while, including one that required a waiver to buy.
I took a pottery class and made a lopsided bowl that my mom still uses to hold her keys.
I used to think my interest in comic books was childish, but I actually appreciate the artwork much more as an adult.
I remember going to the Georgia Aquarium when it first opened and staring in awe at the massive whale sharks.
I rode my bike so far down the Silver Comet Trail once that I cramped up and had to call a friend for a ride.
I got a jury duty summons and spent three days reading magazines in a bleak room before being dismissed.
I ate a greasy burger at the Varsity before a football game and my stomach churned for the entire first half.
I bought an expensive jar of artisan honey from a farmers market in Decatur that just tasted like regular honey.
I walked into a spider web in my backyard and did a panicked martial arts routine trying to get it off me.
I had to hide in my closet during an important phone interview because my neighbor started a lawnmower outside my window.
I tried growing tomatoes on my balcony, but the local squirrels ate every single one before they ripened.
I remember a winter when it snowed in Atlanta and we sledded down a hill on broken cardboard boxes.
I bought a cheap drone to take aerial photos and crashed it into a pine tree on my second flight.
I went on an awkward blind date set up by my mom's friend where we just discussed our accounting jobs for an hour.
I had a major falling out with my best friend in college over borrowed money, and we have not spoken since.
I remember standing at a Midtown rooftop bar pretending to care about crypto while wishing I was home in sweatpants.
I went to a Halloween party as a generic zombie, and someone asked if I was just a tired office worker.
I used to bowl at a cheap late-night alley using the lightest ball and chucking it as hard as possible.
I dated a vegan and tried the diet with her, but secretly ate fried chicken in my car and felt immense guilt.
I got so intensely competitive during a Monopoly game with my cousins that I flipped the board over.
I contributed absolutely nothing at a corporate Escape Room and just stood in the corner holding a flashlight.
I hosted a Super Bowl party with intricate appetizers, but the game was a blowout and everyone left early.
I attended my first traditional Korean wedding for a cousin and had no idea what was happening during the ceremony.
I finally invested in a good mattress after waking up with lower back pain for six months straight.
My laptop crashed right as I started a presentation to the regional manager, and I sweated profusely making small talk.
I switched to sparkling water to be healthier, and now I blindly consume three cases of lime flavor a week.

After those terrible shootings happened at the spas downtown a few years ago, I started going to the community vigils organized by different Asian groups across Atlanta. I stood in the crowd with people from dozens of different backgrounds who were all hurting just like me, and I started proudly calling myself Asian American after that.
I renewed my passport and the clerk yelled at me to keep a neutral expression, making me look like a tired serial killer.
I spent a Sunday trying to fix a leaky bathroom faucet, made it worse, and had to pay a plumber an emergency fee.
I joined a gym in January and actually kept going just because their airtight contract requires a blood sacrifice to cancel.
I found a weird mole and convinced myself it was fatal via Google before a dermatologist just casually froze it off.
I remember pulling number 99 at the Alpharetta DMV when they were serving number 12 and waiting until my phone died.
I bought a robot vacuum that constantly gets stuck under my couch, so I spend more time rescuing it than I save.
I tried a weekend digital detox but caved and checked Instagram after twelve hours out of sheer boredom.
I ate a heavy pasta lunch before a status meeting and legitimately fell asleep with my eyes open for five minutes.
I spent hours seasoning a cast iron skillet only for my friend to cook eggs in it and run it through the dishwasher.
I tried a famous Texas barbecue place on a business trip, and it completely ruined local Georgia barbecue for me.
I only stopped chewing pen caps because a blue pen exploded in my mouth right before a client call.
I tried making sourdough starter during the pandemic, but it smelled like nail polish remover so I threw it away.
I have a specific ragged hoodie I only wear when I am sick, which my mom has tried to throw away multiple times.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about a coworker directly to him, and he definitely saw through my clumsy lie.
I watched a video on changing my car oil to save money before realizing I owned no tools and just drove to Jiffy Lube.
I got caught in a downpour and a paper grocery bag ripped, shattering a jar of pickles all over the parking lot.
I frequently catch myself mimicking my dad's exact mannerisms when annoyed, leading to the jarring realization that I am becoming him.
I threw my back out just by bending over to tie my shoe and had to crab-walk to the couch.
I bought a concert ticket for a Tuesday night but decided to stay home and eat pizza rolls because it felt too late.
I found a burned CD labeled Summer 08 in the attic, but my car stereo immediately spat it back out.
I tried to flirt with a barista in Decatur, and she just handed me my latte with a completely blank stare.
I took a vitamin that turned my pee neon yellow, which freaked me out enough to throw the rest away.
I got stuck behind a tractor on a two-lane rural road for twenty miles and yelled at my dashboard the whole time.
I used a standing desk for a week until my feet hurt so badly I quietly lowered it and never spoke of it again.
I panicked at a Braves game thinking I lost my wallet, but it had slipped between my car seats before I even arrived.
I forgot a guy's name three seconds after meeting him at a networking event and just called him man the whole time.
I bought a huge Ikea houseplant that slowly died over six months while I kept foolishly watering the brown leaves.
I tripped up the stairs at a MARTA station during rush hour and humiliatingly pretended I was just stretching my leg.
I ordered a custom license plate frame that arrived printed upside down, and I was too lazy to return it.
I woke up at 4 AM to watch a lunar eclipse that was mostly blocked by clouds, but the cold air felt nice.
I dropped my keys down a storm drain while holding groceries and had to call a tow truck to fish them out.
